GLOSSARY OF TERMS 
Term 
Definition 
Classified Expenditure 
The expenses and commitments incurred by an authorised agency for the 
collection and dissemination of information related to national security interests 
Contingent Liability 
A potential liability that may occur depending on the outcome of an uncertain 
future event. 
Domestic Arrears 
Domestic arrears refer to short-term debts incurred by Governments against 
unpaid procurement invoices for supply of goods and services during the 
financial year 
External Debt 
Portion of a country's debt that was borrowed from foreign lenders including 
commercial banks, Governments or international financial institutions. 
Garnishee order 
A form of enforcing a judgment debt against a creditor to recover money. 
Nugatory Expenditure 
Expenditure that does not achieve any result 
Off-budget financing 
Off-budget refers to expenditure that is not funded through the budget 
Recruitment 
Refers to the process of attracting, screening, selecting, and on boarding a 
qualified person for a job, provided by an employer in another territory and the 
preparation for their departure 
Revolving Fund 
A fund that is continually replenished as withdrawals are made 
 
 

 
 
 
xviii 
 
 
Foreword 
 
In accordance with the mandate enshrined in Article 163 of the 1995 Constitution of the 
Republic of Uganda, and further amplified in Sections 12 and 18 of the National Audit Act, Cap 
170, I hereby present the Annual Audit Report on the Consolidated Financial Statements of the 
Government of Uganda, as well as the Financial Performance of Public Corporations and State 
Enterprises. 
 
During the audit year ended 31st December 2025, I audited 182 Ministries, Departments, and 
Agencies (MDAs), 85 Public Corporations and State Enterprises, 181 Projects, as well as 145 
Districts and Cities. In addition, I finalized 4,529 audits of Lower Local Governments and 1,228 
Secondary Schools and Tertiary Institutions. Furthermore, I conducted two thematic audits 
focusing on Management of Procurement and implementation of the Parish Development Model. 
 
My Office’s commitment to undertaking audits that add value to society in view of stakeholder 
needs and emerging issues is unwavering. In this regard, I undertook 44 Special Audits and 
Investigations, 24 Value for Money Audits, and 6 Engineering Audits. While individual reports for 
these audits were issued, summaries can also be found in the respective entity/project 
Combined Audit Reports. 
 
As a forward-looking institution, the Office finalized a new strategic plan covering the period 
2025-2030, which was approved by the National Planning Authority. Significantly, our new 
strategic plan was prepared in accordance with the Balanced Scorecard Framework. It 
emphasizes four themes, namely: service excellence, good governance, strategic partnerships, 
and innovation excellence. Through these themes, my office aims to consolidate its role as a 
model Supreme Audit Institution that not only contributes to enhancing public sector 
accountability and transparency but also adds value to society. 
 
I would like to express my appreciation to the Rt. Hon. Speaker of Parliament, the Rt. Hon 
deputy Speaker of Parliament and to Parliament as a whole, particularly the Finance Committee 
and the Accountability Committees, for their continued support, insights and constructive ideas 
aimed at enhancing the quality of my audit reports. I am equally committed to supporting the 
Parliamentary oversight Committees during the discussions of findings in the audit reports. 
 
I also extend my heartfelt gratitude to all stakeholders for the invaluable support throughout 
the audit year, that enabled me to deliver on the mandate. Special mention goes to my staff, 
who worked tirelessly to ensure that this report is produced within the statutory timeline. I am 
deeply grateful for their resilience and professionalism. 
 
Together, let us continue striving for greater accountability and transparency in the 
management of public resources for the benefit of our nation. 
 
 
 
Edward Akol 
AUDITOR GENERAL 
KAMPALA 
 
31st December, 2025 

 
 
 
1 
 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Mandate 
 
In accordance with Article 163(3) of the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, Sections 
12 and 18 of the National Audit Act (NAA), Cap 170, and the Public Finance Management Act 
(PFMA), Cap 171, I am required to audit and report on the public accounts of Uganda and all 
public offices, including the Courts, Central and Local Government Administrations, Universities, 
Public Institutions of like nature and any Public Corporations or other bodies established by Acts 
of Parliament. 
 
Section 12(b) of the NAA, requires my office to perform a range of audits, including Financial, 
Value for Money, Engineering, Information Systems, Special, Government Investment 
Procurements, Treasury Memoranda, Gender and Environment audits, as well as audits related 
to any project or activity involving public funds. Additionally, Classified Expenditure audits are 
conducted to ensure the transparency and proper use of public resources. 
 
In compliance with Article 163(4) of the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, I am 
required to audit and submit accounts to Parliament annually for the year immediately 
preceding. This report is submitted in compliance with the constitutional provision. 
 
Contents of the Report 
 
During the period January to December 2025, I undertook various audit types in line with my 
mandate and the results are as follows; 
 
(i) 
A report and Opinion on the Government of Uganda Consolidated Financial Statements 
of the Government of the Republic of Uganda for the financial year ended 30th June 
2025. 
 
(ii) 
A review of the Consolidated Summary Statement of Financial Performance of Public 
Corporations and State Enterprises for the financial year ended 30th June 2025. 
 
(iii) 
A summary of audit results from performance evaluation of Ministries, Departments, 
Agencies, Commissions, Statutory Corporations and Local Governments. 
 
(iv) 
A summary of audit results from audit of compliance with relevant regulatory 
frameworks. These included Management of Procurement and the Parish Development 
Model (PDM). 
 
(v) 
A summary of audit findings from other specialized audits, Value for Money Audits, 
Special Audits, IT and Engineering Audits, conducted during the year. 
 
(vi) 
Status of implementation of the Treasury Memoranda. 
 
 
 

 
 
 
2 
 
 
Developments during the audit year 
 
a) 
Strategic Plan 2026-2030 
 
In the Audit Year, the Office of the Auditor General (OAG) developed a new Strategic Plan, 
covering the period 2025-2030, which was approved by the National Planning Authority (NPA). 
 
The Strategic Plan sets a clear direction for the OAG and reaffirms our commitment to 
delivering high-quality audits, strengthening public accountability, and safeguarding public 
resources to improve service delivery. 
 
The Strategic Plan is anchored in the Balanced Scorecard Framework, which helps us ensure 
clarity, balance, and measurable indicators and targets. By adopting the Balanced Scorecard 
Framework, the OAG seeks to ensure a holistic view of its performance across four critical 
perspectives, namely; 
 
i) 
Citizen and Stakeholder Perspective: This perspective emphasizes the importance 
of delivering tangible value to citizens and stakeholders. The focus will be on 
understanding needs and expectations, ensuring that audits lead to improvements in 
public services that resonate with the community. 
 
ii) 
Financial Stewardship Perspective: Here, the OAG underlines its commitment to 
responsible management of resources. This entails not just maintaining fiscal discipline 
but also promoting transparency and accountability in the use of public funds. 
 
iii) 
Internal Processes Perspective: Continuous improvement in operational processes is 
vital for achieving efficiency and effectiveness. The OAG will explore innovative 
approaches and optimize workflows to enhance audit practices and broaden its impact. 
 
iv) 
Organisational Capacity Perspective: Recognizing that people and systems are key 
to success, the OAG aims to nurture its workforce and invest in capabilities. This 
perspective prioritizes professional development, training, and the adoption of relevant 
technologies to empower staff. 
 
By focusing on these four perspectives, the OAG aims to consolidate its role as a leading 
Supreme Audit Institution, fostering accountability and transparency within the public sector 
while delivering meaningful contributions to societal welfare. The commitment to measurable 
indicators and targets will further enable the organization to assess its progress and make 
necessary adjustments to ensure that its strategic goals are met effectively.

PART I: REPORTS ON THE CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS 
 
SECTION 1: REPORT OF THE AUDITOR GENERAL ON THE CONSOLIDATED 
FINANCIAL STATEMENTS OF THE GOVERNMENT OF THE REPUBLIC 
OF UGANDA FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30TH JUNE 2025 
 
THE RT. HON. SPEAKER OF PARLIAMENT 
 
Opinion 
 
I have audited the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Government of the Republic 
Uganda, for the financial year ended 30th June 2025, which comprise the Statement of 
Financial Position as at 30th June 2025, the Statement of Financial Performance, the 
Statement of Changes in Equity, and the Statement of Cash Flows, together with other 
accompanying statements for the year then ended, and notes to the financial statements, 
including a summary of significant accounting policies. 
 
In my opinion, the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Government of the Republic of 
Uganda for the financial year ended 30th June 2025 are prepared, in all material respects, in 
accordance with Section 49 of the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA), Cap 171, and the 
Financial Reporting Guide, 2024, as issued by the Accountant General. 
 
Basis of Opinion 
 
I conducted my audit in accordance with the International Standards of Supreme Audit 
Institutions (ISSAIs). My responsibilities under those standards are further described in the 
Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements section of my report. I am 
independent of the Government in accordance with the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of 
Uganda, the National Audit Act, Cap 170, the International Organization of Supreme Audit 
Institutions (INTOSAI) Code of Ethics, the International Ethics Standards Board for 
Accountants Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants (Parts A and B) (IESBA Code), and 
other independence requirements applicable to performing audits of Financial Statements in 
Uganda. I have fulfilled my other ethical responsibilities in accordance with the IESBA Code 
and in accordance with other ethical requirements applicable to performing audits in 
Uganda. I believe that the audit evidence I have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to 
provide a basis for my opinion. 
 
Key Audit Matters 
 
Key audit matters are those matters that, in my professional judgment, are of most 
significance in my audit of the financial statements of the current period. I have determined 
that there are no key audit matters to communicate in my report. 
 
Emphasis of Matter 
 
Without qualifying my opinion, I draw attention to the following matters disclosed in the 
financial statements; 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
6 
 
 
1.1 
Assets Valuation 
 
I draw your attention to the Government’s reported value of property, plant and 
equipment worth UGX.51.2Tn disclosed in Note 24 to the financial statements. I 
noted that the assets being depreciated include those capitalised for the first time in 
FY2023/24 at estimates and/or historical values, as guided by the Accountant 
General. However, no professional valuation has been undertaken to date. 
 
This implies that the carrying amounts of non-current assets may not fully reflect 
their fair value. 
 
The Accounting Officer disclosed in his commentary, that the valuation and 
management of historical assets are being carried out systematically to align with full 
adoption of Accrual accounting across all votes, and this process is ongoing and 
expected to be completed by the end of FY 2025/2026, as guided by the Accountant 
General, to achieve fair presentation. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accountant General to expedite the valuation of assets across 
Government to ensure accurate reporting, transparency, and alignment with best 
practices in public-sector financial management. 
 
1.2 
Trend of Payables 
 
Reported in the statement of financial position is a payables balance of UGX.8.4Tn. 
This reduced by UGX.5.4Tn from UGX.13.8Tn reported last year. 
 
The significant reduction in domestic arrears was due to a conversion of a temporary 
advance from BoU into long-term debt. UGX.7.78Tn was converted from BoU 
reimbursable into Treasury Bonds payable over 10 years. 
 
If this figure is eliminated, the trend of payables still moved upwards by UGX.2.36Tn 
despite payment of UGX0.265Tn in the year under review. 
 
The upward trend is attributed to the failed enforcement of the commitment control 
system and inadequate record-keeping. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Government to further enforce the commitment control system to avoid 
the accumulation of arrears. In addition, the Government Accounting System should 
be used to centrally record any commitment for which payment is not made by the 
close of the financial year. 
 
1.3 
Change in Revenue Recognition Policy 
 
I noted that for the period under review, URA reported gross revenue collections of 
UGX.32.357Tn and net revenue collections of UGX.31.635Tn as shown below; 
 
 
 

 
 
 
7 
 
 
Table 4: Status of revenue collections 
Item 
Amount (UGX Tn) 
Gross Collections 
32.357 
Less Refunds 
0.722 
Net Collections 
31.635 
Source: URA financials 
 
Included in the net tax collections is accrued revenue of UGX 0.868Tn expected from 
the Government. New guidance requires tax revenue from the Government in 
respect of investment subsidies to be recognised when earned. This is a departure 
from previous treatment, where Tax revenue was only recognised when received. 
 
The new guidance implies that all taxes to be paid by the Government on behalf of 
selected companies will be recognized as revenue by URA when earned rather than 
when received. 
 
The Accounting Officer stated that the Liability is recognized in MoFPED (Vote 008) 
Financial Statements and as revenue (cash in transit) in URA financial Statements, 
and going forward, the accounting policies for revenue recognition of intra-
government transactions will be adjusted accordingly to clarify such transactions. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accountant General to include this treatment in the Reporting 
Guidelines for 2026. 
 
Other Information 
 
The Accounting Officer is responsible for the other information. The other information 
comprises the statement of responsibilities, a statement from the Hon. Minister of Finance, 
Planning and Economic Development, a statement from the Secretary to the Treasury, a 
statement from the Accountant General and other supplementary information. 
 
The other information does not include the financial statements and my auditors' report 
thereon. My opinion on the financial statements does not cover the other information, and I 
do not express an audit opinion or any form of assurance conclusion thereon. 
 
In connection with my audit of the financial statements, my responsibility is to read the 
other information and, in doing so, consider whether the other information is materially 
consistent with the financial statements or my knowledge obtained in the audit, or otherwise 
appears to be materially misstated. If, based on the work I have performed, I conclude that 
there is a material misstatement of this other information, I am required to report that fact. 
 
I have nothing to report in this regard. 
 
Management’s Responsibility for the Financial Statements 
 
Under Article 164 of the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda and Section 43 of the 
Public Finance Management Act, Cap 171, the Accounting Officer is accountable to 
Parliament for the funds and resources of the Government. 
 

 
 
 
8 
 
 
The Accountant General is also responsible for the preparation of financial statements in 
accordance with the requirements of the Public Finance Management Act, Cap 171, and for 
such internal controls as the Accountant General determines are necessary to enable the 
preparation of financial statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due 
to fraud or error. 
 
In preparing the financial statements, the Accountant General is responsible for assessing 
the Government’s ability to continue delivering its mandate, disclosing, as applicable, 
matters related to affecting the delivery of the mandate of the Government of Uganda and 
using the Financial Reporting Guide 2024, unless the Accountant General has a realistic 
alternative to the contrary. 
 
The Accountant General is responsible for overseeing the Government's financial reporting 
process. 
 
Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements 
 
My objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as 
a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an 
auditor's report that includes my opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance, 
but is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with ISSAIs will always detect 
a material misstatement when it exists. Misstatements can arise from fraud or error and are 
considered material if, individually or in aggregate, they could reasonably be expected to 
influence the economic decisions of users, taken on the basis of these financial statements. 
 
As part of an audit in accordance with ISSAIs, I exercise professional judgement and 
maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit. I also; 
 
 
Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, 
whether due to fraud or error, design and perform audit procedures responsive to 
those risks, and obtain audit evidence that is sufficient and appropriate to provide a 
basis for my opinion. The risk of not detecting a material misstatement resulting from 
fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, as fraud may involve collusion, 
forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal control. 
 
 
Obtain an understanding of internal controls relevant to the audit in order to design 
audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose 
of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the government's internal controls. 
 
 
Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of 
accounting estimates and related disclosures made by the management. 
 
 
Obtain an understanding of internal controls relevant to the audit in order to design 
audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose 
of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Government's internal controls. 
 
 
Conclude on the appropriateness of management’s use of the going concern basis of 
accounting and, based on the audit evidence obtained, whether a material 
uncertainty exists related to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on 
the government’s ability to deliver its mandate. If I conclude that a material 
uncertainty exists, I am required to draw attention in my auditor's report to the 
related disclosures in the financial statements or, if such disclosures are inadequate, 

 
 
 
9 
 
 
to modify my opinion. My conclusions are based on the audit evidence obtained up to 
the date of my auditor's report. However, future events or conditions may cause the 
government to fail to deliver its mandate. 
 
 
Evaluate the overall presentation, structure, and content of the financial statements, 
including the disclosures, and whether the financial statements represent the 
underlying transactions and events in a manner that complies with the Government 
of Uganda Public Financial Management laws and regulations. 
I communicate with the Accounting Officer regarding, among other matters, the planned 
scope and timing of the audit and significant audit findings, including any significant 
deficiencies in internal controls that I identify during my audit. 
 
I also provide the Accounting Officer with a statement that I have complied with relevant

relationships and other matters that may reasonably be thought to bear on my

applied.

1.4 
Review of Double Taxation Agreements 
 
A Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) is a bilateral agreement between two countries 
that aims to prevent the same income or capital from being taxed twice. This 
situation, known as double taxation, often arises in international trade and 
investment. These treaties are entered into by capital-importing countries, such as 
Uganda, to promote or attract investment by reducing the cost of overseas 
investment for capital-exporting countries. 
Currently, Uganda is party to nine (09) Double Taxation Agreements with several 
countries. I reviewed the operations regarding the treaties and made the following 
observation; 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
10 
 
 
1.4.1 Lack of Key Statistics in Regard to Revenue Foregone vis-à-vis 
Investment Promotion 
 
Tax treaties shift taxing rights away from the capital importer (a developing country) 
towards the capital exporter (a developed country). The capital importer is expected 
to benefit from the welfare gains from increased inward investment, which is 
expected to outweigh the fiscal costs (revenue foregone). 
 
I noted that no centralised statistics highlighted the benefits accruing from the 
existing DTAs, relative to the revenue foregone by them. Reliable statistics would 
enable the country to evaluate the extent to which it benefits from being a party to 
these DTAs. 
Without reliable statistics on the DTAs, it becomes impractical to assess the viability 
of these treaties, leading to inadequate decision-making. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that previously, URA’s income tax returns were not 
designed to capture key information on taxpayers benefiting from Double Taxation 
Agreements 
(DTAs). 
However, 
under 
the 
Government’s 
tax 
expenditures 
management framework, it was agreed that URA would amend the returns before 
the end of FY 2025/26 to ensure that the necessary DTA-related data is collected. 
 
The Accounting Officer further explained that once this information is in place, the 
Government will undertake a cost–benefit assessment starting FY 2026/2027 and 
identify appropriate policy reform measures. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PSST to expedite the assessment of all DTAs to determine the country’s 
benefit from the agreements. 
 
1.5 
Taxation of Digital Services 
 
Over the last decade, world trade has evolved, with a growing proportion of services 
now offered through digital channels. Some of the services include entertainment 
services, Advertising services and other social media, cloud computing and software 
subscriptions from various software providers, betting services through online betting 
platforms, and education services through online tuition providers, among others. 
These services imply that significant income flows out of the country to various non-
resident service providers. 
 
The Income Tax Act was amended in FY 2023/24 to introduce a 5% Digital Service 
Tax for non-resident persons providing digital services to customers in Uganda. I 
noted that during the year 2024/25, UGX.29.583Bn was collected from the Non-
Resident Digital Service providers through Income Tax and VAT. 
 
Section 86(4) of the Income Tax Act, Cap 338, requires a resident company to lodge 
a tax return with the Commissioner, within 15 days after the end of a tax period. I 
reviewed the taxation of digital services and noted the following; 
 
a) 
Although some non-resident digital service providers (DSPs) submitted tax 
returns under the Digital Service Tax (DST) regime, URA lacked a mechanism 

 
 
 
11 
 
 
to verify the accuracy or completeness of the declarations. In effect, URA is 
entirely reliant on self-declarations by the non-resident service providers. 
b) 
UGX.29.583Bn was collected in 2024/25 from 82 Non-Resident Digital Service 
Providers through Income Tax and VAT. The list, however, was not 
conclusive, as it missed many known providers. 
 
Lack of visibility into payments made to non-resident digital service providers limits 
URA’s ability to independently validate DST declarations, which exposes the Authority 
to Revenue leakage due to under-declaration or non-declaration of taxable income. 
The above also implies that some companies are generating revenue in Uganda 
without paying the applicable taxes. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that the Bank of Uganda was in the process of 
procuring a single national payment gateway system. The Ministry was working with 
BOU to ensure that the procured system enables URA to have timely access to all 
information needed to enforce compliance among non-resident digital service 
providers. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PSST to continuously engage the Bank of Uganda to expedite the 
creation of a single national payment gateway system, to enable visibility into 
payments to these Digital service providers. 
 
1.6

Over the last 15 years, the Government has focused on increasing public 
infrastructure investment to reduce the infrastructure gap, thereby improving private 
investment and the business climate and achieving socio-economic transformation. 
 
In line with the PFM regulations, the Development Committee (DC), presided over by 
the PS/ST, was set up to serve as the high-level technical organ responsible for 
performing the ‘gatekeeping’ role within the Public Investment Management System 
Framework. 
 
I reviewed the project performance as reported in the project master file and project 
budget performance data from 2020/2021 to 2024/2025 and noted that the 
government budgeted solely to fund 106 projects worth UGX.13.3Tn. However, only 
UGX.10.07Tn was released to the projects, leading to a shortfall of UGX.3.2Tn 
(24%). Details in the table below;

A further analysis of the project data revealed the following; 
1.6.1 Slow Progress in Implementation of the Projects 
 
Section 5.1 of the Development Committee (DC) Guidelines requires that, in order to 
ensure efficient and effective implementation of public investments in the country, 
the DC undertakes annual portfolio reviews of all ongoing projects in the Public 
Investment Plan (PIP) in line with the DC calendar. 
 
I reviewed the decision matrix of the annual portfolio review as at 30th June 2025 for 
106 GoU-funded projects and noted slow implementation as detailed below; 
 
 
Three (03) projects were downgraded to the pipeline to await funding and re-
inclusion in the PIP. 
 
Thirty-six (36) projects were exited, out of which only five (05) had been 
successfully completed, twelve (12) had reached the end date, six (06) 
projects received various extensions to complete activities in vain, while 
eleven (11) projects had not registered progress as at 30th June 2025. 
 
Seven (07) projects were extended due to numerous unsettled PAPs, re-
scoping of projects, glaring implementation challenges ranging from land 
acquisition, cash flow constraints and delays in completion of designs, among 
others. 
 
Sixty (60) Projects were retained in spite of their implementation challenges. 
 
I noted that there was no evidence on the Integrated Bank of Projects (IBP) 
of evaluation of completed, exited and downgraded projects in relation to the 
planned outputs, outcomes and impacts in line with the established objectives 
in the project design. 
 
I further noted that despite the slow implementation of projects as at 30th June 
2025, the Government on-boarded 149 new projects, solely funded by GoU, worth 
UGX.19.584Tn on 1st July 2025. 
 
It is apparent that the project portfolio's performance is below average, due to the 
evident implementation challenges encountered during project execution. 
 
The PS/ST explained that he had issued a framework for tracking the implementation 
and performance of public investments, aimed at standardising and providing 
strategic direction during project implementation, and that the MoFPED was in the 
process of upgrading the IBP to enhance its robustness and facilitate real-time 
project reporting on both financial and Physical performance. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PS/ST to ensure compliance with the framework to fast-track the 
efficient and effective implementation of projects and enable the attainment of the 
intended objectives. 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
13 
 
 
1.6.2 Lack of a data bank with cumulative costs incurred on project execution 
and other project information 
 
Section 4.31.1 of the Treasury Instructions provides that Projects shall be monitored 
to assess progress relative to the implementation plan by the Implementing agencies 
submitting monthly and quarterly progress reports to identified monitoring agencies 
that shall assess financial and physical implementation. 
 
Section 7.4 of the Development Committee (DC) Guidelines states that the DC shall 
be supported by the IBP to enable smooth operations. The IBP is a single window 
system for all stakeholders involved in the Public Investment Management System of 
Uganda. It also serves as a central repository of information about public projects 
from preparation, budget formulation, execution, implementation, monitoring, and 
evaluation to closure. 
 
I reviewed the Integrated Bank of Projects (IBP) and the project master file and 
noted the absence of cumulative project costs incurred for all projects in the 
portfolio. 
I further reviewed the project performance by agreement report (for projects with an 
external funding component) and revealed that; 
 
 
Three (3) projects (Bukasa Inland Port, Development of BTVET, and 
development of Kabaale International Airport) received full funding, but the 
master file did not indicate the cumulative funding received and spent. 
 
 
Twenty-one (21) sampled Projects on the decision matrix availed could not be 
found on the IBP despite the requirement that all project information should 
be uploaded on the IBP. 
 
There is a risk that projects have received over and above the project's proposed 
costs/value over time due to the lack of effective monitoring of the financial 
implementation of the respective projects. 
 
There is also a risk that the IBP is not updated with all relevant project information 
as required by the Development Committee guidelines. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that there was a planned upgrade of the IBP aimed 
at fully integrating it with other PFM systems to ensure that all project-related 
information from inception to closure is available on the IBP. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PS/ST to implement measures to ensure compliance with the 
Development Committee guidelines, in line with the upload of project data to the 
IBP. 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
14 
 
 
1.6.3 Inconsistent Application of GFSM Frameworks in Budget Preparation and 
Classification 
 
The Government Finance Statistics Manual (GFSM) is a series of guidelines issued by 
the IMF that describe a specialized macroeconomic statistical framework (the 
government finance statistics (GFS) framework) to support fiscal analysis. 
 
The Public Finance Management Act, Cap 171, sets out a legal framework for 
economic management to ensure macroeconomic stability. Section 3(2) of the Act 
provides for the principles that must be based upon while setting the Government’s 
fiscal objectives. 
 
The updated Chart of Uganda Accounts, May 2022, indicates that the Government 
adopted a financial reporting framework that conforms to the 2014 IMF Government 
Financial Statistics (GFS), which requires Governments to align their budget 
classification, reporting, and fiscal analysis to strengthen the worldwide effort to 
improve public sector reporting and transparency. 
 
I noted that whereas Government adopted the GFSM 2014 classification structure in 
its Chart of Accounts for coding and reporting, budget preparation and presentation 
processes were undertaken using the GFSM 1986 framework, yet the GFS 2014 is 
superior to the GFS 1986 in some of the following aspects;

The Accounting Officer explained that the Accountant General had undertaken a

1.7 
Review of UDC Capitalization 
 
State enterprise, Uganda Development Corporation (UDC) is mandated to promote 
and facilitate industrial and economic development by investing in commercially 
viable projects that align with the National Development Goals. 
 
Although UDC is expected to operate with a degree of independence, it is being 
financed through project-specific funding. The government releases funds to UDC 
that are already earmarked for specific projects, leaving UDC with no space to 
conduct proper investment appraisal. 
 
I noted the following; 
 
i) 
Over the last 10 years, UDC has invested UGX.1.3Tn in 22 companies through 
various modalities. Assessment of 10 active companies that provided 
documentation revealed that; 
 
 
8 out of 10 companies recorded net losses for at least two consecutive years. 
 
Kaaro-Koffi Ltd, despite an investment of UGX.3.1Bn, remains non-
operational four years after the initial investment. 
 
Eight companies that UDC loaned UGX.23Bn had not adhered to the agreed 
repayment terms and had neither paid principal nor interest. 
 
An assessment of UDC’s investment income for the year revealed a paltry 
UGX.1.4Bn against a UGX.1.3Tn investment, giving a return on Investment of 
0.09%. 
 
The above analysis shows that the investment decisions made for UDC are not 
yielding returns. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that UDC’s Strategic Plan 2020-2030 envisaged the 
Corporation’s impact to be measured through achievement of high-level outcomes 
anchored upon five fundamental principles, namely; 
 
a) 
Creation of both direct and indirect employment with a focus on productive 
jobs. 
b) 
Utilization of local raw materials/resources to manufacture for both the 
domestic and international markets. 

 
 
 
16 
 
 
c) 
Improving the trade balance position as envisaged in the National Export 
Development Strategy, the National Industrial Development Policy, and the 
National Investment Policy, among others. 
d) 
Development of Local Entrepreneurship. 
e) 
Balanced regional development. 
 
The contribution of UDC and achievements in job creation, trade balance 
improvement, agro-industrial development, and regional equity over the past five 
financial 
years 
include: 
Job 
creation/retention, 
Utilization 
of 
Local 
Raw 
Materials/Resources, Improving the trade balance position, Contribution to Import 
Substitution, Development of Local Entrepreneurship and UDC’s Commitment to 
Balanced Regional Development. 
 
Government will consider financing the Fund to support national priority investments 
that have a high development impact but low returns, or that take too long to turn 
around to profitability, to free UDC capitalization for investment in entities that 
provide good returns on investment. 
 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PS/ST to consider providing capital funding to UDC and then demand 
an expected return on investment.

SECTION 2: REPORT ON THE AUDIT OF COMPLIANCE WITH THE RELEVANT 
REGULATORY FRAMEWORK 
 
I conducted compliance audits on selected key subject matters in line with Section 18 of the 
National Audit Act (NAA), Cap 170 and in accordance with the International Standards of 
Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI 4000)1 on compliance auditing. 
 
The primary objective of the audits was to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence to 
form a conclusion on whether the Government complied with the relevant identified criteria. 
 
The areas of focus for the compliance review were; 
 
 
Management of PDM, and 
 
Management of Procurement. 
 
Audit Criteria 
 
The criteria for the audits were based on Acts of Parliament, regulations, and 
manuals/guidelines that are intended to be followed during implementation of the stated 
interventions. I therefore designed audit procedures to assess the extent of compliance. 
 
Audit Methodology 
 
My audit was conducted based on the information and records provided by the Government 
staff. In executing the audits, various approaches were exercised, which included; 
 
 
Document reviews; 
 
Physical inspections; 
 
Interviewing relevant officials of the Ministry/entity; and 
 
Analyzing data provided. 
 
Audit Findings 
 
The material findings with respect to the compliance criteria for the applicable subject matters 
are as follows; 
 
1.8 
Management of the Parish Development Model 
 
The Parish Development Model (PDM) is a strategy for service delivery by the 
Government of Uganda to improve the incomes and welfare of all Ugandans at the 
household level by transforming 39% of households from a subsistence economy to a 
money economy, as approved by Parliament. In the financial year 2024/25, the Ministry 
of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED) released UGX.1.100Tn to 
10,594 PDM SACCOs as Parish Revolving Funds (PRF) - UGX.1.059Tn and administrative 
costs - UGX.0.41Tn as appropriated by Parliament. 
 
1 ISSAI 4000 - Compliance Audit Standard

the financial inclusion pillar. 
 
I noted that the programme was operating well in aspects of funds disbursement, loan 
application and data capture, and this enabled the disbursement of UGX.1,058.37Bn to 
10,594 PDM SACCOs, in a timely manner.

I noted that 5,123 SACCO bank accounts in 122 LGs, had not yet 
been closed, contrary to the guidance. By 30th June 2025, a 
balance of UGX.4,944,592,705 was outstanding on 4,974 SACCO 
accounts in various commercial banks. 
 
This undermines the attainment of the benefits of using the Wendi 
platform, which include: convenience, security, lower transaction 
costs, transparency and ease of tracking the PDM funds. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed it to low response and non-
compliance by banks, procedural and bureaucratic requirements, 
limited follow-up by SACCO leaders and district management, low 
account balances, and challenges in coordinating account 
signatories.

Conclusion 
 
The Government envisaged that the adoption of the Parish Development Model (PDM) 
strategy would improve service delivery and the incomes and welfare of all Ugandans at 
the household level by transforming 39% of households from a subsistence economy to 
a money economy. 
 
Whereas a lot has been done to implement the strategy, there are still notable areas 
that require improvement, and as such Government should consider implementing the 
recommendations in this report to address the challenges highlighted above for better 
management of the PDM.

1.9 
Management of Procurements 
 
This section highlights my key findings, which have been consolidated for the purpose of 
this thematic report, details of which have been reported in the individual entity/project-
specific reports. 
 
 
1.9.1 Inadequacies in the standardisation of specifications and prices for common 
user works, services and supplies 
 
Section 8 of the PPDA Act, Cap 205, empowers the Authority, where applicable, to 
determine the prices of works, services and supplies which are used in common by two 
or more procuring and disposing entities and which may be subject to common 
procurement; and review the prices as may be necessary. The Authority is also 
mandated to adopt, adapt and update common specifications standards, the use of 
which shall be mandatory to all procuring and disposing entities. 
 
Audit established the following inadequacies; 
 
i) 
The PPDA last undertook price surveys for common user goods in 2022, and this 
only covered Kampala, Mbarara, Mbale, Hoima, Arua and Gulu Districts. 
ii) 
Comparison of the costs for construction of office accommodation for the 
ongoing and recently commissioned projects revealed variances in the costs per 
square ranging from UGX.5.3Mn to UGX.3.7Mn. 
 
Analysis of the costs for construction of a sample of tarmacked roads revealed variances 
for each square meter as detailed below;

In light of the above, it was noticed that government was incurring different costs on 
common user items due to the price variances that ought to be standardized. 
 
Standardization of specifications and prices would eliminate the associated variances on 
costs incurred by various government entities on common user works, services, and 
goods and also provide a benchmark for budgeting purposes. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PS/ST and Executive Director of PPDA, in liaison with other responsible 
ministries and/ or subject matter experts, to undertake standardization of specifications 
and prices for common user works, services, and goods for all Procuring and Disposing 
entities to either comply or explain. 
 
1.9.2 Non-compliance with reservation schemes 
 
Paragraph 2 of the PPDA Guideline number 11 of 2024, Guidelines to promote 
participation of registered associations of women, Persons with Disabilities, requires an 
entity to reserve at least 15% of its annual procurement plan budget for awards to 
registered associations of women, youth, and persons with disabilities. 
 
Contrary to the above, I noted that there was no single Ministry, Department, Agency or 
Local Government out of the sampled 65 entities that reserved procurements for 
registered associations as required by the guidelines. As such, no contract awards were 
made to the registered associations. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed the occurrence to the late release of the guidelines 
by the Public Procurement and Disposal of Public Assets Authority. It was also indicated 
that provisions for special interest groups had been made in the subsequent 
procurement plans. 
 

 
 
 
 
25 
 
 
 
The failure to reserve procurements for registered associations undermines the 
legislator’s objective of promoting the participation of women, youth, and PWDs in 
public procurement proceedings. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officers to ensure that the published procurement plans 
indicate procurements reserved for registered associations to facilitate their participation 
and ensure compliance with the reservation scheme guidelines. 
 
1.9.3 Failure to prepare multi-year procurement plans 
 
Section 60(6) of the PPDA Act, Cap.205 requires an entity that undertakes a 
procurement over a period of more than one financial year to prepare a multi-year 
procurement plan using the guidelines issued. 
 
I reviewed entities’ procurement reports for the financial year 2024/25 and noted that 
64 procurements worth UGX.385Bn were initiated in prior periods and completed in the 
current year; however, these entities did not prepare multi-year procurement plans for 
the procurements as required by the Act. 
 
The failure to prepare multi-year plans creates uncertainty regarding the availability of 
funds, which may lead to project delays and cancellations. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting officers to ensure that multi-year procurement plans are 
prepared for procurements expected to span more than one year for proper planning 
and budgeting. 
 
1.9.4 Ambiguity in the use of lists of prequalified suppliers 
 
Regulation 53 (3) of the PPDA (Rules and Methods) Regulations, SI No. 100 of 2023, 
provides for an entity to develop a shortlist for bidders using the entity’s list of providers 
prequalified for groups of procurements which are similar, or PPDA’s register of 
providers, another entity’s pre-qualified list, or market knowledge. A bidder shall not be 
included unless they are expected to fully satisfy the qualification requirements of 
competence, capacity, resources, and experience required for the execution of the 
procurement. 
 
It was noted that the Regulations do not provide the order in which the prescribed 
sources of developing the shortlist of the bidders apply. Despite having a prequalified list 
of providers for various supplies, services and works at the entity, it was noted that 
some entities were shortlisting bidders other than those on their own pre-qualified lists. 
 
Failure to shortlist prequalified suppliers from the entities' own prequalified lists 
undermines the purpose for which the prequalification process was intended and fogs 
transparency. 

 
 
 
 
26 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Public Procurement and Disposal of Public Assets Authority to review the 
PPDA (Rules and Methods) Regulations, 2023 so as to streamline the order of use of the 
various sources for developing shortlists of bidders. 
 
Conclusion 
 
The evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for my conclusion. 
Based on the work performed and described in this report, except for the findings stated 
above, nothing has come to my attention that causes me to believe that the 
Management of the Parish Development Model and Procurement and disposal of Goods 
and Services in Government is not in compliance, in all material respects, with the 
relevant criteria. 
 
 
 
Edward Akol 
AUDITOR GENERAL 
KAMPALA 
 
31st December, 2025

SECTION 3: REPORT ON PERFORMANCE EVALUATION 
 
In accordance with Schedule 5 of the Public Finance Management Act, Cap 171, on the 
presentation of financial statements, and Section 18 of the NAA, Cap 170, I undertook an 
evaluation of the Government’s actual performance in comparison with its planned activities and 
outputs for the year as well as its mandate. This section presents the findings from the 
evaluation of the performance. 
 
1.10 
Review of Taxation 
1.10.1 Low Tax/GDP ratio 
 
According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), developing countries should 
maintain a tax-to-GDP ratio of at least 15% to ensure they have the funds to invest in 
the future and achieve sustainable economic growth. Tax-to-GDP Ratio represents total 
tax revenue as a percentage of GDP and indicates the share of a Country's output that 
the Government collects through taxes. 
A comparison of the Country’s performance with other economies revealed wide 
disparities, as shown in the table below;

I noted, however, that although URA efforts have yielded significant results, with 
tremendous growth in revenue collection, Uganda's Tax/GDP ratio has stagnated at 
around 13.4%. Below is an analysis of various sectors’ contribution to Tax and to GDP

The table above shows a structural imbalance between economic activity and tax 
revenue, with agriculture, real estate and services contributing significantly to GDP but 
relatively little to tax revenue. Government tax revenue remains heavily concentrated in 
trade and manufacturing. 
 
There is a need to broaden the tax base, enhance compliance in high-GDP but low-tax 
sectors, and rebalance the tax burden to better align revenue collection with the 
economic structure through the tax policy. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that to enhance Uganda’s domestic revenue efforts, 
Government formulated a National Tax Policy, which was approved by Cabinet in FY 
2024/25 and is currently under implementation. He further expounded that Government 
was in the process of finalising the drafting of the Domestic Revenue Mobilisation 
Strategy II (DRMS2), aimed at increasing Uganda’s revenue effort to at least 20% of 
GDP over the medium term. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PSST to expedite efforts to revise the tax policy to align with the growing 
GDP and revenue collection. 
 
1.10.2 Expansion of the Tax Register 
 
The URA Financial statements for FY 2024/25 indicated an addition of 728,640 taxpayers 
to the register, bringing the total number of registered taxpayers to 5,251,874; however, 
only 20% of these are active. 
 
I noted that, whereas efforts were invested in growing the register through the TREP 
program, other clusters of potential taxpayers were not considered for inclusion on the 
register, yet they are expected to yield significant revenue, as explained below; 
 
 
 
Practising Accountants 
 
Out of 289 accountants registered with the ICPAU, only 104 were compliant and had 
filed up-to-date returns; a sample of 10 were registered with URA but had either never 
filed returns or had returns that were not up to date. 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
29 
 
 
 
 
Practising advocates 
 
Out of 1271 advocates registered with the Uganda Law Society, only 292 were 
compliant in terms of having up-to-date Income Tax Returns. 249 were registered with 
URA but did not have up-to-date Income Tax returns, while 61 were not traceable on 
the E-tax system and, therefore, most likely not registered with URA. 
 
 
Similar disparities can be noted in the education, health and engineering 
sectors. 
 
It should be noted that Section 4(8) of the Income Tax Act, Cap 338, bars persons 
providing professional services, such as accountants and advocates, from filing under 
the presumptive tax regime. 
 
The above cases imply that there are still untapped areas that URA has not leveraged, to 
effectively and efficiently collect revenue. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that Government had amended the Tax Procedures 
Code Act (TPCA) to require the possession of a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) 
prior to licensing by any regulatory authority, as provided under Section 4(9) of the 
TPCA. Accounting Officer further explained that URA had been guided to update the tax 
register and enforce compliance to address these gaps. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PSST to institute measures to ensure that the URA enforces the 
requirements of the amended Tax Procedures Code Act (TPCA).

1.11.3 Review of the budgetary allocation by administrative heads versus readiness 
to implement the 10-fold growth strategy 
 
Paragraph 36 of the tenfold growth strategy, 2025, provides that the services sector, 
followed by agriculture and lastly industry, had the highest multiplier effects on the 
economy of 2.61, 2.55 and 2.30, respectively. 
 
Paragraph 39 of the Tenfold Growth Strategy 2025, provides for four anchor areas for 
attaining a sustainable breakthrough into a new and higher economic frontier. These 
four anchor areas, referenced as the ATMS, are; 
 
 
Agro-Industrial Development 
 
Tourism Development 
 
Mineral-based Development plus Oil and Gas (petrochemical industry) and 
 
Science, Technology, ICT and Innovation, including ICT and the Creative 
Industry (Knowledge Economy). 
 
Para 40 of the same strategy provides for enablers to assist the ATMS in the 
achievement of the tenfold growth. These enablers include infrastructure, security, 
human capital, law, and order. 
 
In addition, paragraphs 46, 56 and 100 of the NDP IV, provide that the NDP IV is 
anchored on the Tenfold strategy, which aims to achieve economic growth of 
USD.500Bn within the next 15 years. The strategy emphasises accelerated investment 
and policy prioritisation in these growth pillars to achieve a tenfold increase in GDP by 
2040. In addition, the strategy emphasized enablers. 
 
I reviewed the budgetary allocation to ATMS programs for the FY 2024/25 and noted 
marginal allocations compared to their strategic importance under the Tenfold Growth 
Strategy, as shown in the chart below; 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
32 
 
 
 
Figure 1: Budgetary allocation by ATMS and Other Programs 
 
Source: analysis of information from BPS and IFMS 
Note: The Total revised budget the FY 24/25 is UGX.78.794Tn 
 
The graph above indicates an allocation pattern that does not prioritise productive and 
export-led growth in ATM sectors, which are central to the Tenfold Growth Strategy’s 
implementation framework. 
 
However, while the current budget heavily invests in intermediate programs that form 
the enabling foundation, such as infrastructure, security, human capital and law and 
order, the investment in the ATMS is still paltry. 
 
The above implied that there was a disconnect between strategic priorities and fiscal 
commitments. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that the “ATMS Accelerator Actions Tracker” was 
developed and completed, and that it monitors the extent of allocations to the 
accelerator actions in the budget. He further explained that the allocation of resources to 
the ATMS in FY 2025/26 has been comprehensive and will have a higher multiplier effect 
in the outer years of the strategy, accelerating economic growth. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PS/ST to operationalize program strategies consistent with the Tenfold 
Growth roadmap.

1.12.4 Primary dealership system in the issuance of Treasury Instruments 
 
The Treasury has delegated the process of issuance of Treasury bills and bonds to Bank 
of Uganda. At the moment, Bank of Uganda is using the primary dealership system for 
the issuance of instruments. The primary dealership system limits the bidders for 
Treasury bonds and bills to a few institutional players. Currently, there are eight major 
banks acting as primary dealers in Uganda; however, of these eight, only four are quite 
active. 
 
The major advantage of using the primary dealership system is the reduction in 
refinancing risk and the existence of price discovery through the secondary market. 
However, the benefit of price discovery is currently not met in Uganda, as most primary 
dealers hold the instruments until maturity due to an underdeveloped secondary market. 
 
I performed an analysis of the performance of the private sector commercial lending 
rates, compared to 10-year Government Bonds, using STATA 14.0 for the last three FYs 
to enable an assessment of price discovery and market efficiency. STATA is an 
integrated statistical software package for data management, analysis, and visualisation. 
The analysis compared the Yield to Maturity (YTM) on 10-year Government bonds with 
prevailing private sector commercial lending rates over the same period to assess pricing 
behaviour in the domestic debt market. 
Descriptive statistics examined the level and volatility of bond yields relative to lending 
rates. The yield spread analysis assessed the margin between risk-free government 
borrowing and private sector credit. The results are summarised below; 
 
Table 17: Open market operations

Results from the descriptive analysis 
The average private sector lending rate stood at 18.20% over the period, while average 
Government bond yields were 16.07% (10-year), leaving a narrow margin of 2.13%, 
despite Government securities being risk-free instruments. 
In addition, the volatility (standard deviation) of the 10-year bond yields (0.82) was 
comparable to that of the lending rate (1.03), indicating that Government bond pricing 
exhibited similar instability to private credit markets. 
More critically, spreads turned negative during the three years, reaching as low as -
0.60% (10-year), implying that Government borrowing costs, occasionally exceeded 
private sector lending rates. 

 
 
 
 
37 
 
 
 
The results above suggest that the low yield spreads with bond yields averaging 16.07% 
are an indication of weak price discovery and limited competition in the Government 
securities market 
This exposes Government to the principal risk of the primary dealership system of 
limitation to competition, and the corresponding potential incentive to collusive 
behaviour. This may have the effect of pushing interest rates on Government 
instruments high as the primary dealers seek to maximise profit. 
Management acknowledged the recommendation and planned to select Primary Dealers 
with a mindset to enhance competition in the subsequent selection process. 
 
Recommendation 
 
Treasury is advised to expedite the reassessment of whether the current issuance 
system is optimal and take appropriate steps to address any deficiency. 
 
1.12.5 Review of sovereign credit indicators 
 
Sovereign credit ratings are a condensed assessment of a government’s ability and 
willingness to repay its public debt both in principal and in interest on time. In this, they 
are forward-looking qualitative measures of the probability of default put forward by 
rating agencies. 
I undertook an analysis of selected sovereign credit indicators used to assess a country's 
creditworthiness, reflecting its ability to meet its debt obligations. For this assessment, I 
have assessed the indicators that measure the financial strength of a country. 
The financial strength parameter indicates a country’s fiscal health and its ability to 
manage public resources efficiently. Strong financial indicators contribute to higher 
sovereign credit ratings and investor confidence, while weak indicators can lead to 
reduced creditworthiness and higher borrowing costs. 
a) 
Public Debt to GDP Ratio - Assessment of debt sustainability – 50.29% 
The Debt-to-GDP ratio is a measure that compares what a country owes (total debt) and 
what it produces (manufactures or services). A lower ratio indicates better debt 
sustainability, while a higher ratio suggests increased fiscal pressure and potential 
challenges in meeting debt obligations. 
Objective 1(a) of the National Charter for Fiscal Responsibility FY 2021/22 – FY2025/26 
provides that the total public debt in nominal terms is reduced to 51.2% of GDP in the 
financial year 2024/25. 
A re-computed the debt-to-GDP ratio over the years revealed a generally stable ratio in 
the FYs 2020/21 to 2023/24. However, during the period under review, the debt-to-GDP 
ratio rose sharply to 50.29%. The table and graph below refer;

1.13 
Management of Non-Current Assets 
 
I undertook an assessment of the effectiveness of utilization, maintenance, and 
management of Non-Current Assets across fifty-seven (57) sampled entities, in line with 
the Treasury Instructions, 2017, and the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA), Cap 
171. The review focused on asset utilization and safeguards, maintenance practices, and 
the recording, existence and valuation of Non-Current Assets and the following 
summarized issues were noted; 
 
 
1.13.1 Effectiveness of Utilization and Controls to safeguard Non-Current Assets 
 
During the physical verification and review of asset registers across fifty-seven (57) 
sampled entities, I noted underutilized and idle Non-Current Assets worth 
UGX.378.022Bn in forty one (41) entities, which were not contributing to intended 
service delivery outcomes. 
 

 
 
 
 
41 
 
 
 
I noted that the entities had not put in place mechanisms to detect levels of utilization, 
such as operational plans and utilization reports, monitoring procedures, usage logs, and 
downtime records. There was also limited internal audit coverage and inadequate staff 
training for specialized equipment. 
 
Furthermore, Non-Current Assets valued at UGX.269.939Bn, in ten (10) entities, lacked 
adequate security measures, including appropriate storage, surveillance, fencing on 
vacant land, titling and registration of properties. 
 
These deficiencies indicate misalignment between Non-Current Assets and entity 
mandates, heightening risks of undetected underutilization, misuse, loss, damage, 
inefficient service delivery, resource wastage, unmeasured outcomes, and financial risk 
exposure. 
 
Recommendations 
 
I advised the responsible Accounting Officers to; 
 
i) 
Develop utilization plans aligned to strategic objectives; 
ii) 
Establish comprehensive asset management policies incorporating monitoring 
procedures, performance indicators, robust security measures, and regular 
reporting; 
iii) 
Secure insurance coverage for susceptible assets against risks; and 
iv) 
Conduct regular assessments to identify underutilized or obsolete assets for 
repurposing or disposal under the PPDA Act. 
 
1.13.2 Maintenance of Non-Current Assets 
 
I noted that twenty-eight (28) out of the fifty-seven (57) sampled entities had no 
maintenance plans and reports to document maintenance requirements, such as 
budgets, personnel involved, and schedules. There was also no system for tracking 
maintenance history or forecasting future needs. 
 
Physical verification further revealed non-functional equipment/assets due to lack of 
servicing, worth UGX.10.533Bn, and buildings valued at UGX.61.761Bn showed signs of 
deterioration as a result of neglected repairs and maintenance. 
 
This was attributed to the non-integration of maintenance into broader planning and 
budgeting processes and failure to conduct needs assessments, which results in reactive 
rather than preventive approaches. This leads to asset breakdowns and structural 
deterioration before issues are resolved. 
This inadequate maintenance has led to reduced asset lifespan, potential service 
disruptions, increased operational costs, asset breakdowns and structural deterioration. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
42 
 
 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the responsible Accounting Officers to develop and implement maintenance 
policies with schedules aligned to manufacturer or industry standards, ensure annual 
approval of maintenance plans and budgets, and establish systems for tracking 
maintenance history and costs to maximize the useful life and value of Non-Current 
Assets. 
 
 
 
Edward Akol 
AUDITOR GENERAL 
KAMPALA 
 
31st December, 2025

SECTION 4: REVIEW OF THE CONSOLIDATED SUMMARY STATEMENT OF FINANCIAL 
PERFORMANCE OF PUBLIC CORPORATIONS AND STATE ENTERPRISES 
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30TH JUNE 2025 
In line with Sections 12 and 18 of the National Audit Act (NAA), Cap 170, and the Public 
Finance Management Act (PFMA), Cap 171, I am required to audit and report on Public 
Corporations or other bodies established by Acts of Parliament. 
Section 2 of the PFMA, Cap 171 defines a Public Corporation as an authority established by an 
Act of Parliament other than a Local Government, which receives contributions from public 
funds, and any public body, which in a financial year receives any income from public funds. 
Similarly, a State Enterprise means a body established under any Act other than the Companies 
Act or a Local Government Council, and a Company registered under the Companies Act in 
which the Government or a state enterprise has a controlling interest. 
I reviewed the Consolidated Summary Statement of the Financial Performance of Public 
Corporations and State Enterprises for the financial year ended 30th June 2025, and noted the 
following; 
 
1.14 
Completeness of the Consolidated Summary Statement of Financial 
Performance of Public Corporations and State Enterprises 
Section 50(1)(c) of the PFMA requires the Accountant General to prepare and submit a 
consolidated summary statement of financial performance for all Public Corporations and 
State Enterprises where Government has a controlling interest to the Minister of Finance 
and the Auditor General within three months after the financial year-end. This 
submission is preceded by the Accounting Officers of these institutions preparing and 
submitting their summary financial statements to the Accountant General within two 
months of the end of the financial year, in line with the requirements of Section 49(2) of 
the PFMA. 
Based on my review of the consolidated summary statement for Public Corporations and

45 
 
 
 
1.15 
Review of the Process of Consolidation of the Summary Statement of 
Financial Performance of Public Corporations and State Enterprises 
 
Upon the Accountant General's request for submission of summary statements of 
financial performance from entities, the Accounting Officers of each entity submit their 
respective summaries, based on unaudited financial statements. The Accountant General 
then utilizes the initial submissions to compile the Draft Consolidated Summary 
Statement. 
 
My review revealed variances between the amounts reported in the entity’s audited 
financial statements and their corresponding figures in the consolidated summary 
statement prepared by the Accountant General. 
 
The variances were partly attributed to the failure by some entities to submit adjusted 
summary statements of financial performance post-audit to the Accountant General. In 
addition, the lack of reporting guidelines has hampered the consolidation process. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accountant General to consider issuing reporting guidelines that outline 
the requirements for the submission of summary statements. These guidelines should 
specify the use of only audited and adjusted summary statements to enhance the 
accuracy of the consolidation information. 
 
1.16 
Financial Performance of Public Corporations and State Enterprises 
 
I noted that out of the sixty-two (62) public corporations and state enterprises, fifty-four 
(54) are for-profit or with a commercial orientation, while fifteen (15) operate on a not-
for-profit basis. 
 
Although public corporations and state enterprises have both commercial and service 
delivery mandates, the for-profit entities are expected to operate efficiently, generate 
profits, and pay dividends to Government. Consequently, their financial performance is 
of interest to Government. 
 
As highlighted in my previous reports, the Government Consolidated Summary 
Statement on the financial performance of public corporations and state enterprises 
provides limited insights, focusing only on government shareholding, total income, total 
expenditure, dividends declared, retained earnings, and net worth of entities. However, 
critical performance assessment parameters (metrics), including profitability, return on 
assets, liquidity assessment, and debt analysis, are absent from this reporting 
framework. 
 
To address this gap, I undertook an independent computation of these performance 
ratios based on the audited financial statements of the Public Corporations and State 
Enterprises. 

 
 
 
 
46 
 
 
 
Profit-Oriented Public Corporations and State Enterprises 
 
I assessed fifteen (15) entities from the fifty-four (54) profit-oriented public corporations 
and state enterprises. It is important to note that this analysis excluded newly 
established entities, recently restructured entities and entities in the investment phase. 
These included Uganda National Mining Company (UNMC), Kilembe Mines Limited 
(KML), and Uganda Development Corporation (UDC), which has twenty consolidated 
entities. For Uganda Electricity Distribution Company Limited (UEDCL), the company had 
just operated for only three (3) months, having taken over from Umeme.

b) 
Operating Margin 
 
Operating Margin is the ratio that indicates how much profit an enterprise makes from 
its core business in relation to its total revenues. It is calculated from Operating income 
or EBIT/Total revenue. It measures the extent to which an enterprise is able to pay for 
its operating costs while remaining profitable. A higher operating margin means that the 
enterprise has less financial risk. 
 
I analyzed the operating margins of twelve (12) public corporations and state 
enterprises, with the objective of assessing their ability to cover operating costs while 
maintaining profitability. I noted that only five (5) entities reported operating margins 
higher than 15%, indicating strong performance. These are MNSL (94.96), NHIL (52), 
NEC - Luwero Industries Limited (35), UEGCL (27) and NEC Uzima Limited (24.23). 
 
The entities such as NEC AGRO SMC Limited, Uganda Post Limited and UNOC reported 
improvements in their operating margins compared to the prior year, despite remaining 
below the 15% threshold. This indicates a positive trend for these companies. 
 
However, several entities faced significant declines in their operating margins, 
particularly UETCL decreased from 7.36% to -23%, UBC from -3% to -24%, and UPHL 
from 15.5% to 5.4%. The declines reflect high operational costs and revenue drop, thus 
raising concerns about their financial stability. The table below refers;

c) 
Return on Assets 
 
Return on Assets (ROA) is a financial metric used to evaluate how efficient the company 
uses its assets to generate earnings. A higher ROA indicates more efficient use of assets, 
reflecting strong management performance. Although companies with substantial initial 
investments, such as those in capital-intensive industries, tend to exhibit lower ROA due 
to higher asset bases and potentially lower net income margins, a ROA below 5% is 
generally considered inadequate. 
 
The analysis of ROA for fifteen (15) corporations and enterprises revealed that only 
three (3) public corporations and state enterprises, namely MNSL, UNOC and NEC 
Luwero Industries Limited, achieved a commendable ROA exceeding 5%. The remaining 
twelve (12) exhibited low performance with ROAs falling below the 5% threshold. The

d) 
Dividend Pay-out 
Several public corporations and state enterprises, despite reporting significant profits, 
chose not to distribute any dividends to shareholders, particularly the government. 
These included UNOCL, MNSL, NHCCL and UEGCL, among others. These entities cited 
their intention to retain earnings to fund planned investments/projects as the reason for 
withholding dividends. 
A review of financial statements and the Consolidated Summary Statement of financial 
performance, however, revealed that two entities declared and paid out dividends. 
Although the New Vision Printing and Publishing Company Limited and NHIL declared 
dividends of UGX.3.837Bn and UGX.0.0.271Bn, they paid out UGX.1.390Mn, 
UGX.0.159Bn respectively. I also noted that Housing Finance Bank Ltd, which had 
declared dividends of UGX.32.567Bn, did not pay at all. 
While retaining earnings for reinvestment may be strategically beneficial for growth, it is 
essential to balance this with shareholder returns. Shareholders expect return on their 
investment, especially in profitable entities. 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accountant General to ensure that public corporations and state 
enterprises develop clear dividend policies that specify how profits are allocated between 
reinvestment in business and dividends to shareholders. This will provide clarity and 
establish a framework for consistent decision-making. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
53 
 
 
 
 
 
e) 
Liquidity Assessment 
 
Liquidity is a measure of an organization’s ability to meet its short-term financial 
obligations. The Current Ratio, which compares current assets to current liabilities, is a 
metric used for this assessment, and an ideal (desirable) ratio ranges between 1.5 and 
2, indicating sufficient liquidity to cover liabilities, although acceptable current ratios vary 
between different industries or sectors. 
 
In this analysis of fifteen (15) public corporations and state enterprises, ten (10) entities 
exhibited current ratios above the ideal threshold, suggesting they are generally able to 
meet their short-term obligations. Of the 10, five (5) had exceptionally high current 
ratios (5 and above), raising concerns about the effective utilizing of current assets or 
short-term financing facilities. These included MNSL, NHIL, UACC, UNOC, and UPHL. 
 
Five (5) entities fell below the desirable threshold of 1.5, indicating potential difficulties 
in meeting financial obligations. These included Uganda Printing and Publishing 
Corporation (UPPC), UBC, UETCL, URC and UPL. 
 
Below the threshold, performance was mainly attributed to an increase in payables and 
challenges in receivables management. The Table below refers;

f) 
Debt Analysis 
 
The analysis of debt ratios is crucial for assessing entity financial health and ability to 
meet both short and long-term obligations. The gearing ratio, which measures the 
proportion of an entity's assets financed by debt, is an important indicator of financial 
leverage and risk exposure. A debt ratio exceeding 50% is generally viewed as 
undesirable due to increased financial risk, although this varies from industry to another. 
I assessed eight (8) entities, and noted that six (6) maintained a debt ratio below the 
50% threshold, indicating that owner’s equity was sufficient to cover total debt. 

 
 
 
 
56 
 
 
 
These included NEC Uzima Limited, NEC AGRO SMC Limited, NEC Luwero Industries 
Limited, NHCCL, URC and UPL. 
 
Two enterprises, namely UEGCL and UETCL, had debt ratios above 50%, which raises 
concerns about their financial stability. This was mainly attributed to inadequate funding 
to repay outstanding loan obligations and may further hinder the ability to access future

Overall Conclusion 
The assessment of public corporations and state enterprises has provided valuable insights 
into their financial performance and operational efficiency. The objective of establishing these 
entities was to ensure efficient and effective management of government operations while 
delivering services to citizens. 
While some public corporations and state enterprises are performing well, there is need for 
efforts on those that are unprofitable, because it affects return on assets, ability to pay 
dividends and settle obligations, when they fall due. Implementing the recommended 
strategies can ensure that these entities operate effectively to fulfil their mandates while 
delivering services that meet the expectations of the government and the citizens. By 
developing appropriate financial and non-financial performance assessment indicators for 
Public Corporations and State Enterprises, coupled with establishing a culture of continuous 
improvement, the government can ensure sustainable growth and value creation through 
public enterprises. 
 
 
 
Edward Akol 
AUDITOR GENERAL 
KAMPALA
