2.1.1.2 Procurement and Distribution of Essential Medicines and Health Supplies 
 
The National Medical Stores (NMS) is mandated by Section 4 (a) and (b) of the NMS Act 
Cap. 207 to Procure, Store & Distribute Essential Medicines and Medical Supplies 
(EMHS) to all Public Health Facilities in the Country. The scope of coverage for this 
mandate is 3,432 Health Centres at various levels across different parts of the Country. 
I reviewed the procurement and distribution of EMHS and noted the following; 
 
i) 
The budget availed to NMS for this mandate was below the assessed funding 
requirements by UGX.0.181Tn. A review of the National Annual Needs Analysis 
and Quantification of Essential Medicines and Health Supplies for public health 
facilities in Uganda, compiled by the Ministry of Health and NMS, revealed that 
UGX.1.574Tn was required for NMS to meet the Country's EMHS demands per 
year. However, during the year, UGX.1.393Tn was committed, implying a gap of 
UGX.0.181Tn representing 11% of the required resources. 
 
ii) 
By 30th June 2025, NMS had Non-viable/expired drugs valued at UGX.8.04Bn 
made up of GoU stock worth UGX.0.53Bn and stock from Development partners 
worth UGX.7.51Bn. This represents a 97% decrease from the value of expired 
drugs of UGX.316Bn (mainly Covid Vaccines) as at 30th June 2024. These 
expiries were mainly due to the misalignment between the Country's medicine 
needs and what was procured, and changes in treatment protocols by WHO 
after medicines have been procured. 
 
The above shortcomings in the procurement and distribution of EMHS increase the risk 
of stockouts at health facilities, treatment disruption and death for patients who cannot 
afford to procure the medicines from private pharmacies. 
 
Recommendation 
I advised the Government to ensure that going forward, these challenges are addressed 
to minimise disruptions in the delivery of EMHS. 
 
2.1.1.3 Functionality of ICU and Theatre Equipment 
 
The Ministry of Health procured and delivered Intensive Care Unit (ICU) equipment to 
15 Regional Referral Hospitals (RRHs), three (3) National Referral Hospitals and seven 
(7) General Hospitals in the last five years. The records reviewed showed that the 
equipment was worth UGX.150Bn, and it included Heating, Ventilation and Air 
Conditioning (HVAC) systems for ICU and assorted critical-care equipment for New-born 
Intensive Care Units (NICU) operations. 
 
I noted that although the equipment was delivered to the facilities, several hospitals 
could not utilise this equipment due to gaps in ICU infrastructure, staffing, power 
stability and inadequate oxygen support systems. From my Interviews with hospital 
administrators, biomedical engineers and audit inspections, I confirmed the following; 
 

 
 
 
 
61 
 
 
 
i) 
Unreliable power supply: Five (5) hospitals lacked adequate power backup 
systems to support the continuous operation of critical care equipment. ICU 
units, oxygen plants and diagnostic machines require stable, uninterrupted 
electricity, yet many hospitals did not have generators with sufficient capacity, 
had faulty switching systems or lacked alternative power sources entirely. This 
challenge was observed at Hoima RRH, Jinja RRH, Mubende RRH, Fort Portal 
RRH and Kabale RRH. This affected the installation of ventilators, patient 
monitors and other ICU equipment, which remained boxed or stored in 
temporary rooms instead of being installed and commissioned. 
 
ii) 
Non-functional diagnostic equipment: Several key pieces of diagnostic 
equipment essential to ICU case management were either non-functional or 
overdue for servicing. The X-ray machines at Entebbe RRH, Hoima RRH, and 
Jinja 
RRH 
were 
non-functional 
due 
to 
delayed 
maintenance 
and 
mechanical/technical faults. The non-functional or inadequately maintained 
diagnostic equipment undermines the effective operation of ICU services and 
limits the ability of referral hospitals to provide timely and accurate diagnosis for 
critically ill patients. 
 
iii) 
Inadequate oxygen supply systems: There were gaps in the functionality, 
reliability and safety of oxygen supply systems. Several facilities lacked fully 
installed pipeline systems, had oxygen plants that were not operational, or had 
unresolved technical failures affecting production capacity. These challenges 
were observed at Mubende RRH, Fort Portal RRH, and Kabale RRH. These gaps 
severely limited the hospitals' ability to meet oxygen demand, particularly in 
ICUs, theatres and emergency units where continuous oxygen supply is essential 
to patient survival. 
 
iv) 
Inadequate maintenance budget: The health facilities were grappling with 
challenges of maintenance of the medical equipment due to the inadequate 
budget. For example, oxygen plants require quarterly servicing, yet only nine (9) 
of the 26 oxygen plants were serviced and only once during the year due to 
limited funding. In addition, the funds provided for maintenance of X-ray 
machines could only cover 21 of the 59 machines stationed in the various RRHs. 
The budget for maintenance of this equipment has remained the same at 
approximately UGX.7.6Bn since FY 2015/2016, despite the acquisition of 
sophisticated medical equipment for the Regional Referral Hospitals. This is 23% 
of the required budget of UGX.33Bn. 
 
These challenges collectively affected the capacity of these hospitals to deliver critical 
health care services despite the significant government investment. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer of the Ministry of Health and the Accounting Officers of 
the sampled Hospitals to address these gaps so that citizens can receive the services for 
which the Government made investments in the procurement of this critical ICU 
equipment. 
 

 
 
 
 
62 
 
 
 
2.1.1.4 Staffing Gaps in Critical Care Units 
 
Critical Care units refer to specialised units that provide intensive care to patients with 
life-threatening conditions such as severe injuries or illnesses. These include Intensive 
Care Units (ICUs), High Dependency Units (HDUs), Coronary Care Units (CCUs), 
Neonatal ICUs, Paediatric ICUs, among others. These units require highly specialised 
technology and trained personnel due to the criticality of the cases they handle. 
 
I reviewed the level of staffing in the critical care units of 16 Regional Referral Hospitals 
(RRHs) and five (5) National Referral Hospitals (NRHs) and noted acute staffing 
shortages. For all the staff categories, the understaffing was more than 90% and in

2.1.1.5 Failure to Attract Particular Health Specialists 
 
Objective 4 of the Human Resources for Health Strategic Plan (2020–2030) requires the 
Ministry of Health to ensure the availability of an adequate and appropriately skilled 
health workforce, including specialists and super-specialists who are essential for quality 
service delivery at all levels of care. 
 

 
 
 
 
63 
 
 
 
I observed that Public Health facilities are grappling with the challenge of lack of health 
care specialists, such as Consultant Ophthalmologists, Consultant Pathologists, 
Consultant Psychiatrists, and Medical Officer Special Grade in Anaesthesia and 
Emergency cases. These consultants typically diagnose and treat complex conditions, 
perform specialised medical procedures, and conduct specialised types of medical 
research.

Facilities and compared them with the actual numbers in post and noted significant 
variances as summarised in the table below;

The failure to attract specialists in Public Health facilities was caused by the high entry

2.1.1.6 Management of Routine Immunisation Vaccines 
 
The Ministry of Health, through the Uganda National Expanded Program on 
Immunisation (UNEPI), together with the National Medical Stores (NMS), manages the 
procurement and distribution of vaccines to health facilities. During the year, a total of 
159,902 doses of vaccines worth UGX.30.896Bn were procured and distributed to 
various health facilities. I reviewed the management of these activities and observed the 
following; 
 
i) 
Whereas the national cold chain infrastructure system in Public Health Facilities 
is largely still functional, this infrastructure is fast ageing with no clear plan of 

 
 
 
 
64 
 
 
 
replacement. Almost 50% of the current cold chain equipment was delivered 
over seven years ago, with low and inconsistent preventive maintenance over 
the past seven years. There is a risk that if this infrastructure is not replaced, the 
Health Facilities will not be able to keep vaccines at the required temperatures, 
vaccine efficacy may be affected and disruptions in vaccine access will be 
experienced. 
 
ii) 
Ten (10) districts received 1,739,119 doses of Vaccines worth UGX.17.51Bn 
without undertaking comprehensive needs assessments. The management of 
these districts explained that the estimations are usually done by UNEPI and 
NMS, and the districts have very limited input. This practice increases the risk of 
supply of vaccines that are not needed, overstocking and waste of vaccines 
through expiries. 
 
iii) 
Three (3) districts that received 266,708 doses experienced delays averaging 1-
14 days to receive vaccines. The noted delays were mainly attributed to logistical 
challenges faced by the NMS. These delays increase the risk of Vaccine 
stockouts at the health centres, leading to interruptions in the immunization 
programmes. 
 
iv) 
Twenty-seven (27) districts that received 1,761,507 doses of vaccines worth 
UGX.16.62Bn lacked adequate and appropriate storage facilities for the vaccines. 
The storage spaces were characterised by inadequate pallets, inadequate 
storage space, and a lack of separate storage for expired vaccines, among 
others. The inadequate storage increases the risk of damage to the vaccines and 
the associated financial loss. 
 
The above shortfalls affect the effectiveness of the vaccine distribution programme and 
utilisation and affect the achievement of the Government's vaccination objectives. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer of the Ministry of Health to prioritise routine 
maintenance and replacement of worn-out cold chain equipment in the subsequent 
Ministry budgets and work plans. I also advised NMS to ensure that vaccines are 
delivered in a timelier manner. Further, the Accounting Officers of the districts should 
ensure that vaccine orders are informed by proper needs assessments and that district 
stores are appropriate for the storage of delivered medicines.

The National Teacher Policy 2019, Education Sector Strategic Plan, and competency-
based curriculum agenda aim to improve quality, equity, and relevance of secondary 
education in Uganda, with Uganda National Institute for Teacher Education established 
in July 2024 mandated to coordinate pre-service, in-service, and continuous professional 
development of teachers across six campuses of Shimoni Main, Kaliro, Kabale, Muni, 
Mubende, and Unyama, while Section 3.2 of the National Teacher Policy 2019 requires 
restructuring of teacher education under the Uganda National Institute for Teacher 

 
 
 
 
65 
 
 
 
Education (UNITE) and repurposing of 22 non-core Primary Teachers' Colleges into

availed, leaving funding gap of UGX.72Bn (89%) resulting in recruitment of only 104

2.1.1.8 Delayed repurposing of Non-Core Primary Teachers’ Colleges 
Following the approval of the National Teacher Policy in 2019, the Ministry of Education 
and Sports embarked on implementation of a number of reforms among which was the 
transition of the Primary Teacher Colleges (PTCs) from certificate to Diploma and 
eventually to Degree awarding institutions. This was due to the recommendation by the 
National Teacher Policy to have a Bachelor’s Degree as the minimum qualification for 
teachers at all levels of the Education system by 2031. 
A resolution was passed by Ministry of Education on 21st February 2023 to rationalize 
and repurpose the 46 PTCs. Of the 46, 23 core PTCs were maintained as Teacher 
Training Institutions, while the remaining 23 non-core PTCs were repurposed for other 
educational functions. Shimoni Core PTC was then repurposed into the main campus for 
the National Institute for Teacher Education (UNITE). 
Of the 23 non-core Primary Teachers' Colleges earmarked for repurposing, only four 
(18%) being Erepi PTC, Paidha PTC, Kabwangasi PTC, and Rukungiri PTC were fully 
repurposed and operationalized leaving eighteen (82%) institutions idle or under-utilized 
since 2023. 
 

 
 
 
 
66 
 
 
 
Continued under-utilization of these assets results in avoidable maintenance and 
security costs, delays expansion of secondary, TVET, and health education, and exposes 
infrastructure to deterioration. The delay was attributed to; inadequacies in inter-agency 
coordination, lack of costed implementation plan, funding constraints, and slow legal 
and administrative processes. 
Recommendation 
I advised the Accounting Officer to develop a funded time-bound repurposing plan with 
clearly defined roles, milestones, and monitoring mechanisms to optimize the use of 
existing educational infrastructure and actualise the educational reform in line with the 
National Teacher Policy. 
2.1.1.9 Construction of Stadia and training facilities in Preparation for CHAN and 
AFCON games 
Under the East Africa PAMOJA Bid for Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) and African 
Nations Championship (CHAN) games, the Government of Uganda through the National 
Council of Sports was expected to put in place necessary infrastructure including; one 
stadium with 45,000 sitting capacity, two stadia with 30,000 sitting capacity each, and 
at least five fully functional training grounds, among others. In preparation for the 
tournaments, the government released UGX.941.22Bn for the construction of two stadia 
and one training facility. 
Review of the 2024 CHAN post event report by CAF and physical inspections of the 
facilities,revealed the following status; 
i) 
Hoima City Stadium was completed ahead of schedule. 
ii) 
VIP lounges on first floor of Mandela National Stadium were experiencing lack of 
air conditioning due to under designed AC system failing to accommodate 
increased thermal load caused by large crowds. 
iii) 
Drainage systems at Mandela National Stadium (MNS), Kyambogo University, 
and annexes of MNS were found insufficient to evacuate rainwater efficiently. 
iv) 
Annexes of Mandela National Stadium were facing persistent shortages in 
essential training equipment throughout CHAN 2024, such as; Cones and 
barriers for tactical drills and spatial coordination, Small goalposts for precision 
exercises and goalkeeper training, Rhythmic ladders to support agility and 
footwork routines, Refrigeration units (fridges) for hydration and medical cooling 
needs, Tactical boards for coaching instructions and match preparation, and 
Massage tables critical for recovery and physiotherapy sessions, among others. 
v) 
Maintenance conditions at Mutesa II field being below acceptable standards 
lacking formal pitch maintenance team and appropriate equipment. 

 
 
 
 
67 
 
 
 
vi) 
The construction of Akii-bua stadium and renovations to elevate Mandela 
stadium to CAF/FIFA standards were still expected to be completed by December 
2025. 
vii) 
Mandela National Stadium Annex and Kyambogo University Training Grounds 
was still work in progress, with no clear completion dates. 
viii) 
The contract for renovation of Mandela National stadium had not yet been 
signed. 
The delays were attributed to slow procurement processes and limited funding. 
The Accounting officer explained that with the completion of Hoima Stadium ahead of 
schedule, Akii-bua Stadium was on course to be completed by August 2026 while the 
contract for renovation of Mandela phase two was in the final stages of being 
concluded. 
Recommendation 
I advised management of National Council of Sports to actively seek funding to 
complete the remaining facilities on schedule, enhance project supervision and to 
coordinate closely with CAF as these will ensure compliance and readiness for the 
AFCON games. 
2.1.2 Integrated Transport Infrastructure and Services Program 
2.1.2.1 Outstanding Arrears to Contractors 
During the year under review, I undertook a review of the outstanding arrears to 
contractors for the on-going road projects implemented under the Ministry of Works and 
Transport and the former Uganda National Roads Authority (UNRA). 
Based on my verification procedures I noted that as of 30th June 2025, the total 
outstanding arrears for unpaid completed works on road projects stood at 
UGX.500.347Bn. Included in this balance is UGX.73.991Bn that relates to interest on 
delayed settlement of outstanding certificates. The existence of the outstanding arrears 
was attributed to inadequate budget provisions and non-release of funds for settlement 
for certified works. 
The failure to settle these arrears exposes government to avoidable costs in the form of 
penalties/interest on delayed payments and the risk of litigation. In addition, delayed 
settlement of arrears leads to suspension of road works by the contractors which leads 
to deterioration of already completed works. 
Recommendation 
I advised the Accounting Officer to engage the PSST to prioritise settlement of these 
obligations. 
 

 
 
 
 
68 
 
 
 
 
2.1.2.2 Delays of Works on Road Projects 
 
I reviewed a sample of 67 road projects with a total contract value of UGX.10.625Tn, 
USD.400,043,710 and JPY 5,519,324,131 to assess the progress of works against the 
work programme. The following was observed; 
 
i) 
28 projects worth UGX.3.554Tn experienced significant delays ranging from six 
months to over three (3) years. 
ii) 
13 road projects had been abandoned, or works had been suspended by the 
contractors and at the time of writing my reports. Examples of these roads 
include; Mityana – Mubende- Kyejojo road, Masindi-Biiso-Kabaale-Kiziranfumbi 
and Hohwa-Nyairongo-Kyarushesha-Butole, road, Busega - Mpigi Expressway, 
Najjanakumbi – Busabala Road, Munyonyo Spur Interchange and Service roads, 
Ntungamo-Kabale-Katuna Road, Olwiyo – Pakwach road among others. 
 
The delays were mainly due to the lack of capacity by the contractors, delayed 
payments for completed works which affected the cash flows of the contractors, delays 
in granting the Right-of-Way, and delayed compensation of Project Affected Persons 
(PAPs). The delays had resulted in government paying at least USD.17,695,527.17 in 
commitment charges since the delays in works also affect uptake of loans by 
government. The delays of works also resulted in traffic inconveniences, loss of project 
time, and increased project costs. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer Ministry of Works and Transport (MoWT) to strengthen 
coordination with all responsible stakeholders especially the Parliament and MoFPED, to 
appropriate and provide adequate funds for the road projects. 
 
2.1.2.3 Compensation of Project Affected Persons for Government Projects 
 
I reviewed the status of land compensations for selected government projects and 
noted that there were delays in compensation of PAPs which delayed acquisition of 
Right of Way. The cases where this was noted are summarized below. 
 
i) 
A total of 19,082 PAPs valued at UGX.848.46Bn were assessed for four (4) 
construction projects namely Bukasa Port, SGR project, Tororo- Gulu Metre 
Gauge and Gulu Logistics Hub project. As at 30th June 2025, 11,315 (59%) PAPs 
valued at UGX.315.227Bn had been paid off leaving a balance of 7,767 (41%) 
PAPs worth UGX.533.23Bn as unpaid. 
ii) 
I also observed that 37,595 PAPs were assessed at a value of UGX.1,163Bn for 
seven (7) donor funded projects. As at 30th June 2025, a total 30,998 (82%) 
PAPs valued at UGX.842.446Bn had been paid. The balance of 6,597 (18%) 
PAPs valued at UGX.320.139Bn had not been compensated. 

 
 
 
 
69 
 
 
 
iii) 
In addition to delayed compensation of PAPs, I also noted that out of 1,908.9 
acres acquired for the SGR project, a total of 506.9 acres remained without 
titles. 
iv) 
I further observed that 8,263 land titles were secured from PAPs for projects 
implemented under the former UNRA. Out of these, 4,055 (49%) titles were yet 
to be subdivided to acquire the land titles and returned to the owners (PAPs). 
 
The delay in compensation of PAPs was attributed to the inadequate budgets while the 
delay in titling of acquired land was mainly due to lengthy and bureaucratic land 
expropriation and titling processes involving multiple MDAs. 
 
Consequently, the projects are exposed to encroachment and land disputes, re-
occupation of the land by already compensated PAPs, escalating compensation costs, 
delays in implementation, and possible financial loss to Government. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer of MoWT to engage MoFPED to ensure timely release of 
compensation funds. I further advised the Accounting Officer to strengthen coordination 
with all responsible MDAs to fast-track land titling, evacuate re-occupying PAPs, and 
promptly return remaining titles to rightful owners. 
 
2.1.2.4 Accumulation of Government Debtors owed to Uganda Civil Aviation 
Authority 
 
As at 30th June 2025, Government entities owed the Uganda Civil Aviation Authority 
(UCAA) a total of UGX.152.538Bn, representing 77% of the total trade debtors and 
receivables. These funds related to unpaid for services, security, navigation services and 
rent. The accumulation of long-outstanding Government debtors constrains UCAA’s cash 
flows and exposes the Authority to a heightened risk of revenue loss and impaired 
service delivery. 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer of UCAA to strengthen follow-up measures on 
Government debtors through inter-agency coordination with the supervising Ministries 
and MoFPED to ensure timely recovery of outstanding Government debts. 
 
2.1.2.5 Road Maintenance Grant 
 
Government allocated a Road Maintenance Development Grant of UGX.1Bn to each of 
the 176 Local Governments (LGs), which included; 135 districts, 10 cities, and 31 
Municipal Councils, resulting into a total of UGX.176Bn being transferred to LGs in the 
FY 2024/25. The grant is specifically designed to support road maintenance within these 
LGs. 
 
During my audit of the FY 2024/25, I designed audit procedures to assess the grant 
implementation in LGs, and below are my summary findings; 
 
 

 
 
 
 
70 
 
 
 
2.1.2.6 Road Inventory and Condition Surveys 
 
In accordance with Section 2.1 of the MoWT Road Maintenance Grant Implementation 
Guidelines FY 2024/25, all entities are required to prepare and maintain road inventory 
and condition surveys along with cost estimates. These reports must include, but are 
not limited to, the following information; 
 
i) 
Size and extent of road asset 
ii) 
Locations of culverts, bridges, drifts, road furniture and other key assets on the 
road network. 
iii) 
Size or scope of infrastructure to be maintained. 
iv) 
Functional hierarchy of roads. 
v) 
Volume of traffic. 
I noted that out of 148 LGs, 5 LGs did not have road inventory and condition surveys 
along with cost estimates that detailed the required information. However, 22 LGs had 
databases of roads which described; the size and extent of road assets, but did not have 
the locations of culverts, bridges, drifts, road furniture and other key assets on the road 
network, size or scope of infrastructure to be maintained, functional hierarchy of roads, 
and volume of traffic required by the roads inventory and surveys report. 
 
The absence of detailed road inventory and condition survey data hindered the efficient 
allocation of resources, accurate cost estimation, and appropriate prioritization of road 
maintenance activities. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to limited funding, lack of assessment tools such 
as GPS devices and inadequate staff capacity. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should liaise with MoWT and MoFPED to provide 
technical and financial support to develop comprehensive road inventory and condition 
surveys. 
 
2.1.2.7 Status of LG Road Equipment 
 
Review of the LGs’ status of road equipment in 148 LGs revealed that; 
 
i) 
A total of 19 LGs did not have road equipment units. 
ii) 
A total of 137 LGs had inadequate road equipment units; these included critical 
road equipment such as excavators, motor graders, vibro rollers, dump trucks, 
bulldozers, chain loaders and wheel loaders among others. 
iii) 
A total of 119 LGs had non-functional equipment to undertake road works during 
the financial year. 
 
Limited availability of the road equipment delays implementation of road works, thus 
affects service delivery. 
 

 
 
 
 
71 
 
 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to insufficient funding of the operations of the 
road equipment units, as well as delays in securing additional machinery from the 
Ministry of Works and Transport (MoWT). 
 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of LGs should liaise with MoFPED to secure funding for 
additional machinery to ensure effective and sustainable road maintenance operations. 
 
2.1.2.8 Inspection of Implemented Road Maintenance Works 
 
Field inspection of the implemented road maintenance works in 148 LGs carried out in 
the period between October and December 2025 revealed that; 
 
i) 
A total of 239 roads measuring 1,275 kms in 66 LGs were incomplete at the time 
of audit inspections. 
ii) 
A total of 76 LGs had 228 roads with unsatisfactory works, such as; broken 
culverts, poor drainage, and uneven carriage ways with water ponding among 
others. 
 
This affected timely service delivery. 
 
The Accounting officers explained that maintenance of road works were affected by 
limited funding for road maintenance works, heavy rains, inadequate road construction 
equipment and un-regulated carriage load control on the LG roads. 
 
Recommendations 
 
i) 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should liaise with MoWT and MoFPED to 
provide technical and financial support to develop comprehensive road inventory 
and condition surveys. 
ii) 
The Accounting Officers of LGs should liaise with MoFPED to secure funding for 
additional machinery to ensure effective and sustainable road maintenance 
operations. 
iii) 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should ensure district engineers complete all 
unfinished road works, and all defects on roads should be rectified. 
iv) 
The Ministry of Works and Transport should develop comprehensive guidelines 
on the carriage load control on the LG roads. 
 
2.1.3 Mineral Development Programme 
2.1.3.1 Unlicensed Mineral Dealers 
 
According to section 140(1) of the Mining and Minerals Act, Cap 159, a person shall not 
buy or sell, as either principal or agent, any minerals or tailings unless he or she is a 
licensed mineral dealer. This is meant to ensure accountability and traceability of 
mineral transactions, which helps prevent illegal mining, theft, and smuggling. It also 

 
 
 
 
72 
 
 
 
enables the government to collect the correct taxes, royalties, and fees and reduce 
revenue loss. 
 
A review of the Non-Tax Revenue (NTR) schedule from URA and the Mining Cadaster 
Register revealed that seventeen (17) traders engaged in the buying and selling of 
minerals without mineral rights or a valid mineral dealer’s license. 
Unlicensed mineral operations led to loss of government revenue, undermined 
regulatory control over mineral transactions, and increased the risk of illegal mining and 
mineral smuggling. 
 
Management explained that, in liaison with Police Mineral Protection Unit, the Ministry 
has so far closed over 30 outlets of illegal mineral dealers in Kampala and will continue 
to follow and close up those illegal dealers operations. The Ministry will continue to 
undertake sensitization of URA officials in mineral related businesses and is advanced 
stages of joining the URA single window system where all parties can access Mineral 
transactions. In addition, the Ministry is establishing mineral markets and buying centers 
to formalize and regulate mineral trade in the country. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to enhance monitoring of mining and mineral 
operations and ensure timely collaboration with URA to detect unlicensed mineral 
trading thus improving regulatory oversight. 
 
 
2.1.3.2 Non-Functionality of Beneficiation Centers 
 
Beneficiation centers facilitate the processing of raw minerals locally and enable 
communities access processing equipment for better mineral recovery allowing them to 
earn more from value-added products rather than exporting low-value raw ores. 
I noted that the ministry constructed two beneficiation centers in Ntungamo and Fort 
portal in 2023. However, the essential beneficiation equipment had not been procured 
and installed. 
 
As a result, the centers remain non-functional and cannot support mineral value-
addition initiatives as intended. 
 
Management indicated that the recruitment process of staff for Beneficiation centers has 
been completed, however, the procurement process for the Equipment was completed 
and delivery and installation is expected in March 2026. The Ministry is committed to the 
operationalization of the beneficiation centers. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to fast track the installation of the beneficiation 
equipment to enable the achievement of the intended service delivery. 
 

 
 
 
 
73 
 
 
 
2.1.3.3 Limited Guidance on Mineral Value Addition 
 
Section 3 of the Mining and Minerals Act, Cap 159, outlines the purpose of the Act, 
which includes promoting and facilitating mineral trade, marketing systems, and the 
utilization of mineral products, as well as guiding public private partnerships in mining, 
value addition, and marketing. Further, Sections 127(b) and 130(b) require mineral 
commodities to be exported or imported only at purity levels prescribed by regulations. 
These provisions promote structured and transparent mineral trade, encourage domestic 
value addition through prescribed export purity levels, enhance revenue mobilization, 
attract private investments and support industrial growth ensuring that the country 
derives maximum economic benefit from its mineral resources. 
 
I established that although regulations prescribing purity levels exist for gold, sponge 
iron, and vermiculite, the majority of mineral commodities lack guidance on the 
allowable purity levels required before export. Further, the Ministry has not conducted 
comprehensive assessments to determine the extent to which each mineral can be 
beneficiated or value-added domestically. 
 
Notably, critical minerals such as; tungsten and tantalum lack regulatory purity 
thresholds, yet URA export data shows that these minerals were exported in the period 
under review. This indicates ongoing mining activities in the absence of clear value-
addition requirements. 
 
The absence of clear guidance on mineral value-addition limits the Ministry’s ability to 
enforce value-addition provisions, allows continued export of minimally processed 
minerals, promotes illegal trading, reduces potential government revenue, and 
undermines opportunities for domestic industrial development in the mining sector. 
 
Management explained that the Ministry through the programme has launched a 
consultant to conduct a study on Mineral Value Chain Analysis (MVCA) starting with at 
least five critical minerals. This study will provide a comprehensive assessment to 
determine the extent to which each mineral commodity can be beneficiated in-country, 
which will enhance government’s policy direction on mineral value-addition 
requirements. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to ensure timely completion of the Mineral Value Chain 
Analysis (MVCA) study and operationalize its findings by issuing mineral specific 
beneficiation requirements and putting in place mechanisms to monitor compliance. 
 
2.1.3.4 Outstanding Mineral Sharing Deposits 
 
Section 180 (4) the Mining and Minerals Act, Cap 159, states that royalties shall be 
shared by the Government, Local Governments, sub county or Town Council and owners 
or lawful occupiers of land subject to mineral rights in a ratio of 70%, 15%, 10% and 
5%, respectively. 
 

 
 
 
 
74 
 
 
 
I noted that the Ministry received UGX.5.862Bn into the Mineral Royalties sharing fund 
account in addition to the opening balance of UGX.3.913Bn from the previous period. 
However, UGX.8.33Bn (85%) was paid out leaving an outstanding balance of 
UGX.1.443Bn. Under remittance of the mineral deposits due to the beneficiaries 
undermines the intention of fair distribution of economic benefits arising from mining 
activities among stakeholders and poses the risk of conflict over resource utilization. 
Management explained that whereas the Ministry resolved and disbursed payments that 
were due to Kamwenge and Kitagwenda districts. 
The outstanding deposits for the two district local governments is being processed for 
disbursement while those due to unknown beneficiaries will be disbursed after 
establishment of the true beneficiaries. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to identify bottlenecks leading to non-payment, and 
have them resolved on a case-by-case basis to enable payment of the outstanding 
royalties to the intended beneficiaries. 
 
 
2.1.3.5 Non-payment of Mineral royalties 
 
Section 187(1) of the Minerals Act, Cap. 159 provides that assessed mineral royalties 
shall be due and payable within thirty (30) days from the date of assessment. 
 
A review of mineral royalty records in the Mine Cadaster revealed that payment of 
assessed royalties was not made within the prescribed thirty-day period. Consequently, 
royalty revenues amounting to UGX.2.82Bn remained outstanding beyond the statutory 
timeline. 
 
The delay in remitting mineral royalties denies Government timely revenue required to 
support service delivery. 
 
Failure to pay mineral royalties within the statutory 30-day period leads to delayed 
collection of government revenue, undermines budget execution and indicates 
ineffective enforcement of statutory obligations. 
 
Management explained that the Ministry, routinely serve notices of Non-compliance to 
any breach of the Mining and Minerals Act, Cap 159, which explicitly require the 
concerned licensees to settle all outstanding amounts, which include any payments for 
overdue royalties. The Ministry will continue to engage Attorney General’s Office and 
other agencies such as URA to collect the outstanding revenue. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to strengthen enforcement of the 30-day royalty 
payment requirement by issuing timely reminders, applying penalties for late payment, 
and closely monitoring compliance through the Cadaster system. 
 

 
 
 
 
75 
 
 
 
2.1.4 Sustainable Development of Petroleum Resources 
2.1.4.1 Progress in Oil development activities 
 
Section 10(1) of the Petroleum (Exploration, Development and Production) Act, Cap 
161, indicates that one of the roles of the PAU is to monitor and regulate exploration, 
development and Production of petroleum in Uganda. The Government current target of 
first oil is mid-2026 and there are various key milestones necessary for the realization of 
this aspiration which include; readiness of Kingfisher development field, Tilenga 
development field and East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP). Government has 
undertaken various measures to support the achievement of these milestones. 
 
A review of the Authority’s monitoring reports for June 2025 revealed that the overall 
completion rates for the projects was 57.0% for Tilenga against target of 73.18%, 
69.62% for Kingfisher against target of 73.18% and 62.5% for the East African Crude 
Oil Pipeline against planned target of 72.0%. 
 
I further noted, the National Oil Spill Response and Monitoring Infrastructure Project 
aimed at strengthening Uganda’s preparedness and response capacity to oil spill 
emergencies has not progressed due to inadequate funding. Out of the project 
estimated cost of UGX.59.90Bn, only UGX.1.20Bn was released over the project period 
of FY2022/23 to FY2024/25. 
 
Failure to achieve established project milestones and critical path deliverables poses 
significant schedule risks to the 2026 First Oil target and the absence of a functional 
emergency response capability poses unmitigated environmental and safety risks ahead 
of First Oil. 
 
Management indicated that measures such as pre-commissioning tests , increased work 
shift and establishment of an Inter-ministerial committee ,have been put in place to fast 
track the project implementation. As of November 2025 the status of the progress has 
improved and by November 2025, overall completion rates for the projects were 60% 
for Tilenga, 74% for Kingfisher (all wells necessary for first oil have been drilled) and 
75% for the East African Crude Oil Pipeline. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that the Authority will continue to engage MEMD and 
MoFPED on the issue of funding for the National Oil Spill response and monitoring 
infrastructure project-1780. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to strengthen coordination with MEMD, MoFPED, and 
project licensees to closely monitor and fast-track delivery of critical path milestones for 
Tilenga, Kingfisher, and EACOP to safeguard the First Oil target, and to urgently secure 
adequate funding and implementation timelines for the National Oil Spill Response and 
Monitoring Infrastructure to ensure operational readiness and mitigate environmental 
and safety risks ahead of First Oil. 
 

 
 
 
 
76 
 
 
 
2.1.4.2 Inadequate In country product handling and storage Infrastructure 
 
Objective 3 of the Petroleum Supplies Act, Cap 163, mandates that the Uganda National 
Oil Company Limited (UNOC) import all petroleum products destined for the Ugandan 
market to ensure security of supply. However, some issues undermine this objective. 
 
The Company’s storage capacity at Jinja Storage Terminal (JST) is limited to 30 million 
litres, while the country’s average daily petroleum demand is approximately 6.5 million 
litres. 
UNOC has converted the JST facilities into a commercial hub to supply other marketing 
companies, with trade stocks averaging 5.2 to 7.5 million litres per month, essentially 
matching daily national consumption. This leaves no room for strategic buffer stocks. 
 
The limited storage capacity exposes the country to high risk from both external supply 
shocks and internal operational disruptions, potentially threatening national energy 
security. 
 
Management explained that UNOC is planning to construct an additional storage tank for 
PMS to bring the total capacity of the terminal to 40 million litres, which will cover only 
five days’ stock of the country’s demand. Plans are also under way to construct Kampala 
Storage Terminal (KST), with storage capacity of 240 million litres. This will bring the 
combined storage between JST and KST to 280 million litres sufficient to cover up to 40 
days’ worth of the country’s daily consumption. The only challenge that will remain will 
be on how to finance the stockholding for the 40 days estimated at UGX.1.3Tn. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to fast track the development of additional storage 
facilities and to continue engaging the relevant stakeholders to provide funding for the 
national strategic reserves. 
 
2.1.4.3 Restrictions on vessel Size for importation of PMS 
 
Objective 3 of the Petroleum Supplies Act, Cap 163, is to facilitate the Uganda National 
Oil Company Limited to import all Petroleum Products, destined for the Ugandan market 
to guarantee security of supply of Petroleum Products in the country. 
 
From the review of management reports, I noted that Uganda faced restrictions on the 
delivery vessels sizes for PMS. These were capped at 58,000MT with a maximum 5% 
tolerance. 
 
Whereas UNOC would typically prefer larger vessels to meet market demand efficiently 
and enhance supply security. This restriction constrains the Company’s ability to 
leverage the operational and economic advantages of larger shipments. 
 
Management explained that the Company continues to engage the relevant stakeholders 
to lift vessel capacity restrictions especially for PMS deliveries and as a result, in 
November 2025, UNOC was allowed to deliver an additional 25,000 MT Vessel of PMS. 

 
 
 
 
77 
 
 
 
 
In addition, there are interventions by the Kenyan counter part stakeholders to allow 
UNOC to bring in the preferred vessel size of 85,000 MT from the current 58,000 MT 
which include; increasing the pumping rates from Mombasa to Nairobi and Western 
Kenya depots which will improve evacuation of fuel from Mombasa terminals; and 
enhancing the capacity of PMS storage in Western Kenya. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to continue engaging the relevant stakeholders to 
negotiate for lifting of the vessel size restrictions and to explore alternative supply 
routes in order to enhance supply security and operational flexibility. 
 
 
2.1.5 Sustainable Energy Development Programme 
2.1.5.1 Uptake of available Generation Capacity 
 
In abid to achieve the Vision 2040 target of increasing Uganda’s generation capacity to 
52,481Mw by 2040. In addition to Nalubaale-Kiira, Government constructed Karuma 
600MW and Isimba 183MW using the on-lent loan from EXIM Bank of China of 
USD.1,398,516,759 and USD.567,738,990.96 respectively. 
A review of the quarterly operations and maintenance reports revealed that Nalubaale-
Kiira power plant dispatched 778.8GWh (112%) against declared capacity of 
695.6GWh, Isimba HPP had a Net energy output 1,046.41GWh(72%) against Declared 
available capacity of 1,451.06GWh and Karuma HHP had a net energy output of 
808.27GWh(30%) against Declared available capacity of 2,652GWh. 
 
Further analysis indicates that in the first year of operation, Karuma HPP operated at an 
average of 70MWh and 116MWh in the second year which are below the minimum 
required dispatch of 300MW/h to enable the identification and addressing of the latent 
defects in generating units and associated plant structures, during the defects liability 
period. In addition, the company only realized UGX.148.16Bn (46.8%) out of the total 
expected revenue of UGX.316.42Bn. 
 
In the circumstances the company might not meet the loan and interest repayment 
terms/condition as well as operational and maintenance costs and ably identify defects 
before the expiry of the Defects liability period. 
 
Management attributed the low dispatch to inadequate demand for electricity and 
prioritization of low cost generating plants and private producers who are on capacity 
charge. UEGCL has engaged the regulator (ERA) and UETCL to allow for other players to 
buy the power from UEGCL and improvement of the export infrastructure respectively. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer of UEGCL to continue engagements with MEMD, ERA, 
UETCL and other relevant stakeholders to device mechanisms of increasing demand 
such as; 

 
 
 
 
78 
 
 
 
 
i) 
Promoting establishment of industrial parks and the corresponding connections. 
ii) 
Enhancing cross boarder power trade through the East African Power pool 
arrangement. 
iii) 
Expedite the electricity connections under the Electricity Access Scale Up Project. 
 
2.1.5.2 Electricity Transmission 
 
Instruction 3.9.5 of the Treasury Instructions, 2017, requires budget estimates to be 
based on pre-determined objectives and outputs as provided in the strategic plans of 
the entity. Additionally, Instruction 16.9.1 mandates that the Accounting Officer prepare 
an annual budget for asset maintenance and systematically assess the performance of 
NCAs for functionality, utilization, and physical and financial performance. 
I noted the following; 
 
i) 
Multiple Independent Power Producers (IPPs) were unable to fully evacuate 
power during the period due to grid interruption events attributed to line faults, 
equipment failures, outages of transformers, vandalism incidents, SCADA 
limitations, and other transmission constraints. This resulted into deemed energy 
costs with a total of UGX.26.94Bn recognized as deemed energy obligations in 
the 4 quarters of the financial year. The persistence of these interruptions 
indicates ineffective utilization and reliability of key transmission assets, leading 
to avoidable financial obligations and increased operational costs. 
 
ii) 
I noted major transformers that have remained idle and out of service for 
extended periods without full restoration or replacement as shown in the table 
below;

losses and ensure optimal utilization of key transmission assets. 
 
2.1.5.3 Electricity Distribution 
 
Following the expiry of UMEME’s concession on 31st March 2025, UEDCL assumed 
responsibility for a substantially expanded electricity distribution. By 30th June 2025, 
UEDCL’s asset base had grown from UGX.113Bn to UGX.2Tn, customers from 165,937 
to 2.2Mn, staff from 480 to 2,489, and annual revenue from UGX.111Bn to UGX.661Bn, 
marking a significant operational and institutional scale-up. 
 
An assessment of UEDCL’s post-transition performance revealed service delivery 
challenges particularly in; network reliability, outage management, customer 
responsiveness, complaint resolution, and metering services. 
 
Management attributed the underperformance largely to a deteriorated network arising 
from prolonged underinvestment during the latter years of the concession, regulatory 
budget cuts, vandalism, electricity theft, procurement bottlenecks and staffing 
constraints. 
 

 
 
 
 
80 
 
 
 
Management further indicated that corrective interventions are being implemented and 
they include; the rollout of a loss-reduction strategy coined as the “Wetereze” campaign 
targeting commercial losses, enhanced field monitoring, and community enforcement 
activities as well as development of a five-year distribution network rehabilitation and 
investment plan , deployment of digital customer engagement platforms such as the 
“Social Media Integration and Digital Engagement Platform” and securing PPDA 
accreditation to ease procurement delays . In the meantime 39,996(50%) meters have 
been replaced since April 2025 against a backlog of 79,596 faulty meters. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to implement a fully costed medium to long-term 
network rehabilitation plan, prioritize critical capacity upgrades particularly transformers 
and feeders in high-load areas, strengthen controls against vandalism and theft, and 
fully operationalize and leverage on procurement reforms to sustainably improve service 
delivery. 
 
2.1.6 Agro-Industrialisation Programme 
2.1.6.1 Delays to acquire land and establish a crude palm oil processing mill 
 
Government of Uganda, through the National Oil Palm Project is expected to acquire, 
compensate and hand over the 5,000 ha of land to Oil Palm Buvuma Limited (OPBL). 
The land was expected to have been acquired and handed over by Financial Year 
2019/2020. 
 
In addition, OPBL was expected to construct a crude palm oil processing mill in Financial 
Year 2024/2025 to process fresh oil palm fruit harvested by farmers. 
 
I observed that; 
 
i) 
There was significant delay in compensating landowners by up to 17 months 
after the date of valuation, while in other cases land is yet to be compensated. 
Delayed valuation and compensation of PAPs may lead to increased 
compensation costs as a result of increase in the value of land over time. 
ii) 
By the end of the financial year 2024/2025, OPBL was yet to possess 629ha of 
land. Failure by government to provide the required acreage of land to OPBL 
may result in delays to fully establish the nucleus estate and attain the project 
objectives. 
iii) 
Out of the 4,371 ha that had been acquired and handed over, only 2,650.43ha 
had been cultivated. The failure by OPBL to cultivate the full acreage so far in 
their possession implies that the company may not have the capacity to fully 
cultivate the required land and establish the nucleus estate. 
iv) 
The crude palm oil processing mill was yet to be established by OPBL. Without a 
crude palm oil processing mill, farmers close to the nucleus estate may continue 
incurring costs of transporting fresh oil palm fruit from their gardens to 
Kalangala District for processing. 
v) 
The construction of crude palm oil processing mill was postponed by the investor 
from the earlier planned financial year 2024/2025 to the year 2027 with claims 

 
 
 
 
81 
 
 
 
that it was not a viable investment when still operating the nucleus plantation 
below 5,000 hectares. 
 
 
Recommendations 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer; 
 
i) 
To expedite the compensation of the project affected persons using the 
supplementary funds and ensure that the land acquired is put to immediate use 
for the project activities. 
ii) 
Once the target acreage has been achieved, OPBL should promptly establish the 
crude palm oil processing mill to enable farmers process their harvested fruit 
within Buvuma. 
iii) 
To establish the reasons why OPBL has failed to fully cultivate the land so far 
paid for and handed over. 
 
2.1.6.2 Management of Agricultural Mechanisation Centres 
 
The Ministry has set up five (5) regional mechanisation centres in Buwama, Sanga, 
Kiryandongo, Agwata, and Bunghokho in addition to the National Mechanisation Referral 
Mechanisation Centre in Namalere to lease heavy farm equipment to farmers in the 
regions to increase their farm productivity, reduce reliance on labor, and improve 
efficiency in agricultural production. 
 
I reviewed the management of the regional mechanisation centres and noted the 
following; 
 
i) 
Lack of standard operating procedures/Guidelines; I noted that there 
were no operational guidelines to provide a framework for effective management 
and accountability for the mechanisation centres. As a result, the Ministry lacks 
guidance on the target groups, objectives of the interventions, the constitution 
of management committees and reporting among others. 
ii) 
Inadequacies in the management of the hiring of equipment to 
farmers; The mechanisms in place to account for equipment usage by farmers 
were inadequate, as there was no registers of requests for hire of equipment at 
each centre, or equipment logs to account for machine hours and services it has 
delivered. 
iii) 
Management of hired equipment; MAAIF lacks a standardised assessment 
criteria for identifying farmer beneficiaries to hire out equipment to. When 
equipment develops mechanical issues while hired out, there are no incident 
management reports showing the repair requirements and no logs showing the 
repair history of the equipment. 
iv) 
Revenue collection; There is no record of non-tax revenue generated from the 
hire of the equipment as no revenues could be traced to URA’s revenue 
collection records. 
v) 
Weaknesses observed at the Mechanisation centres; I observed that all 
the six (6) centres did not maintain sufficient records of their operations. Some 

 
 
 
 
82 
 
 
 
of the centres did not have proper offices from which the staff can operate, and 
the offices lacked computers and furniture. They were not equipped with repair 
workshops and equipment service bays. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that the Ministry is developing a mechanisation policy 
to guide the management of the centres. Further, management has engaged MoFPED to 
increase the budgetary allocation to support the mechanisation centres to enable their 
efficient operation. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to fast-track the development and approval of a 
mechanisation policy to streamline the management of the mechanisation centres. In 
addition, I advised the Accounting Officer to develop mechanisms to enhance the 
tracking of the hiring, deployment, use and maintenance of the mechanisation 
equipment.

The Tax Appeals Tribunal is facing a rapidly growing and high-value backlog of tax

awareness of its mandate. The average resolution time was 10 months, as summarized

2.1.8 Governance and Security Programme 
2.1.8.1 Review of the operations in the DNA Central Laboratory 
 
The Directorate of Government Analytical Laboratory (DGAL) was established to provide 
scientific and forensic analytical services to support the administration of justice. During 
the last three (3) years, the demand for DNA paternity testing has increased while there 
has been a trend towards the reliance on forensic science to support investigations. I 
analysed the DNA services to assess how they are delivered, managed and reported on 
and observed the following; 
 
i) 
DGAL identified the establishment of a National Forensic DNA database as a 
flagship initiative in their Strategic Plan (2020/21–2024/25). However, by the 
end of FY 2024/25, DGAL had not established a National Forensic DNA Database 
and the DNA Information System. 
ii) 
DGAL’s DNA division suffers from insufficient laboratory workspace. The limited 
space allows only one (1) analyst to perform the required procedures at a time, 
as the available space does not allow multiple analysts to work concurrently on 
similar procedures. This constraint is leading to substantial delays in case 
processing. 
 
iii) 
In the last five (5) years, the DNA backlog have remained high. Year-end 
backlogs increased from 786 cases in FY 2020/21 to 923 cases in FY 2024/25, 
representing a 17% growth over the five (5) years. 
 
iv) 
The DNA laboratory has four (4) genetic analysers for processing DNA samples. 
However, one analyser was obsolete; another, designated for wildlife DNA 
analysis, was functional but rarely used; a third was frequently used but 
operated below capacity; and the fourth, installed in January 2025, had not yet 
been put to use, eight (8) months after procurement. 
 
The Accounting Officer attributed the challenges to funding gaps. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to liaise with the relevant stakeholders, including 
MoFPED and MIA to mobilise resources and improve the operations of DNA laboratories. 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
84 
 
 
 
2.1.8.2 Review of the operations in the central and regional laboratories 
 
DGAL operates a central and four (4) regional laboratories in Mbale, Gulu, Moroto and 
Mbarara. I assessed the operations of the regional laboratories and observed the 
following; 
 
i) 
The four (4) laboratories are not efficiently and effectively utilised. Only the Gulu 
Regional Laboratory was partially performing limited forensic biology analyses. 
The Mbale and Mbarara laboratories functioned only as exhibit collection and 
sub-sampling centres, while the Moroto laboratory remained non-operational. 
 
ii) 
The four (4) regional laboratories handled 503 cases, representing 8% of DGAL’s 
total workload of 6,109 cases. Gulu accounted for 22% (111 cases) while Mbale 
and Mbarara accounted for the remaining 78% (392 cases) of the total regional 
workload. 
 
iii) 
The headquarters laboratory conducted quarterly outreach visits to regional 
laboratories to collect exhibits and samples for analysis in Kampala. However, 
the limited frequency of these visits caused delayed case transfers and 
turnaround times exceeding the 30-day benchmark set in DGAL’s Strategic Plan. 
 
iv) 
The approved DGAL staff structure provides for 60 positions across the four (4) 
regional laboratories. As of 30th June 2025, only 28 positions had been filled, 
leaving a staffing gap of 32 positions (53%) including two (2) Assistant 
Commissioner roles responsible for overseeing the regional laboratories. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to adopt a phased operationalization strategy for 
regional laboratories, prioritizing the recruitment of critical technical and managerial 
staff in line with the available funding. In the meantime, I advised management to 
review and increase the frequency of outreach visits to regional laboratories to ensure 
timely transfer of samples and exhibits. 
 
 
2.1.8.3 Review of the online business registration by URSB 
 
URSB’s Online Business Registration System (OBRS) was developed to digitalise business 
registration and improve service delivery. Over three (3) years, URSB has invested 
UGX.6.49Bn to design, develop, and maintain the OBRS. The system was launched in 
December 2022. 
 
I reviewed the system and observed the following; 
 
i) 
I noted significant delays in the registration of company names. A review of four 
(4) services offered through the OBRS i.e. company name reservation, business 
name amendments, business name registration, and data updates showed that 
the Bureau did not consistently meet the approved turnaround times. 

 
 
 
 
85 
 
 
 
 
ii) 
I observed regular, recurring OBRS system downtime. Incident logs showed 
multiple system outages between August 2023 and September 2025 due to 
network failures, storage exhaustion, inadequate power backup, and human 
error. These outages prevented users from processing business registration 
applications. 
 
iii) 
I noted that historical business registration records provided to third parties 
through the OBRS contained unredacted personal information, including full 
dates of births of directors, proprietors, or subscribers. 
iv) 
Controls to prevent fraudulent registrations were inadequate. For instance, 
fraudulent entries such as forged signatures and unauthorized filings were only 
addressed when detected or reported. The system is unable to authenticate 
digital signatures or confirm that approvals are submitted by legitimate owners 
of companies. 
 
v) 
Although URSB began the ISO 9001:2015 certification process in August 2018 
and committed to complete certification by 30th June 2024, the Bureau had not 
obtained the certification by the end of FY 2024/25, resulting in a delay of one 
(1) year. 
 
vi) 
The Bureau did not maintain a register of customer complaints for the OBRS, 
including details of complaint types, resolution timelines, or a mechanism for 
clients to track resolution outcomes. As a result, URSB cannot identify recurring 
issues, measure effectiveness in reducing repeat complaints, or assess timeliness 
of resolution of client complaints. 
 
Recommendations 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to; 
 
i) 
Strengthen service availability and limit system downtime by monitoring storage, 
power, and network performance, and establishing redundancy for critical 
servers. 
ii) 
Implement data minimization and redaction controls for records shared with 
third parties. 
iii) 
Benchmark with other government institutions on safeguarding e-signatures and 
consider integrating digital signature authentication into OBRS. 
iv) 
Prioritise the full implementation of ISO 9001:2015 QMS requirements, including 
a comprehensive customer complaints management system. 
 
2.1.8.4 Challenges in implementation of Security Interest in Movable Property Act 
 
Government introduced the Security Interest in Movable Property Act, Cap. 293 in 2019, 
to promote the use of movable assets as collateral for accessing credit to increase 
access to credit for Ugandans particularly women, youth, and low-income earners who 
do not own registered land, which is the preferred collateral for most lenders. 
 

 
 
 
 
86 
 
 
 
To support the initiative, URSB developed the Security Interest in Movable Property 
Registry System (SIMPRS) at a cost of UGX.1.2Bn to automate registration of security 
interests by licensed lenders, including SACCOs, Micro Finance Institutions, commercial 
banks, community-based organisations, and other authorised lenders. 
 
SIMPRS facilitates secured creditors and lenders to register their security interests in 
movable assets such as livestock, farm produce, motor vehicles, machinery, intellectual 
property, electronics, and household furniture while providing the public with notice of 
the existence of these interests. Once a lender registers a security interest, the borrower 
retains the interest until the debt is fully repaid. 
 
A review of the SIMPRS system revealed the following implementation challenges; 
 
i) 
Most movable assets eligible for registration under the Act, such as livestock, ICT 
equipment, household goods, and agricultural produce and tools lack unique 
identifiers making it difficult for lenders to reliably verify legal ownership, 
existence, or traceability of collateral. 
 
ii) 
The Ministry of Trade has no central registry for registering movable equipment 
entering Uganda’s borders, making assets identification and traceability difficult 
and increasing the likelihood that borrowers may use the same asset to secure 
credit from several lenders. 
 
iii) 
Although agricultural warehouse receipts have unique identifiers, URSB cannot 
authenticate them because the Warehouse Receipt System under the Ministry of 
Trade is not integrated with SIMPRS. As a result, lenders cannot verify the 
validity or value of pledged warehouse-stored commodities. 
iv) 
Only licensed lenders are allowed to register interest on the system however, 
due to the absence of integration with Uganda Microfinance Regulatory 
Authority, URSB cannot verify whether a user has an active or expired license in 
real time, exposing SIMPRS to misuse by unlicensed or deregistered lenders. 
 
v) 
SIMPRS has no mechanism to protect lenders from asset depreciation, loss, 
theft, or deterioration, and there are no linked insurance, guarantee, or risk-
mitigation instruments. This gap increases lender exposure and contributes to 
the low uptake of SIMPRS, particularly for high-risk movable assets. 
 
vi) 
The Bureau has no mechanism in place to real time monitor and deregister or 
discharge interests where borrowers have fully settled their loans and only 
present active interests. 
 
Recommendations 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to liaise with all the responsible stakeholders to; 
 
i) 
Introduce unique identifiers for key movable assets eligible for use as collateral 
in order for the system to work as intended. 

 
 
 
 
87 
 
 
 
ii) 
Establish a central registry for movable equipment crossing Uganda’s borders to 
address the risk of multiple pledging of assets. 
iii) 
Integrate the Warehouse Receipt System with SIMPRS to enable lenders verify 
the validity and value of pledged warehouse commodities. 
iv) 
Link SIMPRS with the Uganda Microfinance Regulatory Authority to verify in real 
time whether users are licensed. 
 
2.1.8.5 Registration of Intellectual Property 
 
The Trademarks Act, Cap. 225 protects registered trademarks from unauthorized use, 
imitation, or passing-off, thereby safeguarding brand identity, service credibility, and 
government intellectual property. The Act further provides that a trademark shall be 
registered for a period of 14 years, with the option for renewal thereafter. 
 
I reviewed the trademarks register, records and related reports and observed the 
following; 
 
i) 
Out of a sample of 76 trademarks associated with various Government 
institutions, 56 were not registered, four (4) had expired, six (6) trademarks 
were pending publication, and only 10 trademarks were valid (properly 
registered) and active. 
 
ii) 
There is a significant gap between business registration and trademark uptake. 
Despite URSB having over 850,000 registered businesses, fewer than 11,000 
local trademarks have been registered, implying that over 98% legally registered 
Ugandan companies have no trademarks and therefore lack commercial 
protection, leaving them vulnerable to counterfeiting and unfair competition. 
 
iii) 
I noted that the Bureau has insufficient in-house capacity for patent review, 
especially expertise to conduct substantive examinations in specialized fields 
such 
as 
pharmaceuticals, 
medicine, 
engineering, 
and 
biotechnology. 
Consequently, over the past three years, at least 56 applications that passed 
formality examination were referred to the African Regional Intellectual Property 
Organization (ARIPO) for substantive review, which takes five years or more 
compared to about two years locally. 
 
iv) 
The Bureau has not yet finalized the development of a National Policy on 
Business Formalisation to guide the national agenda, owing to limitations in 
mandate. The lack of which hinders the development of a coherent, multi-
sectoral approach to addressing informality in Uganda, limiting efforts to 
enhance productivity and foster economic growth. 
 
Recommendations 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to; 
 
i) 
Encourage more government institutions to register their trademarks. 
 

 
 
 
 
88 
 
 
 
ii) 
Promote increased trademark registration among businesses through awareness 
campaigns and streamlined processes for registration. 
 
iii) 
Building in-house capacity for patent examinations in specialized fields. 
 
iv) 
Complete the development of the National policy on Business Formalisation to 
provide a framework to guide the transition of informal businesses into formally 
registered businesses. 
 
2.1.9 Regional Balance Development Programme 
2.1.9.1 Limited involvement of the Diaspora in PDM activities 
 
The Parish Development Model (PDM) Pillar 1 requires government MDAs to organize 
and mobilize households and stakeholders, including the Ugandan diaspora, for 
production, processing, and marketing support. 
 
A review of the MoFA PDM Impact and Opportunities for the Ugandan Diaspora 
document, and interviews with MoFA officials revealed that; 
 
i) 
There were no diaspora needs assessments conducted to align diaspora interests 
with PDM priority value chains. 
ii) 
There is no structured mechanism for linking diaspora investors to processing 
plants/factories, storage facilities, or agribusiness ventures under PDM. As a 
result, the level of involvement of Ugandans in the diaspora in agricultural 
investments is low. 
iii) 
There was no evidence of diaspora mobilization for agricultural value chains 
under the PDM such as export markets, technology transfer, off-taker 
arrangements. 
iv) 
MoFA does not systematically collect or share diaspora agribusiness data with 
the PDM Pillar 1 Working Group. 
v) 
No reporting mechanism exists to capture or track diaspora contributions to PDM 
Pillar 1. 
 
This is due to failure by MoFA to prioritize and operationalize diaspora engagement 
within the PDM framework. 
 
Recommendations 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to; 
 
i) 
Streamline PDM activities in its work plans and missions abroad. 
ii) 
Establish a mechanism to systematically capture and share data with all relevant 
stakeholders on implementation of PDM.

Referral Hospitals, Public Universities, and Primary Health Care Services are critically 
understaffed, with vacancy rates of 71%, 68% and 68% respectively. The staffing gaps 
were mainly attributed to inadequate wage provisions and expansion of staff structures, 
particularly in the health sector, without corresponding recruitment. 
The 54% staffing level means that nearly half of all public service positions remain 
unoccupied, hence negatively affecting quality and efficiency of service delivery. 
The Accounting Officer explained that the low staffing levels are mainly due to the 
phased filling of the newly adopted staffing structures for hospitals and health centres, 
as Government gradually strengthens hospital infrastructure. However, Government is 
prioritizing recruitment for the most urgent and critical vacancies. 
In addition, the Ministry has allocated additional wage resources to strengthen 
manpower and raise staffing levels. In FY 2025/2026, Uganda Police Force was allocated
