1,000 prison warders/wardresses. A total of 130 Ministries, Departments, Agencies, and 
Local Governments were cleared to recruit 6,749 employees with wage funding of 
UGX.122.38Bn and UGX.5.48Bn was allocated for newly upgraded Health Centre IIs to 
IIIs. 
Recommendation 
I advised the Accounting Officer to develop and publicise realistic multiyear recruitment 
plans aligned to the government’s wage projections and, in collaboration with MoFPED 
and the Public Service Commission (PSC), progressively fill the staffing gaps, prioritising 
the critical and high impact positions. 

 
 
 
 
90 
 
 
 
2.1.10.2 
Rationalisation of Public Expenditure (RAPEX) 
On 22nd February, 2021, Cabinet approved the policy to merge, mainstream and 
rationalise various government entities to facilitate efficient and effective service delivery 
and eliminate mandate and functional overlaps. 
As of December 2025, 35 bills had been assented to for rationalisation of 40 entities. 
Out of the 40 entities, 23 entities had been successfully rationalised while 17 entities are 
yet to be rationalised. 
Of the 23 rationalised entities, 17 were mainstreamed and their functions transferred to 
successor entities, while six (6) were merged to form new entities. I carried out a 
detailed review of eight (8) rationalised entities and observed the following; 
 
a) 
Payment of terminal benefits following rationalisation 
 
At the time of writing this report, the following observations were noted; 
 
i) 
None of the eight (8) rationalised entities had specific budgets for the payment 
of rationalisation expenses (terminal benefits). Instead, their budgets were 
amalgamated under the successor MDAs. This implied that the individual entity 
budgets may not have been realistic. 
 
ii) 
As of the dates of closure, the eight (8) rationalised entities had 1,917 staff. Out 
of these, 1,492 staff (78%) were absorbed by other government entities, while 
the balance of 425 staff (22%) were not absorbed by any other government 
body. 
 
iii) 
Out of 1,492 staff absorbed by government entities, a total of 1,389 staff 
absorbed by seven (7) rationalised entities were paid UGX.46.80Bn as terminal 
benefits. This was inspite of the Attorney General’s Letter and RAPEX guidance 
by MoPS which provided that where an employee was re-appointed into 
government service, there would be no compensation, as this was considered 
continuity of service. 
 
iv) 
A total of 85 staff who were absorbed from five (5) entities were not paid 
terminal benefits. This implied that the absorbed staff were not entitled to 
terminal benefits. 
 
v) 
A total of 425 staff retired following the rationalisation exercise. Of these, 410 
staff that had retired from six (6) entities had so far been paid terminal benefits 
amounting to UGX.30.4Bn, while 20 staff that had retired from two (2) entities 
had not been paid their terminal benefits. Similarly, a number of retired staff due 
to rationalisation from three (3) entities claimed UGX.2.08Bn. 
 
vi) 
A total of 66 staff were terminated from two (2) entities and entitled to terminal 
benefits of UGX.1.03Bn as provided for in their respective staff regulations, 

 
 
 
 
91 
 
 
 
contracts and human resources manuals. However, they were paid only 
UGX.930.11Mn leaving an unpaid balance of UGX.101.80Mn. 
Recommendation 
I advised the Accounting Officers to bring the matters of ambiguity and inconsistencies 
in the guidance on terminal benefits, including varying interpretations by individual 
entities on who is entitled to receive terminal benefits, and the inconsistent computation 
of the benefits across RAPEX entities, to the attention of the Attorney General, the 
Ministry of Public Service and other relevant stakeholders for further guidance and final 
resolution. 
b) 
Review of assets and liabilities of the Rationalised Entities 
 
RAPEX guidelines required entities to prepare handover reports specifying the assets to 
be transferred to successor entities. At the time of writing this report, the following was 
observed; 
 
i) 
The assets in the handover reports of four (4) rationalised entities worth 
UGX.564.71Mn differed from those disclosed in the fixed assets register. 
Similarly, the assets of three (3) entities worth UGX.54.44Bn differed from those 
in the closure financial statements. 
 
ii) 
Twelve (12) assets valued at UGX.779Mn were left out of the handover reports 
of (1) entity at the time of the closure of the audit. 
 
iii) 
I circularised third parties and observed that seven (7) parcels of land whose 
values could not be established were not included in the handover reports as 
well as the financial statements of one (1) rationalised entity. 
iv) 
One (1) entity had carried out a Board of Survey to ascertain all the assets held 
at the time of closure, while seven (7) were yet to carry out the exercise as 
required by the RAPEX guidelines. 
 
v) 
Physical verification of the land owned at the rationalised entities revealed that 
19 parcels of land in two (2) rationalised entities were encumbered, with 10 
encroached on, while the ownership of seven (7) parcels of land is disputed. 
 
vi) 
79 parcels of land that belonged to four (4) rationalised entities were not titled 
while five (5) parcels of land in one (1) rationalised entity had expired leases. 
 
vii) 
The total receivables of five (5) rationalised entities amounted to UGX.474.79Bn. 
 
viii) 
Five (5) rationalised entities had disclosed liabilities amounting to UGX.932.39Bn 
in their financial statements. This implied that Government is at a risk of loss of 
funds should the creditors sue before settlement of the liabilities. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
92 
 
 
 
Recommendation 
I advised the Accounting Officers of the successor entities to verify the assets before 
including them in their asset’s register and financial statements. I further advised 
Management in the successor entities to verify the liabilities before budgeting for their 
settlement. Where encumbrances on land were observed, management should take up 
the matter and ensure the prompt resolution. 
2.1.10.3 
Underutilization of Prime Land in Kenya 
Uganda Property Holdings Limited (UPHL) owns three large properties in Nyali, Kenya, a 
prime and commercially strategic location with strong potential for high-value 
development. However, physical inspection revealed that these properties, covering a 
combined four acres are currently leased to small, low-value tenants who generate 
minimal rental income relative to the land’s market potential. This underutilization limits 
UPHL’s ability to optimize revenue from its asset portfolio. 
Management reported that proposals for developing maisonettes and flats had been 
prepared and discussed with shareholders, but implementation stalled due to cash flow 
constraints. 
The continued underdevelopment of high-value land reduces the company’s earning 
capacity, weakens long-term financial sustainability, and delays opportunities for 
portfolio growth. 
Recommendation 
I advised UPHL Management to work with shareholders to mobilize the necessary 
investment resources and fast-track the development of these properties to maximize 
utilization and enhance revenue generation. 
2.1.11 Climate Change, Natural Resources, Environment & Water Management 
Programme 
2.1.11.1 
Wetland Encroachment 
 
Contrary to Section 53(2) of the National Environment Act Cap 181 and Regulations 
29(1) and 30(1) of the National Environment (Wetlands, Riverbanks and Lakeshores 
Management) Regulations 2000 requiring 100 meters and 200 meters protected zones 
from highest watermarks of rivers and lakes respectively, and Regulation 10(8) requiring 
five-yearly wetland inventory updates; 
 
i) 
Out of Uganda's wetlands cover of 33,762.6km² The total degraded wetland 
cover was estimated at 6.3% of Uganda’s total land area2. 
 
ii) 
Fourteen major water bodies suffered extensive encroachment; through 
apartment construction, hotels, sand mining, landing sites, washing bays, 
recreation facilities, wastewater discharge, sugarcane plantations, agriculture, 
settlements, quarrying, livestock grazing, cultivation, artisanal mining, brick-
 
2 Paragraph 293 of the NDPIV, Page 173 

 
 
 
 
93 
 
 
 
making, informal markets, unregulated water abstraction, rice farming, palm 
cultivation, charcoal production, illegal logging, and wetland drainage, among 
others3. 
 
iii) 
Despite restoration efforts, the Ministry of Water and Environment demarcated 
only 739.34km² (18%) against planned 4,150km² over three years4. 
iv) 
Whereas the National Environmental Management Authority issued 319 
restoration orders in 2024/25, only 146 (46%) were acted upon leaving 173 
(54%) orders pending5. 
 
The inadequate performance was attributed to limited funding whereby the Ministry 
received only UGX.660 Mn (11%) of the required funding of UGX.6Bn for demarcation of 
wetlands, absence of formal appeals regulations and guidelines and irregular sittings of 
the appeals committee. In addition, the ministry lacks command and control over the 
environmental police which also has only 45 officers responsible for protecting 8,614 
gazetted wetlands covering approximately 37,346.3 km² across 146 districts and 11 
cities6. 
 
The encroachment has led to; physical, chemical, and biological contamination 
manifesting as sedimentation, algal blooms, flash floods, rising water levels, reduced 
water quality, increased treatment costs, endangered aquatic biodiversity, compromised 
ecosystem services and public health risks. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to liaise with Ministry of Finance, Planning and 
Economic Development for necessary resources to enable buffer zone demarcation with 
concrete pillars, restoration of degraded areas, recruitment and control over the 
environmental police, and proactive coordination with NEMA and Local Governments 
regarding water banks and wetlands protection. 
 
2.1.11.2 
Maintenance of Valley Tanks and Dams in the Karamoja Sub-Region 
 
The Ministry of Water and Environment (MWE) and the Office of the Prime Minister, 
constructed 106 valley tanks at an estimated cost of UGX.8.7Bn and five dams at an 
estimated cost of UGX 45Bn across nine (9) districts in the Karamoja Sub-Region to 
support livestock, irrigation, and domestic water use. Upon completion, the 
infrastructure was handed over to communities through Water User Committees 
responsible for operation, management, and maintenance. 
 
During the year under review, the Ministry of Water and Environment received the 
budgeted UGX 1Bn for maintenance of 10 valley tanks and UGX100Mn for the 
rehabilitation of 3 of dams7. 
 
 
3 Interview with the Commissioner, International Transboundary Water Affairs 
4 Wetlands Performance Reports, and interviews with the senior wetlands officer 
5 NEMA annual performance reports FYs 2022 to 2025 
6 Interview with the commandant, environmental protection police unit 
7 Water for production, Karamoja Work Plan 

 
 
 
 
94 
 
 
 
However, inspections of twenty-five valley tanks and five dams conducted in November 
2025 revealed that eighteen valley tanks (72%) were heavily silted, while seven (28%), 
had maintenance challenges, including eroded water inlets, weed invasion, unprotected 
water sources, damaged animal drinking troughs, dilapidated cattle access ramps, and 
eroded embankments. Of the five dams inspected, three (60%) were well maintained, 
one (20%) had maintenance gaps such as overgrown grass and damaged animal 
drinking troughs, and one dam at Kawomeri was non-functional due to lack of water, 
attributed to encroachment of the catchment area. 
Consequently, the silted valley tanks and dams have suffered reduced water storage 
capacity, resulting in limited water availability for livestock and agriculture. This 
condition was attributed to the absence of clear maintenance plans, unclear roles 
between Local Governments and the Ministry of Water and Environment, limited 
community ownership, inadequate practical training of Water User Committees and 
community members in operation, maintenance, and water source protection, 
unprotected catchment areas leading to degradation, and overgrazing due to high 
livestock numbers, particularly affecting valley tanks. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to establish clear maintenance plans and budgets for all 
the 106 valley tanks and 5 dams, clarify the roles of Local Governments and the Ministry 
of Water and Environment, protect water sources through reforestation, and provide 
Water User Committees and community members with practical training in operation 
and maintenance, basic repair skills, and water source protection techniques. 
 
2.1.12 Development Plan Implementation Programme 
2.1.12.1 
Low Tax/GDP ratio 
 
According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), developing countries should 
maintain a Tax-to-GDP Ratio of at least 15% to ensure they have the funds to invest in 
the future and achieve sustainable economic growth. Tax-to-GDP Ratio represents total 
tax revenue as a percentage of GDP and indicates the share of a Country's output that 
the Government collects through taxes. 
 
I noted that although URA’s efforts have yielded impressive results with a tremendous 
growth in revenue collection, Uganda's Tax/GDP Ratio has remained low at around 
13.4%. 
 
A comparison of Uganda’s performance with other economies revealed wide disparities, 
as shown in the table below;

2.1.12.3 
Domestic Arrears 
 
A review of the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Government of Uganda and 
the disclosure in Note 25 revealed that the GoU had accumulated domestic arrears to a 
tune of UGX.8.4Tn as at 30th June 2025, a reduction of 39% from prior year arrears of 
UGX.13.814Tn. 
 
This office is conducting a comprehensive verification of the domestic arrears across all 
Ministries, Departments, Agencies, and Local Authorities. The objective is to determine 
the accurate stock of domestic arrears for the Government. Detailed procedures have 
been designed to ensure that the Government's position on domestic arrears is 
accurately reflected. The detailed findings will be published separately. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the PS/ST to ensure adequate budgeting for domestic arrears and enhance 
enforcement of commitment control for sustainability. 
 
2.1.12.3.1 
Gaps in taxation of digital services allow non-resident companies to 
earn from Uganda without paying taxes 
 
Global trade has shifted toward digital platforms offering entertainment, advertising, 
software subscriptions, cloud services, online education, and betting services. These 
services generate substantial income from Ugandan consumers, much of which flows to 
non-resident companies outside Uganda’s tax jurisdiction. 

 
 
 
 
97 
 
 
 
 
To tax this fast-growing sector, a 5% Digital Service Tax (DST) was introduced in FY 
2023/24. Uganda collected UGX.29.58 billion in FY 2024/25 from 82 compliant providers 
through DST and VAT. 
 
However, my review revealed major providers that are not registered for DST and are 
not paying taxes on income earned from Ugandan users. 
 
This means Uganda is losing revenue to some of the world’s most profitable digital 
multinational companies. URA currently lacks a payment gateway monitoring system, 
making it difficult to quantify how much income these companies earn from Uganda, 
further limiting enforcement. 
 
Management explained that many of the non-compliant companies are based in the 
United States, which strongly resists DST regimes imposed by foreign countries. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised Management to ensure stronger tools and international cooperation, to 
minimise losses of billions in tax revenue from the fast-growing digital services.

completed. 
 
However, traders consistently reported delays in cargo and motor vehicle clearance. To

2024/25.

2.1.12.5 
Contribution of the EFRIS to Domestic Revenue Collection 
Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) introduced the Electronic Fiscal Receipting and 
Invoicing Solution (EFRIS) to digitise tax reporting, combat fraud (like invoice trading), 
and boost revenue by tracking all business transactions in real-time through mandatory 

 
 
 
 
99 
 
 
 
e-invoices/receipts, moving businesses from paper invoices to electronic invoices, aiming 
for transparency and wider tax base inclusion. 
The system was introduced in FY 2020/21 and initially mandatory for only VAT-
registered taxpayers. Effective July 2025, it was expanded to include other businesses 
(even non-VAT registered ones) operating within specific sectors, which include 
wholesale and retail of fuel, real estate, construction, and manufacturing, among others. 
A review of the VAT revenue collections indicates slow growth before the introduction of 
EFRIS in the years 2017/18, 2018/19 and 2019/20, while a significant growth has been 
registered over the 5 years of implementation of the system, as indicated in the table

voluntary compliance.

that are adding value and this is expected to be achieved by 30th June 2026.

duplicate, or non-operational taxpayers. 
ii) 
Develop and implement targeted compliance programs to activate dormant 
taxpayers and encourage newly registered entities to begin filing and paying 
taxes. 
 
2.1.12.6.1 
Operational challenges and conflicting laws in the regulation of the 
Microfinance sector 
a) 
Failure to operationalize the Stabilization Fund 
 
Section 53 and 56 (1) of the Tier 4 Microfinance Institutions and Money Lenders Act 
Cap 61 establishes a SACCO Stabilization fund and SACCO Saving Protection Fund 
respectively, and these are to be managed by the Uganda Micro Finance Regulatory 
Authority. These were intended to provide a safety net for SACCO members against 
SACCOs that have closed. 
 
However, the respective funds have not been operationalized as required due to the 
failure to approve the respective regulations. In addition, SACCOs have found the 
requirement to contribute 0.5% of the average total assets to the SACCO Stabilization 
Fund to be prohibitive. 
 
This exposes the 220 SACCO members to risks of loss in the event of collapse of a 
SACCO. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
101 
 
 
 
b) 
Conflicting laws 
 
There are various overlapping and conflicting laws between the Cooperatives Society Act 
and the Tier 4 Act in regard to: the use of the word SACCO, regulation and supervision, 
reporting of SACCOs and the Establishment of the SACCO Stabilization Fund and the 
Central Financing Facility, Liquidation of SACCOs and SACCO governance. For example, 
on the unclaimed balances, while ‘the Tier 4 Act provides that, unclaimed balances shall, 
after a period of 5 years be transferred to the Regulator for further management, the 
Cooperative Act provides that ‘the abandoned funds be credited to a special reserve 
fund thus the conflicting legal framework and overlapping laws causing a challenge in 
regulating SACCOs and encourage noncompliance issues in implementation. 
 
Recommendations 
 
I advised the Government to; 
 
i) 
Expedite the process of approving the regulations to operationalize the 
respective funds. 
ii) 
Ensure that the Tier 4 Microfinance and Money Lenders (SACCO) Regulations 
2020 and the Cooperative Society Act are harmonised. 
 
2.1.12.7 
Compensations for the Kiteezi mud slide disaster victims 
 
On 10th August 2024, the Kiteezi waste slide occurred affecting over 230 residents of 
Kiteezi in Lusanja – Kansagati Town Council whose properties were destroyed. All of the 
affected persons were to be compensated through KCCA and OPM. Government 
released a total sum of OPM UGX.1.37Bn for the purpose while UGX.2.21Bn was the 
total claim under KCCA as valued by the Chief Government Valuer to be paid out. This 
amount was never released. 
However, at the time of writing this report, none of the claimants under KCCA had been 
compensated and under KCCA while 20 claimants under OPM have so far been 
compensated a total sum of UGX.1.05Bn. 
 
The failure to compensate all affected categories of victims has prolonged the suffering 
of households, whose livelihoods, homes, and properties were destroyed, leading to 
continued social and economic distress. 
 
The Accounting Officers of KCCA and OPM attributed the delay to the need for Cabinet 
approval and delays in securing the necessary funding. The funds have since been 
processed resulting in the payment of 70 out of the 95 affected beneficiaries under 
KCCA while the process of payment of disturbance allowance for the twenty (20) 
households under OPM is also ongoing. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officers to expedite payment of the remaining 25 beneficiaries 
under KCCA and disturbance allowance to the 20 beneficiaries under OPM. In addition, a 

 
 
 
 
102 
 
 
 
proper and detailed justification and report on the management of the disaster and 
compensation of the affected individuals should be prepared for future reference. 
 
 
 
2.1.12.8 
Lack of integration of physical planning 
 
The Physical Planning (Amendment) Act, 2024 assigns NPA the authority to integrate 
physical development planning into national development planning. It NPA’s mandate to 
guide, coordinate, supervise and approve physical development planning frameworks 
nationwide. However, NPA’s contribution to physical development planning is still 
lacking. 
 
Furthermore, the physical development plans lack detailed guidance to effectively guide, 
regulate and ensure the orderly urban and rural development. 
 
A review of NPA’s Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30 and the status report on physical 
planning revealed that, whereas NPA developed the National and two (2) regional 
physical development plans, the following challenges were noted; 
 
i) 
The physical master plan for the Greater Kampala Metropolitan Area, which 
includes Uganda’s Capital City, has not been finalised. 
ii) 
The Physical Planning Committees in all the Local Governments remained non 
operational. 
iii) 
Whereas every local government is expected to have a physical development 
plan, only 18 (13%) out of 135 districts had physical development plans. In 
addition, only three (3) out of 11 cities, 17 out of 31 Municipalities, and 58 out of 
580 Town Councils have physical development plans. 
 
As a result of these gaps, there is a risk of fragmented spatial development in districts 
and cities, and growth of unplanned urban settlements, and congestion leading to 
inadequate service delivery. 
The Accounting Officer explained that the national guidelines and regulations for 
metropolitan, districts and local governments are being developed and shall be 
concluded necessary by the end of FY 2026/2027 after operationalising the Physical 
Planning Amendment Act, 2024. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to fast-track the development and gazetting of the 
national guidelines and regulations for metropolitan planning to operationalise the 
Physical Planning Amendment Act, 2024.

revealed significant delays in the assessment, approval, and certification of both Local

resubmission.

2.1.12.9.1 
Failure by National Planning Authority to fully institutionalise the 
mandate of the Physical Planning 
 
In 2024, the functions of the National Physical Planning Board, including; the 
preparation of the national and regional physical development plans, hearing appeals by 
persons aggrieved by the decisions of physical planning committees, and advising the 
Government on all matters relating to physical planning were transferred to National 
Planning Authority (NPA). 
 
Although the NPA’s mandate was expanded, the Authority has faced challenges in fully 
institutionalising these additional functions, as explained below; 
 
i) 
Lack of enabling guidelines and regulations: Whereas the Authority 
developed guidelines for the approval of local governments’ physical 
development plans, they are yet to be approved and gazetted. 

 
 
 
 
104 
 
 
 
ii) 
Severe staffing gaps: The Authority expanded its staff structure by 52 
positions and created the Department for Economic Planning to accommodate 
the new roles. However, only 32 positions have been filled leaving 20 positions 
vacant. 
iii) 
Delay to approve NSDI: There has been delayed approval of the National 
Spatial Data Infrastructure (NSDI) Policy which is critical for spatial planning. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that the recruitment to fill the established positions 
was halted by the Cabinet Ministerial Committee on Restructuring until the conclusion of 
the ongoing amendment of the Physical Planning Act. Efforts to gazette and disseminate 
the guidelines are still ongoing. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to expedite the gazetting and dissemination of the 
guidelines for physical development plans and approval of the spatial data infrastructure 
policy. I also advise the Accounting Officer to await the outcome of the Cabinet 
Ministerial Committee’s decision before filling the vacant positions. 
 
2.1.13 Innovation, Technology Developments and Transfer Programme 
2.1.13.1 
Review of the construction of the National Biosciences Park facility 
 
During the FY 2021/2022, the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) 
signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with National Enterprise Corporation 
(NEC) to construct a vaccine manufacturing factory at Kakooge in Nakasongola District, 
at a contract price of UGX.74.1Bn. 
 
A review of the implementation of the MoU revealed the following; 
 
i) 
An advance payment of UGX.62.99Bn, or 84% of the contract price, was paid to 
NEC for the construction of the factory under the terms of the MoU. Of this 
amount UGX.40.5Bn was paid in 2022/2023, and UGX.22.49 Bn in 2023/2024; 
however, by the time of the contract’s expiry, no work had been undertaken. 
 
ii) 
Subsequently, in April 2025, STI entered into a new MoU with NEC, and changed 
the scope of work from the construction of a vaccine factory to the design and 
build of a National Biosciences Park facility at Kakooge, Nakasongola district, at a 
contract price of UGX.300Bn. 
 
iii) 
Following the new MOU, a further UGX.26.8Bn was transferred to NEC in June 
2025, bringing the total sum paid to date of UGX.89.8Bn. 
 
iv) 
I inspected the land designated for the construction of the Bio Sciences Park on 
8th September 2025 and noted it was vacant, with no ongoing construction 
activity. In addition, there were no Bills of Quantities or other documented basis 
for the contract price of UGX.300Bn, and no clear multi-year development plan 
had been prepared to guide the implementation of the project. 
 

 
 
 
 
105 
 
 
 
Management explained that a more accurate project cost would be established upon 
completion of the detailed designs, specifications and Bills of Quantities for the National 
Biosciences Park, which is the first deliverable under the new MoU. 
 
The continued disbursement of funds without an established cost basis, such as bills of 
quantities, and an implementation plan exposes STI to significant implementation risks, 
including cost and time overruns, potential loss of funds and difficulties in enforcing the 
contractual obligations. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer of STI, to engage all stakeholders, develop a clear 
concept note for the project, finalise the designs and costs, confirm the availability of 
funds for the multi-year investment and, following the necessary approvals, promptly 
advise NEC to commence the construction. 
 
2.1.13.1.1 
Review of the management of the Technology Business Incubation at 
UIRI 
 
The Uganda Industrial Research Institute (UIRI), through its Technology Business 
Incubation (TBC) Program, plays a critical role in nurturing start-ups (also referred to as 
incubatees), facilitates value addition, and contributes to job creation. Over time, UIRI 
has supported 84 start-up businesses, 46 of which have received direct in-house support 
while 38 have been supported virtually. In the last three (3) years, government has 
provided UGX.4.7Bn to support the incubation initiative. 
 
I undertook a review of the incubation program’ implementation and noted the 
following; 
 
i) 
Since inception in 2006 only five (5) Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) 
have exited the incubation program successfully, while five (5) companies are in 
the process of graduating. 
ii) 
Thirteen (13) incubatees had either expired MoUs implying that the terms 
contained in the agreement may not be binding on or enforceable by either 
party, 
iii) 
Ten (10) incubatees had stayed in the incubator for 5 to 10 years without 
justification. The long stay deprives other potential incubatees from accessing 
the incubation services. 
iv) 
Eight (8) incubatees that had signed MoUs with the Institute were not active 
despite some of them having been allocated specific days to utilise the Institute’s 
facilities. 
 
The above weaknesses affect the programme's effectiveness and attainment of the 
intended objectives. 
 
The Accounting Officer explained that management was in the process of reviewing and 
renewing the contracts of the incubates. In addition, the Accounting Officer explained 

 
 
 
 
106 
 
 
 
that some incubatees stayed longer due to challenges that could result in them 
collapsing if they exited from the program prematurely. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer review and reassess the program and revise the 
strategies applied to make it more effective. 
 
2.1.14 Tourism Development Programme 
2.1.14.1 
Management of concessions at UWA 
 
The Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA) oversees 55 concessions across protected areas to 
promote tourism development, generate revenue, and support conservation objectives. 
Effective concession management requires strong regulatory oversight, complete 
contractual documentation, and consistent monitoring to ensure compliance with 
concession terms and alignment with UWA’s mandate. 
 
However, my audit revealed several weaknesses in the management of concessions, 
including; 
 
i) 
Absence of formal concession agreements for ten operating concessionaires, 
exposing the Authority to legal, financial, and enforcement risks. 
ii) 
Delayed or non-payment of concession fees totaling UGX.18.80Bn, resulting from 
weak compliance, delayed reporting by concessionaires, and insufficient follow-
up by UWA. 
iii) 
Non-operational or significantly delayed concession projects, limiting expected 
tourism infrastructure development and delaying associated revenue streams. 
iv) 
Continued operations under expired agreements, contrary to contractual 
provisions and good governance practices. 
v) 
Lack of audited accounts and audit certificates, limiting UWA’s ability to 
independently verify revenue linked to variable fees such as bed-night charges. 
 
These weaknesses collectively undermine UWA’s ability to safeguard conservation 
interests, enforce contractual obligations, and realize the full economic value of 
concessions in protected areas. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised UWA Management to strengthen concession governance by ensuring timely 
contract execution, instituting structured monitoring mechanisms, enforcing payment 
obligations, regularizing undocumented or expired concessions, and requiring full 
compliance with reporting and audit requirements. 
 
2.1.14.2 
Outstanding compensation claims 
 
The Wildlife Compensation Scheme established under Sections 83 and 84 of the Uganda 
Wildlife Act, Cap 315, is intended to finance compensation for human death, injury, and 
property damage caused by wild animals outside protected areas. The scheme receives 

 
 
 
 
107 
 
 
 
funding from UWA’s revenue collections, Parliamentary appropriations, and other 
approved sources. Compensation claims are expected to be verified by the 
Compensation Verification Committee (CVC) and approved by the Board at market rates. 
However, I identified significant weaknesses in the management of compensation claims 
during the year under review. Analysis of CVC reports and payment records revealed 
that; 
 
i) 
The Committee received UGX.4.09Bn to finance compensation for FY 2024/25. 
ii) 
A total of 1,346 claims were handled, of which 1,308 were verified and 
approved, leaving 38 claims deferred or rejected. 
iii) 
The total approved value amounted to UGX.4.03Bn, yet only UGX.1.08Bn (27%) 
had been paid by year-end, leaving UGX.2.96Bn (73%) unpaid. 
iv) 
The Committee also received 1,109 new claims, but only 164 (15%) were 
verified, leaving 945 claims (85%) pending verification. 
 
These weaknesses indicate inefficiencies in both verification and disbursement 
processes, resulting in a growing backlog of unresolved cases and substantial unpaid 
obligations. 
 
The delays in verifying and paying compensation claims prolong financial hardship for 
communities affected by wildlife damage, weaken trust in the compensation system, 
and may undermine community cooperation in conservation initiatives, thereby 
heightening the risk of human–wildlife conflict. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised UWA Management to strengthen the verification and payment processes 
through improved workflow management, timely disbursement of approved claims, and 
enhanced capacity of the CVC to reduce backlogs and restore confidence in the 
compensation system.

2.1.15.1.2 
Long outstanding pension payments of the former employees of 
Uganda Posts and Telecommunications Corporation – UGX.187.728Bn 
 
Section (L-c) 13 of the Uganda Public Service Standing Orders require that a public 
officer or a beneficiary to whom a pension or gratuity has been granted shall, before the 
pension or gratuity is paid to him or her, satisfy the Responsible Officer as to his or her 
identity in such a manner as the Pensions Authority may from time to time prescribe. 
 
Following a request from the Solicitor General, I undertook a verification exercise of the 
former employees of Uganda Posts and Telecommunications Corporation (UPTC) in 2016 
and a verification report was issued in August 2021, an addendum report issued in 
August 2022 and a special pension audit issued report in December 2024. 
 

 
 
 
 
109 
 
 
 
My review of the implementation of the payments revealed that, although Government 
through the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance has made some progress in 
addressing this long-standing obligation, a substantial balance of UGX.187.728Bn 
remains unsettled due to inadequate funding. 
The delay in settlement undermines the welfare of former UPTC employees, contributes 
to long-term social and economic vulnerability, and negatively impacts public confidence 
in Government’s commitment to honour its obligations. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to liaise with the Ministry of Finance to ensure that 
adequate funds are provided to facilitate full settlement of the outstanding obligation.

2.1.15.1.4 
Accumulation of Unpaid Internet and Leased Line Service Fees by 
Target User Groups-UGX.5.41Bn 
 
Paragraph 4.3.15 of the NITA-U Financial Management Manual (2013) provides that the 
Authority may extend credit to customers but must take all necessary measures to 
recover overdue amounts. Debts outstanding for more than 30 days are subject to debt 
recovery procedures, including issuance of a legal notice within 14 days and, if recovery 
efforts fail, initiation of legal action. Any revenue deemed uncollectible must be verified 
by the Director of Finance and Administration and reported to the Authority Board, with 
recommendations for write-off supported by full details and justification. 
 
For the period under review, 29 Target User Groups (TUGs) had accumulated fees of 
UGX.5.41Bn in lieu of internet and leased line services consumed. However there was 
no evidence for any effort of debt recovery. 
 
Failure by the Target User Groups (TUGs) to remit payments for internet and leased line 
amounting UGX.5.41Bn negatively affects the Authority’s cash flow and limits its ability 
to sustainably manage the NBI/EGI services for all MDAs to which the entire country 
relies on. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to strengthen debt management and recovery 
processes by enforcing debt recovery procedures, including issuance of legal notices and 
initiation of legal action against persistently defaulting TUGs. 
 
 
2.1.16 Sustainable Urbanization and Housing Programme

Delays in titling of land for seed schools, health and road

eliminate theft, losses, wastage, and misuse. 
 
Additionally, Section 2.3 of the Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development 
(MoLHUD) Client's Charter 2024/25–2026/27 provides for an average of 10 days for the 
processing or transfer of land titles through the Uganda National Land Information 
System across the twenty-two Ministerial Zonal Offices. 
 

 
 
 
 
111

were observed in four Ministerial Zonal Offices namely; Mbarara with 29 files (15%),

2.1.17 Manufacturing Programme 
2.1.17.1.1 
Government Investment through UDC - a case for Industrial 
Development 
 
As a state enterprise, Uganda development Corporation (UDC) is mandated to promote 
and facilitate industrial and economic development by investing in commercially viable 
projects that align with the National Development Goals. 
Although UDC is expected to operate with a degree of independence, it is being 
financed through project-specific funding. Government releases funds to UDC, which are 
already earmarked for specific projects, leaving UDC with no space to carry out proper 
investment appraisal. 
 

 
 
 
 
112 
 
 
 
A review of the investment performance over ten years revealed that UDC has invested 
UGX.1.3Tn in 22 companies through different modalities. Assessment of 10 active 
companies that provided documentation revealed the following; 
 
i) 
8 out of 10 companies recorded net losses for at least two consecutive years. 
 
ii) 
One (1) company remains non-operational four years after the initial investment 
of UGX 3.1Bn. 
iii) 
Eight companies that UDC loaned UGX.23Bn had not adhered to the agreed 
repayment terms and had neither paid principal nor interest. 
iv) 
UDC’s investment income for the current year revealed a paltry UGX.1.4Bn 
against a UGX.1.3Tn investment, giving a return on Investment of 0.09% 
 
The above analysis shows that the investment decisions transferred on UDC are not 
viable and are not yielding returns. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Government to consider providing capital funding to UDC and then 
demand for a decent return on investment. 
 
2.1.17.2 
Sub-optimal utilisation of industrial parks 
 
In line with Uganda Investment Authority (UIA) mandate, the Authority established 10 
public industrial parks and supports 5 privately owned parks. Additionally, 7 agricultural 
parks have been developed, with more underway. 
 
These parks are aimed at promoting targeted investment, supporting Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises (MSME) formalization, and enhancing regional competitiveness 
through integrated infrastructure and operational One Stop Centres (OSCs). A review of 
the utilisation of the parks revealed the status as at June, 2025 as follows; 
 
The Government owned parks constitute 4178 acres part of which have been allocated 
to 628 companies. Of these, 307 (49%) are fully operational, 195 (31%) are under 
construction, and 122 (19%) remain in the pre-start phase. 
 
The Authority supports five Public Private parks covering approximately 2523.5 acres of 
which 51 companies had been allocated land, with 45 (88%) of them operational. 
 
The Government owned Agricultural parks total to 23,204 acres in size and have been 
leased to 15 companies with 12 (80%) of them operational. 
 
The intervention has faced challenges as highlighted below; 
i) 
The Authority lacks land titles for several parcels of land across 21 districts in the 
country measuring 26,371.91 acres/41.2 sq. miles. 
 
ii) 
Portions of land in several parks measuring 155 acres remain unallocated to 
active investors. 

 
 
 
 
113 
 
 
 
 
iii) 
UIA received a Presidential Directive in 2016, to establish additional 25 regional 
industrial parks across Uganda. The Authority (UIA) initiated a nationwide land 
mobilization exercise by engaging 16 DLGs and mobilized approximately 56,960 
acres (89 square miles). 
 
However, at the time of audit, the Authority had not established any new 
industrial park in fulfilment of the Presidential directive, 10 years later. 
 
iv) 
Many parks lack critical infrastructure such as solid waste management systems, 
high voltage power, roads and proper drainage channels. 
 
v) 
Kampala Industrial and Business Park, Namanve (KIBP) Project was established 
to develop a 2,200-acre industrial facility. The total project cost is EUR 
215,065,212.41, funded by the Government of Uganda with support from United 
Kingdom Export Finance (UKEF) and Standard Chartered Bank UK. The land has 
been allocated to investors across all sectors. The project commenced on 6th 
July 2020 and after numerous extensions, the new completion date has been set 
at 4th March 2028. As at 30th June 2025, physical progress on the Infrastructure 
Development (Design and Build) stood at 59%. 
 
vi) 
Insufficient infrastructure undermines the functionality and attractiveness of 
industrial parks, constraining agricultural productivity, industrial growth, and job 
creation while failure to develop allocated land undermines UIA’s mandate to 
promote industrial growth and job creation. It results in idle public assets, delays 
in economic transformation, and increased vulnerability to land encroachment. 
I advised Uganda Investment Authority to intensify engagement with key stakeholders; 
to secure dedicated funding and have all the investment bottlenecks addressed. 
 
 
2.1.18 Private Sector Development Programme 
2.1.18.1.1 
Operational challenges and conflicting laws in the regulation of the 
Microfinance sector 
 
a) 
Failure to operationalize the Stabilization Fund 
 
Section 53 and 56 (1) of the Tier 4 Microfinance Institutions and Money Lenders Act, 
Cap 61, establishes a SACCO Stabilization Fund and SACCO Saving Protection Fund 
respectively, and these were to be managed by the Uganda Micro Finance Regulatory 
Authority. These were intended to provide a safety net for SACCO members against 
SACCOs that have closed. 
 
However, the respective funds have not been operationalized as required due to the 
failure to approve the respective regulations. In addition, SACCOs have found the 
requirement to contribute 0.5% of the average total assets to the SACCO Stabilization 
Fund to be prohibitive. 

 
 
 
 
114 
 
 
 
 
This exposes SACCO members to risks of loss in the event of collapse of a SACCO. 
 
b) 
Conflicting laws 
 
There are various overlapping and conflicting laws between the Cooperatives Society Act 
and the Tier 4 Act in regard to: the use of the word SACCO, regulation and supervision, 
reporting of SACCOs and the Establishment of the SACCO Stabilization Fund and the 
Central Financing Facility, Liquidation of SACCOs and SACCO governance. 
 
For example, on the unclaimed balances, while ‘the Tier 4 Act provides that, unclaimed 
balances shall, after a period of 5 years be transferred to the Regulator for further 
management, the Cooperative Act provides that ‘the abandoned funds be credited to a 
special reserve fund thus the conflicting legal framework and overlapping laws causing a 
challenge in regulating SACCOs and encourage noncompliance issues in implementation. 
 
Recommendation 
 
I advised the Government as follows; 
 
i) 
To expedite the process of approving the regulations to operationalize the 
respective funds. 
ii) 
Ensure that the Tier 4 Microfinance and Money Lenders (SACCO) Regulations 
2020 and the Cooperative Society Act are harmonized. 
 
 
2.2 
Observations from other Compliance areas 
 
During the financial year, I conducted audits on other compliance areas whose summary 
findings are provided here. 
 
2.2.1 Management of the Parish Development Model 
 
The Parish Development Model (PDM) is a strategy for service delivery by the 
Government of Uganda to improve the incomes and welfare of all Ugandans at the 
household level by transforming 39% of households from a subsistence economy to a 
money economy as approved by Parliament. In the financial year 2024/25, Ministry of 
Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED) released UGX.1.100Tn to 
10,594 PDM SACCOs as Parish Revolving Funds (PRF) - UGX.1.059Tn and administrative 
costs - UGX.0.41Tn as appropriated by Parliament. 
 
I designed audit procedures to assess whether the PDM programme has been 
implemented in accordance with the PDM policy and guidelines with a specific focus on 
the financial inclusion pillar. Below are my findings;

l) 
Operation of Enterprise Groups 
 
Guideline 2.4 of the Parish Development Model Users 
Handbook Under the Parish Revolving Fund October 2022 
states that A PDM Enterprise Group refers to a group of 
persons whose members share common objectives and are 
engaged in common income generating agri-based activities 
or a range of activities along the agricultural value chain, 
e.g. coffee farming, storage, value addition of agricultural 
produce, etc. A PDM Enterprise Group shall comprise of a 
minimum of 10 and a Maximum of 30 households and shall 
be registered at the sub-county. 
 
i) 
I noted that 6,883 enterprise groups in 72 SACCOs in 
10 LGs were engaged in non-agro-based activities 
along the agricultural value chain. 
 
 
ii) 
I also noted that 4,012 enterprise groups in 1,209 
SACCOs in 67 LGs had less than the required 10 
members while 16,524 enterprise groups in 3,368 
SACCOs in 77 LGs had more than the required 30 
members. 
 
Failure to adhere to the stipulated number of households in 
enterprise groups and engagement in non-agro-based 
activities may affect the attainment of the PMD objectives. 
 
The Accounting Officer attributed this to system errors in 
PDMIS, data entry mistakes, limited access rights for data 
entrants, inadequate guidance and supervision by district 
and sub-county officers, initial lack of restrictions on group 
size, high demand for PRF funds, voluntary movement of 
members between enterprises, and delayed or incomplete 
sensitization of stakeholders on PDM operational guidelines. 
 
 
 
The Accounting Officers 
should 
enforce 
compliance 
with 
PDM 
guidelines 
by 
restructuring 
enterprise 
groups to have 10 to 30 
members, 
restricting 
activities to agro-based 
ventures, and providing 
continuous training and 
supervision 
for 
SACCO 
leaders and data entrants
