PART III: VALUE FOR MONEY AND ENGINEERING AUDITS 
 
3.1 
Value for Money Audits 
 
During the year, I undertook twenty five (25) Value for Money (VFM) audits across a 
broad range of Government programs, fulfilling my mandate as enshrined in Article 
163(3)(b) of the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda (as amended) and 
amplified in Section 21 of the National Audit Act Cap. 170. The audits were completed, 
and detailed individual reports were issued to the respective government entities. 
 
Out of these, five (5) audits were follow-ups on the implementation of 
recommendations from previous VFM audits conducted in earlier years. The remaining 
nineteen (19) audits relate to assessments undertaken during the current year. The 
summaries below present key findings from these VFM reports; 
 
3.1.1 Performance of the Financial Intelligence Authority in the Anti-Money 
Laundering Chain 
 
Introduction 
 
Money laundering is the process of turning illegitimately obtained property into 
seemingly legitimate property and it includes concealing or disguising the nature, 
source, location, disposition or movement of the proceeds of crime and any activity 
which constitutes a crime under Section 119 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act, Cap 
118. Money laundering is a global challenge that has far-reaching consequences on 
financial systems, economies and societal stability since it undermines legitimate 
businesses, reduces government revenues, damages financial systems, undermines 
national economies and currencies, erodes the integrity of a nation's financial 
institutions and distorts economic data leading to ineffective policy planning. 
 
The Financial Intelligence Authority (FIA) faces challenges in effectively monitoring and 
enforcing compliance with the Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Regulations due to limited 
human resources, inadequate inter agency collaboration and insufficient technological 
capacity among accountable institutions. Additionally, there is lack of public awareness 
on AML obligations due to limited FIA engagement with the public. This impacts FIA's 
capacity to swiftly receive, analyse, and distribute intelligence reports to Law 
Enforcement Agencies (LEAs) and other relevant authorities to support investigations 
and prosecutions related to financial crimes, thereby hindering the detection of 
emerging money laundering threats exacerbated by advancements in digital finance. 
 
In light of the above concerns, I undertook a VFM audit to assess the performance of 
the FIA in the AML Chain. 
 
Key Findings 
a) 
Limited reception of Suspicious transaction and activity reports by FIA 
from accountable persons 
 
Audit observed low submission of Suspicious transactions and activity reports by 
institutions in the Financial Services Sector other than banking institutions and foreign 

 
 
 
 
129 
 
 
 
exchange bureaus and non-submission of any suspicious transaction reports by licensing 
authorities and designated non-financial businesses and professions. This was due to 
non-registration of all licensed accountable persons; inadequate inspection and 
oversight of accountable persons for AMLA compliance; inadequate AML training and 
guidance to accountable persons and failure to impose administrative sanctions and 
fines to accountable persons for non-compliance to AMLA provisions. 
 
b) 
Failure by FIA to analyse all the received Suspicious transaction and 
activity reports from accountable persons 
 
FIA failed to analyse 1,086 reports out of 9,061 Suspicious and activity reports received 
by the end of the review period. Out of the 7,975 reports analysed, only 241 resulted 
into generation of intelligence reports and the difference of 7,734 are to be closed while 
gathering more information and intelligence. The pending analysis of reports and hence 
storage of the same was attributed to the delay and/or failure to obtain additional 
information from stakeholders. 
 
c) 
Delays in concluding investigations of disseminated intelligence 
reports 
 
There were delays in finalizing 79% of initiated money laundering investigations by 
selected Law Enforcement Agencies (LEAs) during the review period. The delays in 
concluding investigations was attributed to delayed feedback on information requests, 
limited coordination among stakeholders, parallel investigations, difficulty in tracing 
money launders provided in the FIA intelligence reports, the need to re-profile suspects 
and generate intelligence by LEAs in instances where the FIA intelligence led to wrong 
suspects and the absence of standard timelines for investigating cases. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
The Accounting Officer of FIA, in collaboration with the AML chain stakeholders should; 
 
i) 
Prioritize and establish measures to register all licensed and known non-licensed 
accountable persons operating in the country in compliance with the 
requirements in the AMLA. Prioritization of registration of accountable persons 
should be dependent on any latest National Risk Assessment undertaken for the 
country. 
 
ii) 
Strengthen the sanctions-based regime by imposing administrative sanctions and 
fines to accountable persons on noted non-compliance to the AMLA provisions 
such as failure to register with the authority. This should be in respect to the 
existing latest AML regulations. 
 
iii) 
Implement measures to assess the effectiveness of AML training programs, 
evaluating the extent to which knowledge is shared and skills are applied in 
practice to improve AML compliance. 
 

 
 
 
 
130 
 
 
 
iv) 
Implement ongoing sensitization and awareness campaigns for accountable 
persons, emphasizing their reporting obligations under AMLA. In addition, FIA 
should undertake continuous inspections to accountable persons to review their 
institutional policies and indicators majorly on forming suspicion, review on 
resolved STRs/SARs and transaction monitoring to check compliance with 
amendments periodically undertaken on AML laws and regulations. 
 
v) 
Undertake 
continuous 
sensitization 
and 
awareness 
campaigns 
of 
the 
masses/public on AML issues to allow ease of provision of information by the 
public to accountable persons as they undertake due diligence and KYC. This 
would potentially reduce delays in analysis of STRs/SARs owed to information 
requests made by FIA to accountable persons. 
 
vi) 
Increase their collaboration throughout the execution of all activities in the AML 
chain and increase exchange/sharing of information to address the noted delays 
investigating and concluding ML cases disseminated. In addition, increase 
implementation of capacity building programs focusing on investigation of ML 
cases. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The performance of FIA has improved over the years due to the initiatives undertaken in 
combating money laundering that included among others; 
 
i) 
Instituting mechanisms for reception of suspicious transaction and activity 
reports such as AML trainings and inspections, which enabled the FIA, record an 
overall 34% increase in the number of suspicious transactions and activities 
reported by accountable persons. 
 
ii) 
Establishing 
feedback 
mechanisms 
through 
strategic 
and 
operational 
engagements for information sharing, feedback tracking and reporting of 
outcomes with domestic and foreign stakeholders, which have facilitated 
learning and informed enhancements in reporting, analysis and dissemination 
and investigation by responsible players along the AML chain. 
 
However, to maximize its potential, the authority needs to address the weaknesses 
identified during the audit. These include limited coverage and registration of 
accountable persons in the DNFBP sector, inadequate enforcement of compliance 
through sanctions, insufficient planning and budgeting for AML trainings and 
inspections, incomplete analysis of filed reports, and weak feedback mechanisms. 
 
Addressing these issues will require enhanced coordination and collaboration among all 
AML stakeholders. This will not only enhance the FIA’s efficiency but also secure the 
country’s financial systems from ML activities and improve its capacity to respond to 
evolving Money Laundering threats. 
 

 
 
 
 
131 
 
 
 
3.1.2 Implementation of interventions to transition Households and Institutions 
from biomass use to clean cooking technology coordinated by the Ministry of 
Energy and Mineral Development 
 
Introduction 
 
Clean cooking is fundamental to public health, environmental sustainability and 
economic development. In Uganda, approximately 75% of households and nearly 95% 
of institutions (schools, hospitals, and prisons) continue to rely on traditional biomass 
(firewood, charcoal and crop residues) and inefficient three-stone fires or charcoal 
stoves for cooking. This practice causes severe indoor air pollution and its related 
effects, drives deforestation and increases household expenditure on fuel. 
 
Uganda committed under NDP-III and the Agenda 2030 to raise the share of clean 
energy for cooking through promotion of modern cooking solutions such as the 
Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG), electricity, ethanol, biogas and improved biomass 
stoves. The Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development, through its Clean Cooking Unit 
and various projects has been leading this transition agenda in collaboration with other 
players. 
 
Despite more than 15 years of interventions, reliance on traditional biomass remains 
overwhelmingly high. Considering this, the OAG undertook a Value for Money Audit to 
assess the performance of the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development in 
implementing interventions to transition households and institutions from biomass use 
to clean cooking technologies during the period 2022/23–2024/25. Below is a summary 
of the key findings and recommendations from the audit. The detailed findings are in 
chapter four of this report. 
 
Key Findings 
 
a) 
The share of households primarily using clean cooking energy rose by only 3.9% 
from 16.8% in 2019/20 to 20.7% in 2023/24. This was however still below the 
target of 40% of the population anticipated by 2023/24 in NDP III. Progress was 
heavily concentrated in Central, Eastern and Western regions while the northern 
region (specifically Acholi and West Nile) recorded declines. 
 
b) 
Awareness and sensitization campaigns were limited in scope and focused on a 
few technologies. The sensitizations were also limited in frequency and 
geographic coverage, which affected the objective of the sensitizations to 
demystify the misconceptions by the public about the use and practicality of 
modern clean cooking solutions. 
 
c) 
The selection of beneficiaries and the subsequent installation of clean cooking 
technologies 
was 
not 
informed 
by 
thorough 
needs 
assessments. 
 
This resulted in mismatches between provided technologies and actual 
beneficiary needs, contributing to high abandonment rates and underutilization 
of distributed technologies. 

 
 
 
 
132 
 
 
 
d) 
The absence of robust verification and beneficiary data management systems 
has led to duplication of beneficiaries across the different projects, incomplete 
records, and ineffective targeting, which compromise the equitable distribution 
of resources and the overall effectiveness of clean cooking initiatives. 
 
e) 
The high and unaffordable upfront costs of acquiring clean cooking technologies 
(of up to 2Mn for some technologies) even where subsidies are available, and 
the absence of flexible payment options such as PAYGO has deterred many 
households, especially low-income ones, from transitioning away from traditional 
cooking methods. This has also affected sustainability of the government 
interventions. 
 
f) 
The electricity cooking tariff for households aimed at promoting cooking with 
electricity where households that consume 81-150 units incur a lower cost is not 
meeting its intended objective as almost 75% of the intended beneficiaries are 
not connected to the grid. Even the 25% that are connected rarely consume the 
80 units. 
 
g) 
The infrastructure for refilling the LPG cylinders and ethanol remain inadequate 
outside urban centres. In rural areas, refill points are far from the beneficiaries, 
suffer frequent stockouts, making continued use of the distributed clean cooking 
technologies costly and inconvenient. As a result, beneficiaries often revert to 
traditional fuels or use both systems simultaneously, preventing a full transition 
to clean cooking. 
 
h) 
There was no systematic follow up on beneficiaries after distribution. The 
absence of comprehensive data collection, monitoring reports, and inadequate 
tracking of intervention outcomes have compromised the Ministry’s ability to 
learn from past challenges and make evidence-based corrective and policy 
decisions. 
 
i) 
Government has not developed or implemented effective financing mechanisms 
to mobilize adequate resources for Uganda’s transition to clean cooking. 
Although the Energy Transition Plan (ETP) provides investment estimates, it 
lacks a clear financing strategy, and the MEMD Strategic Plan was not updated 
to align with it. In addition, whereas the MEMD strategy projected that MEMD 
would mobilize UGX.338.03Bn for promoting clean cooking technologies, 
translating to approximately UGX.110Bn - UGX.113Bn p.a., for the three years 
under review, only UGX.26.085Bn was allocated for clean cooking interventions. 
Additionally, the ETP does not detail which interventions the government will 
finance especially those unlikely to attract investment/ donor support. As a 
result, several planned activities remain in the MEMD’s planning documents and 
have not been implemented. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
The Accounting Officer of MEMD should; 
 

 
 
 
 
133 
 
 
 
i) 
Develop and implement a National Clean Cooking Sensitization Strategy outlining 
clear goals, target audiences, delivery channels, and an implementation 
roadmap. The strategy should also integrate clean cooking sensitization 
activities. 
 
ii) 
Fast track the development of an automated beneficiary management system to 
ensure accurate identification, registration, and verification of beneficiaries and, 
to prevent duplication and ensure equitable distribution of resources. 
 
iii) 
Explore and implement financing mechanisms such as effective subsidies, pay-
as-you-go models, and instalment payment schemes to reduce the initial high 
upfront costs and enhance affordability for low-income households and 
institutions. The Electricity cooking tariff needs a review. 
 
iv) 
Establish a clear strategy to expand and regulate clean cooking fuel supply 
chains with a view to increase refill access in underserved areas, partnering with 
private suppliers/stakeholders, and integrating fuel availability planning into all 
clean cooking interventions. 
 
v) 
Institutionalize regular beneficiary follow-up, monitoring and evaluation of clean 
cooking interventions, and develop a comprehensive data system to track 
technologies, beneficiaries and outcomes across all projects and partners. 
 
vi) 
Develop a comprehensive national clean-cooking financing strategy that maps 
key barriers, quantifies funding needs, and establishes clear mechanisms for 
mobilizing and coordinating resources from public, private, and climate-finance 
sources. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
Government, through MEMD and its partners, has made limited progress towards the 
NDP III targets for increased household uptake of clean cooking technologies. While 
there has been a modest increase in the share of households using clean energy for 
cooking, this remains far below the planned trajectory, with regional disparities and 
reversals in some northern sub-regions. 
 
The main interventions, namely LPG project, Electricity Access Scale up project (EASP) 
and Clean Energy Access Project (CEAP), have not achieved their intended outputs at 
scale and have been constrained by inadequate sensitization, weak needs assessment, 
beneficiary targeting, and affordability and accessibility barriers. In addition, the audit 
established that there are gaps in compliance to established standards and inadequate 
refill infrastructure, limited follow-up and monitoring, insufficient financing and poor 
coordination. 
 
As a result, the transition from biomass to clean cooking is progressing slowly and 
unevenly, and there is a high risk that national clean cooking objectives will not be 
realized within the planned timeframe. 
 

 
 
 
 
134 
 
 
 
3.1.3 Provision of Mental Health Services by Ministry of Health 
 
Introduction 
 
Globally, mental disorders account for 13% of the disease burden with Uganda ranked 
among the top six (6) African countries with the highest cases of mental disorders. As of 
2022 it was estimated that 14 million Ugandans (approximately 32% of the country’s 
population) were suffering from some form of mental disorder and only an estimated 
10% of the these patients received treatment. 
 
The Ministry of Health (MoH), through its Division of Mental Health and Substance 
Abuse, is mandated to promote mental well-being, prevent and manage Mental, 
Neurological, and Substance use (MNS) conditions, and coordinate stakeholders to 
ensure effective service delivery. Despite efforts such as enactment of the Mental Health 
Act, Cap 308, introducing the Mental Health Gap Action Program (mhGAP) program, and 
commemorating mental health awareness events, several systemic challenges persist. 
 
Uganda’s mental health services remain underdeveloped and fragmented. Service 
coverage is limited, staffing levels are critically low, and funding allocations remain 
inadequate. The lack of integration of mental health into primary health care, coupled 
with weak community surveillance, stigma, and low awareness among schools and local 
leaders, continues to hinder access and treatment. Without significant investment in 
policy implementation, human resources, community-based care, and inter-sectoral 
coordination, Uganda risks failing to meet both national health objectives and 
international commitments on mental health and well-being. 
 
Against this background, the OAG conducted a VFM audit to assess the interventions of 
MoH ensuring effective provision of mental health services in Uganda for the period 
Financial Years; 2021/22–2023/24. Below are the key findings and recommendations 
from the audit. 
 
Key Findings 
 
The audit revealed a 27% increase in reported Mental, Neurological, and Substance use 
(MNS) cases between 2021 and 2023, indicating a growing disease burden. However, 
the effectiveness of interventions by the Ministry of Health in reversing this trend 
continues to be affected by the following shortcomings; 
 
a) 
Inadequate operationalization of the Mental Health Act Cap. 308 
 
While the Mental Health Act, Cap 308 was enacted in 2019, the Ministry of Health had 
not developed regulations for community mental health intergrattion and emergency 
and voluntary treatment to fully operationalize it six years later. The Mental Health 
Advisory Board and District Mental Health Focal Persons were not fully constituted 
during most of the audit period. As a result, mental health units in regional hospitals 
operated without standardized infrastructure, safety protocols, or clear management 
frameworks. 
 

 
 
 
 
135 
 
 
 
b) 
Inadequate resource allocation and staffing 
 
During the three (3) years reviewed, only 2% (UGX.1.1Bn) of the total mental health 
budget (UGX.58.5Bn) was allocated to the Mental Health Division of the Ministry of 
Health which is responsible for implementing MNS activities. In addition, Uganda had 
only 53 psychiatrists (one per million people) well below the WHO recommendation of 
1: 10,000. Most regional and district facilities lacked trained personnel, medicines, and 
equipment to manage mental health conditions effectively. 
 
c) 
Weak treatment, rehabilitation, and supervision mechanisms 
 
Health facilities lacked adequate infrastructure, specialized clinics for children and 
pregnant mothers, and functional rehabilitation programs. Only a few provided 
psychosocial support or follow-up services. Supervision by the Mental Health Division 
and Regional Referral Hospitals was irregular, and monitoring reports were incomplete. 
216 unaccredited private rehabilitation centres were also operating without oversight, 
posing safety risks to patients. 
 
d) 
Limited awareness and community outreach 
 
Only 19 of the 65 the sampled health facilities (29%), conducted mental health 
outreach activities, and the Ministry did not implement targeted awareness programs for 
faith leaders, traditional healers, or local governance structures. Consequently, 
misconceptions and stigma remain high, with over 60% of individuals seeking care first 
from traditional healers. Most facilities and schools lacked Information, Education, and 
Communication (IEC) materials to promote awareness. 
 
e) 
Weak multi-sectoral coordination 
 
Although MoH initiated plans to establish an inter-ministerial and technical working 
committee on mental health, there was no evidence that this committee was fully 
functional. There was no evidence of approved Terms of Reference or functional 
meetings. The absence of these structures hindered collaboration with key ministries 
such as Education, Gender, and Local Government, leading to fragmented service 
delivery and duplication of efforts. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
a) 
Regulatory and institutional strengthening 
 
i) 
Fast-track approval and implementation of Mental Health Regulations to fully 
operationalize the Act. 
ii) 
Ensure that the inter-ministerial and technical working committees on mental 
health are operationalized and fully functional. 
iii) 
Liaise with the relevant stakeholders to have the minimum standards for mental 
health units approved and fully implemented by all the Health facilities providing 
the MNS service. 
 

 
 
 
 
136 
 
 
 
b) 
Improve Funding and Human Resources 
 
i) 
Prioritize funding of Mental Health activities within the Ministry of Health budget 
especially the service delivery (non-wage) activities. 
ii) 
Fast track the operationalization and filling of the new staffing structure which 
provides for more mental health professionals at the different levels of delivery 
service. 
 
c) 
Strengthen Treatment, Rehabilitation, and Supervision 
 
i) 
Prioritize training of health workers at all levels in matters of mental health 
which include; diagnostics, application of the available treatment protocols, use 
of specialized equipment among others. 
ii) 
Enhance and strengthen regulatory oversight over all private practitioners 
managing mental health matters by ensuring that the Mental Health Advisory 
Board is fully functional. In addition, the Ministry should expedite the approval of 
the minimum practicing standards to facilitate accreditation of practitioners. 
 
d) 
Increase Awareness and Community Engagement 
 
i) 
Enhance allocation of funds meant for mental health activities within the MOH 
budget to facilitate planned community sensitizations and dissemination of IEC 
materials to schools and health facilities. 
ii) 
Fast track and scale up the deployment of the Community Health extension 
works to supplement the Village Health Teams (VHTs) in undertaking 
sensitizations within the communities. 
 
e) 
Enhance Coordination and Integration 
 
i) 
Review and enhance the current coordination frameworks and measures with a 
view of ensuring that coordination among stakeholders is more structured, 
harmonized and more effective. 
 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The Ministry of Health has made good progress in developing laws, policies, and 
awareness programs on mental health. However, there are still areas that need 
attention to improve the provision of Mental Health services. The Mental Health Act, Cap 
308, is yet to be fully operationalized, funding and community awareness for Mental 
health is also still very low. Many facilities and private health care providers lack 
professional mental health staff, struggle to provide proper treatment and rehabilitation 
of patients, and are hardly supervised. Implementation of the recommendation 
proposed in this report will go a long way in improving the provision of mental health 
services in the country. 
 

 
 
 
 
137 
 
 
 
3.1.4 Implementation of Land Administration by the Ministry of Lands, Housing and 
Urban Development through the Ministry Zonal Offices 
 
Introduction 
 
Land administration refers to the processes and systems through which land use, 
ownership, and transfer are managed and regulated. According to international good 
practices and Uganda’s legal framework, effective land administration encompasses five 
core functions; Land registration, Land surveying, Land valuation, Land use planning 
and Dispute resolution. 
 
The Ministry of Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development (MOLHUD) is 
mandated to ensure rational, sustainable, and effective use and management of land; 
orderly development of urban and rural areas; and safe, planned, and adequate housing 
for socio-economic development”. 
 
The Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development (MOLHUD) established Ministry 
Zonal Offices (MZOs) across the country with the pilot phase in 2013 of six (6) MZOs of 
Kampala, Wakiso, Mukono, Jinja, Masaka and Mbarara after the Uganda National Lands 
Information System (UgNLIS) was developed. By 2018, fourteen (14) additional MZOs 
had been rolled-out to Lira, Fort Portal, Kibaale, Masindi, Arua, Gulu, Mbale, Mityana, 
Luwero, Mpigi, Tororo, Soroti, Moroto, Kabale, and Rukungiri MZOs. This was done as 
an effort to decentralize and bring land administration services closer to the people. 
These regional offices are responsible for operationalizing the Uganda National Lands 
Information System (UgNLIS) and providing land services on behalf of MOLHUD. 
 
Despite the creation of Ministry Zonal Offices (MZOs) and introduction of the National 
Lands Information System (NLIS) in 2013 for implementation of land administration in 
Uganda, there are still challenges in the provision of land services such as; delays in 
processing of land titles by the MZOs, land fraud arising from forgeries of land titles and 
fraudulent land transactions, poor inter-agency coordination in regard to MDAs involved 
land administration and MOLHUD meeting its objectives in Land admin, limited 
sensitization 
on 
land 
services 
offered 
through 
land 
administration 
by 
the 
MZOs/MOLHUD. 
 
It is against this background that the OAG conducted a VFM audit on the 
implementation of Land Administration by MOLHUD through the MZOs. Below are the 
summarised key audit findings and recommendations. The detailed findings are in 
chapter 4 of this report. 
 
Key Findings 
 
a) 
Out of a total of 934,645 land registration applications that were received over 
the period, only 657,384 applications were completed. 
 
b) 
Despite the digitalisation, processing of land transactions exceeded the standard 
timelines set in the Client Service Charter, with turnaround times consistently 
longer than the standard for each transaction type across all land offices. 

 
 
 
 
138 
 
 
 
 
The average completion rate per transaction in all the MZOs deteriorated over 
the years from 77% in 2021/22 to 41% in 2024/25. 
 
c) 
The delays were mainly caused by incomplete digitisation and problems within 
the Uganda National Land Information System (UgNLIS), such as missing parcel 
information, incomplete or inaccurate mapping, weak front-desk verification 
processes and survey details that could not be reliably aligned to the cadastral 
map. 
 
d) 
Forged titles, double titling and fraudulent transactions still exist with Wakiso-
Busiro MZO taking the lead for such cases. Although the MOLHUD has made 
some efforts to mitigate land fraud, audit noted that staff at MZOs lack training 
and controls for detecting forged documents, for example, national IDs, land 
titles, LC recommendation letters, etc. 
 
e) 
Despite MOLHUD’s commitment to sensitize citizens, this was not consistently 
done at different levels across MZOs as many clients are unaware of the MLIS 
and required documentation. This has negatively impacted service delivery, 
transparency, and public awareness. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer of MOLHUD to; 
 
i) 
Develop and implement a time-bound data cleaning and digitisation plan to clear 
the backlog of scanned, but uncommitted records on the NLIS that are "stuck at 
Quality Control." 
 
ii) 
Strengthen front-desk verification through continuous training of receptionists 
and data entry clerks on the required documentation and make them responsible 
for verifying all client submissions before acceptance. 
 
iii) 
Provide regular training to lands officers and registrars on fraud detection 
techniques, document verification, and emerging fraud patterns to strengthen 
their ability to identify and respond to suspicious transactions. 
 
iv) 
Develop and issue comprehensive fraud prevention guidelines to all MZOs, 
clearly outlining procedures for fraud detection to ensure consistency in handling 
suspected fraud across zones. 
 
v) 
Strengthen the integration and coordination with NIRA, Courts of Law, Police 
and the public. 
 
vi) 
MOLHUD to prioritize full integration of the NLIS with external databases such as 
NIRA, URA, URSB, and the Passport Office to enable automated verification of 
identity, ownership, and transaction authenticity. 

 
 
 
 
139 
 
 
 
 
vii) 
Develop a national standardised sensitization strategy that guides all MZOs on 
how to conduct regular and uniform outreach programs. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
While the MOLHUD has made significant progress in expanding access to land services 
through the establishment of 22 Ministry Zonal Offices and the rollout of the National 
Land Information System (NLIS), the overall implementation of land administration is 
still falling short of expectations. 
 
The Ministry has improved coverage and processed a large number of land transactions, 
but service delivery remains slow and inconsistent. Most applications are not completed 
within the timelines set in the Client Charter, and a substantial backlog continues to 
grow each year. Despite the NLIS, the rate of completed registration of titles over the 4-
year period of review went down from 77% in 2021/22 to only 41% in 2024/25. The 
main causes of these delays include incomplete digitization of land records, poor data 
quality in the NLIS, weak document verification at the front desk, and limited client 
awareness of required documents. Fraud risk management is still weak, with no unified 
fraud-prevention guidelines, limited internal audits, and detection efforts that rely 
heavily on individual staff experience rather than structured systems. 
 
Significant improvements in data quality, staff capacity, fraud detection and mitigation, 
inter-agency integration, and citizen sensitization are necessary for the Ministry to fully 
achieve its mandate of land administration. 
 
 
3.1.5 Monitoring and Enforcement of Noise Pollution Standards by NEMA and 
selected Cities 
 
Introduction 
 
Noise pollution is defined as the release of uncontrolled, excessive sound that disrupts 
Human Health and Environmental Equality and is an emerging public health and 
environmental issue in Uganda's urban areas. The National Environment Management 
Authority (NEMA) and the Local Governments are responsible for regulating noise levels 
in accordance with the National Environment Act, Cap 181, and the National 
Environment (Noise Standards and Control) Regulations 2003. However, there has been 
persistent public outcry and complaints of unchecked noise levels, particularly in all the 
major cities and urban areas. 
 
The OAG undertook a VFM to assess the effectiveness of NEMA and selected cities in 
monitoring and enforcing noise pollution standards with the objective of ascertaining the 
challenges in regulating noise pollution and providing recommendations to address 
these challenges. 
 
Below is a summary of the key findings and recommendations from the audit. The 
detailed findings are in chapter four of this report. 

 
 
 
 
140 
 
 
 
Key Findings 
 
The audit noted areas of commendable performance for instance: NEMA had conducted 
joint inspections with city authorities and the Environmental Protection Force (EPF) 
during the period under review. NEMA is also in the process of revising the noise 
pollution regulations and acquired sound level meters to aid monitoring. 
 
Despite these efforts, significant challenges remained, with noise levels above 
permissible levels in 28 out of 29 facilities visited. 91% of complaints registered with 
NEMA were due to excess noise from places of entertainment (59%) and places of 
worship (32%). 
 
The audit identified the following performance gaps that are undermining the 
effectiveness of efforts by NEMA and the selected cities to monitor and enforce noise 
regulations across the country; 
 
a) 
There are no formal risk-based assessment procedures to identify and prioritize 
hotspots or sensitive receptors like schools, hospitals, residential areas. NEMA 
and selected cities mainly responded to noise complaints reactively. As a result, 
monitoring and enforcement efforts were not systematically targeted to areas of 
highest risk, limiting effectiveness of regulatory interventions. 
 
b) 
NEMA and the selected cities do not systematically and comprehensively capture 
and track noise complaints. Specifically, complaints received through walk-ins 
and calls were undocumented while only 10.8% and 46% of the complaints 
received in writing were investigated and resolved by NEMA and the respective 
Cities. 
 
c) 
Staffing inadequacies is one of the main challenges affecting the monitoring of 
noise standards. There were only 23 technical staff in NEMA, and 17 staff for the 
eight (8 cities) selected to execute the enormous mandate. Moreover, even 
these do not prioritise noise as there are other competing environment 
responsibilities and cover wide geographical areas resulting in irregular 
inspections and delays in handling noise-related cases. 
 
d) 
There was insufficient equipment for noise monitoring and enforcement with 
only 17 operational sound level meters for both NEMA and selected cities 
(NEMA: 9, cities: 8). In addition, only one facility out of the 29 visited had 
installed sound-level measuring equipment, contrary to the legal requirement. 
This was because none of the city councils made installation a condition for 
approval of occupation. Additionally, the equipment are all not regularly 
calibrated to enable the collection of reliable, credible, and admissible evidence 
on noise levels and trends for decision making and enforcement. 
 
e) 
Furthermore, capacity building for city environmental officers on noise pollution 
was limited. Only one officer (from Masaka) attended NEMA’s Environmental 
Inspector training during the review period, and the training did not cover 
practical aspects of noise measurement or corrective action. 

 
 
 
 
141 
 
 
 
 
Consequently, 
officers 
demonstrated 
inconsistencies 
(and 
at 
times 
contradictions) in their monitoring and enforcement actions. 
 
f) 
Enforcement actions undertaken by NEMA and the selected cities are 
inconsistent, not evidence-based, and often do not result in significant reduction 
of repeat violations due to the absence of structured escalation or tracking 
system, enabling chronic violators to resume operations with impunity and 
leaving noise pollution essentially unregulated despite statutory mandates. Of 
the 16 facilities inspected in Kampala, Jinja, Soroti, Lira, and Hoima, each 
previously subjected to enforcement actions such as verbal warnings, 
improvement notices, or equipment impoundment, 15 (94%) were still found to 
be violating noise pollution standards. 
 
g) 
Only NEMA and KCCA publicised dedicated helplines for reporting noise 
complaints on their websites or social media platforms. There is no structured 
sensitisation efforts in the rest of the selected cities. Throughout the review 
period, 
only 
NEMA, 
KCCA 
and 
Lira 
conducted 
compliance-assistance 
engagements (one each) for polluters; otherwise, engagement was largely 
limited to punitive enforcement. 
 
h) 
Coordination among stakeholders is weak, with roles sometimes mixed up and 
conflicting priorities between revenue collection and environmental compliance. 
 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
NEMA and the cities should; 
 
i) 
Develop a comprehensive, data-driven system to map noise hotspots and 
sensitive receptors, and to flag and prioritise high-risk cases. 
 
ii) 
Fast track the completion and roll out of the Environment Licensing and 
Management Information System (ELMIS) complaint module and ensure that it 
captures all complaints regardless of channel (phone, walk-in, social media, 
etc.), tracks every stage from receipt to closure, flagging repeat offenders, 
among others. 
 
iii) 
Develop, disseminate and enforce Standard Operating Procedures to guide in 
recording, prioritizing, investigating, and providing feedback on noise complaints 
with clear enforcement timelines ensuring that responses are prompt and 
consistent. 
 
iv) 
In consultation with the Ministry of Public Service, prioritize recruitment and 
deployment of more dedicated officers for noise monitoring and enforcement, 
and provide facilitation for after-hours operations. 
 

 
 
 
 
142 
 
 
 
v) 
Ensure enforcement actions are evidence based and all enforcement actions 
undertaken are documented to ease follow up. 
 
vi) 
Develop and implement a targeted communication strategy on noise pollution 
that integrates clear, accessible messages into all sensitisation channels to raise 
public awareness of permissible noise levels, reporting procedures, and 
enforcement actions. This strategy should also strengthen compliance assistance 
through structured, ongoing engagement with noise polluters to promote 
adherence to regulations. 
 
vii) 
Strengthen inter-agency coordination by clarifying institutional roles and 
obligations in the monitoring and enforcement of noise pollution standards. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
While some progress has been made in monitoring and enforcement of noise pollution 
standard by NEMA and selected cities, the efforts remain largely reactive, under 
resourced and poorly coordinated. The absence of structured systems for identifying 
and prioritising noise hotspots, tracking complaints, and enforcing standards, combined 
with inadequate staffing, limited public awareness and weak stakeholder coordination, 
undermines the effectiveness of the current interventions. As a result, the systems in 
place are not yet sufficient to achieve sustained reductions in repeat violations or 
adequately address community complaints. 
 
 
3.1.6 Implementation of the Affirmative Action Programmes by Office of the Prime 
Minister 
 
Introduction 
 
Affirmative action programmes were designed by the Government of Uganda to address 
imbalances of existing marginalized groups and increase opportunities for people who 
are underrepresented in various areas of society. The programmes are implemented by 
the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) through established ministries of Karamoja 
Affairs, Northern Uganda affairs, Luwero-Rwenzori affairs, Bunyoro and Teso affairs. 
 
The affirmative action interventions include infrastructural development projects such as 
construction of dormitory blocks in primary and secondary schools, staff houses, 
classroom blocks, multi-purpose halls, construction and renovation of health centres 
etc.; distribution of material items such as iron sheets, hand hoes, tractors, ox-ploughs, 
sewing machines etc.; distribution of goats, heifers and oxen in northern Uganda and 
Karamoja regions, and supporting community sub projects and micro projects to 
enhance household incomes for youth, women, veterans, Person Living With Disabilities 
(PLWDs) in war-affected areas, refugee settlements and host communities. 
 
I undertook a Value for money audit to assess the extent of implementation of the 
affirmative action interventions by the Office of the Prime Minister. Below are the key 
findings of the audit. 
 

 
 
 
 
143 
 
 
 
Key Findings 
 
Notable progress was observed in the implementation of the affirmative action 
interventions which included the following; 
 
i) 
Distributed 63,944 iron sheets to beneficiary institutions and individuals in 
Northern Uganda, Karamoja region, Luwero-Rwenzori, Teso and Bunyoro sub 
regions. 
ii) 
236 heifers and 74,340 different breeds of goats were distributed to beneficiaries 
in Karamoja region and Northern Uganda. 
iii) 
1,239 micro project groups were supported in various affirmative action regions 
to enhance the social economic welfare and livelihoods of targeted beneficiaries 
iv) 
7,007 hand hoes were distributed to beneficiaries in Bunyoro sub-region for 
livelihood support. 
 
Despite the above notable achievements, the audit identified areas that require targeted 
improvement to enhance implementation of affirmative action interventions and ensure 
realization of the set programme outcomes. The areas are summarized below: 
 
Overall extent of implementation of affirmative action interventions 
 
Out of the selected key 36 activities under the affirmative action outputs, audit noted 11 
(30.6%) were fully implemented, 12 (33.3%) were partially implemented, 11 (30.6%) 
were not implemented and 2 (5.6%), the extent of implementation could not be 
established due to lack of performance targets/ indicators. The failure to fully implement 
the above planned activities was attributed to several factors as discussed below; 
 
i) 
Inadequate planning and budgeting for affirmative action interventions despite 
OPM spending UGX.75,018,000 in the FY 2022/2023 on development planning 
activities such as progress tracking and validation of Busoga Development Plan, 
there were no approved programme plans by NPA for implementation by OPM 
during the National Development Planning period (2020/2021-2024/2025). 
 
ii) 
Failure by OPM to undertake comprehensive needs assessment using a 
participatory approach and involving the targeted beneficiaries to come up with 
the implemented interventions over the years under review in the 32 sampled 
Local Governments (LGs). This resulted into identifying interventions that could 
not be effectively utilized and sustained in the affirmative action regions of 
Northern Uganda, Teso, Karamoja, Bunyoro and Luwero-Rwenzori over the 
three-year period. 
 
iii) 
All the 35 supported beneficiary groups under Luwero-Rwenzori Triangle, 88 
under Teso Affairs, and 46 under Bunyoro affairs started actual micro grant 
projects implementation after the financial year end (30th June, 2024). This was 
due to failure by OPM to transfer funds on a quarterly basis as per the approved 
work plans and the late transfer of grant funds to the LGs which further resulted 
into delayed disbursement of funds to the beneficiary groups by LGs. 
 

 
 
 
 
144 
 
 
 
iv) 
51 out of the 137 sampled beneficiaries who received funding worth 
UGX.229,200,000, had deviated from the initially approved projects after receipt 
of micro grants. This affects the sustainability of the interventions as the 
changed projects were not subjected to the financial evaluation, technical 
capacity assessments, economic and commercial viability evaluations for 
effective implementation. 
 
v) 
Out of the 236 heifers procured and distributed in Northern Uganda and West 
Nile, 67 heifers worth UGX.184,250,000 were not in-calf/ pregnant as per the 
requirements. This affected the anticipated multiplier effect to sustainably 
improve the economic wellbeing of households within the West Nile, Acholi and 
Lango sub-regions. 
 
vi) 
45 heifers out of the sampled 119 heifers worth UGX.327,250,000 had died by 
the time of audit inspection. 221 goats out of the sampled 266 goats were dead 
by the time of audit inspection (September, 2024) two years after actual 
distribution in FY 2022/2023. This affected the realization of the programme 
objectives of improving the social economic wellbeing of households, peace 
building and reconciliation within the sub-regions. 
 
vii) 
9,761 iron sheets worth UGX.673,499,239 out of the distributed 18, 921 iron 
sheets during FYs 2021/2022 and 2022/23 had not been utilized by the 
beneficiary institutions. Non-utilization of the distributed iron sheets by the 
beneficiary institutions defeats the purpose of the intervention. 
 
viii) 
Inadequate monitoring of affirmative action interventions. OPM did not prepare 
annual M&E work plans and budgets for the affirmative action interventions in 
the years under review to guide Government in the identification and allocation 
of funds specifically for routine monitoring. Additionally, there were no tools to 
facilitate routine data collection, analysis and reporting of information on the 
progress of interventions under the various programmes. This resulted into 
failure by OPM and other key stakeholders to track progress of programme 
indicators and measure the impact of the projects. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
I advise the Accounting Officer of OPM to; 
 
i) 
Prioritize the regional development planning activities in the annual work plans 
and budgets to trigger funds identification and allocation by MoFPED to facilitate 
strategic regional development planning for the next five-year period 
(2025/2026-2029/30). 
 
ii) 
Strengthen stakeholder involvement and close collaborations between OPM, local 
Government technical teams and community representatives so as to 
significantly align the interventions with community needs. 
 

 
 
 
 
145 
 
 
 
iii) 
Ensure that micro grant funds are transferred to districts, cities, and 
municipalities in a timely manner according to the approved plan quarterly 
schedules, thereby preventing late disbursement to beneficiary groups. 
 
iv) 
Ensure strict adherence to grant guidelines. OPM and Local Governments should 
establish and enforce clear sanctions for beneficiaries who deviate from 
approved project plans without authorization to ensure compliance and maintain 
the integrity of the program objectives. 
 
v) 
Ensure that Government officials from Ministry of Agriculture, NAADs and DLGs 
responsible for the contract management for procurement and distribution of 
heifers are held accountable for clearance of heifers that were not in 
conformance to quality specifications. 
 
vi) 
Widely engage with District Veterinary Officers and other relevant technical staff 
in MAAIF to determine suitable breeds based on local climate and disease 
profiles. This will enhance the selection of livestock more likely to thrive in the 
respective districts, reducing mortality rates. 
 
vii) 
Undertake comprehensive needs assessments to identify the actual requirements 
of each beneficiary institution, including the quantity of iron sheets needed and 
also evaluating the institutions’ readiness to utilize the materials. 
 
viii) 
Prioritize establishing a comprehensive monitoring and evaluation (M&E) 
framework. This framework should include detailed M&E tools and procedures to 
facilitate routine data collection, analysis, and performance reporting. 
Implementing such a system will enable evidence-based decision-making and 
enhance OPM’s ability to measure the effectiveness of affirmative action 
interventions. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
Government of Uganda through the Office of the Prime Minister has undertaken 
interventions under five designed programmes such as procurement and distribution of 
material items, development of guidelines for affirmative action programme 
implementation, support to micro projects and infrastructure projects of rehabilitation of 
schools, boreholes and roads. 
 
However, the audit has identified gaps that OPM needs to address going forward to 
effectively implement the affirmative actions. These include inadequate planning and 
budgeting for affirmative action interventions, inadequate beneficiary needs assessment 
and identification, delayed implementation of micro grant projects by beneficiary 
groups, implementation of unapproved micro grant projects by beneficiary groups, 
under-utilisation of distributed material items by beneficiaries and inadequate 
monitoring of affirmative action interventions. 
 
Addressing the identified issues requires enhanced collaboration and coordination 
among all affirmative action programmes stakeholders. 

 
 
 
 
146 
 
 
 
3.1.7 Marketing and Branding of Tourism activities by the Ministry of Tourism 
Wildlife and Antiquities and Uganda Tourism Board 
 
Introduction 
 
Tourism remains among the major contributors to Uganda’s economy and continues to 
be on a positive trend. In the year 2024, tourism contributed 6.6% to Uganda’s GDP 
and directly supported 803,691 jobs, representing 7.2% of the country’s total 
employment8 demonstrating tourism’s resilience and continued contribution to job 
creation9. 
 
Marketing of tourism activities involves responsible agencies finding out what the 
customers want, creating products of high value for customers, then pricing and 
publicizing them effectively. Branding, on the other hand, is the creation of an attractive 
identity for a destination that sets it apart from other tourism locations.10 In Uganda it 
involves undertaking both domestic and international promotional activities to popularise 
the explore Uganda brand among other interventions. It also entails registration, 
inspection and licensing of tourism facilities. 
 
Uganda Tourism Board (UTB) takes lead in Tourism marketing and branding in Uganda. 
It is responsible for marketing all tourism products and services in the country both 
internally and externally. UTB performs this task with support from Ministry of Tourism 
Wildlife and Antiquities (MoTWA) and other players in the industry. 
 
I undertook a Value for Money Audit to assess the effectiveness of Tourism and 
branding interventions by UTB and MoTWA and below are the key findings and 
recommendations; 
 
Key Findings 
 
UTB and MoTWA made the following key achievements in relation to marketing and 
branding Uganda; 
 
i) 
Foreign exchange earnings from Tourism improved steadily over the three 
financial years from USD.1.025Bn in 2022/23 to USD.1.28Bn in 2024/25 while 
the Share of Tourism to GDP increased from 5.5% to 5.7% over the same 
period. Although this was lower than the NDP III targets. 
 
ii) 
UTB registered 1,416 and licensed 2,215 tour operators, achieving 283% and 
738% of the targets respectively, which demonstrates notable improvement in 
compliance and formalization of tour operations.

iii) 
The International Congress and Convention Association (ICCA) Africa 2024, 
ranked Uganda 7th, amongst the first 15 MICE events organizing countries in 
Africa. 
 
iv) 
A consistent increase in both domestic and international tourist numbers over 
the three-year period (FY 2022/23–2024/25) was recorded. Domestic tourism 
registered the more significant growth, rising from 1,012,129 tourists in FY 
2022/23 to 2,796,451 in FY 2024/25. 
 
v) 
The tourism policy was reviewed and launched on 26th November 2025. 
 
vi) 
Direct tourism revenue mainly from park entry fees, museums, Uganda Wildlife 
Education Centre (UWEC) and cultural sites increased in the three years under 
review, from UGX.414Bn in FY 2022/23 to UGX.424.6Bn in FY 2024/25. 
 
Despite the above achievements, the audit identified several areas that require targeted 
improvement to enhance overall performance and ensure full realization of the tourism 
marketing and branding interventions by MoTWA and UTB to ensure a competitive and 
sustainable tourist destination in Uganda. 
 
Overall extent of implementation of marketing and branding of tourism 
activities by MoTWA and UTB 
 
Out of the sampled 59 planned activities for implementation by MoTWA (Department of 
Product Development and Investment Promotion) over the three years under review, 46 
(77.9%) were fully achieved, 9 (15.2%) were partially achieved, and 2 (3.4%) were not 
implemented. Similarly, for UTB, out of the 135 sampled activities, 101 (74.8%) were 
fully achieved, 18 (13.0%) were partially achieved, and 16 (11.8%) were not 
implemented. Below are some of the factors explaining the above performance; 
 
a) 
Ineffective legal and regulatory framework 
 
Although MoTWA had developed a number of key policies and regulations, several 
critical frameworks remained either due for review or had not been developed as 
required under the Tourism Act, Cap. 82. The absence and delayed development of 
policies and guidelines for effective regulation of the tourism sector has resulted into a 
number of weaknesses and gaps such as regulatory overlaps, limited enforcement of 
quality standards and inefficiencies in service delivery. 
 
Failure to develop regulations and policies that provide UTB with the mandate to 
inspect, register and license restaurants to ensure compliance with standards, a total of 
4,272 (31.8%) of the cumulative planned target of tourism facilities remained 
unregistered, uninspected and unlicensed over the three-year period. In addition, 1,251, 
representing 28.8%, of the tourism facilities continued to operate with expired licenses. 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
148 
 
 
 
b) 
Inadequate classification and grading of Hotels/Accommodation 
facilities 
 
Only 18% of the strategic plan targets and 47% of the annual work plan targets for 
classification of hotels/ accommodation facilities were achieved over the three-year 
period. As a result, the standardization and competitiveness of Uganda’s tourism sector 
was undermined. 
 
c) 
Lack of a National investment profile of tourism sites and products 
 
UTB had not developed a national tourism investment profile to guide the identification 
and promotion of tourism investment opportunities across the country. This implies that 
Government investments in the tourism sector are not guided by comprehensive 
assessments of tourism needs and growth opportunities. 
 
d) 
Ineffective domestic tourism promotional campaigns 
 
The ministry planned to implement Explore Uganda domestic tourism campaigns but did 
not set target audience/ segment to be reached to guide planning and budgeting for 
such campaigns. Additionally, whereas the ministry planned to implement 12 
campaigns, 10 (83%) were reported to have been achieved leaving 2 (16.7%) un-
implemented due to budget constraints. There was also non-compliance with the 
approved Explore Uganda branding guidelines which undermined the brand’s 
professional image, reduced message clarity, and weakened overall brand recognition 
and credibility. 
 
e) 
Ineffective international tourism promotional campaigns 
 
UTB did not meet the set targets for international arrivals. Out of the planned total 
arrivals of 4,787,292 over the three FYs, 3,460,613 were received indicating a shortfall 
of 1,346,679 (27.7%) of the planned target. Out of the total arrivals, only 264,746 
(19%) were leisure tourists. This results into limited revenue generation from leisure 
tourism. 
 
f) 
Uncompetitive international Bids for MICE events 
 
Out of the 45 bids submitted to international conference organizers (professional 
associations), 18 (40%) were dropped, 14 (31.1%) were lost and only 12 (26.7%) 
passed. It was further noted that of the 12 bids won, only 4 (33%) conferences were 
successfully hosted in Uganda and 8 (67%) conferences did not take place as a result of 
dropped and lost bids. UTB/UCB did not achieve the 130 conferences/ events from 
intergovernmental and non-governmental Association meetings over the five-year 
period. This resulted into loss of MICE potential revenue worth USD.100Mn an 
equivalent of (UGX.361.44Bn). 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
149 
 
 
 
g) 
Failure to conduct Return on Investment (ROI) evaluations for MICE 
Activities by UTB/UCB 
 
Whereas Uganda Conventional Bureau (UCB) conducted expected return on MICE 
investments for forecasting and planning purposes, it did not conduct actual return on 
Investment (ROI) evaluations to assess and measure the economic value of its 
conducted MICE activities despite expenditure of UGX.1.827Bn on MICE activities over 
the three years. As a result, without ROI evaluations, UTB/UCB could not demonstrate 
whether public funds allocated and spent on marketing MICE exhibitions worth 
UGX.1.827Bn yielded the expected economic impact. 
 
h) 
Irregular selection of hosted buyers by both UTB and MoTWA that 
participated in Pearl of Africa Tourism Expo (POATE) 
 
Out of the 79 hosted buyers invited by MoTWA, 56 (55%) had not registered through 
the POATE portal. Similarly, out of the 153 hosted buyers invited for POATE 2023 and 
2024 by UTB, 43 (28%) had not registered through the portal. There is a risk that such 
un vetted and unregistered hosted buyers may not champion the marketing and 
promotion of tourism for Uganda. 
 
i) 
Failure to undertake impact evaluation studies 
 
MoTWA and UTB did not undertake impact evaluation studies on key marketing 
interventions to assess their effectiveness and inform future strategic adjustments. 
These interventions included both domestic and international events/ interventions such 
as; hiring of Market Destination Representatives (MDRs), POATE, participation in 
international expos such as ITB Berlin (Internationale Tourismus-Börse Berlin) and the 
Magical Kenya Travel Expo (MKTE), MITT Russia Expo, and the United States Tour 
Operators Association (USTOA) Conference & Marketplace. This affects evidence-based 
decision-making and may affect realization of strategic tourism outcomes. 
 
j) 
Limited collaboration arrangements between MoTWA and other 
stakeholders 
 
Limited collaboration arrangements between MoTWA and other stakeholders such as 
UTB, Local Governments and UHOA to ensure robust data collection, analysis and 
validation mechanisms such as Data Quality Assessments (DQAs) are put in place to 
ensure reliable reporting of tourism information. 
 
k) 
Lack of integrated systems between the two institutions 
 
Lack of integrated systems between the two institutions to facilitate validation and 
information sharing for evidence based reporting. Whereas UTB has a quality Assurance 
system (QAS) for registration, inspection and licensing purposes, it was not integrated 
with TIMS at MOTWA to ensure data validation and information sharing. This resulted 
into inconsistencies in the reported tourism statistics. 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
150 
 
 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
I advise the Accounting Officers of MoTWA/UTB to; 
 
i) 
Ensure that policy formulation and review activities are prioritized in the annual 
work plans and adequately funded to prevent delays caused by budgetary 
constraints. 
 
ii) 
Strengthen the Quality Assurance function by revising its organizational structure 
to increase staffing levels and establish regional presence for more effective 
decentralized inspection and licensing. Additionally, a hybrid implementation 
model, leveraging temporary or contract field inspectors and accredited third-
party assessors during peak periods may be adopted to ensure timely service 
delivery. 
 
iii) 
Engage Accommodation facilities through targeted sensitization and technical 
support to enhance their preparedness for classification, particularly for higher 
star ratings. In addition, UTB should continuously engage Government to release 
the full budget allocation for classification exercises and enable comprehensive 
nationwide assessments. 
 
iv) 
Prioritize the development of a comprehensive national tourism investment 
profile and catalogue by integrating the activities into its annual work plans to 
facilitate budgetary allocations. 
 
v) 
Conduct comprehensive tourism research and market segmentation studies to 
determine target audiences, regional preferences, and participation trends. This 
will enable evidence-based planning, budgeting, and evaluation of domestic 
tourism campaigns. 
 
vi) 
Advocate for increased and sustained budgetary allocations for international 
tourism activities to ensure consistent participation in global events and 
campaigns. Additionally, the Board should explore alternative funding sources, 
including partnerships with the private sector and development partners, to 
supplement Government funding and maintain Uganda’s visibility and 
competitiveness in international tourism markets. 
 
vii) 
Establish a formal coordination mechanism with key MDAs and Professional 
Associations to jointly plan, budget, and bid for international conferences. This 
framework will ensure clear roles, timelines, and communication channels to 
ensure early engagement and effective collaboration during bid preparation and 
submission. 
 
viii) 
Develop and operationalize a comprehensive ROI evaluation framework for MICE 
activities. The framework will provide clear indicators, data collection tools, and 
analytical methods for measuring both financial returns on MICE investments in 
line with the National MICE Strategy (2017). 
 

 
 
 
 
151 
 
 
 
ix) 
Enforce strict compliance with the POATE hosted buyer’s registration 
requirements by ensuring that only registered and verified hosted buyers are 
invited to participate in the campaign to facilitate monitoring and evaluation of 
the benefits that accrue from their engagements. 
 
x) 
Build and adequately staff dedicated M&E units with skilled personnel to 
effectively plan, coordinate, and implement monitoring and evaluation activities 
within the tourism sector. 
xi) 
Develop and operationalize a comprehensive coordination framework that clearly 
defines the roles, responsibilities, and reporting mechanisms between MOTWA, 
UTB, and key sector stakeholders such as UHOA, UTO, UTA, YUTO, TGFU, and 
USGA to enhance collaboration, planning, and monitoring of tourism promotional 
activities. 
 
xii) 
Operationalize and integrate TIMs with UTB’s Quality Assurance System (QAS) to 
facilitate seamless data validation, information sharing, and evidence-based 
reporting. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
MoTWA and UTB made notable progress in marketing and branding Destination Uganda 
during FYs 2022/23–2024/25, contributing to a strong recovery in tourist arrivals from 
1,826,637 to 4,168,346. Notwithstanding this progress, gaps remain that limit the full 
effectiveness and competitiveness of marketing interventions. In particular, delays in 
reviewing and operationalizing enabling regulations, the absence of comprehensive 
tourism product catalogues, and weak utilization of research to inform investment and 
marketing decisions constrained evidence-based planning. 
 
In addition, non-implementation of some planned domestic and international 
engagements, limited brand awareness in key source markets, capacity gaps among 
staff and stakeholders, and underutilization of digital marketing platforms reduced the 
potential impact of branding efforts. Addressing these weaknesses would enhance the 
effectiveness, reach, and sustainability of MoTWA and UTB’s tourism marketing and 
branding initiatives. 
 
 
3.1.8 Management of the National Special Grant for persons with Disabilities 
implemented by the Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development 
 
Introduction 
 
In Uganda, the disability prevalence rate of persons aged 2 years and above increased 
from 12.4% in 2014 to 13.6% in 2024. Disability categories/ impairments include; 
Physical disability caused by cerebral palsy, amputation of a limb, paralysis of deformity; 
Physical disability including deafness and hard of hearing disability; Visual disability 
including blindness and low vision disability; Deaf and blind disability; Mental disability 
including psychiatric disability and learning disability; Little people; Albinism; and 
Multiple disability. 

 
 
 
 
152 
 
 
 
 
The Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development (MoGLSD) is the lead agency in 
Uganda’s Social Development Sector, mandated to coordinate and implement 
programmes for vulnerable groups, including Persons with Disabilities (PWDs). PWDs 
often face marginalization, exclusion from development benefits, and exposure to 
exploitation and income shocks. 
 
The National Special Grant (NSG) for Persons with disabilities implemented by the 
MoGLSD was introduced in FY 2019/2020; as one of the Special Government 
interventions to address the vulnerability and poverty among people with Disabilities in 
Uganda. The Programme is meant to enable accessibility of funds to Persons with 
Disabilities to actively engage in activities that promote their Social and economic 
welfare. 
 
The OAG conducted a VFM audit to assess the effectiveness of the National Special 
Grants for Persons with Disabilities implemented by the Ministry of Gender, Labour and 
Social Development, in facilitating the achievement of the programme’s intended 
outcomes during the financial years, 2019/20–2023/24. Below are the summarised key 
findings and recommendations; 
 
Key Findings 
 
During the audit, I noted significant progress in the implementation of the National 
Special Grant for Persons with Disabilities (NSG-PWD), including; 
 
a) 
Development and revision of legal and policy frameworks such as the Persons 
with Disabilities Act, Cap. 115, the National Policy on PWDs (2023), and the 
Revised NSG Guidelines (2022) to promote inclusion and protection of PWDs’ 
rights. 
b) 
Disbursement of UGX.38.5Bn to 588 PWD groups between FY 2019/20 and FY 
2023/24. 
c) 
Skilling and graduation of 726 PWD learners across the country in trades such as 
tailoring, carpentry, welding, leatherwork, and hairdressing. 
d) 
Rollout of the Disability Management Information System (DMIS) to 181 Local 
Governments (LGs) to improve programme management and reporting. 
e) 
Progressive increase in programme budget allocation to UGX.15.9Bn in FY 
2023/24, surpassing the Global Disability Summit commitment of a 30% 
increment from UGX.9.6Bn in FY 2021/22. 
 
Despite the notable achievements, the study identified areas of improvement that need 
to be addressed as indicated below; 
 
a) 
Planning and Budgeting 
 
i) 
There was no up-to-date national database of Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) 
as at 30th June 2025 to support evidence-based planning and budgeting. The 
NSG programme continued relying on outdated data from the 2014 Census and 
2016 UBOS survey, which does not reflect current disability demographics as 

 
 
 
 
153 
 
 
 
required by the Persons with Disabilities Act Cap. 115. As a result, programme 
coverage remained low, with only 68,252 PWDs (2.5%) benefiting out of the 2.7 
million reported in the 2024 Census. 
 
ii) 
The review of Indicative Planning Figures (IPFs) for 18 sampled Local 
Governments in FY 2023/24 revealed that the allocation criteria were mainly 
input-based (resource envelope) and general population-driven, without using 
disaggregated disability data by type, age, or gender to guide needs-based 
allocations. Consequently, some LGs with higher PWD populations received 
fewer resources. 
 
iii) 
There was limited grant coverage, as only 588 out of 905 Local Governments 
(65%) that is; Districts, municipalities, cities and five (05) divisions of Kampala 
city, received PWD funds over the five-year period, leaving 317 LGs (35%) 
without support. 
 
b) 
Extent of implementation of the NSG Programme activities 
 
i) 
Out of 61 sampled NSG programme activities, 33 (54.1%) were fully 
implemented, 23 (37.7%) were partially implemented, and 5 (8.2%) not 
implemented, a few examples of these activities included; the development of 
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for PWD centres, stakeholder 
consultations, and verification of institutional PWDs for support. 
 
ii) 
Of 103 sampled group projects, only 27 (26.2%) maintained their approved 
projects, 8 (7.7%) changed projects without approval, and 68 (66%) split after 
receiving funds. The most affected categories were goat rearing (22%) and 
produce buying & selling (17.6%), while enterprises like savings and credit, 
poultry keeping, and events management remained stable. 
 
iii) 
Funds totaling UGX.2.19Bn were disbursed to 808 PWD groups without 
verification, and no verification reports were available for Quarter 3 and Quarter 
4 of FY 2023/24, creating risks of funds being released to non-existent (“ghost”) 
groups. 
 
c) 
Monitoring, coordination and evaluation of the National Special Grant 
for PWD Programme 
 
i) 
MOGLSD did not prepare annual Monitoring & Evaluation (M&E) work plans or 
budgets for the FY 2019/2020- FY 2023/ 2024 dedicated to the NSG Programme, 
limiting systematic tracking of progress and accountability. 
ii) 
Although comprehensive tools were developed for routine data collection and 
reporting, the M&E officers did not use them to monitor programme 
implementation. 
iii) 
No monitoring reports were produced for FY 2019/2020 despite the release of 
UGX.420Mn for operational activities, including grant monitoring. Furthermore, 
there was no evidence that findings from later monitoring reports were 
discussed or acted upon. 

 
 
 
 
154 
 
 
 
iv) 
The Ministry failed to conduct a mid-term evaluation by the FY 2022/2023 to 
assess progress against key outcome indicators such as PWD income 
improvement, participation in economic programs, and entrepreneurship skills 
development. 
 
d) 
Disability Management Information System 
 
i) 
Although planned for full deployment in 2019, the DMIS was only rolled out to 
181 Local Governments by FY 2023/24. This was delayed by COVID-19 
disruptions, procurement challenges, and lack of prioritized user training. 
ii) 
Key modules such as group registration, applications, grievance handling, 
appraisal, disbursement and reporting were either underused or non-functional, 
resulting in incomplete group data and unresolved beneficiary complaints. 
 
iii) 
Historical data from FYs 2019/20–2022/23 was not migrated into the system, 
undermining audit tracking since inception. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer of the MoGLSD to; 
 
i) 
Conduct a comprehensive nationwide survey, in collaboration with UBOS, to 
obtain accurate, disaggregated data on PWDs by disability type, gender, age, 
and geographical location. The data should inform a robust and equitable 
resource allocation framework consistent with NSG programme principles of 
inclusivity and fairness. 
ii) 
Enforce clear deadlines for submission of beneficiary PWD groups through the 
Disability Management Information System (DMIS) to facilitate real-time tracking 
and compliance. 
iii) 
Strengthen technical support to Local Governments (LGs) through continuous 
training and regional support teams to enhance timely project appraisal and 
verification. 
iv) 
Reinforce monitoring and evaluation frameworks to track progress against 
targets, address emerging challenges, and realign activities where funding 
shortfalls affect implementation. 
v) 
Expedite integration of the DMIS with IFMS and Bank of Uganda Banking System 
(BBS) Connect in collaboration with MoFPED and NITA-Uganda to operationalize 
the disbursement module and ensure secure, automated transfers to beneficiary 
accounts. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
While the Government of Uganda, through the MoGLSD has made notable progress in 
implementing the NSG Programme for PWDs, weaknesses remain in programme design, 
execution, and oversight. The Key gaps include limited funding, the absence of an up-
to-date PWD database, and underutilization of the DMIS, weak monitoring and 
evaluation systems, inadequate entrepreneurship and business development support, 
and lack of an effective grievance-handling mechanism. 

 
 
 
 
155 
 
 
 
These challenges have constrained the overall effectiveness of the grant through 
inequitable resource allocation, limited reach and quality of support provided hence 
limiting the programme’s ability to deliver sustainable socio-economic transformation for 
beneficiaries. 
 
Strengthening data-driven planning, stakeholder coordination, institutional capacity, and 
system functionality remains critical to improving programme effectiveness, inclusivity, 
and long-term programme impact. 
 
3.1.9 Evaluation of the Business Registration and Licensing, and Tourism 
Competitiveness Development interventions under the Competitiveness and 
Enterprise Development Project 
 
Introduction 
 
The Value for Money audit on the Competitiveness and Enterprise Development Project 
(CEDP) evaluated the implementation of the Business registration and licensing, and 
Tourism competitiveness development interventions in supporting the competitiveness 
of business and tourism industry in Uganda. 
 
CEDP was implemented by the Private Sector Foundation Uganda with beneficiary 
agencies including Uganda Registration and Services Bureau, Ministry of Tourism, 
Wildlife and Antiquities, Uganda Wildlife Authority, Uganda Tourism Board, Uganda 
Wildlife Conservation and Education Centre, Uganda Hotel and Tourism Training 
Institute and Uganda Wildlife Research and Training Institute, Uganda Museum. The 
project aimed at the establishment of one-stop shop for business registration, an e-
registry which is a virtual platform for business licensing and the streamlining of 
business registration and licensing procedures and infrastructural developments in the 
tourism sector. 
 
The audit evaluated the implementation of two components of the CEDP: Business 
Registration and Licensing Reforms component which was implemented under CEDP-P 
and the Tourism Competitiveness Development component which was implemented 
under both CEDP-P and CEDP-AF. The audit covered the ten (10) financial years from 
2014/15 to 2024/25 in line with the project lifespan, covering both the original and 
additional financing. Regarding the Business Registration and Licensing Component, I 
noted the following; 
 
a) 
Construction 
and 
operationalization 
of 
the 
Uganda 
Business 
Facilitation Centre (UBFC): The construction of the UBFC was completed and 
key agencies occupied it without commissioning and hand over by MoFPED. 
There is underutilization of space by NITA-U and the Presidential CEO Forum on 
the 9th and 10th floor. The delay to rectify defects and formally hand over the 
UBFC to beneficiary agencies, has compromised the building’s functionality and 
safety. MoFPED will need to address the identified construction snags and fast-
track the commissioning and formal handover of the building. MoFPED should 
also reassess the space allocation to NITA-U and the Presidential CEO Forum 
and reallocate any unused space in order to optimize utilization of the UBFC. 

 
 
 
 
156 
 
 
 
b) 
Utilization of the One Stop Business Centre: The physical One Stop 
Business Centre (OSBC) at the UBFC is underutilized indicating that it has limited 
relevance in the current digital business environment. As a result, the project’s 
objective of reducing the administrative burden of formalizing a business has 
been only partially realized, as investments were directed toward a physical 
facility with minimal impact instead of strengthening the online digital platforms 
that could have delivered more sustainable benefits. MoFPED should review the 
continued relevance and effectiveness of the physical One Stop Centre, in 
improving the ease of doing business in Uganda. 
 
c) 
Implementation of Business Licensing Reforms: The project made a 
significant contribution toward initiating and partially implementing business 
licensing reforms, however failure by MoFPED to fully operationalize a 
transactional e-licensing platform and complete the rationalisation of licenses has 
hindered the achievement of the project’s objective of reducing the business 
licensing burden. To address this, MoFPED, through the Private Sector 
Development Unit, should complete the implementation of key BLRC 
recommendations and allocate resources to upgrade the existing e-licensing 
portal into a fully transactional system. 
 
d) 
Operationalisation of the Online Business Registration System. 
Persistent user challenges such as difficulties in account creation, payment 
processing, system errors, and limited online support have reduced the 
convenience and effectiveness of the platform. These issues hinder the project’s 
goal of fully reducing the cost and time burden of business registration and limit 
the system’s contribution to a more competitive and investor-friendly business 
environment. To address this, URSB should strengthen the functionality and user 
support of the OBRS by addressing recurring system errors, improving account 
management features, and enhancing responsiveness of the helpdesk. 
 
Regarding the Tourism Competitiveness Development Component, I noted the 
following; 
 
a) 
Construction and equipping of the Crested Crane Hotel in Jinja: There 
was a delay of approximately 38 months to complete construction and equipping 
works at the Hotel. At the time of the audit in September 2025, installation of 
equipment, furniture and fixtures was pending completion. Key facilities 
originally within the approved scope, such as hostels, a health club, and a spa, 
were not constructed despite their importance in achieving the 3-star hotel 
rating. To address this, PSFU should prioritise completion of the outstanding 
works and address identified design and construction defects, ensuring that 
essential facilities originally planned are incorporated or alternatives are 
provided. 
 
b) 
Sustainability of UHTTI as a centre of Excellence: The Uganda Hotel and 
Tourism Training Institute (UHTTI) long-term sustainability as a Centre of 
Excellence is at risk as the institute continues to face a substantial funding 
shortfall, with the current government subvention inadequate to meet the full 

 
 
 
 
157 
 
 
 
cost of training and the shortage of qualified teaching staff which undermine the 
delivery of practical, competency-based training. To address this, the Board of 
UHTTI should revise the institute’s staffing structure and recruitment plan and 
also develop a resource mobilization strategy to diversify the institute’s funding 
base to support long-term institutional sustainability. 
 
c) 
Refurbishment of Uganda Wildlife Education Centre (UWEC): The 
chimpanzee enclosure, which includes a protective moat, was incomplete and 
could not retain water which is supposed to prevent the chimpanzees from 
crossing to access humans. The upgraded animal hospital lacked a reliable 
electricity backup system in the event of power outages which poses a risk of 
interruption of veterinary services. UWEC management, in collaboration with 
UWA, should urgently install a backup power system at the wildlife hospital and 
address drainage issues at the chimpanzee island so as to safeguard animal 
health services, protect research materials, and improve the visitor experience at 
the centre. 
 
d) 
Upgrade of the Uganda Wildlife Research and Training Institute 
(UWRTI): CEDP substantially improved infrastructure at the Institute (UWRTI). 
However, it was observed that the GIS laboratory was not in use since the GIS 
software had not been installed in the computers, and the research boat had not 
been put to use since acquisition in November 2024. In order to realise the 
gains from the infrastructure developments done by CEDP at the institute, the 
UWRTI will need to address the internet connectivity problem and the training 
gap for boat operators. 
 
e)
