Upgrading of the Uganda Museum: The civil works were still ongoing at the 
time of the audit with a delay of six months. This was mainly due to delayed 
payments to the contractor, slow approval of design and delayed approval of 
VAT exemption requests. As a result, the museum remains closed to the public, 
delaying the realization of the intended benefits of increased visitor numbers. 
 
Therefore, MoFPED should ensure timely payment of approved IPCs and 
expedite review and approval of design changes to ensure completion of the 
remaining works within the revised project timelines. 
 
f) 
Design and implementation of the Tourism Information Management 
System (TIMS): The development of the Tourism information management 
system was completed, however, it has not been rolled out for use by other 
MDAs because it is still being hosted on the domain of the developer. NITA-U 
was unable to host the system due to limited capacity. The system is also not 
integrated with the Tourism Satellite Account. To address this, MoTWA should 
fast-track the full operationalisation of TIMS and ensure integration the Tourism 
Satellite Account (TSA) and other relevant systems such as UTB and UBoS data 
platforms. 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
158 
 
 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
Overall, the performance of the CEDP against the four outcome indicators for the 
Business Registration and Licensing and Tourism Competitiveness Development 
components was commendable, as all targets were fully achieved by July 2024. 
However, these results were achieved despite several planned activities not being fully 
implemented, indicating that some interventions and the related expenditures were not 
critical to the attainment of the stated outcomes. 
 
However, to maximize the gains from the project, the stakeholders highlighted in the 
report need to address the weaknesses identified in the audit that included the delayed 
completion of works; underutilization of key facilities; and partial implementation of 
business licensing reforms. These gaps pose a risk to sustaining the project gains and 
achieving deeper, long-term impacts such as higher tourist spending, improved service 
quality, and strengthened sector competitiveness. Addressing the above issues will 
improve service delivery efficiency, enable long-term sustainability of project 
interventions and enable achievement of the full value of the project investment. 
 
 
3.1.10 Management of Remand Homes and the Rehabilitation Centre by the Ministry 
of Gender, Labour and Social Development in Uganda 
 
Introduction 
 
The management of Juvenile Offenders (JOs) in Uganda, is pivotal in safeguarding 
children's rights while striving to promote social justice. The Children Act, Cap 62, 
defines JOs as individuals under the age of 18 who come into contact with the justice 
system due to suspected or accused criminal activity. 
 
According to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, the African Charter and the 
Ugandan Children’s Act, Cap 62 (Part 10, Section 8), it is a fundamental principle that 
children who commit offenses should not be detained with adults, but instead housed in 
separate children facilities known as Remand Homes. 
 
Currently, Uganda has seven (7) remand homes and one national rehabilitation centre 
dedicated to the protection, rehabilitation, and reintegration of JOs. These facilities face 
significant challenges, including overcrowding, aging infrastructure, inadequate health 
facilities/sickbays, lack of access to education and inadequate rehabilitation services, 
among others. 
 
In light of the above challenges, the Office of the Auditor General undertook a value for 
money audit to assess and provide insights into the management of remand homes and 
the rehabilitation centre in the period 2022/23 to 2024/25. Below is a summary of the 
key findings and recommendations from the audit. 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
159 
 
 
 
Key Findings 
 
i) 
Six (75%) out of eight Remand Homes and Rehabilitation Centre (RRCs) were 
overcrowded, with juvenile populations exceeding their recommended holding 
capacities. Specifically, these centres are operating at capacity levels ranging 
from 110% to 229%. The most affected, being Fort portal and Mbale RRCs 
housing juvenile populations of 129% and 122% above their individual 
recommended holding capacities of 45 each. 
 
ii) 
All eight (8) RRCs lacked a resident medical practitioner or health personnel, 
contrary to Rule 11(1) of the Children’s Home Rules, 2013 that requires the 
RRCs to employ the services of a registered nurse as a full time staff member. 
Audit however noted innovation. Despite the RRCs lacking resident medical 
practitioners or health personnel, the RRCs developed informal working 
arrangements with nearby government medical facilities, where doctors and 
other medical personnel visited when needed. As a result, out of the 203 JOs 
sampled, 143, representing 70% received medical check-up immediately on 
admission. 
 
iii) 
Out of 9,204 JOs admitted to various RRCs in the period of study, 5,757, 
representing an average of 63%, lacked Social Inquiry Reports. This delayed 
court proceedings, leading to overstay on remand. 
In addition, the resettlement of juveniles upon release becomes a challenge due 
to scanty information of the child’s social and family background. 
 
iv) 
There were significant gaps in dietary provisions for juveniles on lifelong 
medication. Eighteen (18) juveniles, representing 9%, were not provided with 
specific menu/diet tailored to their medical conditions, which can jeopardize or 
complicate existing health conditions. 
 
v) 
All the eight RRCs were understaffed. The ratios of Probation and Social Welfare 
Officers (PSWOs)/ Assistant PSWOs to the juveniles, averaged 1:37 across the 
facilities, way above the recommended ratio of 1:8, for older children. 
 
vi) 
Except for Arua, and Kampiringisa, the other six (75%) remand homes lacked 
sufficient facilities/playgrounds for outdoor games like football, volleyball 
basketball. The remand homes could only provide some indoor games such as 
Ludo. 
 
vii) 
From a sample of 82 juveniles with minor offenses, 34, representing 41%, had 
been remanded for more than the recommended three months, contrary to 
Section 94(5) of the Children Act, Cap 62. Similarly, 20 out of a sample of 44 
juveniles on capital offences, representing 45%, had been remanded for more 
than six months. 
 
viii) 
Only 35 juveniles (25%) out of 140 juveniles, who had expressed interest in 
formal education at Kampiringisa National Rehabilitation Centre, were accessing 

 
 
 
 
160 
 
 
 
education at either primary or secondary level, due to lack of on-site schools 
(own schools). 
 
ix) 
Although skilling programmes were being offered in hairdressing, tailoring, 
shoemaking and agricultural activities, other skilling activities like carpentry and 
tailoring were not offered due to lack of modern and functional equipment. 
Some equipment, dating as far back as the 1950s, was dilapidated and 
unsuitable for effective skills training. 
 
x) 
There were delays in the resettlement of juvenile offenders who had completed 
their committal orders. At the time of audit (October 2025), out of 413 juveniles 
at the Centre, 115 (29%) had completed their committal orders but had not yet 
been reintegrated into their communities. 
 
xi) 
All 971 juveniles resettled during the three-year period under study were 
released without start-up resources, which undermines the ability of rehabilitees 
to utilise the skills acquired during rehabilitation, thereby increasing the risk of 
recidivism and negatively affecting their livelihoods. 
 
xii) 
The study noted absence of structured follow-up mechanisms after JOs are 
released and/or resettled. This contravenes the principle of continuous care 
under the Children Act and weakens the sustainability of rehabilitation outcomes. 
 
xiii) 
Since the enactment of the Children’s Act in 1997, specific rules or regulations 
have never been formulated to govern the management of RRCs, resulting in 
RRCs operating without a structured framework, leading to inconsistencies in 
management. 
 
xiv) 
Coordination at the national level, which is meant to involve various Ministries, 
Departments, and Agencies (MDAs) including the Office of the Director of Public 
Prosecutions (ODPP), the Judiciary, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs, among 
others, has not been effective. The absence of regular, structured meetings and 
interactions among these entities hampers effective administration of juvenile 
justice. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
The MoGLSD should; 
 
i) 
Enforce the use of diversion programs (alternatives to detention) for minor 
offenses, as encouraged by international standards to reduce the number of 
children in detention, prevent stigmatization, and promote rehabilitation within 
the community. 
 
ii) 
Carry out sensitization and capacity building to empower the LCs, the Police and 
the district probation officers to handle minor offences by encouraging mediation 
and caution in the settlement of cases to avoid unnecessary remanding of 
children. 

 
 
 
 
161 
 
 
 
In addition, encourage parents/guardians participation in court proceedings to 
enhance the support system for juveniles to promote quicker resolution of cases 
and/or bail application. 
 
iii) 
Expedite the rehabilitation and expansion of existing RRCs, completing the 
ongoing construction in Kabale and Masindi Remand Homes and possibly 
constructing new juvenile facilities to match the population demands. Develop 
and implement a comprehensive policy for regular maintenance of rehabilitation 
facilities, ensuring that all structures are kept in good condition to uphold health 
and safety standards. 
 
iv) 
In collaborate with other government agencies come up with advocacy 
programmes targeting specific needs of boys in homes, communities and schools 
to mitigate peer pressure and behavioural related challenges. In addition, 
programs should be designed and widely disseminated to empower parents, 
family and community to reduce violence against children, improve family 
wellbeing and positively influence behaviour of children. 
 
v) 
In collaboration with the stakeholders, consider facilitating virtual court hearings 
for juvenile cases to minimize travel limitations and delays in case processing, to 
address case backlogs. The use of age scanning machines should be explored at 
regional level to weed out over age persons being remanded in juvenile facilities. 
 
vi) 
Continue engaging the Local Governments, under which the RRCs fall, to ensure 
adequate facilitation, training and build capacity for the district probation and 
social welfare officers to bridge the knowledge and skilling gap to enable them 
prepare timely SIR reports, to attend court sessions to quicken juvenile court 
proceedings and ease resettlement of JOs after release. 
 
vii) 
Establish links with Ministry of Health, National Medical Stores and District Health 
Officers to ensure that medical requirements of RRCs are planned for so that 
RRCs become service points for drugs and other medical supplies. In addition, 
consider designing guidelines on provision of specialized nutritional care tailored 
to the specific health needs of juveniles, in order not to jeopardize their existing 
health conditions. 
 
viii) 
Liaise with relevant authorities to expedite the recruitment of additional staff for 
the RRCs to handle medical examinations of JOs and any associated medical 
emergencies and support the needs of juveniles by improving care and services, 
which enhances overall welfare and development outcomes. 
 
ix) 
Engage the Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development to survey and 
title the available land at RRC in order to provide an accurate assessment of the 
current land boundaries and secure it from encroachers. In addition, inventory of 
all land resources available be maintained at each RRC, detailing sizes, current 
usage to enable better land management and proper planning for recreational 
facilities. 
 

 
 
 
 
162 
 
 
 
x) 
Conduct a comprehensive review of land utilization at the RRCs and develop 
programs not only for recreational and skilling activities but also for food 
production and income-generating initiatives. 
 
xi) 
Prioritize the establishment of education facilities within juvenile rehabilitation 
centre. In addition, transitional education and skills-based programs should be 
introduced to rehabilitees who are not inclined to pursue formal education, to 
enable them acquire market-relevant vocational skills and improve their 
employability upon reintegration into society. 
 
xii) 
In the short term, liaise with the Judiciary to expedite cases involving school-
going children and support such juveniles to obtain bail, where appropriate, to 
enable continuity of education while complying with court processes. 
 
xiii) 
Establish partnerships with vocational training institutions to provide structured 
skilling and vocational training, aimed at preparing juveniles for future 
employment and reducing the risk of recidivism. In addition, facilitate the 
acquisition of modern and appropriate equipment, including carpentry, tailoring, 
and metal fabrication tools, to enhance the quality and relevance of skilling 
programmes. 
 
xiv) 
Consider planning and deepening collaboration with civil society organizations 
and development partners to provide start-up resources to enable juvenile 
offenders to effectively utilize acquired skills for sustainable livelihoods upon 
reintegration. 
 
xv) 
Liaise with districts to advocate for enhanced facilitation of PSWOs to effectively 
prepare families and offer psychosocial support to both the parents and JO’s for 
better reintegration outcomes. In addition, budget for systematic follow-up of 
released juveniles to enable tracking of progress and the provision of timely 
support, which is critical for successful reintegration. 
 
xvi) 
Liaise with other government departments and agencies to ensure rehabilitees 
benefit from existing government programmes like the Parish Development 
Model and Presidential Skilling Hubs, to support their socio-economic 
reintegration. 
 
xvii) 
Acquire or develop a software-based tracking system to aid in the monitoring of 
juveniles after reintegration and to support decision-making on child protection 
and rehabilitation outcomes. In addition, guidelines should be developed for 
follow-up to ensure reintegrated juveniles receive continued supervision and 
support, thereby reducing the risk of recidivism. 
 
xviii) 
Prioritize the development of rules or regulations to guide the management of 
RRCs to enhance accountability and oversight, ensuring that the rights and well-
being of children in these facilities are effectively protected. 
 

 
 
 
 
163 
 
 
 
xix) 
Prioritize and budget for funding to facilitate meetings of relevant stakeholders at 
national level to discuss challenges and make recommendations regarding the 
implementation of child protection and juvenile justice policies. This would 
facilitate better communication, data sharing, and joint initiatives among 
stakeholders. 
 
xx) 
Develop coordination guidelines that provide explicit guidance on inter-agency 
collaboration, referral pathways, information sharing, and accountability within 
the juvenile justice system. 
 
General Conclusion 
 
The historical context of the RRCs, combined with the increase in Uganda's population, 
underscores the urgent need for reforms in the juvenile justice system. Although the 
Juvenile system is fulfilling its mandate, the findings in this report, call for urgent need 
for improvements in the management and care of juveniles within the justice system, to 
meet contemporary needs, while upholding the rights of juveniles during their 
rehabilitation and reintegration into society. 
 
 
3.1.11 Regulation of Private Health Care Practice in Uganda 
 
Introduction 
 
Private Health Care practice refers to individuals and organizations that are not owned 
or directly controlled by governments and are involved in providing health services. This 
includes facilities and practitioners that deliver care independently of public systems, 
whether for-profit or not-for-profit. 
 
Regulation of private healthcare practice is critical in safeguarding the population as an 
estimated 54% of Uganda’s population seeks health care services from private health 
facilities. Regulation of private healthcare practice entails setting and enforcing 
standards of health practice, registration and licensing of health professionals and 
private health facilities, inspection and supervision and exercising disciplinary control 
over both professionals and health facilities which is a mandate of the Ministry of Health 
and health regulatory councils. 
 
Several regulatory challenges to private healthcare practice have been documented and 
published and include but not limited to loose regulatory oversight of the operations of 
private health practice leading to increased infiltration of unqualified individuals, limited 
investigation and resolution of reported medical negligence and malpractice cases 
leading to a backlog of cases and inadequate enforcement to ensure adherence to the 
health standards among others. 
 
In light of the above, I assessed the efforts by the Ministry of Health (MoH) and the 
Regulatory Councils in regulating private healthcare practice to promote safe and quality 
health care and protect the public from malpractice. Below are the key findings and 
recommendations of the audit. 

 
 
 
 
164 
 
 
 
Key Findings 
 
i) 
Incomplete databases for private health practitioners and facilities as they only 
provide for professionals and private health facilities that seek registration. This 
limits planning for regulatory interventions for all facilities and professionals 
operating in the country. 
 
ii) 
Inconsistencies in numbers of registered private health facilities by MoH and 
regulatory councils as the Ministry of Health was unable to reconcile and account 
for 10,458 registered private health facilities captured in the regulatory councils’ 
databases but missing from the National Health Facility Registry which 
undermines the effectiveness of regulatory oversight over private healthcare 
practice. This data gap limits the Ministry’s capacity to plan, coordinate, and 
monitor, enforce compliance with minimum standards, and take timely corrective 
or enforcement action against non-compliant facilities. 
 
iii) 
Failure by the regulatory councils to Gazette licensed health facilities and 
professionals. UMDPC, UNMC and AHPC failed to gazette an annual average of 
1,804; 406 and 295 licensed private facilities respectively in the three years 
under review. Limited gazetting of private health facilities and professionals 
limits public awareness of those qualified to provide health services. 
 
iv) 
Inadequate Inspection and support supervision of Private Health Facilities and 
Professionals; 
 
a) 
Failure by Regulatory Councils and MoH to set clear targets at planning and 
budgeting for inspections and support supervision. MoH and regulatory councils 
did not adequately plan and execute inspections and support supervisions during 
the review period due to absence of clear inspection targets, schedules, and 
documented coverage plans. The inadequate inspections limited the Ministry and 
regulatory councils’ ability to ensure quality health service delivery and poses 
risks to patient safety. 
 
b) 
Gaps in the inspection reports. None of the reviewed inspection reports from the 
MoH and the regulatory councils indicated whether previously identified issues 
had been addressed. Furthermore, follow-up on prior findings is primarily 
conducted verbally, with no provision for documenting these actions in the 
inspection reports. 
 
c) 
Limited Follow up of inspection and supervision recommendations. Audit noted 
49 out of the 189 facilities inspected had not taken any action on the inspection 
recommendations. Additionally, councils do not maintain a follow-up matrix to 
track implementation of issued performance improvement recommendations. 
 
v) 
Inadequate enforcement of compliance with health standards in private 
healthcare practice. Audit noted that all selected 27 facilities recommended for 
closure were still operating, with no evidence of reassessment or formal approval 
to reopen. 

 
 
 
 
165 
 
 
 
Non-compliance 
to 
health 
standards 
that 
resulted 
into 
the 
closure 
recommendation were observed to still be existing. Additionally, out of the 39 
sampled private facilities with issued corrective actions and recommendations, 
none of the facilities fully addressed the recommended corrective actions, with 
36.67 percent implementing none and 63.33 percent only partially implementing 
them. 
 
vi) 
Limited Complaint and dispute resolution by Regulatory Councils; 
a) 
Audit observed a total of 204 cases were pending to be resolved before the 
different regulatory councils’ disciplinary committees/tribunals. 
 
b) 
Audit noted councils take a considerably long time to conclude cases received as 
AHPC, UNMC and UMDPC took 12, 37 and 24 months respectively on average to 
resolve complaints. 
c) 
Limited of sensitization of the public on reporting complaints. Audit noted that 
although the councils undertake sensitization activities, these are not directed 
towards complaint reporting by the public which may be aggrieved. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
I advise the Accounting Officers of the MoH and the regulatory councils to; 
 
i) 
Develop a comprehensive database for private health facilities and professionals 
incorporating both the registered and unregistered persons to facilitate better 
planning for activities such as inspection, supervision and enforcement. 
 
ii) 
Regularly update the National Health Facility Registry system with data on all 
registered facilities in the country to provide users with accurate information on 
the facilities and the services they are allowed to offer. 
 
iii) 
Prioritise the planning, budgeting and allocation of resources for gazetting of all 
the registered and licensed private health facilities and professionals in 
compliance with the existing statutory obligation or coming up with a policy or 
guideline for publication of this information on the councils’ websites. 
 
iv) 
Prioritize joint inspections by all regulatory councils to minimize duplication, 
reduce costs, and ensure comprehensive assessment of health facilities and all 
professional cadres in the facilities. 
 
v) 
Establish and operationalize monitoring and evaluation units to support planning 
and target setting for interventions/activities in the councils. 
 
vi) 
Revise and amend the existing legal provisions in the councils’ Acts and 
regulations to provide for empowerment to enforce compliance to health care 
standards. 
 
vii) 
Undertake stakeholder consultations to establish a standard for complaint 
investigation and verification to prevent prolonged delays and improve the 

 
 
 
 
166 
 
 
 
efficiency of the complaint handling processes. Client charters for the same 
should be developed. 
 
viii) 
Strengthen public sensitization and awareness campaigns on complaint reporting 
coupled with dedicated multi-channel reporting platforms. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
Ministry of Health and her regulatory councils have undertaken measures to regulate 
private health care practice in the country. However, these have been ineffective to 
ensure adequate compliance to established standards and guidelines. Whereas the 
Ministry and the regulatory councils undertake registration and licensing; inspection and 
support supervision of private health care professionals and facilities and complaint and 
dispute resolution, gaps that need to be addressed to improve regulation of the private 
practice were identified. These included inconsistencies in registration figures by Ministry 
of Health and Regulatory councils, limited gazetting of registered and licensed private 
health facilities and professionals, inadequate inspection and support supervision of 
private health facilities and professionals, limited enforcement of compliance with health 
standards in private health care practice and delays in complaint handling and dispute 
resolution. 
 
Addressing the identified issues requires enhanced collaboration and coordination 
among all health sector stakeholders. This will not only ensure compliance to 
established health standards and guidelines but ultimately promote safe and quality 
health care and protection of the public from malpractice. 
 
 
3.1.12 Efficiency of Operations of Public Universities in the delivery of Education 
Services 
 
Introduction 
 
Public universities in Uganda are established by the Minister responsible for education, 
by statutory instrument, on the recommendation of the National Council for Higher 
Education (NCHE) and by resolution of Parliament and maintained out of public funds. 
Public universities are mandated to provide higher education, promote research and 
learning, disseminate knowledge, and expand access to tertiary education. There are 
ten public universities namely: Makerere University, Mbarara University of Science and 
Technology, Kyambogo University, Gulu University, Busitema University, Kabale 
University, Lira University, Muni University, Soroti University, and Mountains of the Moon 
University. These institutions operate under the governance of their respective councils 
and senates, within the national legal and policy framework overseen by the Ministry of 
Education and Sports and regulated by the NCHE. 
 
Public universities play a critical role in supporting national development through human 
capital formation, research, and innovation. Over the three financial years FY 2022/23–

 
 
 
 
167 
 
 
 
2024/25, Government invested UGX.2.65Tn in the ten public universities11, 
supplemented by a 32% increase in staffing and a 49% expansion in infrastructure. 
Notwithstanding this significant investment, persistent concerns have been raised 
regarding delayed completion of postgraduate programmes, underutilisation of 
resources, and inefficiencies in academic and administrative operations. 
 
It was on this basis that the Office of the Auditor General undertook, a Value for Money 
Audit to assess how efficiently public universities utilise financial resources, human 
resources, and student enrolment to maximise key outputs, particularly the number of 
graduates produced and the volume and quality of research generated. 
 
To measure efficiency, the audit applied the Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) 
technique by comparing each university’s mix of inputs (financial resources, staffing 
levels, and student enrolment) against its outputs (graduates produced and research 
outputs), enabling the identification of both efficient and inefficient institutions. The 
results provide evidence-based insights to guide public universities, the Ministry of 
Education and Sports, and NCHE on areas requiring attention to improve performance 
and enhance value for money across the Education sector. Below is a summary of the 
key findings. 
 
Key Findings 
 
The audit established some positive measures adopted by the public universities as well 
as areas that require improvement in order to ensure the public universities remain 
effective and competitive. 
 
1) 
Overall performance of the Public Universities 
 
Over the last five years, Uganda’s public universities have demonstrated tangible 
innovation and problem-solving solutions that extend beyond the classroom into national 
development outcomes. For example, Makerere University has made notable progress in 
translating research into practical solutions through the development of home grown 
COVID-19 rapid antibody test kits, the MakSol solar-powered cooker, and innovations in 
stabilised/interlocking soil blocks. In addition, Kyambogo University has strengthened its 
research and innovation capacity through the Business Incubation and Innovation 
Centre by promoting applied research, supporting entrepreneurship, and enhancing 
industry–academia linkages to improve skills development and industrialization 
outcomes. 
 
While Mbarara University of Science and Technology (MUST) has expanded its role as a 
science and technology leader by graduating large cohorts of professionals and 
advancing gender representation in university leadership, including the appointment of 
its first female Vice-Chancellor, which underscores progress in inclusive academic 
governance and Gulu University has been recognized internationally for its community 
impact, receiving the Most Impactful University in Rural Transformation and Community 
Development award for its practice-oriented programmes that equip graduates to 
 
11 Makerere University, Mbarara University of Science and Technology, Kyambogo University, Gulu University, Busitema University, Kabale University, 
Lira University, Muni University, Soroti University, and Mountains of the Moon University 

 
 
 
 
168 
 
 
 
address rural socio-economic challenges and drive community-focused development 
across agriculture, education, health and business sectors. 
 
Busitema University has distinguished itself through impactful research and innovation, 
including hosting a 4 MW solar power station on its campus that supports renewable 
energy education and contributes to the national grid; securing competitive research 
grants and producing high-impact projects in areas such as sustainable agriculture, HIV 
self-testing interventions, and food security; as well as earning recognition as one of 
Uganda’s visionary public universities, reflecting its advancing academic and community 
development role. 
 
Collectively, these examples indicate a positive trajectory where public universities are 
increasingly translating research into practical products, prototyping solutions, and 
strengthening industry/community relevance through applied innovation. 
 
2) 
Results of DEA 
 
i) 
The audit noted that although universities are spending more money each year, 
the results they produce are not increasing at the same pace. For instance, 
although the average university expenditure rose from UGX.84.3 Billion in FY 
2022/23 to UGX.90.9 Billion in FY 2024/25, research outputs declined sharply 
from an average of 204.8 to 76.23 over the same period. Similarly, although 
student enrolment and staff numbers increased from an average of 5,975 to 
7,859 students and from 826 to 864 staff the number of graduates rose only 
modestly (from 2,278 to 3,448), while research outputs declined significantly, 
from an average of 205 outputs to 76 outputs, indicating a lack of proportional 
growth in outputs. 
 
ii) 
Over the three years under review (2022/23–2024/25) audit established three 
levels of efficiency across the ten public universities as shown below: 
 
a) 
Kyambogo University, Lira University, and Mbarara University of Science and 
Technology (MUST) maintained full efficiency across all the three years12, 
demonstrating strong internal management and optimal use of available financial, 
human, and student resources. 
 
b) 
Kabale University, Mountains of the Moon University, and Soroti University 
progressively improved their efficiency scores and had attained full efficiency by 
FY 2024/25 relative to the other public universities in utilization of inputs. 
 
c) 
Gulu University and Busitema University exhibited recurring inefficiencies across 
the three-year period. The evidence shows that these inefficiencies were not 
driven by institutional size, resource constraints, or enrolment scale, but by 
internal management challenges, weak supervision systems, and suboptimal 
utilisation of available resources. 
 
 
12 Financial years 2022/23–2024/25 

 
 
 
 
169 
 
 
 
3) 
Key Factors that influence Operational Efficiency of the Public 
Universities 
a) 
Delayed Completion of Graduate Studies 
 
The study observed prolonged completion periods for master’s programmes 
caused by ineffective supervision, delayed marking, and inadequate dissertation 
support. This resulted into a total of 1,019 graduate students from Makerere, 
Kyambogo, Mbarara, and Gulu Universities exceeding the standard two-year 
study duration, increasing the universities’ costs per graduate and affecting the 
number of graduates. 
 
b) 
Weak Research Management and Low Completion of Funded Projects 
 
Despite substantial Government investment in research through the Research 
and Innovation Fund (RIF), completion of funded research projects remained 
extremely low. 
I noted that: 
 
i) 
Research funds were frequently disbursed late, often in the second quarter of 
the financial year, disrupting project timelines. 
 
ii) 
88% of researchers across universities were simultaneously engaged in multiple 
projects, which reduced focus and contributed to a large backlog of unfinished 
work. For example, some researchers at Makerere, MUST, and Busitema 
University were listed on more than four concurrent projects and delivered no 
completed output within the planned timeframes. 
 
c) 
Low Academic Staff Participation in Research Activities 
 
I found that academic staff participation in research was low across eight universities 
with exception of Makerere and Mbarara Universities. The publication rates for the 
period under review were as follows: 
 
i) 
Gulu University:11 out of 259 staff (4%) published research. 
ii) 
Kabale University: 28 out of 320 staff (9%) published research. 
iii) 
Kyambogo University, only 70 out of 418 staff (17%) published research. 
iv) 
Lira University, only 22 out of 116 staff (19%) published research. 
v) 
Busitema University, only 62 out of 286 staff (22%) published research. 
vi) 
Soroti University, only 35 out of 99 staff (35%) published research. 
vii) 
Muni University, only 38 out of 107 staff (36%) published research. 
viii) 
Mountains of the Moon University, only 66 out of 139 staff (47%) published 
research. 
 
The low participation in research activities across the universities was attributed to 
inadequate mentoring structures, limited training in proposal development, and weak 
incentives for junior researchers. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
170 
 
 
 
d) 
Dissemination of Research Findings 
 
The Public Universities13 lacked standardised procedures to ensure that research outputs 
reached stakeholders such as policymakers, local communities, industry partners and 
peer reviewers. For instance, mobile technology prototypes at Gulu University were 
demonstrated only once and never made accessible afterwards and Agricultural 
innovations at Busitema University were shared without adaptations for local farmers’ 
language or technical literacy. As a result, innovations remained un-utilised or under-
utilised, which made research visibility to remain low, affecting Webometrics 
performance. 
 
e) 
Operation of Unaccredited Campuses and Teaching of Unaccredited 
Programmes 
 
I noted that the following universities were operating un-accredited campuses and Study 
Centres: 
 
i) 
Makerere University study centres in Mbale and Lira, 
ii) 
Gulu University study centres, in Kotido, Hoima/Masindi & Kitgum 
iii) 
Busitema University, in Tororo study centre & Kabwangasi campus 
iv) 
Kyambogo University study centres, in Bushenyi, Paidha & Soroti 
 
Additionally, Mbarara, Busitema, Kabale, Muni, Mountains of the Moon, Lira, and Soroti 
Universities continued to admit students to 64 academic programmes with expired 
accreditations due to weak enforcement by NCHE and inadequate internal tracking 
systems. 
 
f) 
Inadequate Oversight and Inconsistent Application of Accreditation 
Standards by NCHE 
 
I identified the following systemic weaknesses within NCHE’s accreditation processes; 
 
i) 
Reviewers frequently produced. reports that were not aligned with the NCHE 
performance assessment tools for desk review which affected the soundness 
conclusions reached. 
 
ii) 
Reviewers frequently recommend accreditation despite reaching conclusions that 
are not supported by the NCHE instruments. 
 
iii) 
The accreditation process is ineffective as evidenced by monitoring reports that 
indicate significant non-compliance in critical areas such as staffing, and 
infrastructure (e.g., laboratories) within a short period after accreditation of 
Programmes. 
 
 
13 Makerere University, Mbarara University of Science and Technology, Kyambogo University, Gulu University, Busitema University, 
Kabale University, Lira University, Muni University, Soroti University, and Mountains of the Moon University 

 
 
 
 
171 
 
 
 
iv) 
Absence of records on follow-up or quality assurance checks by NCHE staff on 
reports submitted by reviewers to ensure reliability and integrity of accreditation 
decisions. 
 
g) 
Weak Internal Quality Assurance Systems in Universities 
 
Although all universities had Quality Assurance Units, most of them were not functioning 
effectively because; 
 
i) 
There was no evidence of staff teaching evaluations for three consecutive years 
at Gulu, Lira, and Busitema Universities. 
ii) 
Makerere and MUST conducted student evaluations inconsistently, and results 
were not analysed for improvement. 
 
The follow-up on NCHE directives was irregular across universities. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
I advised the Accounting Officers of the public universities to; 
 
i) 
Establish and enforce an integrated, automated timetabling and teaching-
monitoring system to ensure full delivery of planned contact hours by academic 
staff. 
 
ii) 
Develop and implement strict timelines for instruction, marking and submission 
of results. and postgraduate supervision, supported by an electronic results-
tracking system that alerts management to delays. 
 
iii) 
Introduce a Research Monitoring and Evaluation framework requiring researchers 
to submit periodic progress reports, evidence of outputs, and final deliverables 
before full release or closure of research funds. 
 
iv) 
Fast track the accreditation of all unlicensed campuses and study centres by 
submitting complete documentation to NCHE and designating responsible quality 
assurance focal persons to regularly follow up progress of the applications until 
approvals are granted. 
 
v) 
Conduct internal reviews of all campuses/ branches / centres for compliance with 
NCHE requirements and close or improve those that do not meet the minimum 
standards and re-allocate the resources. 
 
vi) 
Ensure that no new study centres are opened without prior NCHE approval. 
 
vii) 
Develop and implement standardized research dissemination guidelines that 
define the procedures, responsibilities, channels, and approval processes for 
dissemination of research outputs. 
 

 
 
 
 
172 
 
 
 
viii) 
Prioritize and ring-fence budgets for research dissemination within Research & 
Innovation Fund (RIF) and other grant allocations, to ensure that researchers 
have adequate resources for stakeholder engagement, research publication and 
translation of findings into user-friendly formats. 
 
ix) 
NCHE should develop and enforce a sanctions regime (warnings, suspension of 
admissions, or closure directives) for non-compliance. 
 
x) 
NCHE should maintain and regularly update a publicly accessible register of 
accredited universities, campuses, branches, centres and programmes to guide 
students, parents, and other stakeholders. 
 
xi) 
NCHE should advocate for enhanced Government financing to allow NCHE to 
independently and fully fund all accreditation activities, including physical 
inspections, thereby eliminating reliance on university payments. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
While Government has been improving investments in public universities over the study 
period that are reflected in increased funding, staffing, and enrolment, these 
improvements have not translated into proportional improvements in the output of 
graduates, research outputs, or overall institutional efficiencies. DEA results show that 
several universities continue to operate below optimal efficiency levels, not because of 
inadequate resources, but due to internal managerial and operational challenges such as 
inadequate 
course 
planning, 
inconsistent 
assessment 
processes, 
inadequate 
postgraduate supervision, limited monitoring of research, and inefficiencies in academic 
administration. Oversight institutions, particularly NCHE and Ministry of Education and 
Sports (MoES), have also fallen short in consistently enforcing Programme accreditation, 
monitoring campus operations, and ensuring that teaching and research activities meet 
established national benchmarks. 
 
Furthermore, the operation of unaccredited campuses, admission of students to 
unaccredited programmes, limited research participation among academic staff, 
inadequate dissemination of research findings, and inadequate quality assurance 
practices further undermine the integrity of Uganda’s higher education system. 
 
To improve efficiency and strengthen institutional performance, public universities must 
prioritize reforms in governance, quality assurance, research management, and 
academic processes, while NCHE and MoES must reinforce their regulatory and 
supervisory roles to ensure compliance and sustainable improvement across the sector. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
173 
 
 
 
3.1.13 Licensing and Investor Support Services by Uganda Investment Authority 
Introduction 
 
Uganda provides investment incentives to attract investors, support emerging industries, 
and create employment opportunities. These incentives come at a significant cost to the 
government, making it essential that only eligible investors benefit from them and that 
their performance is properly monitored after receiving support. The Uganda Investment 
Authority (UIA) is mandated to register qualified investors and track their progress to 
ensure that the incentives lead to the intended economic outcomes. 
 
In recent years, the number of domestic investors applying for incentives has continued 
to grow, rising from 147 applicants in FY2022/23 to 159 in FY2023/24 and further to 
186 in FY2024/25. This upward trend demonstrates increasing interest in the incentive 
scheme and highlights the need for an efficient, transparent, and well-coordinated 
registration, monitoring, and evaluation system. 
 
Given this growing demand and the critical role that investment incentives play in 
stimulating industrial growth and job creation, it became necessary to undertake a study 
to assess how effectively UIA manages this responsibility. The main objective of the 
study was to determine whether UIA properly registers eligible investors for incentives 
and whether it adequately monitors and evaluates their performance after receiving 
support, ensuring that Government resources contribute meaningfully to Uganda’s 
economic development. 
 
Uganda Investment Authority (UIA) has put in place systems and structures to register 
and license investors who apply for investment incentives and to monitor their 
performance after accessing these incentives. These include the One Stop Centre, the 
eBiz licensing system, and the My Investor Monitoring and Evaluation platform. 
However, the audit established that these mechanisms have not been fully effective in 
ensuring timely licensing and comprehensive monitoring of investors. 
 
Below are the key findings and recommendations; 
 
Key Findings 
 
i) 
The number of domestic investors applying for investment incentives has been 
increasing over the last three years. Applications grew from 147 in FY2022/23 to 
159 in FY2023/24, and further to 186 in FY2024/25. This trend shows that more 
investors are interested in accessing incentives. 
 
ii) 
The rise in applications has put more pressure on the Authority’s registration 
processes. These processes still face delays due to incomplete applications, 
unclear guidance on the online system, and the absence of some key agencies 
on the platform. The average time taken to license a domestic investor in FY 
2023/24 was 7 days, rising to 11 days in FY 2024/25. 
 
iii) 
A significant number of investor applications were deferred because they either 
lack the required documents or contain errors. 

 
 
 
 
174 
 
 
 
Many investors did not regularly check the online system for feedback, which 
delays corrections and prolongs processing times. Deferred cases grew from 29 
in FY2022/23 to 64 in FY2023/24, and further to 79 in FY2024/25. 
 
iv) 
Some approvals could not be completed within the One Stop Centre because not 
all relevant agencies were fully integrated. As a result, investors often had to 
follow manual processes, which slows down access to investment incentives. 
 
v) 
Planned regional One Stop Centres in Namanve, Mbarara and Arua were not 
established, and existing facilities, such as the one in Mbale, could not be 
operationalised. Investors in upcountry areas, therefore, have limited access to 
timely support and must rely on the central Office. 
 
vi) 
UIA lacked a dedicated Monitoring & Evaluation (M&E) Officer, and M&E 
activities were carried out separately by departments without central 
coordination. This fragmentation leads to inconsistent data, duplication of effort, 
and limits the Authority’s ability to track investor performance and assess the 
effectiveness of investment incentives. 
 
vii) 
Investor performance data was mostly self-reported, with minimal verification 
through field visits or checks. Only 28% of licensed domestic investors submitted 
complete information via the online system, reducing the reliability of data for 
decision-making and weakening the Authority’s capacity to monitor compliance 
and the impact of incentives. 
 
viii) 
The My Investor online system experienced frequent downtime, slow loading, 
and was not integrated with the eBiz licensing system, requiring investors to re-
enter information. These limitations discourage submissions, necessitate costly 
manual follow-ups, and reduce efficiency, data accuracy, and the overall 
effectiveness of UIA’s monitoring and reporting. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
I advised UIA to; 
 
i) 
Improve the eBiz platform by incorporating clear visual instructions, step-by-step 
prompts, and tooltips to guide investors in completing applications and uploading 
required documents. Implementing pre-submission checks or automated alerts 
to notify investors of missing or incomplete documents before formal submission 
will help reduce errors and deferrals, making the application process smoother 
and more efficient. 
 
ii) 
Fast-track the full integration of all agencies involved in the investment process 
into the eBiz system. This will enable investors to access all services through a 
single portal, minimising manual follow-ups and ensuring approvals can be 
completed seamlessly within the One Stop Centre. 
 

 
 
 
 
175 
 
 
 
iii) 
Enhance communication with applicants by using digital tools and automation, 
such as online tracking dashboards, automated reminders, and phone 
notifications. These measures will help investors understand why their 
applications were deferred and what corrections are needed, ensuring timely 
responses and faster access to investment incentives. 
 
iv) 
Prioritise establishing regional One Stop Centres to ensure equitable access to 
investment services across the country. In the interim, the Authority can 
collaborate with existing regional government offices and agencies to provide 
core OSC services through shared spaces or co-location arrangements. 
 
v) 
Strengthen integration with all critical regulatory and approving agencies within 
the OSC to ensure end-to-end service delivery for investors. Coordinated 
mechanisms and digital integration will reduce processing delays, enhance 
efficiency, and improve the overall management of investment incentives. 
 
vi) 
Fill the vacant M&E Officer position and establish a centralised M&E framework 
to coordinate all monitoring activities across departments. Develop and enforce 
standardised tools, guidelines, and reporting templates to ensure consistent data 
collection, analysis, and reporting, improving accountability and evidence-based 
decision-making. 
 
vii) 
Enhance the reliability and usability of the My Investor system by integrating it 
with the eBiz platform to remove duplicate data entry and improve data 
consistency. In the short term, work with NITA-U to reduce system downtime 
and set clear service-level standards; in the medium to long term, acquire 
dedicated ICT infrastructure to ensure stable system performance. 
 
viii) 
Increase investor participation through targeted sensitisation, training, and 
support to ensure timely and complete submission of performance data. 
Strengthen verification mechanisms using site visits, mandatory documentation, 
and a risk-based approach to prioritise high-risk investors, reducing reliance on 
costly physical follow-ups and improving data reliability. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
While UIA undertakes investor registration, licensing, facilitation, and monitoring, the 
audit identified several gaps that limit effective management of investment incentives. 
These include delays in processing some licence applications due to incomplete 
submissions and system limitations, inadequate integration of key regulatory agencies 
into the One Stop Centre, failure to establish regional One Stop Centres, weak 
communication with applicants on deferred applications, and challenges with the 
functionality and integration of the M&E system. In addition, the absence of a dedicated 
M&E Officer and limited verification of self-reported data constrain effective performance 
tracking. 
 
To effectively deliver its mandate in managing investment incentives, UIA needs to 
address the identified weaknesses by strengthening system integration, improving 

 
 
 
 
176 
 
 
 
licensing efficiency, enhancing investor communication, expanding regional service 
access, and reinforcing the M&E framework. Addressing these issues will improve timely 
access to investment incentives, enhance accountability for incentive beneficiaries, 
support evidence-based decision-making, and ultimately strengthen the impact of 
investment incentives on investment growth, job creation, and economic development in 
Uganda. 
 
3.1.14 Implementation of Solar Powered Water Supply and Irrigation Systems by 
Ministry of Water and Environment 
 
Introduction 
 
Water is vital for human, animal, and plant life. Clean, safe water is essential for 
domestic and industrial use, while its absence leads to disease, mortality, and reduced 
industrial output. Agriculture also relies on water from planting to harvest, and limited 
access affects both subsistence and commercial farming. 
 
The NDP III prioritises sustainable water resource management through a dedicated 
program on Natural Resources, Environment, Climate Change, Land, and Water. This 
aligns with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 6 and 2, focused on universal access 
to water and sanitation, food security, and sustainable agriculture. 
 
Given Uganda’s rain-dependent, agriculture-driven economy, inconsistent rainfall poses 
serious risks. To reduce this vulnerability, the Ministry of Water and Environment, 
through the Directorate of Water Development (DWD), initiated a project to implement 
687 solar-powered irrigation and water supply systems across Uganda. The initiative 
comprised 252 irrigation schemes and 435 water supply systems. Planned for 
implementation over three years, the project had received UGX.161.15Bn by the end of 
FY 2023/2024. However, progress was hindered by the delayed commencement of 
construction due to the absence of feasibility studies and designs, among other 
challenges that delayed service delivery to intended beneficiaries. 
 
In response, I undertook a VFM audit to evaluate the implementation of solar powered 
irrigation schemes and water suppy systems by DWD in the Ministry of Water and 
Environment. The key findings and recommendations for improving performance are 
summarised below; 
 
Key Findings 
 
i) 
Out of the 1,009 sites handed over by the DWD to the contractor, 162 (16%) 
sites were marked as failed at feasibility study stage. This led to increased 
implementation costs of Euro 320,344.98, by way of undertaking new 
feasibilities studies as a result of abandoning failed sites. 
 
ii) 
Similarly, 58 schemes (21 Irrigation and 37 Water Supplies) failed at the design 
phase resulting into a financial loss of Euro 208,530 paid to the contractor for 
designs that were not implemented. 
 

 
 
 
 
177 
 
 
 
iii) 
By the project deadline of June 2024, only 122 out of the planned 687 schemes, 
representing 18%, had been completed. 
 
iv) 
Inadequate project costing led to the removal of 141 (21%) planned schemes 
from the original scope. Secondly, although 257 schemes had been set for 
construction, only 122 (47%) were substantially completed, and of those, 22 
(18%) had been commissioned for use, indicating a low rate of 
operationalisation. 
 
v) 
Additionally, construction failures affected 17 of the approved schemes, 
comprising 3 irrigation and 14 water supply systems. These failures resulted in a 
financial loss amounting to Euro 61,120.82. The failed sites at construction 
phase was attributed to inadequate sensitization of beneficiaries about land 
requirements leading to landowners withdrawing consent. Of the 17 failed sites, 
15 (88%) were caused by land withdrawal. 
 
vi) 
An inspection of forty-three constructed schemes revealed that fourteen (14) of 
the schemes were non-functional, while sixteen (16), though functional, were 
not in use. In these cases, farmers were mistakenly waiting for the delivery of 
seedlings, even though the provision of seedlings was not included in the 
project’s scope of deliverables. Furthermore, there were instances of vandalism 
due to the neglect. 
 
vii) 
DWD did not appoint or approve rural water committees and associations 
responsible for the administration of the water supply systems and the collection 
of funds for operations and maintenance. Additionally, DWD did not allocate any 
funding for the operation and maintenance of the rural water supply systems. 
 
viii) 
Only 8 (36%) of the 22 substantially completed urban water supply sites were 
handed over to umbrella institutions. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
The Directorate of Water Development should; 
 
i) 
Plan and budget for the pre-project implementation fund, and to ensure timely 
and adequate sensitisation of beneficiaries, and particularly landowners, 
regarding their obligations. 
 
ii) 
Ensure that detailed designs are initiated only after the completion and 
validation of feasibility studies, and to also strengthen internal supervision 
mechanisms to ensure that design-related challenges are identified and 
addressed proactively. 
 
iii) 
Under-take market assessments for project targets before costing and launching 
future projects. Conduct a comprehensive needs assessment, and to further 
formulate a database and monitoring mechanism that will provide up to date 
information on the areas that need their services, 

 
 
 
 
178 
 
 
 
 
iv) 
Ensure timely decentralisation of project management assignments so as to fast 
track timely supervision and approval of project assignments, 
 
v) 
Ensure that MOUs are signed, clearly outlining the terms and conditions, and 
implications of any breach of each party’s obligations, 
 
vi) 
Plan and budget for the timely site takeover and commissioning fund as part of 
the project implementation costs, 
 
vii) 
Enhance security measures for substantially completed sites to prevent 
unauthorised access and reduce the risk of vandalism before the commissioning, 
 
viii) 
Prioritize sustainability strategies for both rural and urban water schemes by 
including 
detailed 
action 
plans 
for 
operations, 
maintenance, 
funding 
mechanisms, and community involvement to ensure the long-term functionality 
of the water systems, and 
 
ix) 
Expedite the development of the irrigation schemes framework, which should 
outline clear guidelines for the establishment, operation, and sustainability of 
irrigation systems. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The DWD has made commendable progress in implementing solar-powered irrigation 
and water supply systems, with completed sites contributing to improved agricultural 
output, higher incomes, and better living standards. Despite this progress, by June 
2024, only 257 of 687 sites (37%) were under implementation and just 139 (20%) 
substantially completed. Key challenges included; inadequate feasibility studies, leading 
to 162 failed sites due to poor water sources and land issues; design flaws that caused 
58 scheme failures and a EUR 208,530 loss; and 32 sites abandoned due to landowner 
disputes over compensation. Weak market and needs assessments, delayed regional 
team deployment, slow design approvals, and consultant payment delays further 
hindered progress. 
 
To enhance sustainability and performance, DWD should always undertake 
comprehensive pre-feasibility and market assessments, adequate planning budgets, 
early community engagement, and stronger supervision. For completed schemes, 
maintenance structures, source protection, and clear operational frameworks are 
essential. Addressing these root issues will be key to unlocking the full benefits of solar-
powered systems and securing long-term gains for the citizens. 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
179 
 
 
 
3.1.15 Implementation of Uganda Communications Universal Service and Access 
Fund in increasing access and usage of Digital Devices and Services in 
Unserved and Underserved Areas of Uganda 
 
Introduction 
 
Information and communication technology (ICT) forms the backbone of today's digital 
economy and has enormous potential for improvement of people's lives worldwide. 
Relatedly, Social Development Goal (SDG) 9 aims at improving the extent and quality of 
ICT infrastructure and extension of networks into underserved, remote and rural areas. 
The Uganda Communications Universal Service and Access Fund (UCUSAF) operated by 
the Uganda Communications Commission (UCC) is aligned to the Uganda National Vision 
2040 that identifies ICT access and utilization as both a development enabler and as a 
major business opportunity. Accordingly, the fund’s operational guidelines are geared to 
address the issues of ICT Access, Adoption and Usage in the unserved and underserved 
areas of Uganda. 
 
Furthermore, the Uganda's Fourth National Development Plan (NDP IV) recognizes the 
crucial role of ICT in driving economic growth and development. The NDP IV aims to 
leverage on ICT to enhance productivity, value addition, and service delivery across 
various sectors, including agriculture, industry, and government agencies. Key focus 
areas of the NDP IV include digital infrastructure development, skills enhancement, and 
cybersecurity that require effectiveness in implementation UCUSAF projects. 
 
Accordingly, I undertook a value-for-money audit to assess whether UCUSAF has 
effectively implemented interventions for increased access and usage of digital devices 
and services in the unserved and underserved areas of Uganda. The interventions 
included; mobilization of resources to implement the intended activities, subsidies for 
the construction of Base Station Transceiver equipment (Service Towers), distribution of 
mobile device equipment and establishment of Public Access Centres (PACs), digital 
literacy trainings for Youth, Women, elderly, teachers and PWDs, and digital literacy 
programs. Below are the key findings; 
 
Key Findings 
 
a) 
Failure to charge the maximum allowed rates on the levy on the Gross 
Annual Revenue 
 
I observed that the Commission levied a rate of 2% on telecom operators (MTN Uganda 
Ltd, Airtel Uganda Ltd, ATC Uganda Limited and Tangerine Ltd). Section 68 of the UCC 
Act, Cap.103 (schedule 5) states that; the rate of gross annual revenue payable by an 
operator to the Commission shall not be less than 2% and shall not exceed 2.5%. The 
Commission would have realized UGX.8.075Bn extra revenue, if a higher rate of 2.5% 
was considered. 
 
I further noted that out of the gross annual revenue (GAR) collected by the 
Commission, 50% is remitted to the Consolidated Fund for information communication 
technology development, 8% to UCC/MoICT/UICT and the remaining 42% to UCUSAF 

 
 
 
 
180 
 
 
 
for rural communications, contrary to Section 68 (4) that requires the Commission to 
share the Gross annual revenue collected between Uganda Consolidated Fund (for 
information communication technology development) and USCUSAF (for rural 
communications) in the ratio of one to one. 
 
b) 
Delayed establishment of Telecommunications cellular mobile network 
infrastructure 
 
Out of the 68 planned towers, only 19 towers (28%) had been completed by the 
time of audit for the four financial years. The delayed completion of network 
infrastructures, and on boarding of a single mobile operator on the developed 
infrastructure limit the expansion of communication services to unserved and 
underserved communities. 
 
c) 
Delayed delivery of tablet devices to the intended beneficiaries 
 
Out of the 19,044 planned supply, delivery and distribution of tablet devices in various 
identified areas across the country in the period under audit, only 18,709 (98%) devices 
had been supplied to UCUSAF. Of this, 12,709 (68%) tablet devices were distributed to 
the intended household beneficiaries in the period of acquisition while the distribution of 
6,000 (32%) tablet devices supplied in FY 2021/22 was rolled over to the subsequent 
financial years, thus causing a delay. 
 
d) 
Insufficient ICT laboratories and Devices versus user demands 
 
The Commission continues to promote digital inclusion through the establishment of ICT 
School Laboratories, there remains a significant gap between the high cost of 
implementing these facilities and the national demand for such interventions. The 
average cost of establishing an ICT laboratory, according to the UCC technical team, 
ranges between UGX.110–120 million for a 20-computer grid-powered lab and 
UGX.170–180 million for a similar solar-powered setup. For 40-computer laboratories, 
the cost increases to UGX.210–240 million (grid) and UGX.340–360 million (solar). 
These estimates exclude recurrent operational requirements such as internet 
connectivity, equipment maintenance, software updates, security and surveillance 
systems, and periodic refresher training for instructors. Given the increasing number of 
secondary schools (8,658 secondary schools as per the Education Management 
Information System (EMIS) and the resources available, the Commission is unable to 
scale the programme at a pace that aligns with the nationwide demand for ICT learning 
facilities. 
 
e) 
Sustainability concerns on the laboratory and public access projects 
 
A total of 20 (33%) projects (16 ICT labs and 04 PACs) out of the 60 visited were not 
operational due to the issues of solar system failure, software upgrades, faulty N-
computing devices, activation challenges of N-computing application, inability to change 
passwords and update antiviruses licences due to lack of support in internet connectivity 
and refresher trainings on how to troubleshoot simple ICT issues. These were coupled 
with security concerns such as equipment not being engraved, lack of CCTV cameras, 

 
 
 
 
181 
 
 
 
fire extinguishers, lab attendants, security personnel, dust protective gears and 
protective maintenance to safeguard the ICT investment. 
 
f) 
Support given to Non-Government Organizations and Community 
Based Organizations without MoUs 
 
Out of the 18 public access projects selected for inspection, 11 (61%) were NGOs and 
CBOs supported with a 10 seater ICT center, a printer and some with internet package. 
These however did not sign Memorandum of Understanding (MoUs), clarifying 
expectations between parties and obligations in the collaboration. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
i) 
The Board and Management of UCC should explore increasing the levy towards 
2.5% to enable the Fund generate more revenue which will enable them 
implement most of the unfunded priorities and community demands. 
 
ii) 
UCC Management should engage the Mobile Network Operators and contractors 
of 
telecommunications 
cellular 
mobile 
network 
infrastructure 
prior 
to 
implementation for a streamlined on boarding process and timelines that are in 
tandem with the contractual terms. 
 
iii) 
The Accounting Officer of UCC should ensure that the procurement processes 
are expedited as per planned timelines. 
 
iv) 
UCC Management should ensure that the bottlenecks in its supply and 
distribution of tablets to intended beneficiaries are ironed out without 
jeopardizing the intended objectives of the Fund. 
v) 
The Management should ensure an improved and effective contract 
management processes by strengthening oversight mechanisms on the contract 
managers and follow up on the adherence of set procurement implementation 
plan timelines for timely supply and installation of quality ICT equipment and 
internet services to beneficiary schools/institutions. 
 
vi) 
The Board and Management of UCC should consider incorporating sustainability 
arrangements in the design of future projects in order for the implemented 
projects to survive beyond UCUSAF support. 
 
vii) 
UCC Management should always ensure that MoUs are signed before 
implementation of any projects in order to protect the interests of the Fund, and 
especially avoiding loss of funds in non-operational projects. 
 
viii) 
UCC Management should review the bottlenecks affecting the attainment of 
targeted number of trainings, and revisit the costing and mode of the trainings. 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
182 
 
 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The UCC established and has administered a Universal Service Fund to effect 
communication interventions with an overall goal of ensuring that those unserved and 
underserved areas get access to communications services that are comparable to those 
in the served areas, the demand for ICT within communities has increased tremendously 
and the Commission through UCUSAF has had to continuously design programs to 
address the demand gap. However, even with the available resources, the Fund cannot 
meet the total demand given that the main revenue base (communications sector) 
already bears a significant tax burden which is ultimately passed on to consumers 
coupled with community resistance in providing land for communications equipment, 
differing planning cycles and varying priorities of Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) to 
on-board the towers, high rate of device failure, delays in implementation of planned 
interventions and several sustainability concerns on the implemented projects. The 
Government should address the bottlenecks through policy guidance, mobilization of 
resources and strategic collaboration towards digital inclusion. 
 
 
3.1.16 Effectiveness of Interventions by the Office of the Prime Minister in 
facilitating achievement of Uganda’s Nationalised SDG Targets by 2030 
 
Introduction 
 
In 2015, Uganda committed to implementing the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable 
Development and subsequently integrated the 17 Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs) into its national development frameworks, including the National Development 
Plans (NDPs) and aligning them with Vision 2040. The Office of the Prime Minister 
(OPM) was designated as the lead institution responsible for coordinating SDG 
implementation across government, non-state actors and development partners through 
established coordination structures and Technical Working Groups (TWGs). 
 
The 
Government 
allocated 
UGX.31.4Bn 
to 
the 
Strategic 
Coordination 
and 
Implementation Department and the Monitoring and Evaluation Department of OPM 
over FY 2020/21–2024/25 to strengthen SDG coordination and tracking. Uganda has 
been an active participant in global SDG review processes, presenting three Voluntary 
National Reviews (VNRs). Despite these efforts, the national and international 
assessments indicate that Uganda remains off track on a significant number of SDG 
targets. As the country enters the final five years to 2030, concerns persist regarding 
coordination effectiveness, localisation and popularisation of SDGs, and the adequacy of 
monitoring and reporting systems to inform policy decisions. 
 
In light of the above concerns, I undertook a Value for Money Audit to assess the 
effectiveness of interventions by the Office of the Prime Minister in facilitating the 
achievement of Uganda’s nationalised SDG targets by 2030 and below are my findings; 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
183 
 
 
 
Key Findings 
 
i) 
According to the 2025 UN Sustainable Development Report, Uganda ranked 142 
out of 167 countries with an SDG index score of 55.8 out of 100, slightly above 
the Sub-Saharan Africa regional average of 53.9. Gains are notable in health 
(SDG 3), clean water (SDG 6), and energy access (SDG 7), but challenges persist 
in poverty reduction (SDG 1), food security (SDG 2), education quality (SDG 4), 
and gender equality (SDG 5). 
 
ii) 
Although the OPM is mandated to operationalise the SDG coordination 
Framework, the audit established that the framework was not fully functional. 
The National SDG Taskforce did not meet as required, and only 25% of planned 
Technical Working Group meetings were held over five years. Two critical 
TWGs—Coordination, Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting, and Finance and 
Resource Mobilisation performed poorly, failing to deliver most of their mandated 
responsibilities. The TWG responsible for Coordination, Monitoring, Evaluation 
and Reporting did not meet at all, during the period and achieved none of its 14 
responsibilities. 
 
iii) 
The audit identified duplication of roles between the SDG Secretariat and the 
Coordination, Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting structures within OPM, 
resulting in unclear accountability and weakened oversight. 
 
iv) 
The awareness and understanding of the SDGs remained low at the local 
government and community levels. SDG communication materials were not 
existing in the districts visited, and most local leaders interviewed lacked basic 
knowledge of the SDGs and their relevance to service delivery. 
 
v) 
Whereas SDGs were substantially integrated into national planning frameworks 
(SDG target alignment under NDP III was at 95%, improving to 97% under NDP 
IV), localisation at sector and district levels and the practical integration of the 
“Leaving No One Behind” (LNOB) principle remained weak. District Development 
Plans did not explicitly map priorities to SDG targets or indicators, limiting 
effective tracking of local contributions to national SDG outcomes. Furthermore, 
only one of the ten sampled districts had undertaken a Voluntary Local Review 
(VLR), constraining evidence-based local reporting and accountability. 
 
vi) 
The audit noted improvements in national SDG data availability, raising from 41 
indicators with available data in 2019 to 127 in 2024. However, significant 
weaknesses remained in data disaggregation required to operationalise the 
Leave No One Behind principle. Less than two-thirds of the required 
disaggregation categories for core indicators under Goals 1–7 were captured in 
the national SDG indicator framework. In addition, the national SDG assessments 
relied heavily on secondary or outdated survey data, with no clearly articulated 
assessment methodology, systematic baseline-to-target analysis, or results-
based evaluation tools. 
 

 
 
 
 
184 
 
 
 
vii) 
Inadequate engagement of MDAs and local governments in indicator profiling 
and target-setting exercises, further limited the production of inclusive, 
disaggregated data. As a result, Uganda’s annual SDG assessments over the 
three years served more as institutional updates than evaluative reviews, 
characterised by descriptive reporting, limited indicator application, and weak 
linkages between national plans, local data, and global targets. This SDG 
reporting risks masking inequalities, undermining evidence-based targeting of 
vulnerable populations, and weakening the credibility of progress assessments. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
To enhance the effectiveness of SDG coordination and accelerate progress towards the 
2030 Agenda, the Accounting Officer of OPM, should; 
 
i) 
Review and clearly define the mandates of the SDG Secretariat and the 
Coordination, Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting TWG to eliminate duplication 
of roles, and liaising with the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic 
Development to mobilise earmarked funds in the SDG roadmaps to support TWG 
activities. 
 
ii) 
Strengthen SDG awareness and localisation by formally disseminating the SDG 
Communication and Advocacy Strategy to all MDAs and Local Governments, 
accompanied by annual communication and popularisation calendars; and 
institutionalising SDG integration into detailed planning and budgeting through 
guidance that links programme outcomes to specific SDG targets and indicators, 
in collaboration with the National Planning Authority. 
 
iii) 
Enhance use of indicators and LNOB by working with UBOS and NPA to fully 
integrate applicable SDG indicators into the National Standard Indicator 
framework and providing technical guidance to MDAs and LGs on indicator 
profiling, target setting and use of NSI indicators; and appointing SDG focal 
persons at district level to spearhead SDG-related activities. 
 
Strengthen monitoring, reporting and data systems by institutionalising indicator profiling and 
target-setting through annual SDG target-setting exercises; ensuring that the Coordination, 
Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting TWG meets quarterly, produces an action matrix, and 
integrates outputs into departmental scorecards and National Annual Performance Reports 
(NAPR) reports 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The OPM has established a foundational policy framework and achieved key national 
milestones, such as integrating SDGs into development plans and preparing Voluntary 
National Reviews. However, the overall impact has been hampered by operational gaps. 
Coordination structures, including the National SDG Taskforce and Technical Working 
Groups, have struggled with inconsistent meetings and overlapping roles, which has 
derailed policy decisions for effective implementation of SDGs. This lack of functional 
oversight is compounded by a disconnect at the sub-national level, where limited 

 
 
 
 
185 
 
 
 
community awareness and a lack of technical guidance for local governments have 
hindered the "localisation" of the SDG goals. Furthermore, despite improvements in data 
collection, monitoring systems still fail to fully capture the "Leave No One Behind" 
principle due to insufficient data disaggregation, making it difficult to effectively track 
and address the needs of the most vulnerable populations. 
 
As Uganda transitions to NDP IV implementation and enters the final phase of SDG 
implementation towards 2030, the OPM needs to evolve from procedural oversight to 
results-oriented coordination interventions. This shift necessitates institutionalizing 
accountability within SDG structures, streamlining internal mandates to eliminate 
redundancy and duplication, revitalising SDG popularisation and localisation at sub-
national level, and enhancing inclusive monitoring and reporting systems. Addressing 
these issues is critical to accelerating progress, improving coherence across national and 
local interventions, and ensuring that Uganda’s SDG implementation effectively reaches 
those furthest behind within the remaining timeframe. 
 
 
3.1.17 Effectiveness Of The Ministry Of Health And Public Health Facilities In The 
Management Of Health Care Waste 
 
Introduction 
 
Health Care Waste (HCW) refers to all waste generated from healthcare activities, 
including both infectious and non-infectious materials. Unsafe handling, storage, 
treatment, and disposal of HCW exposes health workers, patients, waste handlers, and 
surrounding 
communities 
to 
infections, 
toxic 
emissions, 
and 
environmental 
contamination. The Ministry of Health (MoH), through the Department of Environmental 
Health, is mandated to regulate and oversee HealthCare Waste Management (HCWM) 
across the country. 
Despite Government efforts including the development of Water Sanitation and Hygiene 
(WASH) Guidelines (2022), National Environment Waste Management Regulations 
(2020) and the ongoing construction of five (5) regional incinerators, HCW continues to 
be unsatisfactorily managed across many public health facilities. National assessments 
have highlighted widespread weaknesses in segregation, storage, treatment, and 
disposal practices. 
 
In light of these concerns, I undertook a Value for Money audit to assess the 
effectiveness of the Ministry of Health and public health facilities in managing Health 
Care Waste and to identify areas of improvement to reduce public health risks and 
below are my findings. 
 
Key Findings 
 
i) 
Although the Ministry has developed several policies, regulations and guidelines 
to guide HCWM, gaps still exit in the current HCW management regulatory 
framework. For example, there was no requirement for facilities to measure or 
report HCW volumes, there were no clear indicators for treatment efficiency and 
emissions control, and there were no standards for the designs for common user 

 
 
 
 
186 
 
 
 
waste Pits among others. These resulted in adhoc and ineffective planning for 
HCW management, challenges in performance measurement and ineffective 
treatment of waste. 
 
ii) 
For the period FY 2022/23–2024/25, MoH did not have an operational national 
HCWM strategic plan to guide sector-wide planning and budgeting. This resulted 
into HCWM activities at national, local government and facility levels to be 
fragmented and inconsistently implemented. Although a new HCWM Strategy 
(2025/26–2029/30) has since been developed, this is yet to be disseminated, 
popularised and implemented. 
 
iii) 
There were no specific allocations for HCWM in the budgets and workplans of 
both the Ministry of Health and the Health facilities visited. Because of this, 
major HCWM activities such as construction of incinerators was purely reliant on 
the development partners who have since withdrawn their funding. The Ministry 
in response has planned to allocate UGX.5Bn to bridge the funding gap left and 
guided that Health facilities allocate 10% of their PHC funding to HCWM. 
However, the average annual PHC funding available for HWM amounts to 
approximately UGX.60,000 for HC II facilities, UGX.120,000 for HC III facilities, 
UGX.600,000 for HC IV facilities, and UGX.7,500,000 for hospitals. This is 
unlikely to have any meaningful impact. 
 
iv) 
Although MoH conducts periodic WASH assessments which cover HCWM 
activities, there was no follow-up with the Health facilities on the extent of 
implementation of corrective actions. As such, weaknesses such as poor 
segregation, inadequate storage, and unsafe disposal continued to occur across 
facilities despite being repeatedly identified through regular reviews. There were 
also other shortcomings regarding monitoring of HCW activities which include 
lack of a module in the DHIS2 system to capture data on HCW volumes, and lack 
of appropriate data capture and analysis tools at the Health Centres. This
