affected planning for HCWM interventions. 
 
v) 
Although the MoH established national and regional WASH/HCWM steering 
committees, no coordination meetings were held among MoH, NEMA, local 
government councils, District Health Offices, and the health facilities during FY 
2022/23–2024/25. This lack of engagement limited harmonization of HCW 
interventions across the sector. 
 
vi) 
Inappropriate waste segregation, collection, storage, treatment and disposal 
practices and systems were observed at all the Health Facilities visited. These 
were characterised by mix up of infectious and non-infectious Waste in the same 
bins, unmatched binliners, unlabelled waste bags, absence of dedicated 
temporary storage spaces, absence of temperature and emission meters at 
incinerators, and the use of inappropriate treatment and methods like open 
burning of waste. These collectively affected the effectiveness of HCWM in the 
health facilities. 
 
 

 
 
 
 
187 
 
 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
The Accounting Officer of the Ministry of Health should; 
 
i) 
Fast-track dissemination and implementation of the recently developed HCWM 
Strategy (2025/26–2029/30), operational guidelines, regulations and SOPs to 
ensure that all health facilities apply harmonised standards for HealthCare Waste 
quantification, treatment, emissions control and final disposal. 
 
ii) 
Prioritise HealthCare Waste management by providing sufficient resource at the 
national and facility levels. Specifically, the Accounting Officer is advised to fast-
track the implementation of sustainable financing model, including the polluter-
pays principle, to address chronic underfunding, and reduce reliance on 
development partner support. 
 
iii) 
Operationalise WASH-MIS/DHIS2 for routine HealthCare Waste management 
data capture and reporting, and establish clear mechanisms for tracking and 
enforcing corrective actions arising from monitoring and supervision activities, in 
order to strengthen evidence-based planning, budgeting and oversight, and 
improve accountability across all levels of HealthCare Waste management. 
 
iv) 
Engage with the local governments and relevant regulatory bodies, to strengthen 
supervision of HealthCare Waste management in both public and private health 
facilities so as to close existing oversight gaps, improve adherence to national 
standards, and protect health workers, patients and surrounding communities 
from risks associated with poor waste management practices. 
 
v) 
Ensure that national, regional and facility-level HCWM and IPC coordination 
structures are fully functional, meet regularly and operate under clear roles, 
performance indicators and reporting requirements, to enhance coordination 
among stakeholders, support implementation of agreed actions, and reinforce 
integration of HealthCare Waste management within broader infection 
prevention and control systems. 
 
vi) 
Disseminate and enforce implementation of the recently developed HCWM 
guidelines at facility level to ensure effective control of waste at source and 
strengthen 
compliance 
with 
national 
HealthCare 
Waste 
management 
requirements. 
 
vii) 
Assess HealthCare Waste storage needs nationwide and develop strategies to 
address gaps in compliant storage facilities to prevent unsafe accumulation, 
reduce exposure risks, and strengthen compliance with national standards. 
 
viii) 
Fast-rack the proposed remedial interventions regarding the un-completed 
incinerators and intensify resource mobilization efforts through engagements 
with the Ministry of Finance and the development partners given that this is a 
heavy resource requirement endeavor. 
 

 
 
 
 
188 
 
 
 
The management of health facilities should; 
 
i) 
Ensure availability of color coded bins and liners at all waste generation points to 
prevent waste mixing and lower treatment and disposal costs and enhance 
regular monitoring within the health facilities to sstrengthen accountability, and 
implement targeted improvements that enhance safety and compliance with 
national HCWM standards. 
 
ii) 
Enforce strict adherence to prescribed HealthCare Waste collection schedules 
and container fill limits in order to prevent reduce occupational injury and 
infection risks. 
 
iii) 
Establish and enforce formal contracts with licensed waste handlers where onsite 
treatment is inadequate, to ensure timely offsite treatment, prevent waste 
accumulation and use environmentally acceptable treatment and disposal 
methods. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The Ministry of Health has made important strides in the management of HealthCare 
Waste such as establishing guidelines and developing HCW infrastructure. Public health 
facilities have attempted to implement measures aimed at managing HCW appropriately 
however, there is a lot that need to be addressed by both the Ministry of Health and the 
Management of Health Facilities. 
 
The existing policies and practices are ineffective characterised by weak enforcement of 
regulations, inadequate funding, poor segregation and treatment practices, lack of 
reliable waste data, and limited monitoring. These have resulted in unsafe handling and 
disposal of HealthCare Waste and exposure of patients, waste handlers, public and the 
environment to risk. 
The timely and effective implementation of the recommendations provided in this report 
will go a long way to improve the current situation. 
 
 
3.1.18 Management of Road Weighbridges by the Ministry of Works and Transport 
 
Introduction 
 
Road weighbridges are a critical infrastructure for enforcing axle-load limits and 
protecting road infrastructure from premature deterioration. Effective axle-load control 
contributes to road safety, reduces maintenance costs, and supports efficient domestic 
and regional trade. In Uganda, the Ministry of Works and Transport (MoWT) is 
mandated to manage weighbridge operations under the Roads Act, Cap. 346, the East 
African Community (EAC) Vehicle Load Control Act, 2016 and the Traffic and Road 
Safety (Weighbridges) Regulations, 2010. 
 
At the time of the audit (October 2025), axle-load enforcement was undertaken through 
a network of eight (8) fixed and six (6) mobile weighbridge stations across the country. 

 
 
 
 
189 
 
 
 
Despite this number of weighbridge stations, vehicle overloading remained prevalent 
and continued to contribute significantly to faster road deterioration, increased road 
maintenance costs, traffic congestion, and safety risks. 
 
I undertook a Value for Money audit to assess the effectiveness of MoWT in managing 
the national weighbridge system to protect road assets and support safe and efficient 
road transport. The audit covered a period of three years from FY 2022/23 - FY 2024/25 
in regard to aspects of planning, deployment, operation, enforcement, and stakeholder 
engagement in weighbridge management. All eight fixed and six mobile weighbridge 
stations were inspected, alongside selected highways with and without weighbridge 
coverage. 
 
Key Findings 
 
a) 
Inadequate Profiling and Deployment of Weighbridge Stations 
 
Weighbridge deployment was not guided by comprehensive risk assessments, traffic 
volumes, or overloading patterns. Only five (5) corridors14 out of the country’s thirty-
seven (37) priority Class A and B road corridors were covered by operational fixed 
weighbridges, while six mobile units were overstretched across vast geographical areas. 
Several constructed stations remained non-operational, and major corridors lacked 
enforcement presence, contributing to accelerated road deterioration. 
 
b) 
Weak utilisation of weighbridge data for planning and policy 
 
Although weighbridge stations generate large volumes of axle-load and traffic data, this 
information was not systematically analysed or used to inform enforcement strategies, 
infrastructure planning, or deployment decisions. Data from mobile weighbridges was 
not integrated into the central system, resulting in the ministry conducting costly parallel 
traffic surveys to inform network planning and weighbridge deployment. 
 
c) 
Operational and Technological Weaknesses 
 
Weighbridge operations were undermined by outdated and inconsistent weighing 
technologies, incomplete transition to multi-deck systems, prolonged equipment 
downtime, and non-compliance with mandatory calibration requirements. None of the 
eight fixed weighbridges complied with the prescribed quarterly calibration schedule, 
compromising measurement accuracy, enforcement credibility, and public trust. 
 
d) 
Staffing and Capacity Constraints 
 
Three out of the eight fixed stations operated below the approved staffing levels, with 
some lacking designated controllers. Extended shifts, fatigue, and absence of regionally 
accredited training increased procedural errors, inconsistent enforcement, and collusion, 
thereby weakening axle-load control effectiveness. 
 
 
 
14 Kampala-Malaba, Kibuye-Katuna, Busega-Fortportal-Mpondwe, Kampala-Kafu-Nimule, and Malaba-Kamdini 

 
 
 
 
190 
 
 
 
e) 
Ineffective Enforcement and Deterrence Mechanisms 
 
The audit identified inconsistencies between vehicle licensing practices and prescribed 
axle-load limits, particularly for Sino-trucks. Weak tracking of repeat offenders, limited 
automation, and manual enforcement processes reduced the deterrent effect of 
penalties and allowed persistent non-compliance. 
 
f) 
Limited Stakeholder Engagement and Compliance Promotion 
 
MoWT conducted limited and irregular stakeholder engagement activities. Out of the 
planned 156 stakeholder engagements over the three-year period, only five were held. 
Sensitisation of transporters, drivers, and local communities was inadequate, reducing 
awareness of axle-load regulations and undermining voluntary compliance. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
To enhance the effectiveness of weighbridge management and protect road 
infrastructure in the country, the Accounting Officer of Ministry of Works and Transport 
(MoWT) should; 
 
i) 
Develop and implement a national weighbridge deployment strategy informed by 
risk-based corridor analysis, traffic data, and overloading patterns. 
 
ii) 
Fast-track operationalisation of non-functional stations and expansion of 
weighbridge coverage on high-risk corridors. 
 
iii) 
Establish an automated, integrated weighbridge data management system 
covering all fixed and mobile stations to support enforcement, planning, and 
policy decisions. 
 
iv) 
Enforce mandatory calibration and preventive maintenance schedules in 
collaboration with UNBS. 
 
v) 
Address staffing gaps, standardise training in line with EAC requirements, and 
strengthen supervision at weighbridge stations. 
 
vi) 
Accelerate automation through CCTV, ANPR, and weigh-in-motion technologies 
to enhance transparency, accountability, and deterrence. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
Overall, the MoWT has not effectively managed the national weighbridge system to 
adequately protect road assets or support safe and efficient transport. While the 
ministry has established a legal and institutional framework for axle-load control, the 
identified gaps in the profiling and deployment of weighbridge stations, utilisation of 
weighbridge data, operational reliability and calibration of equipment, staffing and 
automation of controls, enforcement of axle-load limits, and stakeholder engagement 
have constrained the system’s ability to deter overloading and preserve road assets. 

 
 
 
 
191 
 
 
 
As a result, large sections of the national road network remain inadequately monitored, 
axle-load violations persist, and premature road deterioration continue to impose 
avoidable costs on Government. 
 
 
3.1.19 Programmatic Audit Report of the Global Fund - Malaria Grant implemented 
by Ministry of Health for the period 1st January to 31st December 2024 
 
Introduction 
 
Uganda continues to bear a high malaria burden, ranking 3rd globally in malaria cases 
and 10th in malaria-related deaths according to the World Malaria Report (WMR) 2024. 
In 2023, the country suffered an estimated 12.57 million malaria cases (4.8% of the 
global total) and 15,363 deaths (2.7% of global malaria mortality). 
 
To address this burden, the Government of Uganda has implemented a range of malaria 
control interventions, including the mass distribution of over 28 million Long-Lasting 
Insecticidal Nets (LLINs), Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) in 13 districts, integrated 
community case management (iCCM) in 67 districts, and expanded access to diagnosis 
and treatment with Artemisinin-Based Combination Therapies (ACTs). 
 
During the audit, notable progress was observed in the implementation of the Global 
Fund Malaria Grant for the period ending December 2024. Indoor Residual Spraying 
(IRS) surpassed the national coverage target of 85%, reaching 95% of households and 
contributing to an estimated 80% reduction in malaria incidence within the targeted 
districts. 
 
Malaria case management also showed improvement, with 95% of confirmed cases 
receiving treatment during the year. In-patient malaria deaths declined to 1.9 per 
100,000 people, well below the national target of 3.6, reflecting strengthened clinical 
care and the cumulative impact of malaria control interventions. The combined funding 
from the Global Fund and the Government of Uganda reached 82.4% of the estimated 
commodity requirements, reducing the financing gap to 17.6%. 
 
In addition, the Malaria Programme Review (2024) highlighted notable progress, 
including reductions in malaria mortality, incidence, test positivity rates, and outpatient 
malaria visits, alongside improved and sustained malaria testing and treatment coverage 
across health facilities countrywide. 
 
Against this background, the Office of the Auditor General (OAG) conducted a 
Programmatic Audit of the Global Fund Malaria Grant to assess the efficiency and 
effectiveness of systems, human capacity, and processes supporting delivery of the 
grant’s commitments for the period 1st January to 31st December 2024. 
 
The audit examined the implementation of key malaria interventions by the Ministry of 
Health, reviewed the extent to which programmatic targets were achieved, and 
assessed compliance with national and global malaria standards. 

 
 
 
 
192 
 
 
 
It further evaluated the adequacy of oversight arrangements, supply chain and 
commodity 
management, 
diagnostic 
and 
treatment 
services, 
vector 
control 
interventions, and data quality. Below are the key findings of the audit. 
 
Key Findings 
 
Despite the above notable achievements, the audit identified several areas that require 
targeted improvement to enhance overall programmatic performance and ensure full 
realization of the Malaria programmatic outcomes. These areas are summarised below 
and detailed in chapter four of this report. 
 
Overall extent of achievement of annual malaria programmatic targets 
 
The performance against the 2024 national targets was mixed. Inpatient malaria deaths 
were lower than the target, showing progress in case management; however, malaria 
still accounted for 4.5% of all deaths, slightly above the 4% target. Outpatient malaria 
burden remained high (37.2% vs. target of 18.6%), confirming that malaria continues 
to dominate facility attendance. Confirmed malaria cases and test positivity rates were 
lower than the national targets, partly reflecting effective IRS and LLIN interventions, 
though results varied by level of care. The observed under performance in some of the 
areas was attributed to different factors as discussed below. 
 
i) 
Oversight by the Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM) remained limited, with 
monitoring efforts focusing more on HIV and TB other than malaria. Follow-up 
on malaria-specific supervision reports was inadequate, reducing the 
effectiveness of corrective actions. This further resulted in less attention to 
national malaria reduction and elimination strategies. 
 
ii) 
The Grant coordination and oversight by the Funds Coordination Unit (FCU) was 
not effectively done as only 50% of the FCU responsibilities were fully 
implemented. Key functions such as routine verification of reports, performance 
reviews, and systematic documentation relied heavily on verbal feedback and 
email exchanges, limiting objective assurance. This weakened the effectiveness 
of the FCU’s oversight and internal control role over Global Fund operations. 
 
iii) 
Procurement planning and supply chain management gaps were also observed. 
The estimated national malaria commodity need was USD.73.7M, yet available 
financing covered only 83.4%, leaving a deficit of USD 12.2M. Quantification 
gaps were also noted, including exclusion of essential items such as gloves and 
blood slides due to weak reporting on stock status. Facility inspections revealed 
shortfalls in storage infrastructure, poor records management, inadequate 
temperature monitoring, mixing laboratory chemicals with medicines, and 
insufficient fire safety equipment. This has undermined effective service delivery 
and may compromise the achievement of programmatic outcomes. 
 
iv) 
Malaria case management and diagnostic services showed inconsistent 
compliance with national guidelines. Some facilities treated patients without 
laboratory confirmation, while others left large proportions of confirmed cases 

 
 
 
 
193 
 
 
 
untreated—particularly Regional Referral Hospitals. Night-time diagnostic 
services were unavailable in 25.6% of facilities due to staffing gaps. Microscopes 
were poorly maintained, with 79.5% operating without being serviced. Stock-
outs of key commodities such as Artesunate, MRDTs, and ACTs were frequent 
hindering timely treatment. 
 
v) 
Vector control interventions showed mixed performance. Although LLIN 
coverage at household level was high, 87% of sampled facilities lacked nets in 
maternity and paediatric wards, leaving high-risk inpatients unprotected. 
Planning and logistical weaknesses left 13,763 structures unsprayed. Insecticide 
usage rates varied widely, and significant volumes remained unused. Community 
engagement 
was 
weakened 
by 
inadequate 
IEC 
materials, 
language 
inconsistencies, poorly timed radio talk shows, and limited posters. IRS waste 
collection by NMS was delayed for up to six months, posing environmental and 
public health risks. This affected the intended impact of vector control 
interventions and exposed some communities to preventable malaria 
transmission. 
 
vi) 
Data quality and reporting were affected by incomplete and inconsistent 
submissions across multiple platforms. Essential commodity reporting was weak, 
reporting rates varied significantly by level of care, and discrepancies were noted 
between facility data and DHIS-2. Fragmentation across systems (DHIS2, eLMIS, 
EMR) contributed to persistent data quality challenges. This affected the integrity 
of malaria surveillance systems for effective malaria case management. 
 
Key Recommendations 
 
i) 
UCCM should strengthen its oversight role on the malaria grant through 
dedicated monitoring and reporting for each disease, rather than focusing 
predominantly on HIV/AIDS and TB. 
 
ii) 
FCU should improve its documentation and assurance processes, including 
establishing clear performance indicators and increasing verifiable evidence for 
grant coordination functions. 
 
iii) 
MoH in collaborate with MoFPED should develop a long-term malaria commodity 
financing strategy to reduce reliance on donor funding and close recurring 
funding gaps. 
 
iv) 
MoH in collaboration with partners should prioritize the expansion or renovation 
of storage facilities to create adequate space, including separate areas for 
expired medicines and laboratory chemicals to avoid contamination and mix-up 
of commodities. 
 
v) 
MoH in collaboration with Health Service Commission (HSC) and Local 
Governments (LGs) should recruit and deploy the required health cadres in line 
with the approved staffing structure to support effective malaria case 
management across all levels of care. 

 
 
 
 
194 
 
 
 
 
vi) 
MoH through its regional equipment maintenance workshops prioritize and 
allocate dedicated funding for the regular servicing and replacement of 
microscopes and other critical laboratory equipment to further improve 
diagnostic services. 
 
vii) 
MoH should prioritize procurement of modern blood slide dryers (air ovens) for 
all health facilities to standardize drying times and improve turnaround times. 
 
viii) 
MoH should enhance IRS planning and execution by involving districts in micro-
planning, improving timeliness and quality of equipment delivery, and ensuring 
accurate enumeration of sprayable structures. 
 
ix) 
Improve IEC delivery by providing timely, translated, and adequate 
communication materials, and guide districts on peak-hour scheduling of radio 
talk shows. 
 
x) 
MoH should strengthen national data quality systems through harmonization of 
reporting tools, routine validation, and improved integration of logistics and 
HMIS platforms so as to improve surveillance systems. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The Ministry of Health, together with Development Partners, has made commendable 
progress in implementing key malaria interventions including; expanding access to 
diagnostic and treatment services, conducting large-scale LLIN distribution campaigns, 
and surpassing IRS coverage targets, numerous programmatic gaps continue to hinder 
the full achievement of the malaria programme outcomes for 2024. The audit revealed 
persistent weaknesses such as recurrent stock-outs of essential malaria commodities, 
inadequate storage and inventory management practices, limited functionality and poor 
maintenance of diagnostic equipment, and insufficient human resource capacity to 
provide 24-hour case detection and timely treatment. 
 
In addition, there were challenges in the oversight and coordination mechanisms, data 
quality gaps,low reporting rates at lower-level facilities. The identified challenges 
affected the achievement of several annual targets under the UMRESP and, if not 
addressed, may slow national progress towards malaria reduction and elimination 
strategies for the country. 
 
 
3.1.20 Follow up Report on the Value for Money Audit on the Management of 
Petroleum Data 
 
Introduction 
 
In December 2016, the Auditor General issued a VFM audit report on the Management 
Petroleum Data by the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development (MEMD) and 
submitted the report to Parliament. 

 
 
 
 
195 
 
 
 
Key issues were noted and recommendations made in the report related to the access 
to and submission of reports on acquisition of petroleum data, review of recoverable 
expenditure related to petroleum data, verification of petroleum data and reports, data 
storage and safety, and dissemination of petroleum data. 
 
I undertook a verification of the extent to which these recommendations were 
implemented and noted the following; 
 
Overall performance 
 
The Petroleum Authority made commendable progress in implementing the 
recommendations of the 2016 VFM audit report. Out of the 12 recommendations, six 
(50%) were fully implemented and six (50%) were partially implemented. Some of the 
key interventions made by the Authority include; 
 
a) 
Development of a Compliance Management System (COMS), integrated with key 
PAU databases, though it remains 70% complete and not fully operational. 
 
b) 
Development of several guidelines including a revised Data Management Policy 
(2022) and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) on data dissemination, 
Petroleum sale of data regulations, among others to guide in the management of 
petroleum data. 
 
c) 
Clear separation of critical roles and responsibilities in its data management 
systems, reducing fraud risk and promoting stronger accountability and internal 
control mechanisms. 
 
d) 
Establishment of a modern ICT data centre for storage of electronic data and a 
seismic tape storage and transcription facility. Significant progress has also been 
made in development of the Crane Database, including onboarding all 
exploration wells and integration with the GIS Geodatabase and PAU Factsite. 
 
e) 
Development/ acquisition of several software tools including MAGMA software, 
Petrel, Electronic Document and Records Management System (EDRMS), E&P 
Factsite among others which has improved the verification for petroleum data, 
the storage and its dissemination to the public. 
 
However, key areas such as compliance tracking, staffing adequacy, long-term data 
back-up capacity, and full data onboarding remain a challenge. To address these 
challenges, management of the Authority is advised to; 
 
i) 
Fast track the full operationalisation and enforcement of the compliance 
management system (COMS) to ensure real time monitoring of licensee 
compliance. 
 
ii) 
Adopt a phased approach to complete the development of the Crane Database, 
with clear targets and measurable milestones against which progress can be 

 
 
 
 
196 
 
 
 
objectively assessed, to avoid the perception that the system is perpetually 
under development. 
 
iii) 
Expedite completion of data migration and the onboarding of all outstanding 
petroleum data onto the Crane Database. 
 
iv) 
Prioritise establishment of a fully functional offsite disaster recovery site to 
ensure continuity of critical ICT operations in the event of system failures, 
natural disasters, or other disruptions, to safeguard the integrity, availability, and 
resilience of organizational data and services. 
 
v) 
Address the staffing gaps in the department to enhance optimal performance 
and fully mitigate the risk of inadequate segregation of duties. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The Petroleum Authority of Uganda (PAU) has made commendable progress in 
implementing the 2016 Value for Money audit recommendations. The Authority has fully 
implemented six (6) of the 12 recommendations and partially implemented the balance 
of six (6) which has resulted in in better management of petroleum data. However, the 
follow-up has also identified areas that still need attention of management. These 
include critical gaps in compliance tracking, staffing shortages, inadequate long-term 
offsite data backup, and incomplete data onboarding. The recommendations of this 
follow-up if implemented will considerably address these gaps and further improve the 
management of petroleum data in the country. 
 
 
3.1.21 Follow up Report on Value for Money audit on Utilisation of the District Water 
and Sanitation Conditional Grant by Selected District Local Governments 
 
Introduction 
 
In December 2015, the Auditor General issued a report to Parliament on the Utilisation 
of the District Water and Sanitation Conditional Grant (DWSCG) by selected District 
Local Governments (DLGs). The audit report highlighted weaknesses in the 
management and utilization of the District Water and Sanitation Conditional Grant 
(DWSCG) in the selected District Local Governments (DLGs). The weaknesses identified 
were in the areas of procurement, contract implementation and financial management 
in the utilisation of the DWSCG, which affected the ability of the selected districts to 
effectively deliver safe and sustainable water and sanitation services to the 
communities. 
 
The OAG undertook a follow-up of the 2015 audit report to assess the extent of 
implementation of the audit recommendations, given that the extent to which Ministry 
of Water and Environment (MWE) and the select DLGs addressed the issues raised 
would have a bearing on access to water and sanitation services and infrastructure in 
the rural areas of the implementing districts. 
 

 
 
 
 
197 
 
 
 
Scope of the Follow up 
 
The previous audit covered three (3) Financial Years (FY) 2012/13, 2013/14 and 
2014/15. The follow-up hence evaluated progress made by the MWE and the select 
DLGs in implementing audit recommendations from FY 2014/2015 to-date. 
 
Summary of status of implementation of the Recommendations and actions 
taken by MWE and the selected DLGs 
 
Audit noted that MWE and the selected DLGs have made some progress in 
implementing the Auditor General’s 2015 Value for Money audit recommendations. Out 
of the 53 recommendations made in the AG’s report of December 2015; 
 
i) 
31 (58%) audit recommendations were fully implemented; 
ii) 
13 (25%) audit recommendations were partially implemented; 
iii) 
3 (6%) audit recommendations were not implemented; and 
iv) 
6 (11%) of the recommendations were overtaken by events and no longer 
applicable. 
 
A summary of the status is presented in the Figure below; 
 
Figure 2: Status of implementation of DWSCG VFM Audit Recommendations 
 
Source: OAG analysis of responses and supporting documentation from MWE and districts visited 
 
The follow-up review revealed progress in implementation of audit recommendations 
with 58% fully implemented and a further 25% on track. Key improvements were 
observed in compliance with procurement regulations, adherence to engineering design 
requirements, adoption and use of durable materials in construction works for water 
facilities, and enhanced mobilisation and sensitisation of communities for sustainable 
development and use of water facilities. 
 
However, despite the above progress made, some challenges still need to be addressed 
to achieve efficient and effective Utilisation of the District Water and Sanitation 
Conditional Grants (DWSCG) by the Select DLGs, as highlighted below; 
 

 
 
 
 
198 
 
 
 
i) 
Delays in procurement, inadequate staffing for the Procurement and Disposal 
Units (PDU), and gaps in documentation of contract management processes 
continue to pose challenges in the select DLGs implementing the DWSCG grants. 
 
ii) 
The select Districts have also not resolved the issues of stressed water sources, 
which results in water scarcity during dry seasons. 
 
iii) 
Vandalism and periodic breakdowns of water facilities are also still being 
reported. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The Ministry of Water and Environment and the select District Local Governments 
(DLG)s have demonstrated a commendable commitment to addressing the Auditor 
General’s recommendations from 2015, with notable progress in the implementation of 
the District Water and Sanitation Conditional Grants (DWSCG). The report reveals that 
out of fifty-three (53) key recommendations, (58%) were fully implemented, (25%) 
were partially implemented, (6%) weren’t implemented and only 6 representing 11%, 
was overtaken by events because it was not practicable. 
 
Addressing the remaining challenges is crucial in ensuring development of sustainable 
water facilities and achievement of the objectives of the DWSCG towards reliable water 
access for all communities. 
 
 
3.1.22 Follow up Report on the VFM Audit On Government’s Efforts to Achieve 
Gender Equality 
 
Introduction 
 
In 2013, the Auditor General issued a Value for Money audit report to Parliament on 
Governments efforts to achieve gender equality. The audit report highlighted 
performance gaps in the efforts by the Ministry of Gender Labour and Social (MoGLSD) 
to achieve gender equality. The report made recommendations to address the identified 
performance gaps to with a view of enhancing gender equality. 
 
I undertook a verification of the extent to which these recommendations were 
implemented and noted the following; 
 
a) 
The overall progress in implementation of the recommendations of the 2013 
Value for Money report by the MoGLSD was unsatisfactory. Out of the 28 
recommendations that were given, three (11%) were fully implemented, four 
(14%) were partially implemented, while twenty-one (75%) were not 
implemented at all. 
 
b) 
There were some achieved actions by the MoGLSD towards the promotion and 
realisation of gender equality. For example, the Ministry has; 
 

 
 
 
 
199 
 
 
 
i) 
Developed the National Gender Mainstreaming Guidelines 2024 to guide all 
stakeholders in systematically integrating gender concerns into planning and 
implementation. 
 
ii) 
Revised the National Gender priority indicators, which are critical for putting the 
spotlight on gender inequality. 
 
iii) 
Been pivotal in ensuring that the Equal Opportunities Commission is fully 
constituted and functional. 
 
Despite these actions, the MoGLSD did not perform well in some of the critical areas for 
example; 
 
i) 
There was no training and proper supervision of Gender Focal Point Persons in 
all Local Governments. This negatively affects the progression towards the 
achievement of the government gender equality goals. 
 
ii) 
The MoGLSD had not constituted Gender Committees in the different MDAs and 
Local Governments, which has continued to affect the progress towards 
achievement of the Government gender equality goals. 
 
iii) 
Critical pieces of Legislation such as the Marriage and Divorce bill, Sexual 
Offences Bill and the HIV/AIDS Prevention and Control Bill were yet to be passed 
and enacted into law by Parliament. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The VFM audit report that was issued in 2013 made several recommendations to 
improve gender equality and mainstreaming within government. However, most of these 
recommendations have remained un-implemented. 
 
This can only exacerbate the challenges faced by government and further hinders 
achievement of full gender mainstreaming by Government entities. Management of 
MoGLSD should therefore prioritise implementation of all the recommendations that 
were either partially or not implemented at all if the noted/observed gender 
mainstreaming challenges are to be addressed.

3.1.24 Follow up Report on the VFM Audit on the Procurement and Distribution of 
Essential Medicines and Health Supplies by the National Medical Stores 
 
Introduction 
 
In 2016, the Auditor General issued a Value for Money audit report to Parliament on the 
Procurement and Distribution of Essential Medicines and Health supplies by the National 
Medical Stores (NMS). The audit report highlighted shortcomings in the pricing, planning 
and timeliness in the delivery of Essential Medicines and Health Supplies (EMHS). These 
gaps affected the efficiency with which NMS procured and distributed EMHS to health 
facilities. The report made recommendations to address the identified performance gaps 
as a way of improving service delivery. 
 
I undertook a verification of the extent to which these recommendations were 
implemented and noted the following; 
 
a) 
The National Drug Authority (NMS) made significant progress in implementing 
the recommendations of the 2016 Value for Money audit report. Out of the 11 
recommendations, four (4) (36%) were fully implemented, five (5) (46%) were 
partially implemented, one (1) (9%) recommendation was overtaken by events 
and one (1) (9%) was not implemented. 
 
b) 
There have been areas of commendable improvements in the procurement and 
distribution of EMHS by NMS for example; 
 
i) 
Prices at which NMS procures Anti-retroviral (ARVs) drugs from the approved 
local manufacturer are now comparable with the prices at which donors supply 
ARVs to government under other health programmes which has made the NMS 
price more competitive. These prices can even be brought lower through 
renegotiation of the MOU with the supplier. 
 
ii) 
Standardising the Mark-up NMS charges with what is provided for in the 
approved budgets has reduced budget distortions and made the cost of 
procuring EMHS more comparable and competitive across the various health 
facilities. 
 
iii) 
The price market survey data currently used by NMS is more reliable and 
accurate due to strengthening quality control systems regarding this data. This 
has resulted in more market reflective prices for EMHS supplied by NMS. 
 
Despite these notable improvements however, there are still areas that require redress 
by NMS key among which include; 
 
i) 
The continued procurement of ARVs and Anti-Cancer Treatments (ACTs) from 
the approved local manufacture in dollars (USD) continued to expose NMS to 
significant exchange rate losses which limited NMS’s purchasing power derived 
from the available resources. 
 

 
 
 
 
203 
 
 
 
ii) 
There are still notable challenges in the planning, procurement and distribution 
of EMHS. These include delivery of un-ordered EMHS, excess and under 
deliveries, unplanned among others. 
 
iii) 
There are significant delays in delivery of EMHS and responding to customer 
complaints and queries. The noted average delays to deliver supplies ranged 
between 19 to 69 days. On the other hand, NMS delayed by an average of 
between 16 to 572 days to respond to customer queries. The unresolved 
complaints also increased by 208% while the partially resolved complaints more 
than doubled during the three (3) year period 2022/2023 to 2024/2025 covered 
by the follow-up audit. 
 
Overall Conclusion 
 
The National Medical Stores has demonstrated a commendable commitment to 
addressing the Auditor General’s recommendations from 2016 with notable progress in 
the Procurement and Distribution of Essential Medicines and Health Supplies. However, 
there are shortcomings that have been highlighted by the report that NMS need to 
urgently address. Failure to address these shortcomings can only result in in more 
inefficiencies in the procurement and distribution of EMHS.

The key findings are presented below; 
 
 
3.2.1 Engineering audit of Infrastructure Projects Implemented by Kampala Capital 
City Authority under the Kampala City Roads Rehabilitation Project 
 
The Kampala City Roads Rehabilitation Project (KCRRP) is part of a citywide 
infrastructural improvement program aimed at tackling congestion in the city of Kampala 
through improvement of road network, upgrading of traffic junctions, and enhanced 
drainage capacity to mitigate flooding on the streets. The project entails; improvement 
of 62Km of roads, 123km of non-motorized traffic facilities, provision of street lighting; 
provision of scheduled Eco bus services with supporting infrastructure (bus depot and 
dedicated lanes). Complementary initiatives include: Women and youth skills and 
entrepreneurship development, and institutional support to boost project execution 
capacity. 
 
The project estimated to cost USD.288Mn including compensation and resettlement 
costs (net of taxes) is financed by Bank Group (ADB and ADF), the Global Environmental 
Fund (GEF) and the Government of Uganda (GoU). Of the total project cost, USD.275Mn 
covers the costs of civil works, consultancy services and provision of goods. I conducted 
an engineering audit on all the five (05) contracted lots (Lot 1-5) for the civil works 
under the Kampala City Roads Rehabilitation Project, worth UGX.717.98Bn 
 
Below is a summary of key findings and observations resulting from the engineering 
audit; 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
205 
 
 
 
a) 
Initiation and Planning 
 
I reviewed the overall initiation and strategic planning of the KCCRP project and noted 
that: 
 
i) 
There was no evidence of collaboration with and submission of designs for 
review and approval to MoWT contrary to the requirements of the Roads Act 
Cap. 346. 
 
ii) 
There was inadequate inclusion of infrastructure for some Non-Motorized Traffic 
in the designs contrary to the project objectives. 
 
iii) 
The lotting adopted lacked a clear and logical basis. Roads located within the 
same locality were allocated to different lots creating operational and logistical 
challenges for the Contractors and Supervisors. 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to; 
 
i) 
Engage with the MoWT prior to initiation of future projects and ensure that road 
designs prepared are submitted to MoWT for review and approval. 
 
ii) 
Ensure that NMT user requirements are incorporated and implemented in future 
road projects. In addition, the safety of the NMT users should be prioritised in 
the designs. 
 
iii) 
Ensure that for future projects, roads are grouped following a clear and logical 
basis to optimise efficiencies during execution of the works. 
 
iv) 
Develop a standardised methodology for prioritisation of roads to be 
rehabilitated/developed. 
 
b) 
Review of the Engineer’s Estimates 
 
I reviewed the Engineer’s estimates for all the five lots and noted that; 
 
i) 
There were inconsistencies in the figures quoted in the PPDA Form 5, the 
evaluation reports and the availed detailed BoQs across the five lots. These, 
compromise the reliability of Indicative Planning Figures used during budgeting 
which may result in inadequate budget provision to complete the works or 
increase the risk of budget inflation 
 
ii) 
There were discrepancies between the quantities in the Engineer’s estimates and 
the quantities derived from the tender drawings, with the variances for the 
sampled items ranging from 1% to 2446%. Such inconsistencies increase the 
risk of variations during implementation or having inflated contracts 
 
 

 
 
 
 
206 
 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to establish the actual Engineer’s estimates for the 
projects and going forward, to ensure thorough review and reconciliation of tender 
documentation prior to procurement in order to prevent recurrence of such 
inconsistencies. 
 
c) 
Procurement Issues 
 
I noted that; 
 
i) 
There were delays ranging from 116 to 838 days in the procurement of the 
works contractors and supervising consultants. These affected the timely 
commencement of the works. 
 
ii) 
The minimum average turnover requirement set for the Lots 1 and 4 was less 
than that recommended as per ADB procurement guidelines. This created a risk 
of selection of contractors without the financial capacity to execute the works as 
required. 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to; 
 
i) 
Fast-track training of staff in bid document preparation to improve efficiency and 
minimise delays in future procurements. 
 
ii) 
Ensure that, going forward, the annual turnover requirement used in the 
procurement of works is in line with the relevant procurement guidelines. 
 
d) 
Delayed Acquisition of Right of Way 
 
I established that there were delays ranging from of up to 1030 days in acquisition of 
right of way (RoW) for lots 1,2, 4 and 5. These hindered project progress due to lack of 
site access. 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to ensure that going forward, RoW is secured before 
commencement to minimise delays in execution of the works. 
 
e) 
Design Review Issues 
 
I established that; 
 
i) 
The design reviews on all the lots were delayed by 7-8 months beyond their 
stipulated completion timelines. This hindered the timely approval of the design 
recommendations and subsequently affected the Contractors’ sequencing and 
timely completion of works. 
 
ii) 
For Lots 1, 2 and 3, the ground investigations undertaken for some of the roads 
were inadequate increasing the risk of variations during implementation as well 
unjustified changes to design parameters. 
 

 
 
 
 
207 
 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to ensure that going forward: 
 
i) 
Design reviews for the agreed scope are submitted within the agreed timelines. 
ii) 
Adequate ground investigations are conducted during the design phases 
 
f) 
Review of Relocation of Utilities 
 
I reviewed documentation relating to relocation of utilities and noted that; 
 
i) 
On Lots 1,2,3 and 5 there were delays of up to 882 days in the completion of 
relocations. 
 
ii) 
The relocation costs for Lots 3 and 4 increased by 112% and 94% respectively 
beyond the original estimate. 
 
iii) 
On lots 2, 3, 4 and 5, the sub-contract amounts for water relocations were 
overstated by UGX.636.5Mn due to inclusion of unrequired items and errors in 
computation of supervision costs. 
 
iv) 
There was no breakdown for supervision fees worth UGX.614.3Mn for relocations 
for Lots 1, 2 and 3. 
 
v) 
A total of UGX.640.2Mn was irregularly paid for backfilling and murram 
compaction on Lots 3, 4 and 5 and change of pipe specification during 
implementation on Lot 5. 
 
Failure to adequately plan and execute the relocation works resulted in increased cost of 
relocations, delays in completion and affecting progress of the works. 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to; 
 
i) 
Ensure adequate scoping of all relocation works is undertaken prior to tendering 
of the main civil works. 
ii) 
Ensure adequate review of BoQs provided for relocation utilities. 
iii) 
Supervision fees provided by the utility owners are adequately detailed. 
iv) 
Review the irregular payments and recover any overpayments accordingly. 
 
g) 
Progress of Works 
 
I noted that; 
 
i) 
There were slippages in progress of works on all the lots, with physical progress 
lags ranging between 3.77% and 34.21% and delays in sectional handover 
between 285-834 days for Lot 1. 
 
ii) 
Liquidated damages of UGX.12.76Bn on Lots 2 and 3 for failure to achieve 40% 
physical progress in 60% of the allocated time per section as defined in the 
contracts, remained unclaimed. 

 
 
 
 
208 
 
 
 
iii) 
The liquidated damages clause in all the contracts was ineffective as it could not 
be applied if the contractor achieved 40% physical progress in 60% of the 
allocated time but failed to complete the works within the overall completion 
timeline resulting in forfeiting of the damages, as was the case for Lot 1. 
 
Slow progress not only denies the intended users timely usage of the infrastructure but 
also prolongs the negative effects of construction activities on businesses and lives of 
the surrounding communities. In addition, unclaimed or forfeited damages deny 
Government compensation for failure by the contractors to deliver the project works in 
time. 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to; 
 
i) 
Compel the contractors to institute measures to accelerate the progress of the 
works to ensure timely completion. 
 
ii) 
Claim the liquidated damages of UGX.12.76Bn due to the Employer. 
 
iii) 
Ensure that going forward, the contracts penalise contractors for failure to 
achieve completion of works in the allotted time. 
 
h) 
Irregularities in Application of Price Adjustment 
 
I reviewed the application of price adjustment and noted that; 
 
i) 
The price adjustment clauses in the contracts considered that all cost elements 
of works would be applicable from the start of the application and did not 
provide for cases where some cost elements in the formula were not yet used in 
the works. This resulted in generation of an adjustment multiplier using some 
inputs that were not yet due which can result in an unfair payment. 
 
ii) 
For Lots 3 and 4, the indices used for computation of the foreign component of 
VoP were different from those of the source country of the inputs contrary to 
contract requirements. This resulted in an irregular payment of USD.1,385,646; 
iii) 
For Lot 3, an overpayment of USD.9,259 resulting from failure to update the 
foreign base indices as contractually required. 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to ensure that; 
 
i) 
Going forward, price adjustment formulas are provided for each of the different 
construction components of works. In addition, in cases where one formula is 
used, guidance is provided regarding use of cost elements not yet due to 
prevent ambiguities in application. 
 
ii) 
The inconsistencies in the sources of indices being used for price adjustment are 
resolved for all the contracts. 
 
iii) 
The overpayment of USD.9,259 is recovered. 

 
 
 
 
209 
 
 
 
i) 
Review of Payments to Contractors 
 
I reviewed the payments to contractors and noted that; 
 
i) 
Except for Lot 4 where timeliness of payments could not be established due to 
unprovided payment vouchers, payments to all the other contractors 
experienced delays of up to 321 days. Arising from these delays, the Contractors 
for Lots 1, 3 and 5 projects had claimed financing charges totalling to 
UGX.699Mn and USD.115,325. 
 
ii) 
Overpayments totalling to UGX.1.217Bn had been made on Lots 3, 4 and 5 as a 
result of use of higher-than-contractual percentage rate for overhead charges 
and profit on provisional sums. 
 
iii) 
Interest rates contrary to those specified in the contracts had been adopted in 
the computation of financing charges on delayed payments resulting in over 
certifications of UGX.291.6Mn and USD.15,229.12 on Lots 1, 3 and 5. 
 
iv) 
An overpayment of UGX.52.7Mn was made on Lots 4 and 5 resulting from 
double payment of personal protection and site safety items. 
 
Delays in payments result in a financial loss in form of avoidable financing charges while 
overpayments expose Government to a risk of financial loss if not recovered. 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to ensure that; 
 
i) 
Going forward, payments to contractors are made within the contractual 
timelines and any financing charges due to the contractors are not included in 
the payment certificates. 
 
ii) 
The overpayments totalling to UGX.1.217Bn are recovered. 
 
j) 
Mobilisation of the Contractors 
 
I established that; 
 
i) 
Apart from the Lot 1 contractor, all the other contractors had failed to mobilize 
adequate equipment as per the contract provisions. 
 
ii) 
All the contractors had failed to deploy some of the expected approved 
personnel as per the contract provisions. 
 
iii) 
For Lots 3 and 4 where the contractor was the same, some of the equipment 
was being shared contrary to contract requirements. 
 
Failure to adequately mobilise equipment and personnel may result in delays in 
completion, poor workmanship and poor-quality works. 
 

 
 
 
 
210 
 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to ensure that the contractors adequately mobilise 
equipment and personnel for timely completion of the works. 
 
k) 
Implementation of Works Contrary to Availed Designs 
 
I noted that on Lots 3 and 5, some of the pavement layers implemented on Muzito, 
Ssuuna II, Masiro and Mugema Roads, were contrary to those specified in the availed 
design review reports. This resulted in an additional cost of UGX.3.01Bn. 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to ensure that for future projects, the implemented 
pavement structures are in accordance with the design report and drawings.

3.2.2 Value for Money Audit/Assessment on Selected Infrastructure Projects 
Implemented by Entities Participating in the Greater Kampala Metropolitan 
Area Urban Development Program 
 
The Government of Uganda, through the Office of the President - Ministry of Kampala 
Capital City and Metropolitan Affairs (MKCC&MA), is implementing the Greater Kampala 
Metropolitan Area Urban Development Program (GKMA-UDP). The program spans five 
fiscal years, beginning in 2023/24 and is being implemented in the nine GKMA 
implementing entities of Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA), the District Local 
Governments of Wakiso, Mukono and Mpigi, and the Municipalities of Kira, Nansana, 
Makindye-Ssabagabo, Mukono and Entebbe. 

 
 
 
 
215 
 
 
 
In line with the funding requirements, I conducted an audit/assessment on twenty-four 
(24) infrastructure projects comprising Roads and Building with a total cost of 
UGX.487.6Bn15 implemented by Local Governments (LGs) participating in the GKMA-
UDP. 
 
For the financial year 2024/25, with the exception of GKMA financed projects 
Municipalities of Kira and Mukono Municipalities, which had attained significant physical 
progress, all the other GKMA financed projects in the remaining seven entities had very 
low physical progress. As such, for these seven entities, the assessment only focussed 
on non-GKMA financed infrastructure projects. 
Presented below is a summary of the key findings, the details of which are included in 
the consolidated audit report covering all nine entities, as well as in the individual audit 
reports issued separately; 
 
i) 
Only Mukono DLG and Makindye Ssabagabo MC completed all their projects that 
had reached the initial completion stage, at the time of audit, within the original 
contractual timelines. In the remaining seven entities, completion of projects 
that had reached their initial completion dates exceeded the planned timelines 
by between 17 and 310 days. 
 
ii) 
I undertook measurements on some of the executed work items and noted that 
there were inconsistencies in some of the quantities certified resulting in 
overpayments of UGX.846.6Mn16. 
 
iii) 
With the exception of Nansana MC, Entebbe MC, Makindye Ssabagabo MC and 
Mukono DLG, I noted delays in payments to contractors, consultants and/or 
suppliers across all the other entities. 
 
iv) 
Out of the nine entities assessed, only Makindye Ssabagabo MC, Entebbe MC 
and Nansana MC provided evidence of conducting all the required material tests 
for their projects. The remaining six entities conducted only partial material 
testing, thereby increasing the risk of incorporating substandard materials, which 
may adversely affect the quality and durability of the works. 
 
v) 
The physical inspection of works revealed defects on all the road projects 
implemented by the entities. The observed defects included, unjointed stone 
masonry, honeycombing, surface voids in concrete, damaged culverts and head 
walls, incomplete sealing of culvert joints, cracks on the asphalt concrete, rigid 
pavement failure, etc. For the building projects, apart from the project in 
Nansana MC and one (01) project in Wakiso DLG, defects were observed on all 
the projects in the remaining seven (07) entities. These defects included: honey 
combed and damaged ramps, columns beam and lintels, uneven floor tiling in 
the classroom, crooked and poorly finished chalk rail, roofing timber pieces not 
completely covered by treatment agent, lightning arrestor installed without a 
ground inspection chamber, rust on structural steel members etc. 
 
15 This cost is inclusive of the contract sums for the two KCCA projects implemented under KCRRP 
16 This figure is exclusive of overpayments for the two KCRRP projects. The overpayments for these are reported under the KCRRP 
section

vi) 
Out of the nine entities assessed, only Makindye Ssabagabo MC provided

I advised the respective Accounting Officers to ensure that; 
 
i) 
Measures are put in place to ensure that works are completed within the 
stipulated timelines. 
ii)

iii)

PART IV: INFORMATION SYSTEMS, FORENSIC AND SPECIAL AUDITS 
 
This Section provides a summary of findings from Information Systems (IS), Special and 
Forensic Audits. 
 
4.1 
Information Systems Audits 
 
Introduction 
 
Sections 12 (1) (d) and 21 of the National Audit Act (NAA), Cap 170, mandate the AG to 
audit all Government investments and to carry out special audit engagements, which, 
among others, include Information System Audits. In addition, Paragraph 18 of the 
International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI) 1315, requires external 
auditors to consider whether the audited entity has responded adequately to the risks 
arising from IT by establishing effective general IT and application controls and evaluate 
whether these are effectively implemented to maintain the integrity of information and 
the security of the data processed by such systems. 
 
Furthermore, INTOSAI GUIDE 5100, requires SAIs to conduct examination of controls 
related to IS to ensure that internal IT controls that maintain confidentiality, integrity, 
and availability of data have been adopted by public sector entities. Relatedly, the 
transition by governments and public sector entities to computerized IS and electronic 
processing triggered significant changes that present high-risk control environment. 
 
Based on my annual risk assessment, all Government Information Systems were 
assessed and ranked in accordance with the OAG Risk Audit Framework. 
 
Objectives of IS Audits 
 
The overall objective of the IS Audits was to evaluate the integrity, consistency, and 
availability aspects of the systems and data processes, mainly focusing on General, 
Application, and specific controls. 
 
The audit reports were redacted to remove critical system sensitive information for 
purposes of confidentiality and protecting the systems from external parties who may 
use audit information for unauthorized access. 
 
Audits Undertaken 
 
Eighteen (18) IS audits were undertaken as separate audit engagements and separate 
reports were issued to the Accounting Officers of the respective entities. Given the 
sensitive nature and risk of issuing IS reports to the general public, fifteen (15) report 
findings are not presented in this Consolidated Report. 
 
Below are the redacted executive summaries of three (3) issued reports; 
 
 

 
 
 
 
218 
 
 
 
4.1.1 Information Systems Audit of EMIS and TELA at the Ministry of Education and 
Sports 
 
Introduction 
 
I undertook an audit of the Education Management Information System (EMIS) and 
Teacher Effectiveness and Learner Achievement (TELA) at the Ministry of Education and 
Sports (MoES) to establish whether the systems are safeguarding the entity’s assets, 
maintaining the integrity of stored and communicated data, operating efficiently, and to 
make recommendations for improvement of the systems. 
 
The two systems are core Government of Uganda digital platforms implemented by 
MoES to support evidence-based planning, service delivery, and accountability in the 
education sector. 
 
The EMIS serves as the central repository and data warehouse for education sector 
information, capturing data on learners, teachers, institutions, infrastructure, and 
performance indicators across all districts. It supports policy formulation, budgeting, 
monitoring, and reporting, and interfaces with several sector systems such as 
examination bodies and inspection platforms. 
 
The TELA is a teacher and learner attendance and performance monitoring system, 
designed to improve teacher time-on-task and learner attendance through mobile and 
web technologies. It has been rolled out in phases, starting with government schools 
and later extending to private institutions, and supports attendance tracking, enrolment 
management, and performance analytics. 
 
Together, the systems represent a major investment in digital transformation of the 
education sector. Below is a summary of the areas of improvement that the audit noted;

governance

ensure that IT initiatives are aligned 
with the Ministry’s strategic objectives. 
6. Parallel IT Units within the Ministry 
 
The existence of parallel and project-based 
IT units operating outside the mainstream IT 
department 
has 
resulted 
in 
blurred 
accountability, 
inefficiencies, 
and 
inconsistent oversight of education systems. 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to 
streamline IT staffing arrangements by 
integrating project-based IT personnel 
into the central IT department and 
aligning all IT functions under a single 
governance and reporting structure. 
7. Non-Operational EMIS Modules and 
Functionalities 
 
Several critical EMIS modules, including 
Licensing, 
Projects 
and 
Monitoring 
& 
Evaluation, Help Desk, Messaging, and 
school-level 
data 
modules, 
were 
not 
operational at the time of audit, limiting the 
system’s usefulness. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to 
enforce the full implementation and 
activation 
of 
all 
contracted 
EMIS 
modules 
and 
apply 
contract 
management measures to ensure timely 
delivery of outstanding functionalities. 

 
 
 
 
220 
 
 
 
SN 
Area of Improvement 
Recommendation 
8. Absence of a Business Case for TELA 
Acquisition 
 
The 
Ministry 
did 
not 
prepare 
a 
comprehensive business case prior to the 
acquisition of TELA, resulting in limited 
assessment 
of 
value 
for 
money, 
sustainability, and alignment with existing 
systems. 
 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to 
institutionalise 
the 
preparation 
of 
comprehensive business cases for all 
major 
IT 
investments 
to 
support 
informed decision-making and ensure 
value for money. 
9. Implementation 
of 
TELA 
with 
Unresolved System Bugs 
 
TELA was implemented with known technical 
defects that affected system stability, user 
confidence, and effective utilisation. 
 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to 
ensure that all identified system bugs 
are resolved through structured testing 
and acceptance processes before full 
operational rollout. 
10. Use of TELA by Unlicensed Schools 
 
TELA was found to be in use by schools that 
were not duly licensed by the Ministry, 
undermining regulatory controls and the 
integrity of captured data. 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to 
integrate TELA with the school licensing 
function and restrict system access to 
only duly licensed education institutions. 
11. Deactivation of GPS Functionality in 
TELA 
 
The deactivation of GPS and geofencing 
features weakened the system’s ability to 
independently verify teacher presence and 
increased the risk of manipulation of 
attendance records. 
 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to

enforce

and 
geofencing controls to strengthen the

data captured through TELA. 
12. Failure to Track School Help Requests 
in TELA 
 
The TELA help-request and support tracking 
functionality was not operational, limiting 
visibility over user challenges and system 
support effectiveness. 
 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to 
operationalise the help-request tracking 
module to enable effective monitoring of 
system issues, response times, and user 
support performance. 
 
Conclusion 
 
The audit established that while EMIS and TELA represent important investments in the 
digital transformation of the education sector, significant weaknesses persist in system 
integration, governance, internal capacity, and functionality. Without urgent corrective 
action to address these gaps, the Ministry risks under-realising the benefits of these 
systems, and compromising data integrity.

4.1.2 Information Systems Audit of the Prisons Information Management System 
at Uganda Prisons Service 
 
Introduction 
 
I undertook an audit of Prisons Information Management System (PIMS) at Uganda 
Prisons Service (UPS). The acquisition and development of the PIMS started in 2015. 
The system was designed as a centralized, real-time, three-tier system to manage 
prisoner admission, sentence computation, classification, transfers, biometrics, health 
records, rehabilitation, discipline, discharge, and reporting across all prison stations 
nationwide. The system was expected to support all 253 prisons in Uganda and 
integrate with other Justice, Law and Order Sector (JLOS) systems to enable seamless 
information exchange. 
 
The audit sought to assess whether PIMS and the surrounding IT environment 
adequately safeguard assets, maintain data integrity and security, operate efficiently, 
and support UPS in achieving its strategic and operational objectives. Below is a 
summary of the areas of improvement that the audit noted; 
 
Table 55: Key Findings and Recommendations - PIMS 
SN Area of Improvement 
Recommendation 
1 
Unfilled Positions in the ICT Department 
 
The approved ICT structure at UPS provides 
for seventy-six (76) positions; however, only 
twenty-four (24) were filled at the time of 
audit. The shortage of ICT staff limits 
effective system administration, increases IT 
risk exposure, and constrains the realisation 
of UPS’s digital transformation objectives. 
 
 
I advised the Accounting Officer to 
assess and prioritise the critical unfilled 
ICT positions and engage the Prisons 
Council to obtain approval for phased 
recruitment within the available wage

and

PIMS has remained in a prolonged pilot phase 
since its acquisition in 2015, with rollout

to

Conclusion 
 
I observed that the system has improved the management of inmate records in 
locations where it has been piloted and demonstrates potential to enhance operational 
efficiency, data accuracy, and service delivery across the Service. 
 
However, I noted that the benefits of PIMS have not been fully realised due to 
weaknesses in IT governance, project management, system rollout, capacity, 
integration, and operational controls. 

 
 
 
 
223 
 
 
 
Notably, PIMS has remained in a prolonged pilot phase for nearly a decade without a 
clear, funded rollout plan; several critical modules are either underutilised or not 
operational; key prison operational processes remain manual; and integration with other 
justice sector systems has not been achieved. 
 
 
4.1.3 Information Systems Audit of the Electronic Licensing System for National 
Forest Authority 
 
Introduction 
 
The National Forestry Authority (NFA) is mandated to manage Uganda’s Central Forest 
Reserves (CFRs) and promote sustainable forest cover in line with national development 
priorities. Given Government’s limited capacity to undertake large-scale tree planting, 
NFA relies on private sector participation through the licensing of individuals and entities 
to undertake commercial tree planting, harvesting, and other authorised activities within 
CFRs. 
 
Historically, NFA’s licensing processes were largely manual, requiring applicants to 
physically submit forms at NFA offices. This approach was time-consuming, costly, 
prone to errors, and constrained service uptake. The absence of a direct digital interface 
between the Forest Management Information System (FMIS) and the public further 
limited efficiency, transparency, and oversight in the licensing process. 
 
To address these challenges and improve service delivery, NFA embarked on the 
development of an Electronic Licensing (e-Licensing) System. The system was intended 
to provide a centralised online platform through which citizens could apply for, process, 
and manage licenses for activities such as tree planting, harvesting, ecotourism, 
research, and other approved uses within CFRs. The system was also designed to 
integrate with other government platforms, automate payment validation, enhance 
accountability, improve revenue collection, and support data-driven decision-making. 
 
Implementation of the system was planned in phases. Phase I focused on automating 
the application, issuance, and transfer of tree planting and harvesting licenses, while 
Phase II aimed to extend coverage to additional license categories and integrate the 
system with NFA’s FMIS and other national e-Government platforms. The intervention 
aligned with Government’s broader digital transformation agenda and was expected to 
modernise forestry service delivery while strengthening forest governance.

Conclusion 
I observed that the implementation of the Electronic Licensing System by the National 
Forestry Authority was a well-intended initiative aimed at modernising forestry service 
delivery, improving transparency, enhancing revenue administration, and supporting 
sustainable management of Central Forest Reserves. The system design envisaged 
comprehensive automation, integration with key government platforms, and the 
enforcement of statutory and operational controls. 
However, the audit established that the system had not achieved its intended objectives 
due to weaknesses in ICT governance, system implementation, application controls, 
database security, and operationalisation. The system was not fully commissioned, most 
core modules were either not implemented or not operatonal.
