PART V: HIGHLIGHTS FROM LOCAL GOVERNMENT AUDITS 
 
5.1 
Management of Essential Medicines and Health Supplies in Health Centre IVs 
 
The Essential Medicines and Health Supplies (EMHS) management ensures that all 
Health Centre IVs are adequately stocked with the medicines and supplies necessary to 
deliver primary health care, emergency treatment, surgical services, and diagnostic 
services. 
 
Stock-outs of essential medicines and supplies remain a prevalent and critical problem 
across most health facilities, undermining the delivery of primary healthcare and the 
ability of Health Centre IVs to provide emergency and surgical services as mandated. 
 
Stock-outs of EMHS were confirmed for key tracer medicines such as antibiotics, 
antimalarial, laboratory reagents, and emergency theatre supplies. These shortages 
directly compromise timely diagnosis and treatment, increase the risk of patient 
morbidity and mortality, and diminish public confidence in the health system. 
 
I conducted an audit in 136 Health Centre IVs in 135 LGs to assess the management of 
EMHS and below are the findings; 
 
5.1.1 Inadequacies in Procurement Planning and Budgeting 
 
Paragraph 3.4.2 of the EMHS Manual, 2023 requires the health facilities to prepare 
procurement plans to guide the ordering of EMHS from the central warehouses/National 
Medical Stores. 
 
I noted that five (05) Health Centre IVs in five (05) Local Governments did not prepare 
budgets or procurement plans to guide the ordering of EMHS from the central 
warehouse. I further observed that one (01) health facility did not submit their budgets 
or procurement plans to NMS as required. 
 
In addition, seven (07) health facilities in seven (07) Local Governments submitted their 
budgets/procurement plans late, with delays ranging from 13 to 103 days. The absence 
of, and or late submission of, procurement plans distorts NMS’ planned annual delivery 
cycles to the districts. 
 
Consequently, health facilities were unable to deliver the desired clinical outcomes, and 
patients were frequently compelled to purchase drugs using their own meagre resources 
from local drug shops and private pharmacies. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to frequent changes in IPFs and budget ceilings, 
which constrained effective planning, while delays occurred because procurement plans 
were often prepared later than the first quarter and some health facilities waited for 
guidance from National Medical Stores before starting the planning process. 
 
Recommendation 
 
NMS should ensure timely and consistent communication of IPFs and budget ceilings to 
reduce plan revisions. The Accounting Officers of the LGs should ensure that the health 
facilities begin planning in the first quarter using established guidelines. 

 
233 
5.1.2 Inadequate IPF Ceilings versus the Assessed Requirements 
 
Paragraph 3.4 of the EMHS Manual 2023 provides budget ceilings for procurement of 
EMHS in each health facility. 
 
A total of 19 facilities in 18 LGs received IPF ceilings below the assessed EMHS 
requirements. As a result, health facilities experienced shortfalls ranging between 
UGX.11,928,149 and UGX.551,808,239 during the year. In addition, seven (07) facilities, 
had 565 vital items worth UGX.386,025,330 that were not budgeted for. 
 
Consequently, NMS was unable to deliver the desired EMHS to the health facilities, thus, 
causing stock outs that frequently compelled patients to purchase drugs using their own 
meagre resources from local drug shops and private pharmacies. 
 
 
The Accounting Officers explained that inadequate IPFs are determined by the Ministry 
of Health and NMS, and the districts have no control. Consequently, the procurement 
plans are prepared within issued IPF ceilings, variances are carried forward to the next 
financial year, and concerns are communicated to the Ministry of Health for possible 
review and additional support. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should engage MoH to advocate for realistic IPFs, 
timely communication of price changes, and early notification of new drug introductions. 
Persistent funding gaps should be documented and escalated to the Ministry of Finance 
during budget formulation. 
 
5.1.3 Non-Adherence to Procurement Plans 
 
Paragraph 3.4.5.6 of the EMHS Manual 2023: Procurement plan performance monitoring 
requires the Accounting Officer to develop a perfect procurement plan where the 
submitted orders are not over/under 10% of the approved procurement plan for that 
financial year. 
 
A total of 32 health facilities in 31 LGs ordered EMHS outside the approved plan. I also 
noted that across these facilities, 3,844 EMHS items were over-ordered, while 1,128 
items were under-ordered. As a result, 25 different EMHS items expired due to 
overstocking. 
 
As a result, patients were compelled to purchase drugs using their own meagre 
resources from local drug shops and private pharmacies. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed procurement variances to NMS system restrictions, 
fixed procurement plans with limited adjustment, varying IPFs, and NMS supply 
practices based on available stock rather than orders. Additional causes included 
fluctuating disease patterns, increased patient load, price changes, and capacity gaps in 
forecasting. 
 

 
234 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should improve forecasting capacity, conduct regular 
reconciliations, and prioritize demand-based ordering. In addition, the Accounting 
Officers should engage NMS to enhance planning flexibility, ensure timely 
communication on IPFs and pricing, and align supplies with actual facility needs. 
 
5.1.4 Delayed Submission of Orders to NMS 
 
Paragraph 4.1.1.4 of the EMHS Manual 2023 requires the Health Facility to submit 
orders according to the suppliers’ order and delivery schedules except for emergency 
situations. 
 
I noted that 10 health facilities in 10 LGs submitted orders late (past the scheduled 
ordering dates) with delays ranging from 3 to 122 days. 
 
The delayed submission of orders disrupted the scheduled supply cycle, resulting in late 
or missed deliveries from NMS, which undermined service continuity. 
 
The Accounting Officers cited system and network challenges as the main cause of 
ordering delays, acknowledged internal lapses, committed to timely future orders, and 
noted that EMHS ordering and delivery schedules are largely controlled by NMS. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should ensure timely EMHS ordering by enforcing 
adherence to ordering schedules, improving internal oversight, and putting in place 
contingency measures for system or network downtimes. In addition, the Ministry of 
Health should engage NMS to address system reliability and improve coordination on 
order processing and delivery schedules. 
 
5.1.5 Receipt of Short-Dated EMHS (Shelve Life) 
 
Paragraph 5.3.3. (10) (Verification Process)- of the EMHS Manual 2023 requires the 
receiving team to Pay special attention to expiry dates and reject items with short expiry 
dates, particularly if it is unlikely that they will be consumed before they expire (4 
months for EMHS and 3 months for laboratory supplies). 
 
Paragraph 5.3.9 of the EMHS Manual 2023 further requires a health facility in-charge to 
fill and submit a discrepancy report to the warehouse (such as NMS, JMS, and others) 
within one (1) week of receiving a consignment that has discrepancies. 
 
I noted that eight (08) health facilities in eight (08) LGs received EMHS with a shelve life 
of less than 4 months, which led to the expiry of some drugs. I was not provided with 
evidence of rejection of short shelve life deliveries as required by the EMHS Manual 
2023. 
 

 
235 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to limited control over HIV commodities due to 
push supply and redistribution, staffing gaps and the failure to implement the internal 
controls committed to rejecting short shelf-life drugs. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should engage the MoPS to address the staffing gaps 
and enforce acceptance criteria for all EMHS to ensure effective oversight and prevent 
wastage. 
 
5.1.6 Delayed Deliveries by NMS 
 
NMS has standard delivery dates for the six (06) delivery cycles per annum, based on 
zones. 
 
A comparison of the standard delivery dates of NMS with the actual delivery dates at 
health facilities revealed that 102 health facilities in 101 Local Governments received 
EMHS deliveries late, with average delays ranging from 1 to 148 days. 
 
Consequently, late deliveries contributed to EMHS stock-outs which compelled patients 
to purchase drugs using their own meagre resources from local drug shops and private 
pharmacies. 
 
The Accounting Officers stated that delays in the delivery of EMHS were beyond the 
control of the District and health facilities, as delivery scheduling and logistics are solely 
managed by NMS. The Accounting Officers further explained that although orders are 
submitted on time, delivery delays were attributed to NMS logistical, financing, routing, 
and supply chain challenges, with management limited to following up, notifying NMS, 
and mitigating shortages through redistribution and supplementary funding. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should formally track delivery schedules, 
documenting delays, escalating persistent non-compliance to the Ministry of Health, and 
implementing contingency measures such as timely redistribution and alternative 
sourcing to minimize stock-outs of EMHS. 
 
5.1.7 Blood Supply Chain Weaknesses 
 
Paragraph 11.4 of the Uganda Essential Medicines and Health Supplies Management 
Manual 2023 provides that blood to be ordered routinely to ensure sufficient stock of 
supply in the health facility. Order quantities should be based on stock at hand and 
current demand or trend analysis with respect to clinical use in the respective facility. 
 
Review of health facility records showed significant gaps in blood availability and storage 
capacity across 78 sampled health facilities. 
 

 
236 
 
A total of 67 health facilities experienced under-supply of blood. Out of 49,081 
units ordered, only 27,298 units were delivered, leading to a deficit of 22,279 
units. 
 
A total of 13 health facilities lacked functional cold-chain storage facilities, 
undermining safe blood preservation. 
 
I noted that 34 facilities recorded blood stock-outs lasting between 3 and 365 
days. 
 
These deficiencies elevate the likelihood of service disruptions, jeopardise patient safety, 
and increase patient morbidity and mortality. 
 
The Accounting Officers stated that blood shortages were largely beyond the District’s 
control and were due to limited supply at regional blood banks and Uganda Blood 
Transfusion Service (UBTS), driven by low blood donor turnout, scarcity of certain blood 
groups, high demand for blood, power supply and equipment challenges, and funding 
constraints. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should ensure formal follow-up with regional blood 
banks and the UBTS through documented requisitions, regular stock reconciliations, and 
escalation of persistent shortages to higher authorities. In addition, facilities should 
ensure reliable power supply, adequate storage equipment, proper documentation, and 
contingency arrangements to minimize service disruptions arising from blood shortages. 
 
5.1.8 Management of Expired EMHS 
 
Guideline 18.0 of EMHS 2023 requires expired EMHS to be segregated from EMHS with 
longer shelf life and stored in a designated area. A separate register should be made to 
record all expired stock, stock cards must be adjusted to reflect this as a negative 
balance, and the DHO/MCHO/CHO and NMS must be notified. 
 
Inspection of the EMHS stores revealed that several items had expired during the year, 
and weaknesses were noted in the management of expired stock. These included; 
 
 
A 
total 
of 
44 
health 
facilities 
had 
expired 
medicines 
valued 
at 
UGX.2,648,823,144. 
 
A total 15 health facilities had expired medicines improperly stored, whereby 
some expired EMHS were stored alongside usable stock, and in inappropriate 
spaces like office corridors and wards. 
 
I further noted that expired EMHS had not been collected by NMS. 
 
Improper management of expired EMHS may lead to their misuse, hence causing a 
health hazard to society. 
 

 
237 
The Accounting Officers explained that EMHS expiries were due to short shelf-life 
deliveries, low consumption, changes in treatment guidelines, and inadequate storage 
and record-keeping. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should enforce inventory and expiry management 
controls by ensuring proper storage, timely update of expiry registers, and regular 
redistribution of near-expiry items. Supplies with short shelf-life should be rejected, and 
staff should be trained in effective stock management. Regular supervision and 
monitoring should be conducted to minimize wastage and ensure expired EMHS are 
promptly segregated and returned to NMS. 
 
5.2 
Implementation of USE Capitation Grant in Local Governments 
 
Government of Uganda (GoU) introduced the Universal Secondary Education (USE) 
program to subsidize school fees, providing textbooks and other instructional materials 
for both students and teachers, meeting the costs of co-curricular activities, school 
administration and maintenance, among others, for O-level leaners. Similarly, the 
Universal Post O’ Level Education and Training (UPOLET) program aimed at increasing 
access to secondary school education beyond “O” Level was built on the success story of 
USE. 
 
The implementation of the programme has resulted in increased enrolment in secondary 
schools from 0.95 million students in 2007 to 1.4 million in 2017, an increment of 32% 
in ten (10) years, and to 4.6 million students by 2024; comprising males (2.0 million) 
and females (2.6 million) in traditional and government-aided Secondary schools across 
the country17. This has led to overcrowded classrooms and low teacher morale, 
insufficiency of learning materials, high students-to-teacher ratios, thus adversely 
affecting the quality of education among other challenges. 
 
I designed audit procedures to assess the grant implementation in Local Governments 
(LGs) and below are my findings; 
 
5.2.1 Receipt of USE Capitation Grants in relation to Actual Student Enrolment 
 
Paragraph 5.1.1 (1) of the Planning, Budgeting and Implementation Guidelines for Local 
Governments for the Education and Sports Sector, 2021 states that the allocation of the 
capitation budget for schools and tertiary institutions will be pre-loaded into the PBS by 
the MoES using the verified enrolment figures and approved list of schools and tertiary 
institutions in Local Governments. The allocation for primary and secondary schools is be 
based on the approved unit costs per school and per learner. Each Secondary school 
should be given annual USE unit costs of UGX.175,000 per normal learner, UGX.192,500 
for SNE learners and UGX.1,230,000 for SNE learners in exclusive schools, and 
UGX.270,000 for UPOLET learners. 
 
I noted the following; 
 
17 The UBOS abstract 2023 & The national housing and population census 2024 

 
238 
i) 
Based on the EMIS enrolment of 804,227 students in 1,098 funded Secondary 
Schools in 146 LGs sampled, my re-computations revealed that the expected 
USE/UPOLET 
Capitation 
Grant 
was 
UGX.155,368,989,261, 
however, 
UGX.128,714,815,508 was received by the LGs, leading to an under-receipt of 
UGX.26,654,173,753. The underfunding affected subsequent disbursement to 
schools, thus affecting the implementation of planned school activities. 
 
ii) 
Similarly, based on the EMIS enrolment of 15,220 students in 17 funded 
Secondary Schools in 2 LGs, my re-computations revealed that the expected 
USE/UPOLET 
Capitation 
Grant 
was 
UGX.2,646,720,000, 
however, 
UGX.2,801,270,000 was received by the LGs, resulting in excess funding of 
UGX.154,550,000. The over-funding distorts planning and implementation of USE 
activities. 
The Accounting Officers explained that under and over funding was due to delays in 
uploading data on EMIS by school head teachers and irregularities in attendance of 
school by the learners. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of LGs and the MoES should ensure that the EMIS is regularly 
updated and only validated learners’ enrolment should be submitted to MoFPED for 
accurate planning, budgeting and release of funds. 
 
5.2.2 Students not captured on EMIS but actually enrolled at Secondary schools 
 
Paragraph 5.1.1 (5) of the Planning, Budgeting and Implementation Guidelines for Local 
Governments for the Education and Sports Sector 2021 states that the District/Municipal 
Education office is required to verify and confirm the list of schools and tertiary 
institutions, their enrolment and budget allocation in the Programme Budgeting System 
(PBS), and notify the MoES in writing, if a school or its enrolment have been listed 
incorrectly or missed. 
 
A review of the enrolment numbers in the Education Management Information Systems 
(EMIS) and Actual enrolment as per school records in 687 sampled schools in 131 LGs, 
revealed that 67,138 students were not on EMIS and this lead to a shortage of funding 
to the tune of UGX.13,306,233,669. 
 
As a result, this affected total funding of schools and caused financial pressure on the 
inadequate resources, thus affecting service delivery at the respective schools. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to; capacity gaps among Head Teachers in the 
usage of EMIS, failure to provide NINs by the parents, bad network in some regions and 
absenteeism by learners in schools. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of LGs should engage MoES to continuously train head teachers 
on the use of EMIS, and upgrade the EMIS to improve its efficiency. 

 
239 
In addition, engage head teachers to sensitize parents on the need for timely 
submission of their NINs to enable student enrollment on the EMIS, and attendance of 
learners in schools. 
 
5.2.3 Receipt of hard-to-reach capitation grants (Secondary) supplement 
 
Paragraph 5.1.1 (2) of the Planning, Budgeting and Implementation Guidelines for Local 
Governments for the Education and Sports Sector, 2021 states that the capitation grants 
for schools that have significantly higher costs in delivering education services because they 
lie in hard-to-reach areas (as classified by the Ministry of Public Service) may be 
supplemented by a hard- to-reach capitation of up to UGX.2,000 per learner, in line with 
greatly increased resources for Education Offices. 
 
There are 24 LGs gazetted by the Public Service Ministry as hard- to- reach and the 
schools in these areas are required to access additional special facilitation up to 
UGX.2,000 per learner. They include; Abim, Amuru, Adjumani, Bundibugyo, Bukwo, 
Buvuma, Sigulu Islands in Bugiri, Malonge Islands in Mayuge, Kaabong, Moroto, 
Nakapiripirit, Pader, Kitgum, Gulu, Nwoya, Koome Islands in Mukono, Kalangala, Kisoro, 
Kanungu, Lamwo, Namayingo, Napak and Ntoroko Districts. 
 
I noted that 103 schools in 19 LGs did not receive the special facilitation and this led to 
a deficit of UGX.1,254,485,671. 
 
Failure to make considerations for hard to reach areas as provided by the Guidelines 
may affect the delivery of education services in those areas due to the perceived high 
cost of delivering education services in those districts. 
 
The Accounting Officers explained that they were not aware of the hard-to-reach 
capitation grants supplement for hard-to-reach areas and promised to bring the matter 
to the attention of relevant authorities for consideration. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of LGs should engage the MoES and MoFPED to ensure that 
schools in the hard-to-reach areas are paid the capitation grants supplement to cater for 
the high cost of delivering education services in the affected districts stipulated in the 
guidelines. 
 
5.2.4 Expenditure on ineligible activities 
 
Guideline 2.3.2 of the Budgeting and Implementation Guidelines for Primary and 
Secondary Schools, 2019 provides a list of eligible and ineligible expenditures for which 
the capitation grant may be used. 
 
I noted that 84 schools in 22 LGs spent a sum of UGX.2,156,599,789 on ineligible 
activities. This mainly related to salaries to locally recruited staff that were not on the 
government payroll, and administrative expenses. 
 

 
240 
As a result, key planned eligible activities were not implemented and this adversely 
affected delivery of education services. 
 
The Accounting Officers explained that this was due to inadequate staff on government 
payroll which forced the respective head teachers to use part of the capitation grant to 
pay privately recruited teachers. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers in LGs should engage MoES and MoPS to recruit the requisite 
number of teachers in Secondary schools and who should be enrolled on the 
government payroll. 
 
 
5.2.5 Failure to prepare Annual Financial Statements 
 
Guideline 2.3.1 of the Budgeting and Implementation Guidelines for Secondary Schools, 
2019 states that each school is required to prepare an annual budget and financial 
statement capturing funds from all sources to the school and expenditures incurred from 
those sources. The school budget should outline all planned activities and ensure that 
expected revenues match planned expenditures for the new financial year. 
 
I noted 319 sampled Secondary schools in 75 LGs, did not prepare annual financial 
Statements in the academic year under audit. 
 
Absence of financial Statements negatively affects oversight over expenditure, income, 
assets and liabilities of the school thus creating opportunities for misappropriation. 
 
The Accounting Officers in LGs attributed the non-preparation of financial statements to 
limited skills and capacity of bursars and accounts staff, and inadequate financial 
reporting skills among head teachers, highlighting the need for targeted training and 
capacity building. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of LGs should ensure schools have qualified bursars who should 
be mandatorily trained on financial statement preparation, with support and supervision 
from the District Chief Finance Officers (CFOs) and the District Internal Audit 
Departments to ensure compliance. In addition, Head Teachers should be trained in 
general financial management literacy. 
 
5.2.6 Staffing levels in the Secondary Schools 
 
Paragraph 4.1 of the Planning, Budgeting and Implementation Guidelines for Local 
Governments for the Education and Sports Sector 2021 states that the Education 
Department must prepare a recruitment plan and submit it to the Human Resource 
Management (HRM) Department for the vacant positions of teachers and 
District/Municipal Education Offices. 

 
241 
 
I noted that in 705 sampled Secondary schools in 124 LGs, out of 30,539 required staff 
as per the approved structure, only 16,980 (56%) were filled leaving 13,443 (44%) 
posts vacant. Some of the critical vacant positions included the head teachers, deputy 
head teachers and instructors. 
 
Failure to have adequate staffing affects the supervision and delivery of education 
services to students. 
 
The Accounting Officers explained that LGs were faced with inadequate wage bill and a 
ban on recruitment by the Ministry of Public Service. In addition, they explained that 
recruitment and appointment of secondary school teachers is a responsibility of the 
Education Service Commission and Ministry of Education and Sports and they had no 
control. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting officers of LGs should engage the MoPS and MoES to approve and 
recruit requisite number of staff in Secondary schools. 
 
5.2.7 Physical inspections of USE Schools’ Infrastructure 
 
During physical inspection of schools’ infrastructure conducted between September to 
December, 2025, I observed the following in 157 LGs sampled; 
 
i) 
136 schools lacked science laboratory while 270 schools had laboratories that 
were not adequately equipped. 
ii) 
182 schools lacked a library while 233 schools had libraries which lacked 
essential books. 
iii) 
251 schools had no teacher accommodation facilities. 
iv) 
380 schools had inadequate classroom facilities leading to congested classrooms. 
v) 
233 schools had pit latrines that had been condemned and were in use. 
vi) 
237 schools had very old and damaged iron sheets. 
vii) 
252 schools had some classrooms with cracked walls and posed a danger to 
human life. 
 
Inadequate support infrastructure affects the learning environment which may lead to 
students’ poor performance, thus impairing the intended purpose of the USE capitation 
grant by government. 
 
The Accounting Officers in LGs explained that this was due to inadequate funding to 
secondary schools, as capital developments in Secondary Schools are handled by the 
Ministry of Education and Sports. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of LGs should engage the MoES and MoFPED to allocate 
adequate funds for rehabilitation and construction of school infrastructure such as 

 
242 
science laboratories, libraries, classrooms, pit latrines, and staff accommodation to 
enhance delivery of education service. 
 
5.3 
Audit of Local Revenue 
 
Local revenue collection is a cornerstone for service delivery and development in Local 
Governments. Over the years, Local Governments have faced persistent challenges in 
meeting local revenue targets, revenue leakages, spending at source, and poor record-
keeping, among others. To address the challenges, the Government introduced 
the Integrated 
Revenue 
Administration 
System 
(IRAS) 
in 
the financial 
year 
2019/2020 and the E-logrev (Electronic Local Government Revenue System) in financial 
year 2016/17. 
 
The total local revenue collection increased by UGX.66.98Bn (54%) from UGX.124.89Bn 
in the Financial Year (2021/22) to UGX.191.87Bn in Financial Year (2023/24). 
Despite the increase in local revenue collections, there are still notable challenges facing 
the Local Governments. 
 
I designed audit procedures to establish whether Local revenue in LGs in the financial 
year 2024/25 was appropriately budgeted, collected and accounted for, and noted the 
following; 
 
5.3.1 Local Revenue Performance as per IRAS/E-logrev 
 
I reviewed the Approved Budget and the IRAS/E-logrev Annual Revenue Performance 
/collection report for the Financial Year 2024/25 and noted that out of the budgeted 
total local revenue of UGX.248,849,478,844 in 124 LGs, a sum of UGX.196,329,205,208 
(79%) was collected leading to a revenue shortfall of UGX.52,861,936,899 (21%). 
 
Revenue shortfalls affected the implementation of planned activities, thus affecting 
service delivery. 
 
The Accounting Officer attributed the revenue shortfall to taxpayer’s resistance, capacity 
gaps, the IRAS system challenges, inadequate staff in the revenue collection department 
especially in the new urban councils and the inadequate Point of Sale (POS) gadgets 
which aid in field revenue management activities. 
 
Recommendations 
 
i) 
The Accounting Officers of the Local Governments should undertake all 
necessary revenue mobilization strategies to enhance local revenue collection in 
the Local Governments such as sensitization drives on taxation for both tax 
payers and parish chiefs. 
 
ii) 
The Accounting Officers of the Local Governments should liaise with the Local 
Government Finance Commission to help resolve the challenges affecting the 
IRAS/Elogrev system. 
 

 
243 
5.3.2 Lack of Local Revenue Management Committees/Non-Functional Local 
Revenue Management Committees 
 
Section 4.3.1 of the LGFAM, 2007 requires establishment a Tax Assessment Committee 
for every Local Government. In addition, the Local Government Revenue Mobilization, 
Allocation and Utilization Manual, 2017 requires Local Governments to establish 
Enumeration and Registration Committees (ERC) and Appeals Tribunal Committee 
(ATC). 
 
I reviewed the constitution and functionality of the committees and noted the following; 
 
i) 
Out of 136 sampled LGs, 105 did not constitute the Tax Assessment Committee. 
ii) 
Out of 136 sampled LGs, 105 LGs did not constitute the Appeals Tribunal 
Committee. 
iii) 
Out of 136 sampled LGs, 103 did not constitute the Enumeration and 
Registration Committees. 
iv) 
A total of 32 LGs had constituted committees that were not functional (8 LGs for 
Tax Assessment Committee; 12 LGs for Appeals Tribunal Committee; and 12 LGs 
for Enumeration and Registration Committees). 
 
The absence/non-functionality of these committees leads to unfair tax assessments, 
weak revenue mobilization, and increased taxpayer grievances, thus leading to under-
collection of local revenue. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to the recent adoption of the IRAS and absence 
of the required resources to facilitate the committees. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the Local Governments should ensure that the requisite local 
revenue management committees are constituted in consultation with the Local 
Government Finance Commission since the introduction of IRAS requires alignment of 
the Committees. 
 
5.3.3 Failure to Collect all Tendered Local Revenue 
 
Regulation 88 (2) (a-h) of the Local Government PPDA regulations, 2006 states that a 
contract document shall clearly identify the obligations of each party. In addition, 
detailed obligations are stated in the contract agreement between the entity and the 
tenderer. 
 
I noted that 728 Contractors in 54 LGs who were awarded contracts to collect revenue 
worth UGX.17,376,992,770, only remitted UGX.11,203,135,109, leading to a shortfall of 
UGX.6,173,857,661. 
 
The under-remittance is a breach of contractual obligations resulting into low revenue 
generation which negatively impacts on service delivery. 
 

 
244 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to; 
 
i) 
The foot and mouth disease that caused quarantine and affected operation of 
markets in the affected districts. 
ii) 
The negative effect of the ban on fishing activities in the districts surrounding the 
water bodies. 
iii) 
Non-compliance by the contractors to implement their obligations as stated in 
the contracts. 
 
Recommendations 
 
i) 
The Accounting Officers of the Local Governments should liaise with MAAIF to 
carryout vaccination of animals to curb the spread and effects of Foot and Mouth 
(FMD) disease and sensitize the fishing communities on how to meet the 
standards of fishing on the various lakes. 
ii) 
The Accounting Officers of the Local Governments should ensure that local 
revenue collection agreements include punitive measures to curb non-compliance 
by the Contractors. Meanwhile, all outstanding revenue should be collected from 
contractors. 
 
5.3.4 Challenges affecting Implementation of IRAS 
 
Through interviews and documentary review in a sample of 30 Local Governments, the 
following challenges were noted on the usage, connectivity, and navigation of the local

5.4 
Road Maintenance Grant 
 
Government allocated a Road Maintenance Development Grant of UGX.1Bn to each of 
the 176 Local Governments (LGs), which included; 135 districts, 10 cities, and 31 
Municipal Councils, resulting into a total of UGX.176Bn being transferred to LGs in the 
FY 2024/25. The grant is specifically designed to support road maintenance within these 
LGs. 
 
During my audit of the FY 2024/25, I designed audit procedures to assess the grant 
implementation in LGs, and below are my summary findings; 
 
 
 

 
246 
5.4.1 Road Inventory and Condition Surveys 
 
In accordance with Section 2.1 of the MoWT Road Maintenance Grant Implementation 
Guidelines FY 2024/25, all entities are required to prepare and maintain road inventory 
and condition surveys along with cost estimates. These reports must include, but are not 
limited to, the following information: 
 
i) 
Size and extent of road asset. 
ii) 
Locations of culverts, bridges, drifts, road furniture and other key assets on the 
road network. 
iii) 
Size or scope of infrastructure to be maintained. 
iv) 
Functional hierarchy of roads. 
v) 
Volume of traffic. 
 
I noted that out of 148 LGs, only five (05) LGs had road inventory and condition surveys 
along with cost estimates that detailed the required information. However, 143 LGs had 
databases of roads which described; the size and extent of road assets, but did not have 
the locations of culverts, bridges, drifts, road furniture and other key assets on the road 
network, size or scope of infrastructure to be maintained, functional hierarchy of roads, 
and volume of traffic required by the roads inventory and surveys report. 
 
The absence of detailed road inventory and condition survey data hindered the efficient 
allocation of resources, accurate cost estimation, and appropriate prioritization of road 
maintenance activities. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to limited funding, lack of assessment tools such 
as GPS devices and inadequate staff capacity. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should liaise with MoWT and MoFPED to provide 
technical and financial support to develop comprehensive road inventory and condition 
surveys. 
 
5.4.2 Status of LG Road Equipment 
 
Review of the LGs’ status of road equipment in 148 LGs revealed that; 
 
i) 
A total of 19 LGs did not have road equipment units. 
ii) 
A total of 137 LGs had inadequate road equipment units; these included critical 
road equipment such as excavators, motor graders, vibro rollers, dump trucks, 
bulldozers, chain loaders and wheel loaders among others. 
iii) 
A total of 119 LGs had non-functional equipment to undertake road works during 
the financial year. 
 
Limited availability of the road equipment delays implementation of road works, thus 
affects service delivery. 
 

 
247 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to insufficient funding of the operations of the 
road equipment units, as well as delays in securing additional machinery from the 
Ministry of Works and Transport (MoWT). 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of LGs should liaise with MoFPED to secure funding for 
additional machinery to ensure effective and sustainable road maintenance operations. 
 
5.4.3 Inspection of Implemented Road Maintenance Works 
 
Field inspection of the implemented road maintenance works in 148 LGs carried out in 
the period between October and December 2025 revealed that; 
 
i) 
A total of 239 roads measuring 1,275 kms in 66 LGs were incomplete at the time 
of audit inspections. 
 
ii) 
A total of 76 LGs had 228 roads with unsatisfactory works, such as; broken 
culverts, poor drainage, and uneven carriage ways with water ponding among 
others. 
 
This affected timely service delivery. 
 
The Accounting officers explained that maintenance of road works were affected by 
limited funding for road maintenance works, heavy rains, inadequate road construction 
equipment and un-regulated carriage load control on the LG roads. 
 
Recommendations 
 
i) 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should liaise with MoWT and MoFPED to 
provide technical and financial support to develop comprehensive road inventory 
and condition surveys. 
 
ii) 
The Accounting Officers of LGs should liaise with MoFPED to secure funding for 
additional machinery to ensure effective and sustainable road maintenance 
operations. 
 
iii) 
The Accounting Officers of the LGs should ensure district engineers complete all 
unfinished road works, and all defects on roads should be rectified. 
 
iv) 
The Ministry of Works and Transport should develop comprehensive guidelines 
on the carriage load control on the LG roads.

249 
5.5.1 Legal and Regulatory framework for Secondary Schools, Tertiary Institutions 
and Other Institutions 
 
5.5.1.1 Absence of a defined accounting framework for Secondary Schools and 
Tertiary Institutions 
 
A review of the Education (Pre-Primary, Primary and Post-Primary) Act Cap. 247, the 
Universities and Other Tertiary Institutions Act Cap. 262, and the Technical and 
Vocational Education and Training Act, 2025 revealed that these laws do not prescribe 
an accounting framework to be used by secondary schools, tertiary institutions, and 
other education institutions. In addition, the Accountant General has not specifically 
guided these institutions regarding the accounting frame work to apply. 
 
In contrast, the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA) Cap. 171 which governs 
financial management for all government institutions requires the preparation of 
financial statements in accordance with a prescribed accounting framework applicable to 
government votes, local governments, and public corporations. However, because the 
laws in the education sector do not define an accounting framework, schools and 
tertiary institutions lack clear statutory guidance aligned to the PFMA Cap 171. 
 
Absence of a prescribed accounting framework results in unreliable financial statements, 
which limit the usefulness of financial information to stakeholders and weakens 
accountability. 
Recommendation 
 
The Ministry of Education and Sports should engage the Ministry of Finance, Planning 
and Economic Development (Accountant General) to align the education sector laws 
with the PFMA Cap. 171 and issue clear guidance on the accounting framework that all 
primary schools, secondary schools and tertiary institutions must use. 
 
5.5.1.2 Accounting Periods for Secondary Schools, Tertiary Institutions and Other 
Institutions 
 
I noted that although the Education Act Cap. 247, is consistent with the PFMA in 
defining the financial year as 1 July to 30 June, secondary schools operating under this 
Act continue to apply a calendar-year reporting cycle when preparing and submitting 
their financial statements. This practice is not aligned with the PFMA requirements for 
government entities. 
 
This inconsistency leads to secondary schools preparing and submitting financial reports 
on timelines that differ from the government financial year, resulting in misaligned 
budgets, work plans, and financial reporting, thus reducing the comparability and 
usefulness of financial information. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Ministry of Education and Sports in consultation with MoFPED should provide clear 
guidance to secondary schools requiring them to prepare and report financial 

 
250 
information using the Government of Uganda’s financial year in accordance with the 
Education (Pre-Primary, Primary and Post-Primary) Act Cap. 247 and PFMA, Cap 171. 
 
5.5.1.3 Impact of the New Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) 
Act 2025 on the Business, Technical, Vocational Education and Training 
Institutions (BTVET) 
 
The TVET Act 2025 in Uganda, gazetted on March 14, 2025, establishes a framework for 
promoting, coordinating, and regulating Technical and Vocational Education and 
Training (TVET). The Act aims to streamline TVET systems, enhance skills development, 
align with industry needs, and promote accountability within the sector. It introduces a 
TVET Council, develops a qualifications framework, regulates trainers, and consolidates 
TVET governance. 
 
a) 
Existence of the Governing Boards of former BTVET Institutions 
 
Section 51 (1) of the Technical and Vocational Education and Training Act, 2025 
provides that there shall be established a Governing Council of seven (7) members for a 
TVET provider at a level of Technical College, National Polytechnic or National Technical 
University. However, the Education (Board of Governors) Regulations 2008 provided eight (8) 
members of the BOG while the Universities and Other Tertiary Institutions Act, Cap 262 provided 
for 17 members. 
 
This implies that the implementation of the TVET Act enacted on 14 March 2025 
required the dissolution of the existing boards, some of which had just been approved. 
 
I noted that there was no clear guidance issued to manage the transition in regard to 
the dissolution and interim management of the institutions. As a result, no formal 
governance or oversight mechanisms were established during the transition period, 
leaving operations to be managed solely at the discretion of the existing institutional 
management staff. This gap in oversight supervision may increase the risk of operational 
mismanagement at these institutions. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Ministry of Education and Sports should issue formal guidance to institutions on the 
dissolution of existing boards and the establishment of interim governance 
arrangements during the transition under the TVET Act. In the meantime, the 
Accounting Officers of the affected institutions should ensure that a temporary oversight 
mechanism is put in place. 
 
5.5.2 Status of phased out Primary Teachers’ Colleges 
 
I noted that 23 Primary Teacher Colleges (PTCs) earmarked for repurposing into 
alternative institutions (such as TVET centres, secondary schools, health-training schools 
and Technical Agro-vet Institutions) had not been operationalized at the time of audit. 
The institutions remain idle, with no active programs, no deployed staff, and no 

 
251 
approved budgets for their new mandates. Most facilities visited were vacant and not 
utilized. 
 
The continued inactivity at these institutions resulted in idle public infrastructure, 
increased risk of deterioration and theft of assets, and delayed realization of the 
intended benefits of the education and skilling reforms. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Ministry of Education and Sports should issue clear operationalization guidelines for 
each repurposed PTC. In addition, strengthen coordination with the responsible agencies 
to ensure timely takeover, activation and repurposing of these institutions. 
 
5.5.3 Accumulation of Payables 
 
The Notes to the Financial Statements for 255 secondary schools disclose payables 
amounting to UGX.35,629,190,629 incurred in AY 2023 and UGX.36,781,493,807 
incurred in AY 2024, representing an increase of UGX.1,152,303,178 (3%). 
 
Similarly, the Notes to the Financial Statements for 49 tertiary institutions report 
payables of UGX.6,403,495,094 for FY 2022/23 and UGX.7,744,458,999 for FY 2023/24, 
representing an increase of UGX.1,340,963,905 (21%). 
 
An increase in the payables balance implied that the Accounting Officers were not 
following financial commitment control procedures which could lead to litigations and 
associated costs, thus affecting the credibility of the institutions. In addition, this may 
create a financial burden to government while managing transition arrangements for the 
repurposed institutions. 
 
The Accounting Officers mainly attributed the accumulation of payables to delays in 
receipt of funds, inadequate releases from Central Government, and shortfall in student 
fees collections. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should enforce financial commitment controls, prioritize 
essential payments, and improve internal revenue collection. Where significant funding 
gaps exist, the affected institutions should engage the MoES through the Local 
Government administration to address the matter. 
 
5.5.4 Outstanding Receivables 
 
The Notes to the Financial Statements for 278 secondary schools disclosed receivables 
amounting to UGX.28,441,446,505 incurred in AY 2023 and UGX.30,494,213,455 
incurred in AY 2024, representing an increase of UGX.2,052,766,950 (7%). 
Similarly, the Notes to the Financial Statements for 57 tertiary institutions reported 
receivables of UGX.5,171,875,535 for FY 2022/23 and UGX.5,902,977,865 for FY 
2023/24, representing an increase of UGX.731,102,330 (14%). 

 
252 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed the failure to recover school fees to widespread 
financial constraints among parents, government policies that restrict schools from 
enforcing strict fee payment, negative community perceptions and political interference 
discouraging payment, and high dropout or transfer rates coupled with weak fee-
collection controls. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should improve school fees collection mechanisms by enforcing 
agreed payment policies, enhancing regular engagement with parents and community 
leaders to improve compliance, and introducing stricter follow-up measures such as 
structured payment plans, timely reminders, and recovery committees. Additionally, the 
school should implement clear controls such as exam clearance requirements, and digital 
payment platforms to ensure timely and complete settlement of fees. 
 
5.5.5 Implementation of the approved budget 
 
Paragraph 3.1 of the Simplified Guidelines on Budgeting, Accounting and Reporting for 
Secondary Schools, 2017, provides that Head Teachers are responsible for the financial 
management of the school, including planning, budget preparation, and records 
management and reporting. 
Section 94(1) Universities and Other Tertiary Institutions Act, Cap 262, provides that the 
Governing Council shall, within three months before the end of each financial year, 
make and submit to the Minister for approval estimates of the income and expenditure 
of the institute for the next ensuing year. 
 
I noted the following; 
 
5.5.5.1 Approval of the Work Plan and Budget 
 
Section 3.2.5 of the Simplified Guidelines on Budgeting, Accounting and Reporting for 
Secondary Schools 2017 provides that the Head Teacher and the School Bursar shall 
present the revenue and expenditure budget/estimates to the school management 
committee in charge of finance for their review, and once agreed, the budget shall then 
be submitted to the Board of Governors (BoG) for review and approval as required. 
 
Section 90 (1) of the Universities and Other Tertiary Institutions Act Cap 262, provides 
that the Governing Council shall, within three months before the end of each financial 
year, make and submit to the Minister for approval estimates of the income and 
expenditure of the institute for the next ensuing year. 
 
I noted that in AY 2023 and AY 2024, the work plans and budgets of 29 and 24 
Secondary Schools respectively were not approved by the respective Boards of 
Governors (BOGs). 
 

 
253 
Similarly, in FY 2022/23 and FY 2023/24, the work plans and budgets of 11 and 9 
Tertiary Institutions respectively were not approved by the respective Governing 
Councils (GCs). 
 
The absence of formal approval of work plans and budgets by the respective Boards of 
Governors and Governing Councils undermines institutional governance and oversight. 
In addition, this increases the risk of misaligned priorities, thus affecting education 
service delivery. 
The Accounting Officers attributed this to limited resources to facilitate Board activities, 
and the expiry of some Board’s/GC’s term of office. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should come up with robust revenue enhancement plans to 
secure funds to facilitate the activities of the oversight bodies. In addition, the 
Accounting officers should ensure timely nomination of new Boards/GC members before 
the expiry of their term to prevent any lapse in governance and maintain uninterrupted 
oversight. 
 
5.5.5.2 Overall Budget Revenue Performance 
 
Regulation 23(b) of the Education (Board of Governors) Regulations 2008 requires the 
board to receive funds on behalf of a school by way of tuition and other fees by parents 
for the welfare of the students. 
 
Section 94(2) of the Universities and other Tertiary Institutions Act, Cap 262, requires 
annual estimates to include all the income and expenditure of the Institution for that 
financial year. 
 
I reviewed the performance of revenue against the approved budget for 384 Secondary 
schools and 79 Tertiary Institutions and the following are my observations;

9.0% of the approved budget. In AY 2024, the schools received UGX.862.80Bn out of an 
approved budget of UGX.932.19Bn, leading to a shortfall of UGX.69.80Bn, corresponding

Recommendation

5.5.6 Assessment of Service Delivery 
 
Guideline 6 of the Ministry of Education and Sports Planning, Budgeting and 
Implementation Guidelines for Local Governments for the Education and Sports Sector 
2021/22 stipulates the minimum quality standards/norms for schools. 
A review of the academic year 2024, I noted that secondary schools did not meet the 
minimum quality standards as follows; 
 
i) 
A total 221 secondary schools recorded classroom to student ratios exceeding 
the recommended 1:60 standards, resulting in congested classrooms that strain 
infrastructure and pose health and safety risks, ultimately diminishing the overall 
quality of teaching and learning. 
 
ii) 
A total 193 secondary schools had fewer than the minimum required four (4) 
staff accommodation units, a shortage that limits teacher availability on campus 
and reduces the level of learner support, thereby affecting overall learning 
outcomes. 
iii) 
A total 176 secondary schools recorded desk to student ratios exceeding the 
recommended standard of 1:3, indicating inadequate seating facilities. This 
shortage limits learners’ comfort and concentration, restricts effective classroom 
engagement, and ultimately undermines the overall quality of teaching and 
learning. 
 
I further noted that the 2024 New Lower Secondary Curriculum Framework specifies 
that classrooms should, at a minimum, have furniture arranged to facilitate group work 
and provide adequate seating for all learners. However, many schools currently fall 
below the minimum desk and classroom standards. The introduction of the new 
curriculum, which demands additional space and resources, is likely to further strain 
existing infrastructure, thereby compromising effective curriculum implementation and 
teaching quality. 
 
This underscores the urgent need for government policy review and strategic resource 
planning given that the framework has not explicitly guided on any detailed numeric 
standards or exact furniture/sitting arrangement requirements. 
 
The Accounting Officers explained that limited funding, low parental fee contributions, 
and insufficient stakeholder resources, combined with rapid enrolment growth and 
expansion to A-Level, strained existing infrastructure. While temporary measures and 
phased construction were underway, they were constrained by limited resources, and 
the schools were awaiting government interventions such as Uganda Secondary 
Education Expansion Project (USEEP) and UGIFT to address the gaps. 

 
256 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should enhance resource mobilization, prioritize phased 
infrastructure expansion, and coordinate closely with the Ministry of Education and 
Sports and stakeholders to ensure timely implementation of projects such as USEEP and 
UgIFT to address overcrowding and facility gaps. 
 
The Ministry of Education and Sports should establish and enforce minimum classroom 
and furniture standards that will support effective implementation of the New Lower 
Secondary Curriculum and enhance the quality of teaching and learning. 
 
5.5.7 Staffing 
 
Section (A-a) 14 of the Public Service Standing Orders 2021 provides that the Ministry of 
Public Service shall have the overall responsibility for ensuring proper implementation of 
structures and terms and conditions of service for the Public Service. Furthermore, 
Indicator 3(a) of the basic requirements and minimum standards indicator for Education 
Institutions require a school to have a staff establishment as laid down by the Ministry of 
Education and Sports and Public Service. 
 
Section 6(1)(g) of the Education (Pre-Primary, Primary and Post-Primary) Act, Cap. 247, 
states that Government through its relevant agencies shall be responsible for recruiting, 
deployment and promotion of both teaching and non-teaching staff. 
 
Section 89 of the Universities and Other Tertiary Institutions Act Ca 262 requires the 
Secretary, Registrar, Bursar, other senior administrative officers and academic staff to 
be appointed by the Education Service Commission on the recommendation of the 
Appointments Committee through the Governing Council. Additionally, Section 90(2) 
provides that Subject to section 89, the academic staff, administrative staff, and any 
other employees shall be appointed by the appointments committee. 
 
I observed the following; 
 
i) 
During the AY 2024 and FY 2023/24, 126 Secondary Schools and 26 Tertiary 
Institutions did not have an approved staff establishment/structure making it 
difficult to determine existing staffing gaps and this may result in 
over/understaffing in various departments, potentially affecting the operations of 
the school and institution. 
 
ii) 
In AY 2024, only 11,665 (65%) of the required 17,894 staff positions were filled 
across 238 secondary schools. Similarly, 
in FY2023/24, only 2,283 (57%) of 
the required 4,026 staff positions were filled across 57 Tertiary Institutions. 
 
iii) 
Consequently, to address the staffing gaps highlighted above, 231 Secondary 
Schools in AY 2024 locally recruited 8,628 staff who, although included within 
the reported filled positions, were not on the Government payroll. This placed an 
additional financial burden of UGX.61,343,868,842 on the schools and resulted in 

 
257 
accumulated salary arrears of UGX.1,599,535,860. Similarly, in FY 2023/24, 48 
Tertiary Institutions locally recruited 1,367 staff that are also included among the 
filled positions, leading to an extra cost of UGX.7,260,299,467 and salary arrears 
totalling UGX.72,988,750. 
 
iv) 
A review of a sample of 65 secondary schools revealed inconsistencies between 
the approved staff establishment and the staffing requirements derived from the 
minimum Teacher Student Ratio. While the minimum standard indicates a need 
for 5,461 teachers, the approved staff establishment provides for only 3,517, 
resulting in a significant shortfall. This gap demonstrates that the current staff 
establishment is inadequate to meet service delivery needs. 
 
Furthermore, the introduction of the 2024 New Lower Secondary Curriculum 
which includes additional learning areas and competency-based pedagogical 
approaches requires more human resources for effective implementation. 
Without a corresponding adjustment of the staff establishment, the staffing 
shortfall is expected to widen, potentially affecting instructional quality and 
overall curriculum delivery. 
 
v) 
In a sample of five (05) secondary schools and two (2) tertiary institutions, 68 
teaching positions that had fallen vacant due to transfers or retirements 
remained un-replaced by the Ministry of Education and Sports as of December 
2024. Unlike new positions that require additional wage provisions, these 
vacancies only required straightforward replacement within the existing wage 
bill. 
The non-utilization of the available wage for these positions results in unspent 
balances at the Higher Local Government level, which are consequently returned 
to the Treasury. This situation highlights a systemic control weakness in staff 
recruitment, appointment and deployment processes that is likely to reflect a 
broader issue across the majority of schools and institutions. The delays 
contributed to teaching gaps and negatively affected service delivery in the 
affected institutions. 
 
This overstretches the available staff beyond their capacity and creates job-related 
stress thereby negatively affecting the level of education service delivery. In addition, 
this creates a burden on the financial resources of the school which is often transferred 
to parents through increased fees. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed the staffing gaps to constraints within the available 
wage bill at the local governments, which limited the Ministry of Education and Sports 
(MoES) from recruiting and deploying additional staff. They further noted delays in the 
recruitment and clearance processes involving MoES, Municipal Authorities, and the 
Education Service Commission. In several institutions, mandatory staff movements 
including transfers, retirements, promotions, and deaths created vacancies that were not 
replaced in a timely manner. Additionally, the absence of an approved staff 
establishment or structure in some schools further hindered formal recruitment and 
deployment. 
 

 
258 
Recommendations 
 
The Accounting Officer of the MoES, in collaboration with the MoPS and Local 
Governments, should expedite the development, approval, and rollout of standardised 
staff establishments for all secondary schools and tertiary institutions to ensure accurate 
determination of staffing needs. MoES should further review and align the approved 
staffing 
structures 
with 
actual 
enrolment, 
minimum 
Teacher–Student 
Ratio 
requirements, and the human resource demands of the 2024 New Lower Secondary 
Curriculum. 
 
Additionally, the MoES should enhance recruitment, appointment, and deployment 
controls to ensure timely replacement of staff vacancies within the existing wage bill and 
prevent the return of unspent wage funds to the Treasury. Government should also 
develop a clear framework for absorbing locally recruited staff into the payroll to reduce 
financial pressure on institutions and minimise cost burdens passed on to parents. 
 
5.5.8 Board of Governors and Governance Councils 
 
Regulation 3 of the Education (Board of Governors) Regulations 2008 provides that 
there shall be a board of governors for every post-primary school. 
 
Section 75(1) of the Universities and Other Tertiary Institutions Act Cap. 262 provides 
that there shall be established for each Public Tertiary Institution a Governing Council, 
which, shall be a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal and may 
sue or be sued in its name. 
I conducted a review of the existence and composition of Boards of Governors (BOGs) 
and Governing Councils (GC), the tenure of members and the frequency of meetings 
and observed the following; 
 
i) 
In AY 2023, 23 Secondary Schools did not constitute BOGs, this number 
increased to 34 Secondary Schools in AY 2024. 
 
ii) 
In AY 2024, 58 Secondary schools did not have full Board member 
representation while seven (07) Secondary Schools had more than the required 
number of Board representation. 
 
iii) 
Similarly, in FY 2023/24, four (04) Tertiary Institutions lacked full representation 
on their Governing Councils, whereas 23 institutions exceeded the prescribed 
number of council members. 
 
iv) 
In AY 2024, 25 Secondary Schools had expired Boards with an expiry period 
ranging between two (02) to 35 months. Similarly, in FY 2023/24, five (05) 
tertiary institutions had expired Governing Councils with an expiry period ranging 
between three (03) to seven (07) months. 
 
v) 
In AY 2024, 59 secondary schools’ Boards did not meet the required Board 
sittings in the year, while three (03) secondary schools’ Boards held more than 
the required Board sittings. 

 
259 
 
vi) 
Similarly, in FY 2023/24, 15 Tertiary Institutions’ Governing Councils did not have 
the required Council meetings. 
 
The inadequate composition of Boards of Governors (BOGs) and Governing Councils 
(GCs), coupled with expired appointments and irregular meetings, undermines their 
effectiveness, weakens oversight, and may compromise institutional accountability and 
governance. 
 
I further noted that the enactment of the TVET Act, 2025 introduced changes to the 
composition and size of governing bodies for Technical and Vocational Education and 
Training institutions. Specifically, the Act reduced the number of required board 
members, rendering some of the existing fully constituted boards non-compliant with 
the new legal provisions. As a result, several board members currently serving were 
appointed under the provisions of the previous law, and therefore their appointment 
letters are now inconsistent with the updated legal framework. This has created 
uncertainty regarding the validity of current board compositions and may affect 
governance and decision-making within the affected institutions unless corrective 
measures are taken. 
 
The Accounting Officers acknowledged the gaps in board composition, expired 
appointments, and irregular meetings, citing delays in member clearance and approvals 
by MoES, the Public Service Commission, and local authorities. 
In addition the Accounting Officers attributed the failure to hold all mandatory BOG’s 
meetings to limited funding, delays in appointing or approving Board members, and 
disruptions caused by member unavailability, transfers, or death 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should engage the MoES and other stakeholders to ensure 
timely appointment of Board members and budget adequately for all mandatory BOG 
meetings. The schools should also consider other effective options, such as virtual 
meetings, and plan meeting schedules early to minimize conflicts and ensure statutory 
compliance. 
 
5.5.9 Lack of Land titles 
 
Indicator 12(xiii) of the Basic Requirements and Minimum Standards Indicators for 
Education Institutions, 2010 requires Schools to have land titles for the land on which 
they are located. 
 
I noted that 36 Secondary schools and 11 Tertiary Institutions did not have titles for 55 
pieces of land measuring 1,214 acres in which they were located. 
 
There is a risk of loss of these pieces of land in case of encroachment or disputes. 
The Accounting Officers attributed delays in land titling to ownership disputes, shared 
land arrangements, and lengthy administrative or legal processes involving surveys, 
court cases, and approvals. They also cited limited funding, high compensation 

 
260 
demands, and procedural backlogs, along with boundary issues and transitional periods, 
as key factors slowing progress. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should engage relevant authorities and stakeholders to resolve 
ownership and boundary issues and expedite the land titling process. They should 
secure clear agreements, allocate adequate funding for surveys and legal requirements, 
and maintain proper documentation to prevent delays and safeguard institutional 
investments. 
 
5.6 
Audit of Lower Local Governments for FYs 2021/22 - 2023/24 
 
I undertook financial audits in a total of 2,053 Lower Local Governments (LLGs), which 
included: 1,487 Sub-counties for the FYs 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24, and 568 Town 
Councils for the FY 2023/24 resulting in a total of 4,440 reports. 
 
A trend analysis on the audit opinions issued on LLGs revealed that; 
 
i) 
Out of the 568 Town Council reports, 528 had unqualified audit opinions, 36 had 
qualified audit opinions, three (03) had adverse audit opinions while one (01) 
had a disclaimer of opinion. The pie chart below summarises the Town Council 
audit opinions for FY 2023/24. 
Figure 4: Town Council Audit Opinions for FY 2023/2024 
 
 
ii) 
Out of 3,872 sub-county reports over the 03 years, a total of 3,332 were 
unqualified, 449 were qualified, 23 had adverse opinions, while 68 had disclaimer 
of opinion as illustrated in figure 5 below; 
 
 

 
261 
Figure 5: Sub-County Audit Opinions for three FYs 
 
Source: OAG analysis 
 
For the three (03) financial years audited in the sub counties, unqualified audit 
opinions increased from 683 to 931, qualified audit opinions increased from 95 to 
180, the adverse audit opinions increased from 3 to 13 while the disclaimer of 
opinions reduced from 26 to 19. 
 
The increase in the qualified audit opinions and the adverse audit opinions was 
attributed to failure to prepare financial statements and supporting accounting 
records; non-recognition, incorrect valuation, and failure to depreciate PPE; 
significant misstatements of revenue, expenditure, cash balances, net worth, 
reserves, and opening balances; unaccounted-for funds and unsupported 
expenditures; and the use of inappropriate reporting templates. 
 
The following cross cutting issues were noted; 
 
5.6.1 Accumulation of Payables 
 
I noted that 133 LLGs had a total of UGX.6,126,682,346 as outstanding payables at the 
end of the financial year 2023/24. The payables of these LLGs had increased by 
UGX.565,067,111 (9%) from the previous financial period. 
 
An increase in payables implied that the Accounting Officers were not following 
commitment control procedures which could lead to litigation and its associated costs, 
thus affecting the credibility of the institutions. 
 
The Accounting Officers largely attributed the increase or accumulation of payables to 
delayed fund releases, local revenue shortfalls, inadequate funding, operational delays, 
and long-standing obligations, with many committing to settle the arrears in the 
subsequent financial years. 

 
262 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers of LLGs should improve financial management by enforcing 
commitment control systems, ensuring expenditures match available funds, and 
improving the accuracy of revenue forecasting. They should also enhance local revenue 
collection and follow up on delayed remittances from Central Government and District 
authorities. 
 
5.6.2 Outstanding Revenue Arrears 
 
I noted an increase in the revenue arrears in 146 LLGs from UGX.3,000,318,963 in the 
year ended 30th June 2023 to UGX.4,048,993,085 in the year ended 30th June 2024 
leading to an increase of UGX.1,048,674,122. 
 
I noted that minimum effort had been made by the Accounting Officers to recover the 
outstanding revenue arrears. Failure to collect the revenue arrears affected 
implementation of planned activities. 
 
The Accounting Officers primarily attributed revenue arrears and under-collection issues 
to systemic challenges including the introduction of the Integrated Revenue 
Administration System (IRAS), which caused delays in revenue remittance and some 
mismanagement. Other significant factors were relocation of taxpayers, closure of 
businesses, local disputes affecting revenue sources, delays in fund transfers by district 
authorities, insufficient staffing and resources for enforcement. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers in LLGs should fully integrate and streamline revenue 
administration systems, ensure proper training for staff and taxpayers, enhance 
enforcement by equipping collection teams, and improve taxpayer awareness through 
community engagement. They should also coordinate promptly with district authorities 
for timely remittances, and establish strong monitoring and reporting mechanisms to 
boost accountability, improve revenue recovery, and support the councils’ financial 
stability. 
 
5.6.3 Lack of Strategic Plans 
 
I noted that the 94 LLGs with a total budget of UGX.11,513,111,034 did not have 
strategic plans to indicate their vision, mission, goals, objectives and how they will be 
achieved contrary to Section 37(3) of the Local Government Act Cap 138. The summary 
is in the table below;

Most Accounting Officers attributed this shortcoming mainly to inadequate funding and 
resource constraints, which hindered the preparation and implementation of 
development and strategic plans. They also cited capacity gaps, particularly in planning 
and staffing shortages, as additional challenges. Some reported that strategic plans 
were in progress or awaiting approval. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers in LLGs should improve financial resource mobilization by 
enhancing local revenue collection and actively engaging development partners and 
government agencies for additional funding. In addition, they should implement 
capacity-building initiatives to strengthen technical skills in strategic planning and 
improve coordination to ensure timely approval of strategic plans.

The Accounting Officers attributed the challenges to contractors abandoning

5.6.7 Under Staffing 
 
I carried out an assessment of the staffing levels at the LLGs in financial year 2023/24 
and noted that out of the approved staff structure of a total of 31,109 positions in 1,209 
LLGs, 13,455 (43%) positions were filled leaving 17,654 (57%) vacant. 
 
Understaffing overstretches the available staff beyond their capacity, creates job-related 
stress to the fewer staff and negatively affects the level of public service delivery to the 
community. 
 
The Accounting Officers majorly attributed the understaffing to the limited wage bill and 
the government ban on the recruitment of new staff other than on replacement basis 
due to wage budget ceilings. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should engage the District to liaise with the Ministry of Public 
Service and MoFPED to come up with a plan of filling the vacant positions to enable 
effective service delivery at LLGs. 
 

 
266 
5.6.8 Untitled Land 
 
Instruction 16.13.11 of the Treasury Instruction, 2017 states that a government entity 
shall be considered to have control for land if it has the title. If the government entity 
does not have title to the land, the entity shall not be considered to have control. 
 
I noted that in the financial year 2023/24, a total of 241 LLGs did not have land titles for 
the 737 pieces of land measuring approximately 3,637 acres. 
 
There is a risk of loss/encroachment on the LLGs’ land and associated costs, thus 
hampering service delivery. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed the lack of land titles to inadequate funds to 
undertake the process of surveying the land and processing the land tittles. Delays are 
also caused by disputes over ownership, squatters, and coordination challenges with in 
government offices. 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should explore alternative funding sources, such as; grants, 
development partners, local revenue mobilization or cost-sharing initiatives. They should 
also amicably resolve land ownership disputes by seeking legal advice from the Office of 
the Attorney General.

A re-computation of the transfers from the Higher Local Governments (HLGs) in the 
financial year 2023/24 revealed that 668 LLGs were expected to receive 
UGX.34,402,952,072 from the HLGs. However, only UGX.30,823,334,604 (90%) was 
received resulting into a shortfall of UGX.3,579,617,468.

Failure to remit funds negatively affects the implementation of the planned activities at

The Accounting Officers attributed this to the lack of bank accounts by the lower local

Recommendation

and ensure timely remittance of their respective shares to support planned activities. For 
joint activities implemented by the LLG and parishes, clear agreements should be 
documented to define funds usage and responsibilities. 
 
5.6.11 Unaccounted for funds 
 
Review of documents supporting payments made in financial year 2023/24 revealed that 
payments amounting to UGX.422,067,137 made in 21 LLGs remained un-accounted for 
by close of the financial year contrary to Regulation 33 (4) of the Public Finance 
Management Regulations of 2016 and Regulation 42 and 43 (2) of the LGFAR 2007. 
 
 

 
268 
Consequently, I could not confirm that the funds were utilized for the intended purpose. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed the failure to account for funds to the delayed 
submission of supporting documentation by the responsible officers. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should ensure that the responsible officers are handled with 
disciplinary action. 
 
5.6.12 Inadequate Facilities for Garbage Collection and Disposal 
 
Section 1(w) Part 3 of Schedule 5 of the Local Government Act Cap. 138 provides that 
an Urban Council should establish, acquire, erect, maintain, promote, assist or control 
(with the participation of the citizens) sanitary services for the removal and disposal of 
night soil, rubbish, carcasses of dead animals and all kinds of refuse and effluent. 
 
I noted that 320 Town Councils lacked adequate garbage collection equipment, such as; 
garbabe collection trucks, skip loaders, tractors, among others as at the end of the 
financial year 2023/24. 
 
On inspection, 275 Town Councils lacked skips or gazetted garbage collection points but 
rather, dumped garbage at road sides. 
 
The heaps of garbage created an unsightly environment and unbearable stench for the 
neighbouring communities and have therefore become a public health nuisance. 
 
The Accounting Officers explained that the funding allocated to garbage management 
was insufficient and therefore could not facilitate the procurement of garbage collection 
and disposal facilities. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers together with the respective districts should lobby for funds 
from MoFPED and development partners to purchase garbage collection equipment. 
 
5.6.13 Lack of the landfill in Town Councils 
 
Section 1(w) Part 3 of Schedule 5 of the Local Government Act Cap. 138 provides that 
an Urban Council should establish, acquire, erect, maintain, promote, assist or control 
(with the participation of the citizens) sanitary services for the removal and disposal of 
night soil, rubbish, carcasses of dead animals and all kinds of refuse and effluent. 
 
Regulation 78 (1) of the National environment (waste management) Regulations of 2020 
provides that a waste handler shall ensure that placement of waste in the landfill is 
undertaken in a manner that ensures stability of the mass of waste and associated 
structures. 
 

 
269 
I noted that 254 Town Councils did not have landfills or designated sites for dumping, 
sorting and recycling of solid waste. 
Consequently, garbage had been dumped and piled on road sides and unauthorized 
public places which endangered the health of the surrounding communities. 
 
The Accounting Officers attributed the shortcoming to resource constraints. 
 
Recommendation 
 
The Accounting Officers should lobby resources through the districts to acquire the 
landfills for the Town Councils.

The audit of TMs for the remaining 48 (11.6%) entities were ongoing and will be 
completed within the audit year 2026. 
 
6.2 
Treasury Memoranda Audits planned for audit year 2026 
 
During the audit year 2025, I received an additional six (6) Treasury Memoranda whose 
audits are planned for the audit year 2026. The results of these audits will be included 
in my subsequent report to parliament. These are; 
 
i) 
Treasury Memorandum on the Report of the Auditor General for the Financial 
year ended 30th June 2023 Volume I: Treasury Operations and 
Consolidated Financial Statements. 
ii) 
Treasury Memorandum on the Report of the Auditor General for the Financial 
year ended 30th June 2023 Volume II: Central Government Ministries. 
iii) 
Treasury Memorandum on the Report of the Auditor General for the Financial 
year ended 30th June 2023 Volume III: Missions Abroad. 
iv) 
Treasury Memorandum on the Report of the Auditor General for the Financial 
year ended 30th June 2023 Volume IV: Public Universities, Referral 
Hospitals and Specialized Health Facilities. 
v) 
Treasury Memorandum on the Report of the Auditor General for the Financial 
year ended 30th June 2023 Volume V: Local Governments.

year ended 30th June 2023 Volume VI: Commissions, Statutory Authorities

Opinion

I noted that;

Minister (OPM) 
Development 
plan 
implementation 
 
Governance 
and

Natural 
resources, 
environment, 
climate 
change, 
land and water 
 
Regional 
balance 
development 
Unqualified 
 
 
 
 
i) 
The Ministry had verified stock of outstanding commitments amounting to 
UGX.181.46Mn at the year-end. 
ii) 
Out of UGX.58.44Bn released for management of disasters, only UGX.8.27Bn 
(14%) was spent leaving an unspent balance of UGX.50.17Bn (86%) which was 
not transferred back to the contingencies fund Account by 31st July 2025 
iii) UGX.1.68Bn released for Kiteezi victims was diverted to purchase of relief items 
and implementation of disaster related activities in other parts of the country 
without approval by the minister. 
iv) UGX.0.32Bn which related to disturbance allowance for houses destroyed during 
Kiteezi landslide was not paid to the victims. 
v) 
The Ministry did not reserve any procurements for registered Associations under 
the reservations scheme. 
vi) Three (3) procurements worth UGX.10.38Bn were not carried out despite the 
receipt of the related funds, while three (3) contracts worth UGX.0.73Bn were 
not completed. 
vii) 21 procurements relating to repair of motor vehicles amounting to 
UGX.149.65Mn were conducted using Micro Procurement Method instead of 
Request for Quotation method. 
viii) There was a low bidder turnout for 117 procurements worth UGX.4.63Bn, with 
most procurements attracting less than 3 bidders. 
ix) There were evaluation irregularities such as rating suppliers with expired tax 
certificates and NSSF certificates as administratively compliant. 
x) 
Seven (7) procurements worth UGX.2.15Bn experienced delays averaging 54 
working days. 
xi) The entity faced a number of challenges in the use of e-GP, including; 
inadequate oversight, insufficient documentation, processing procurements out 
of the system, inadequate documentation and failure to generate monthly 
reports from the system. 
xii) There were no maintenance logs maintained to document activities, costs, or 
personnel involved in use of assets. Additionally, there was no system for 
tracking maintenance history or forecasting future needs for NCAs. 
xiii) Some of the entity land is not titled, while 12 pieces of land were not recorded in 
the fixed Assets Register.

Uganda

Development 
Plan 
implementation 
Unqualified 
i) 
I noted that although URA efforts have yielded significant results, with 
tremendous growth in revenue collection, Uganda's Tax/GDP ratio has remained 
low at around 13.4%, below the recommended average of 15%. 
ii) I noted that of the 5,252,874 registered taxpayers, only 2,524,666 (48%) were 
valuable, implying that they generated revenue for the Authority. This implies 
that a relatively small proportion of taxpayers shoulder the revenue burden, 
which may lead to inequitable taxation, taxpayer fatigue, and reduced voluntary 
compliance. 
iii) Out of the 1,440,752 provisional returns expected, only 21,285 were filed, 
representing 1.4%. Of 184,714 provisional returns for non-individuals expected, 
only 37,470 were filed, representing 20.3%. 
iv) Taxpayers were penalised for erroneous filings consistent with the submitted 
audited financial statements, suggesting that the financial statements were 
inaccurate and/or fraudulent. No punitive measures were undertaken for the 
preparers of the attendant financial statements. 
v) Over 1,000 objections were processed beyond the required 90 days, which 
exposes the Authority to significant revenue risks, as taxpayers are legally 
entitled to treat delayed cases as deemed allowed. 
vi) There was no customisation for multinational companies regarding transfer 
pricing information to enable clear declaration of related party transactions and, 
therefore, facilitate audits and return examinations, as well as support business 
intelligence through simplified analysis. 
vii) During my physical inspection of bonded ware houses, I noted that URA 
requested Yuasa Investments Limited to accommodate 41 siezed motor 
vehicles to free up space at the URA headquarters in 2019, however, these have 
been abandoned for over 6 years without payment of storage costs.

Judicial

Administration 
of

Unqualified 
i) 
The Commission had no budget provision during the year to settle the
