2023/2024. These payables, relating to PAYE, had remained outstanding since 
the FY 2020/2021. 
ii) 
Out of the approved staffing level of 196, only 101 positions were filled (52%), 
leaving a staffing gap of 95 positions (48%). 
iii) JSC does not regularly assess its long-term assets to ensure that they are 
functional, utilised and in good condition to deliver value for money. This 
increases the risk of undetected underutilization or misuse of NCAs, leading to 
inefficient resource allocation and unmeasured service delivery outcomes. 
iv) Fourteen (14) motor vehicles valued at UGX.1.29Bn had exceeded the 
recommended five (5) years of useful life by the time of audit but are yet to be 
disposed of. The old fleet increases the risk of high vehicle maintenance costs, 
continued loss in net book value and replacement costs, and potential service 
disruptions due to frequent breakdowns. 
v) JSC did not reserve any procurements in the plan for registered Associations as 
required by the guidelines and no contracts were awarded to these registered 
Associations. This undermines the regulator’s objective of promoting the 
participation of women, youth, and PWDs in public procurements, who are 
considered disadvantaged groups. 
vi) Some procurements in JSC’s detailed procurement plan were not clearly defined 
as the plan included broadly defined activities such as staff training, welfare and 
entertainment, workshops, meetings and seminars as subjects of procurement 
instead of the actual goods or services to be procured. The failure to include 
specific procurements defeats the purpose of procurement planning. Whereas 
JSC planned to procure goods and services worth UGX.6.57Bn, procurements 
worth UGX.6.068Bn were executed, leaving goods or services worth 
UGX.504.16Mn un procured. 
vii) Fifteen (15) procurements worth UGX.6.067Bn conducted during the financial 
year were processed manually outside the e-GP system, without justification.

iii) Out of the planned procurements worth UGX.1.99Bn, contracts worth 
UGX.156.8Mn were awarded, representing an implementation rate of only 8%. 
iv) A review of the overall performance of the strategic plan (2022/23-2024/25) 
revealed a 40% underfunding to support the strategic plan objectives, leading to 
an underachievement with only two (02) out of the planned eleven (11) 
interventions outlined in the strategic plan undertaken. There was also a failure 
to align the 2025/26-2030/2031 strategic plan with the UDC strategic plan. 
v) I assessed the extent of implementation of non-payroll outputs, with budgeted 
expenditure worth UGX.2.116Bn and noted that 7 outputs with budgeted 
expenditure worth UGX.0.287Bn were fully implemented and 4 outputs with 
budgeted expenditure worth UGX. 1.829 Bn were not implemented. 
vi) Financial performance analysis of the Company revealed several issues i.e. the 
Operating margin though good had a slight dip of 2% from prior year to current 
year’s; a Surplus of UGX.1.34Bn after tax in the year slightly down from prior 
year’s UGX.1.36Bn; a Return on assets of only 0.73% which is below the 
required 5% thus suboptimal and inefficient utilization of assets; a high liquidity 
ratio of 8.1 implying that the Company is not efficiently using its current assets 
or its short-term financing facilities coupled with delayed payment of dividends. 
vii) I noted that the entity acquired an unsecured loan of UGX.5.5Bn to fund the 
acquisition of a Country Hotel at an interest rate of 10% payable in ten years. 
The acquisition was premised on projected cumulative profitability of 
UGX.5.163Bn in the first three years, implying an average annual profit of 
UGX.0.843Bn that would have helped to partially settle the loan obligations. 
However, to date, the investment has made a cumulative loss of UGX.214Mn, 
implying that the acquisition does not contribute anything to the loan settlement.

Summary of Key Findings 
I noted that; 
xi) 
A review of the Prison population and capacity trends over the last five years 
reveals a persistent congestion problem within the Uganda Prisons Service, 
despite gradual improvements in infrastructure. 
xii) 
The remand prisoners constituted 48% of the total inmate population as of 
June 2025, which was above the UPS target of 46%. 
xiii) Despite a 28% increase in Uganda Prisons’ staff from 8,814 (FY 2020/21) to 
11,276 (FY 2024/25), the staff-to-prisoner ratio has remained at 1:6 – 1:7, 
significantly above the ideal ratio of 1:3. 
xiv) Over 50% of UPS’ staff do not have permanent houses provided by UPS, on 
average 29% of staff over the five years are housed in uniports or mud and 
wattle houses. 
xv) 
Out of the 269 Prisons, only 228 (85%) have access to clean and safe water. 
The 41 (15%) Prisons that do not have access to clean and safe water, obtain 
their water from unprotected shallow wells and streams. 
xvi) A review of UPS’ health infrastructure revealed that out of the 269 Prisons, 
only 90 (33%) have modest health facilities. In addition, 25 (9%) Prisons do 
not have trained medical staff stationed at the Prisons, 262 (97%) Prisons do 
not have isolation centers for sick prisoners with transmittable diseases, and 
only 10 (4%) Prisons have established psychiatric spaces. 
xvii) Of the required 316 staff at Murchison Bay Hospital, only 133 positions are 
filled representing 42% staffing levels. 
xviii) Although the national cotton productivity standard is 800 kgs per acre , UPS 
produced an average of 291kgs per acre in the five (5) years, accounting for 
only 36% of the national standard. 
xix) An analysis of the overall staffing for the rehabilitation department revealed 
that it has only 65 staff who are attached to only 40 Prison stations in the 
country. 
xx) 
Most Prison units lack qualified and adequate teachers and instructors to 
deliver both formal and vocational (informal) education programs to inmates. 
xxi) UPS fully implemented seven (7) recommendations while Five (5) were 
partially implemented, in the Treasury Memorandum on the Report of the 
Public Accounts Committee of Parliament on the UPS for the financial year 
2020/21.

resolutions, case files, or follow-up, undermining regulatory enforcement and 
public protection. In addition, the Council does not have a client charter.
